blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions
blocks.text: Muhammad Ashrafa,1, Muhammad Sohail Ahmad b,c,⇑,1, Yusuke Inomata c, Nisar Ullah a,⇑, Muhammad Nawaz Tahir a,d, Tetsuya Kida b,c, ⇑ a Department of Chemistry, King Fahad University of Petroleum and Minerals, Dharan 31261, Saudi Arabia b 2D Nanomaterials Division, Institute of Industrial Nanomaterials, Kumamoto University, 2-39-1 Kurokami, Chuo-ku, Kumamoto 860-8555, Japan c Department ofAdvanced Science and Technology, Kumamoto University, 2-39-1 Kurokami, Chuo-ku, Kumamoto 860-8555, Japan d Interdisciplinary Research Center for Hydrogen and Energy Storage (IRC-HES), King Fahd University of Petroleum and & Minerals, Dhahran 31261, Saudi Arabia

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > abstract
blocks.text: Transition metal (TM) catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are the utmost versatile and reliable methods for the production of many industrially important fine chemicals. The utilization of transition metals nanocatalysts in organic transformations, specifically the Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions, have enticed the vigilant eye of researchers and technologists due to; (i) high surface area, (ii) higher number of surface atoms leading to large number of catalytic active centers, and (iii) chemical stability. Moreover, being colloidal, nanomaterials combine the properties of both homogeneous and heterogeneous. i.e., solubility in different solvents and ease in the separation of catalysts. This improves the overall catalytic efficiency and cost. Therefore, these pseudo-homogeneous nanocatalysts are gaining a great deal of attention due to their broad substrate scope and ease of handling. This review article focuses on the recent advances in developing nanostructured catalysts and their utilization for selective carbon–carbon bond-forming reactions, e.g., Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira coupling reactions.

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > abstract
blocks.text: The main focus is laid on the reactions catalyzed by nanocatalysts derived from transition metals such as Pd, Pt, Cu, Ag, Ni, Fe, Au, and Zn, expounding the conception and rationale based on the reactivity improvement and the recyclability of the nanocatalysts are presented here. The heterogeneous catalysis, essential in daily chemical transformations, is demonstrated, implicating significant functions presented by the nanocatalysts, related pros and cons, recyclability, and efficiency.

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: TM-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are amongst the most powerful tools that find widespread applications in synthesizing natural products, functional materials, pharmaceuticals, and agrochemicals [1,2]. Among them, Suzuki-Miyaura (Suzuki), Mizoroki-Heck (Heck), and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions are considered the most versatile and broadly applied reactions for the formation of CAC, C@C, and C„C, respectively [3,4] (Scheme 1).

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: These three reactions have significant practical and theoretical significance in pharmaceuticals, polymers, and natural product synthesis. These reactions are also used for the intra-cellular synthesis of therapeutic molecules [5]. Traditionally, these reactions are catalyzed by homogeneous Pd-complexed catalysts and ligands such as phosphor and N-heterocyclic carbene [6–8]. Despite signif icant advancements in attaining higher activity, enhanced selectivity, and broader substrate scope, homogeneous Pd catalysts suffer from liabilities such as toxicity and post-processing procurement of most of the ligands used, expensive downstream separation [9] of residual metal from the final product below the maximum allowable level, and reusability of the catalyst [10]. Moreover, the use of toxic solvents, cumbersome multi-step synthesis involved in their preparation, tedious handling due to their air sensitivity, and laborious chromatographic purification of the product also pose a challenge. Consequently, homogeneous Pd catalysts are far from industrial realism [11,12].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Recently, heterogeneous metal catalysis has been gaining much attention due to its superior catalytic activity, broad substrate scope, and ease of handling [13]. The nanocatalysts are easy to recover by filtration or centrifugation, allowing reusability of the catalyst after the completion of the reactions [3,14,15]. A great part of the former heterogenous catalysis community is emerging into the nanoparticle community, as highlighted in the special issue of the prestigious journal ‘‘Chem. Rev.”(nanocatalysts) [16]. Moreover, nanocatalysts-based transformation is considered a nonhazardous and greener approach, which is desirable for sustainability and economic viability [17]. In addition, nanocatalysts that are built up on TM nanoparticles (NPs) such as Au, Cu, Pd, and their alloys can drive a wide range of C C cross-coupling reactions and C-Het (N, S, N) bond formations with enhanced catalytic activity, broad substrate scope, and improved yields [15]. These catalyst systems are generally free from ligands and the requirement of air and moisture-sensitive conditions [15].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Materials in the nanosize regime bear the highest surface area and the highest number of surface atoms that can be further tuned through the synthesis method employed. This leads to higher catalytic efficiency due to; (i) increasing the contact between the substrate and catalytic center, (ii) offering many catalytic active sites per unit volume as compared to bulk heterogeneous counterpart, (iii) higher zeta potential values, and (iv) due to unique surface chemistry associated with the nanomaterials [18,19].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Consequently, TM NPs based nanocatalysts have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional homogeneous complexes and demonstrated a plethora of applications in medicinal chemistry, electronics, and industrial settings [20–23]. In particular, the application of TM NPs based nanocatalysts in Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions has witnessed phenomenal growth in the past decade. For instance, a search on Scopus for articles published since 2010 on the subject matter described in this review is illustrated in Fig. 1.

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: The data show that in recent years, there has been remarkable growth in the utility of nanocatalysts for coupling reactions. However, issues of their low selectivity, the requirement of harsher reaction conditions, leaching of metal species from the support, and side product formation need to be addressed [24]. Likewise, the controversy of whether it is the surface of NPs (heterogeneous pathway) or the leached metal species in the solution (homogeneous pathway) involved in the catalysis process also requires further attention. As a result, searching for efficient pseudo-homogeneous nanocatalysts with superior performance to relinquish the liabilities of the homogenous transition metals catalysts remains an ongoing challenge within the field [23,25]. In this contribution, the development progress for synthesizing colloidal nanocatalysts has paved the way to address some of these questions [26–29].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: The synthesis of nanocatalysts with controlled size, shapes, and structures has enabled conforming nanocatalysts activities and selectivities. Likewise, the architectures of well-defined nanostructured supporting materials have also made meaningful advancements in the field [30–32]. The use of nanocatalysts of TM NPs is considered a process involving TM NPs on the nanoscale (1 nm to 100 nm in diameter) on solid support ( e.g., SiO _2, Al _2O_3, Fe _2O_3, MgO, CeO _2, TiO _2,, and others) as solid catalysts and reactants of dif ferent phases (e.g., gas or liquid). Generally, the NPs are grown onto a support surface such as alumina, silica, or carbon-based material by impregnation of metal salts, followed by the reduction of these precursors salts to zero-valent metal NPs [33]. These systems are, therefore, up-and-coming for their potential utilization in the industry [34].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Since these supports and resulting nanocatalysts bear a high surface area, even small amounts of dispersed metal NPs onto support can lead to higher efficiency when compared with their bulk counterpart (larger size particles) [35–37]. Moreover, the dexterity to integrate the precise nano-sized (1 to 100 nm (Fig. 2) [38,39] objects into the nanostructured composite affords unprecedented opportunities to generate multiple catalytic interfaces with the elaborated spatial arrangement on a single platform to exploit their synergistic effects [40].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Earlier review articles that summarize applications of nanocatalysts in cross-coupling reactions are relatively specific, such as A 3 (aldehyde, amine, alkyne) coupling reactions [42,43], Pd NPS catalyzed polyols coupling reactions [44], while some are majorly concentrated on either composition of the nanocatalyst used or the type of reaction explored. For example, Somorjai et al. reviewed the main concepts of using metal nanoparticles in organic transformation [39]. Some other group-published work includes diverse organic transformations by selective metals (mostly Pd, Pt) nanocatalysts [40–43] with a focus on C C and/ C–X coupling reactions catalyzed [44,45]. Astruc and co-workers explored the metal NPs catalyzed semi-heterogeneous catalysis as a frontier among heterogeneous and homogeneous catalysis [47]. Likewise, another short review on TM NPs catalyzed C C bond construction highlights the nanocatalysts role in an aqueous medium for catalytic C C bond formation [48]. Recently, a detailed review of the polyol synthesis of Pd NPs with different sizes and shapes and their use in cross-coupling and hydrogenation reactions were reported [44].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Recently, Hong et al. reviewed the use of Pd nanoparticles with a special focus on the role of support materials on the in Pd-NPs catalyzed Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira crosscoupling reactions [49]. To the best of our knowledge, a comprehensive review dedicated to different TM NPs (Pd, Pt, Cu, Ni, Fe, Au, Ag, and Zn) nanocatalysts is lacking in the literature. Therefore, in this review, we will summarize recent advances in Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions catalyzed by TM nanocatalysts, focusing on literature reports majorly spanning from the year 2010 to 2021. We begin with the design of nanocatalysts, with a focus on the size, shape, and role of support material. Then we will give recent advances in transition metals (Pd, Pt, Cu, Ni, Fe, Au, Ag, and Zn) NPs catalyzed C C bond-forming reactions. Lastly, we will conclude and give the future prospects and main challenges of the field.

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2. The design of nanocatalysts
blocks.text: The nanocatalysts catalytic efficiency, selectivity, and recyclability depend on the nanoparticles’ size, shape, composition, and assembly, and their instauration with the support. Nanocatalysts may be deigned as nanocrystals, clusters of metals, metals oxide, and nonoxides of various sizes and shapes. These may involve no support materials or may be supported on carbonaceous materials, polymers, metal oxide, or porous materials such as siliceous mesocellular foam [50]. The rational design of nanocatalysts is important to achieve enhanced catalytic activity, chemical and thermal stability, selectivity, and high efficiency [51]. The tailored nanomaterials would necessitate tuning their chemical and physi cal properties as efficient nanocatalysts through particle size, shape, surface composition, and surface reactivity [52]. It is widely known that electron transfer occurs between the catalyst surface and the reactive species in all key steps of the catalytic reactions, including the reactants adsorption, intermediates diffusion, and the desorption of the products [53].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2. The design of nanocatalysts
blocks.text: Thus, tuning the spatial and energy distribution of valence electrons at the catalyst surface would enhance the catalytic efficiency, such as the activation energy barrier, which in turn is linked to the reactivity and selectivity of the catalysts [54,55]. Based on frontier molecular orbital theory, adsorption and bonding of reactants on the surface of the catalyst are dependent upon matching their energy levels to those of the catalyst surfaces as well as the symmetry and spin state of the reactant’s molecular or atomic orbitals [56,57]. These properties of nanomaterials can be achieved/tuned by altering their size, lattice framework, morphology, quantum size, and electronic effects from nanopore confinement [58–65]. Likewise, the support’s size, shape, and composition are critically important in the design of catalysts [62,63]. In addition, nanocatalysts’ thermal and chemical stability is also very important since catalysts can be deactivated because of surface aggregation, leaching, phase changes, and sintering [64,65].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2.1. Size effect
blocks.text: One of the foremost importance of using nanocatalysts is their small size because this is directly linked with other parameters such as high surface area, chemical stability, and reactivity responsible for the enhanced catalytic activities. Therefore, in the past year, enormous work has been dedicated to nanosized catalysts to understand the effect of particle size on their catalytic and electronic properties in numerous transformations, more specifically, coupling reactions [66,67]. When the size of the NPs decreases, the ratio of surface to the bulk atoms increases, denoting that more surface atoms eventually be accessible for the reactions. However, catalytic activity is not often in direct proportion with the increased surface area of smaller NPs [68]. The surface of nanocatalysts with assorted facets can offer diverse binding force strength and configuration, which prolong different active sites, steps, and corners of surface terraces. Therefore, the size and shape of the NPs significantly affect their catalytic performance [69–76].

blocks.text: Likewise, exposure of the crystallographic planes and accessibility of catalyst active sites fitted into the porous structure onto the solid support is also critical for catalytic activity and selectivity [73,74]. The higher performance of nanocatalysts is considered due to the phenomenon of nano-effects, which is believed to result due to structural, quantum size, and electronic effects [58,59,75].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2.1. Size effect
blocks.text: The wet impregnation method is a widely employed technique for preparing transition metal nanocatalysts [76]. However, compared to the solution-phase synthesis of metal nanoparticles, the impregnation method offers poor control over the particle size and size distribution of resulting metal NPs. Nevertheless, the method is still prevalent today due to its scope of scalability and low cost. Other methods for the synthesis of metal nanocatalysts include coprecipitation, which could be in-situ precipitation of the metal and the support using sol–gel protocols [77] or using post-functionalization to deposit the colloidal nanoparticles onto the support [78] or polymer-assisted method that involves polymer as a template to nucleate and stabilize NPs [79,80]. A decrease in the size of the catalyst produces a dominant effect on the surface atoms at edges and corner positions [81,82]. This affects the catalytic activity by creating under-coordinating states on the surfaces. It was found that the fractions of metals on surface atoms having coordination numbers of 4,7,9 in octahedral NPs or 3,6,8 cubic NPs present strong dependences on the size of NPs [83].

A low reaction rate was obtained when the Pd precursor was utilized without a polymer, implying the reaction doesn’t occur through solution-phase catalysis by leached Pd particles. A quantitative relationship was found between the initial reaction rates over various stabilized Pd NPS and the number of low-coordinated (defect) Pd surface atoms calculated using statistics for face-centered cubic (fcc) cuboctahedron [87]. According to the d-band center theory, the catalyst’s reactivity depends on the d-band valence electrons near the Fermi level. Consequently, the reactant adsorption, activation, and dissociation are directly related to that metal’s d-band center of gravity [95]. Therefore, tuning the spatial and energy distribution of the valence electrons at the surface is important for the reactivity and selectivity of the catalyst. The current literature widely suggests that adsorption energies dependent upon the size of adsorbates on the surface of catalyst atoms rely on the coordination numbers [96–103]. For instance, the surface atoms of catalysts with low orbitals coordina tion numbers exhibit more adsorption for a specific molecule than higher coordination numbers [84,100]. Computational studies have also suggested that the activation energies of adsorbate for the chemisorption on the surface of Pt NPs catalyst decreases with size.

blocks.text: To conclude, size is one of the key parameters influencing any catalyst’s catalytic performance, especially transition metalsbased nanocatalysts in different chemical reactions [102]. Its influence is complicated in many cases, such as if the rate-determining step is the dissociation of an intra-molecular bond of a reactant molecule, then it is expected that the metal atom has a lower coordination number and exhibits higher catalytic activity [103–109]. Metal atoms with smaller coordination numbers on the surface have stronger adsorption energy, which could reduce the activation barrier to dissociate the reactant molecules and hence accelerate the catalytic process. The size-dependent catalytic activity is favored when the dissociation step acts as the rate-determining step. While in some cases, this trend is opposite to the above statement, in that case, the metal surface atoms have lower coordination numbers, dramatically dissociate a chemical bond, and tightly bind the dissociated species.

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2.2. Shape effect
blocks.text: The shape of NPs plays a significant role in the catalytic performance of nanocatalysts since NPs with different shapes are synthesized by stabilizing certain facets and allowing the other facets to grow [108,109]. This strategy could tune the synthesis with nanocatalysts with exposed active facets and defined atoms on the corners and edges [110,111]. Packing the atoms in nanocatalyst surfaces has been found in various shapes such as spherical, cubic, tetrahedron, octahedron, and truncated octahedron [112–119]. It has been demonstrated that contrasting atomic arrangements and interactions of different crystal faces of the same crystal could have significantly different distributions of valence electrons, resulting in entirely different molecular adsorption and reactivity [116,117]. Thus, the controlled design of the metal NPs crystals with uniform surface facets is necessary for enhanced catalytic activity and selectivity of the product [118]. These surfaces of metal NPs with specific shapes are composed of either pure (100) facets, pure (111), or vicinal surfaces with (730) facets containing denser steps or kinked atoms that result in lowering the coordination number [119].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2.2. Shape effect
blocks.text: Therefore, controlled synthesis of these shapes provides the prospects to systematically explore the surface structure to tune the catalytic activity and selectivity of the catalytic reactions in organic synthesis [84,111]. The lowindex facets such as (100), (110), and (111) of magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) are preferably exposed due to the lower surface energy and hence more stability. The variations in structural aspects stem mainly from the differences in the atomic packing on the catalyst surfaces [120]. Therefore, the structural variations between different crystallographic surfaces intrinsically influence the dissociation, adsorption, coupling, and interactions of the adsorbed intermediates in the catalytic reactions [84].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2.2. Shape effect
blocks.text: A good fraction of the catalysis research was devoted to tailoring metal deposits’ shape on oxide surfaces. One parameter that controls the particle geometry is the metal-support interaction, which is typically small for wide-gap oxides, causing the metals to grow in a 3D fashion [121]. Various approaches were developed to modify this parameter, for instance, by introducing defects and species (OH functionalities) into the oxide surface or using polar oxide terminations with high metal oxide adhesion[122]. Alternatively, electron-transfer processes across the metal oxide interface may be exploited to alter the growth morphology of metals. This approach has been demonstrated for thin fil oxides on metal support first [123]. The shapes of metal nanoparticles, particularly in wet chemistry synthesis, can be controlled in the twilight zone of kinetic and thermodynamic control [115]. This is mostly controlled by the capping ligands, solvents, and temperature by controlling the nucleation and growth steps [124–130]. El-Sayed et al. reported that Pt NPs have cubic, tetrahedral, and spherical spiracles shapes (Fig. 6).

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2.2. Shape effect
blocks.text: These shapes were controlled by altering the concentration of capping materials to the concentration of Pt cations used in the reductive hydrogen method at room temperature [127]. Later on, the same research group reported the Pt NPs with various shapes as nanocatalysts for electron transfer reactions [66,128]. The tetrahedral-shaped Pt NPs showed excellent catalytic activity with the lowest activation energy (14 kJ mol 1), whereas cubic-shaped Pt NPs exhibited low catalytic activity, having the highest activation energy (26.4 kJ mol 1). The sphericle-shaped Pt NPs displayed moderate catalytic activity due to exposed facets and fewer catalytically active atoms on the surface of NPs. Thus, tetrahedral-shaped Pt NPs exhibiting (111) facets had a large fraction of atoms on the edges and corners of the surface. On the other hand, cubic-shaped Pt NPs contained (100) facets on the surface with smaller fractions of atoms on the edges and corners of the surfaces. Due to these exposed facets and catalytically active atoms on the surface of tetrahedral NPs, the tetrahedral Pt NPs proved more active than cubic Pt NPs [128].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2.2. Shape effect
blocks.text: The shape dependence of NPs on the reactivity in C C bond formation, e.g., in the Suzuki reaction, has been demonstrated by Bokhoven et al. [74]. The catalytic activity tends to increase from spherical to tetrahedral shapes of Pt NPs, which was linked to the (111) facets of tetrahedral shapes that bear the maximum catalytically active sites on the surface of NPs. Likewise, Huang reported the synthesis of Pd nanorods and branched Pd nanostructures for the C C coupling reaction [129,130]. The study concluded that both nanorods and branched NPs were proved to be very active catalysts with comparable chemical stability and recyclabil ity. However, the nanorods had a little edge (92 % yield) over star shape (90 % yield).

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2.3. Support materials
blocks.text: In the case of supported metal catalysis, the support materials have been considered to be inert, and their prime role was to increase the stability of the metal particles by immobilizing and dispersing them to improve the active surface area. Later, the Tauster group introduced the term strong metal-support interaction to elaborate on the unexpected chemisorption properties of H_2 on noble metal NPs supported by TiO _2 [63]. Further, the importance of the support materials has been explored at a fundamental level, commonly utilizing model catalysts. In short, the role of the support materials in catalysis is somewhat more complex and yet to be explored. Support material can play direct or indirect roles during a catalytic transformation. These provide precise defect sites onto which the metal NPs can be immobilized in the case of metastable particles [131]. In addition, the support can enable the electronic interactions between metal NPs and provide functionalities to the nanomaterials, such as acidic sites or basic sites that improve the stability, activity, and selectivity of the catalyst [132,133].

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 2.3. Support materials
blocks.text: Earlier studies have shown that the catalysts inherent activity and selectivity may vary strongly, contingent on the size of the metal NPs (>7 nm in diameter). Yet the size is not solely responsible for varying catalyst efficiencies. The choice of catalyst support is captious even for materials having the same geometry, for which mass transport differences can be ruled out [13]. This frequently turns out that some support materials catalyze unwanted side transformations, in many cases, the clarification is less frivolous [134]. In some cases, the NPs catalytic activity decreased upon recyclability. Therefore, a stabilizer such as a polymer ligand and surfactant was used to overcome the mentioned issues [135]. A series of supporting materials such as CNTs [136], colloidal support [137], silica [137], metal NPs support [138], polymers [139], carbon [140], and graphene [141] have been reported. On the other hand, using magnetic NPs as catalyst support could also enable the effective separation of catalysts from the reaction mixture with the help of an external magnet [142].

blocks.text: In the Sonogashira reaction, the cross-coupling of aryl or vinyl halides with terminal alkynes to produce conjugated enynes and aryl alkynes is also catalyzed by Pd, using copper (I) as a cocatalyst. The reaction finds many applications in synthesizing natural products, pharmaceuticals, and other important molecular frameworks [183–190]. Although Pd-catalyzed Sonogashira reaction- under homogenous conditions that employ complexes of Pd(II) salts and phosphine ligands display high activity, it is quite challenging to recover from reaction mixtures [187]. This makes its recycling complicated for reuse [187]. Therefore, the heterogeneous Pd nanocatalysts, consisting of an active catalytic Pd species supported on solid support, have been a focus of recent research interest from the scientific community [114–120].

He concluded that the low generation of metallodendrimers or metallosters usually optimizes the efficiency and recyclability of catalysts [190]. Later in 2007, they reviewed Pd NPs as catalysts in C - C coupling reaction as homogeneous or heterogeneous pre-catalysts and whether these NPs are intentionally performed or produced from Pd derivatives such as Pd ( OAc) _2. Besides, the lower amount of catalyst loading is crucial for the development of green Pd-assisted nanocatalysts to catalyze C C cross-coupling reactions.[7] Seminal studies from the groups of Beletskaya, Reetz, and de Varies showed the Pd NPs can catalyze Heck and Suzuki-Miyaura reactions with aryl iodide and, in some cases, aryl bromides at parts per million levels [7,193,194]. As a result, researchers coined the term ‘‘homeopathic” Pd catalysis. The catalytic efficiencies achieved ‘‘homeopathic” (0.1 and 0.0001 mol percent catalyst loading achieved TON = 660 and TON = 540 000 respectively) behavior matter the PdNP size and stabilization type. The TON increased with decreas ing the Pd/substrate ratio, which suggested a leaching mechanism.

blocks.text: Platinum as nanocatalysts for cross-coupling reaction has been utilized to a limited degree compared to Pd NPs because the oxidative and reductive elimination steps are slower than those of Pd NPs. However, Narayanan et al. have synthesized tetrahedralshaped poly(vinylpyrrolidone) stabilized Pt NPs to catalyze the Suzuki coupling reaction of aryl halide-like iodobenzene and phenylboronic acid (Scheme 17) [66]. They concluded that the morphology of the Pt NPs could be altered from spherical to tetrahedral shape through tailoring reaction parameters which, in return, greatly affect the progress of the Suzuki coupling reaction [200]. In comparison, spherical shape Pt NPs were found to be more active than tetrahedral shapes. However, the authors further investigated that the Pt NPs are not chemically stable under reaction conditions. This leads to a rapid decrease in the catalytic activity of the nanocatalyst.

This also differentiates the colloidally synthesized Pt-based nano-catalysts from normally used heterogeneous catalysts [201]. Kim et al. developed a block copolymer with tunable micro and mesoporous structure loaded with 2 nm size Pt NPs as a nanocatalyst and utilized in ligand free Suzuki cross-coupling reaction (Scheme 18) [202]. The higher catalytic reactivity and efficiency of Pt-HPP (Hierarchically porous polymer) to a challenging substrate like aryl halide is striking, especially in aryl chloride, where the stronger C-Cl bond disfavor oxidative addition reaction. The screening of the prescribed substrate scope revealed Pt-HPP mostly works well, but electrondeficient substrates lowered the desired yield of selective product. This Pt-loaded polymer support (Pt-HPP) outperformed mesoporous/microporous based supports and indicated higher TOF and better reusability, confirming the hierarchically porous nature of Pt-HPP.

For the Heck CAC coupling reactions, Pd and Ni-based catalysts are more frequently reported in the literature. While the other heavier members of its group, such as Pt, barely perform in the same manner. Therefore, there are only some salts or complexes of Pt, catalytically active for Heck reaction due to its dissolution in organic solvents such as dimethylformamide, etc. However, Estefania et al. recently reported Pt NPs as very active species, and these clusters efficiently catalyzed the Heck C C coupling reaction. The author also differentiated the barriers in the first elementary mechanistic steps with small nano-size catalysts (Scheme 19) [205]. These are conventionally found for organometallic compounds and, with the oxidative addition step not the rate-determining step of the reaction.

blocks.text: Recently, the use of iron (Fe) based catalysts in organic transformations, particularly in C C bond-forming reactions, received significant attention due to their excellent catalytic and magnetic properties [206–215]. In this contribution, iron, as zerovalent or multivalent, is used either as a catalyst or as magnetic support material [209–218]. As an example, Akiyama et al. used sulfurcoated Au-supported iron (0) (SAFe(0)) nanoparticles as ligandfree nanocatalysts for Suzuki coupling and C H amination reaction [212]. Detailed spectroscopic analyses showed that the iron (0) NPs with a size of 6–10 nm, which tend to be easily oxidized to iron (III), were stable in air when immobilized in SAFe(0) with selfassembled multilayers. The catalyst was simple to treat in the air and could be reused in reaction processes with a low iron leaching rate showing a great catalytic activity for forming aCC bond in an excellent yield of 67–95 % (Scheme 20).

blocks.text: In the other study, Cu_20 NPs supported on rGO, synthesized using a simple solution-phase reduction approach, and employed efficiently to catalyze the Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions [238]. The catalyst Cu _20/rG0 nanocomposites exhibit high selectivity and catalytic activity towards the coupling reaction of aryl halides with phenylacetylene in ligand-free conditions. In the catalytic mechanisms, Cu_20 NPs first activated the phenylacetylene to produce copper (I) acetylide compounds in the presence of a base. These compounds reacted with aryl halides to form diphenyl ethylene (Scheme 27). After five cycles, the catalytic activity of the reaction slightly decreased due to leaching and partial oxidation of Cu O in strongly basic conditions. The Cu _20/rG0 nanocomposites heterogeneous catalyst is a good option to provide future direction for the replacement of palladium-based catalyst for the Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions [238].

The coupling reactions between aryl halides and terminal alkynes have been carried out in the presence of Cu NPs using an organic base (Scheme 28) [240]. Phenylacetylene reacts with a Cu cluster, forming a [alkenyl-Cu] cluster, which further reacts with the aryl halide and finally leads to the product by reductive elimination steps [241]. Notably, the positive charge generated during the oxidative addition is shared between the Cu atoms in the cluster, which is advantageous in contrast to the monoatomic copper complexes. The side chain of tryptophan has been applied to reduce Au ions in HAuCl to metallic Au and the functionality of carboxylic acid to stabilize the AuNPs. blocks.text: Song et al. reported water-dispersible Au@Pd core–shell and Au-Pd alloy NPs for the Heck coupling reaction [22]. In a conventional Heck coupling reaction, Pd (0) phosphine complex system has been employed as an effective catalyst in controlling the reactivity and selectivity in the reaction, which enters the catalytic cycle of the C C bond coupling reaction among unsaturated hydrocarbon and aryl halides. In the last step, bases were added to eliminate halides and reduce Pd(II) to Pd(0) [257]. For instance, styrene, methyl acrylate, and n-butyl acrylate were applied as unsaturated hydrocarbon and iodobenzene was utilized as aryl halide (Scheme 30). Au@Pd NPs presented a 99 % yield of the product after many times recycling of catalytic reactions. Cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) was introduced as an additive to improve the activity of the catalyst. The cationic surfactant enhanced the catalytic activity effect by chelating the Pd NPs, a phosphine-free catalyst. [258] Song and co-workers utilized four different types of Au@Pd core–shell NPs at room temperature, as a result, the emulsion phase surrounded the Au core-NPs.

blocks.text: Silver (Ag) nanoparticles catalyzed organic transformations have also attracted the interest of researchers in the past ten years because of the unique catalytic properties of Ag NPs such as efficient reactivity, specific selectivity, prolonged stability, and easy recyclability during catalytic reactions [273,274]. The application of heterogeneous AgNPs in general organic transformation reactions has proven to be an effective strategy in developing crosscoupling reactions in terms of efficiency and selectivity [274]. The hybrid NPs of bimetallic Pd-Ag supported on carbon quantum dots (CQDs) is an emerging nanohybrid efficient catalyst for the Suzuki coupling reaction of aryl halides like bromides and chlorides under ligand-free ambient environments (Scheme 35). The nanohybrid catalyst showed heterogeneous character and enabled easy isolation and recyclability [275].

blocks.text: To explore the substrate’s scope, the catalytic efficiency rate of Ag NPs for the CAC coupling reactions, especially Suzuki coupling reactions, depends on the substrate substituents in the aryl halides and aryl boronic acids. The existence of electron-donating substituents in aryl halides and aryl boronic acids forces the reaction to complete in a short time, while on the other hand, the presence of electron-withdrawing groups or substituents requires a longer time for the completion of reactions. It was observed that the presence of polar nature in electron-donating moieties on the surface of catalyst facilitates better interactions and contact sites with the substituents than those of electron-withdrawing moieties [275]. blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 4. Conclusion and future perspective
blocks.text: This article demonstrates that the TM-based NPs catalyzed C C cross-coupling reactions have witnessed phenomenal growth in the past decade (Fig. 1). The C C coupling transformation finds its utility in producing biomaterials, fine chemicals, natural products, and medicine [315]. More specifically, the Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira reactions have been widely exploited to generate diverse structural frameworks and chemical entities. Since homogeneous Pd catalysts are far from industrial realism, heterogeneous metal nanocatalysts have emerged as a promising alternative owing to their superior catalytic activity, broad substrate scope, and ease of handling. Moreover, the ease of recovery and reusability makes their use a non-hazardous and greener approach, which is important for sustainability and economic viability. For a higher catalytic activity, stability, and recyclability of the heterogeneous metal nanocatalysts system, careful design of the nanocatalysts size, shape, and morphology is important. Likewise, the architectures of well-defined nanostructured supporting materials have also made meaningful advancements in the field.

blocks.section: Transition metal nanoparticles as nanocatalysts for Suzuki, Heck and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions > 4. Conclusion and future perspective
blocks.text: Moreover, the dexterity to integrate the precise nano-sized (1 to 100 nm objects into the composite nanostructured affords unprecedented opportunities to generate multiple catalytic interfaces in a single nanostructured catalyst to exploit the synergistic effects between these catalytic interfaces. Mechanistic understanding of a chemical process is equally important. The organic transformations usually follow multistep complex reaction pathways, which need to be fully understood to understand the role of nanocatalysts. A pedagogical approach is required to empower the synthetic chemist with the suitable software and computational chemistry tools needed to design their reaction, prediction flowcharts, and probe reaction pathways was envisioned. Computational chemistry tools such as first principle ab initio and density functional theory could be a strong means to predict the mechanism and kinetics of the chemical transformation. Computational modeling of nanocatalysis due to the variety of nano sizes of the NPs becomes quite complex.

Acquiring ‘chemical accuracy’ through computational modeling would necessitate considering all aspects of the catalyst environment, such as support, pressure, temperature, solvent, and other surface-bounds species [317]. The atomistic approaches, combined with machine learning tools, can achieve the desired accuracy required to shape optimum nanocatalysts [318].

blocks.text: Similarly, the dynamic model for understanding reaction condi tions in a real reaction environment, such as atomic mobility within each NPs can also be employed. Finally, new numerical tools are in high demand to understand the assembly of NPs into super architectures and their influence on catalytic reactions [319,320]. Artificial intelligence technology could be a viable solution to solve grand challenges in organic transformations which need in-depth chemical intuition. Advanced hardware, enhanced algorithms, and growing storage capacity would allow scrutinizing variables beyond the ability of human beings and detection of hidden patterns in insignificant and core scale datasheets. The future of advancement and approaches will ultimately assist the engineering and design of nanocatalysts for the efficient routes (retrosynthesis and prediction of products) with their improvement (optimization of reaction parameters) to identify new chemical matter.

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > abstract
blocks.text: An organic additive, Diazine Black (DB), was employed as a leveler for microvia filling using copper electroplating. DB is a derivative of Janus Green B (JGB), which is a common leveler used for copper fill of submicron or micron circuit metallization in electronic products. This study determined the optimal DB concentration for achieving the best filling performance. The electrochemical behavior of DB and its interaction with other additives, such as a suppressor and an accelerator were characterized using galvanostatic measurements. These electrochemical analyses helped explaining the filling mechanism of the plating formula containing the DB. Various surface morphologies and the crystalline orientation of the plated copper films caused by different DB concentrations were characterized by a scanning electron microscope (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD), respectively. The corresponding chemical activity of the surface atoms of the plated copper films caused by different DB concentrations was characterized using a test of etching rate.

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Recently, multifunction and portable electronic products have become part of the mainstream of consumer electronic products. Not only the motherboard of electronic products but also the packaging substrates of integrated circuit (IC) chips need a high-density interconnection (HDI) made by a process using stacked microvias [1,2]. For example, the motherboard of cellular phones uses HDI to integrate more functions.

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Because the diameter of the microvia has shrunk to less than 65 -m, and even as low as 50 -m, several metallization technologies such as filling with resin and conductive paste have not met the demands of process integration [1,2]. Instead, researchers believe that a more promising technology is to fill microvia using copper electroplating because this filling technique has been employed successfully to fabricate the interconnections of IC chips, such as via and trench metallization [3–13]. The microvia filling technology using copper electroplating is implemented using a specific plating formula that contains a suppressor, an accelerator, and a leveler [14–17]. The suppressor and the accelerator are basic additives for the microvia filling; the addition of a leveler can significantly improve the filling yield and extend the operative range of the accelerator concentration [16,17].

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Janus Green B (JGB) is a familiar leveler that bears one quaternary ammonium cation and one chloride ion. It preferentially adsorbs at the protrusion to inhibit the copper deposition rate because of the selective adsorption of the quaternary ammonium cation [18]. Therefore, a proper addition of JGB results in a copper deposit with a mirror-like surface. It is an effective reagent for carrying out a void-free filling in dual damascene metallization [4,5,7,8,10]. With regard to the electrochemical and adsorptive behaviors of JGB on the copper electrodeposition, Li et al. [18] and Bozzini et al. [19] presented detailed results using various instruments to identify the molecular structures of adsorbed JGB and the byproduct thereof. In addition, JGB can interact with polyethylene glycol (PEG) to form a composite suppressor whose adsorptive behavior is strongly convection dependent [16,17]. Hence, the addition of JGB can significantly enhance the filling performance of a plating formula because the forced convection acting on the board surface is always stronger than that at the bottom of the microvia during electroplating [20,21].

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: The behavior of the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of a plating formula has been demonstrated to be an indicator that can determine whether the plating formula is a good candidate or not for the microvia filling [17,22,23].

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Recently, many new levelers have been evaluated to determine their effectiveness as additives to copper electroplating for submicron via filling [11–13,24]. These new levelers also have the quaternary ammonium cations, except for polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) [13]. A preliminary evaluation of filling performance using the CDA metrology has shown that the derivative of JGB, namely, Diazine Black (DB), can compete with JGB in filling performance [17]. However, except for a patent [25] which claimed that DB is an effective leveler for copper fill, no detailed research has been undertaken to study DB as a leveler for the microvia filling. Therefore, in this study, we investigated the use of DB as a leveler, including the filling performance of the plating formula, the chemical interactions among the additives, the surface morphology of the copper deposit, and the influence of DB on the crystalline structure. In PCB fabrication, the etching process for patterning circuits is a subsequent step after copper plating. In this study, the influence of the DB concentration on the etching rate of the plated copper film was examined using an etching solution composed of H_2O_2 and H_2S0_4

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.1. Electroplating
blocks.text: The electroplating conditions, procedures, and pretreatment methods have been detailed elsewhere [16,17]. PCB fragments with microvias formed by CO _2 laser ablation were used as test samples for filling plating. The size of the PCB fragment was 1 0 × 6 cm ^2 The via density was 500 in array of 2 0 × 2 5. The distance between two microvias was 220μm or 320μm (from center to center), depending on the diameter of the microvia. The specification of the microvias was described in the caption of cross-section images of these microvias. Before metallization, the microvias were conducted through a so-called desmear process to remove the smear that was formed by laser ablation on the microvia bottom. The desmear process can thoroughly clean copper surface of the via bottom to make sure of good conductivity at the interface between the filled copper and the inner copper pad after plating. Following the desmear process, electroless copper plating was used for sidewall metallization of the microvia. Following that, a plated copper layer with a thickness of ^2 - 3 -m was deposited on the sidewall to increase the thickness of the copper seed layer for the prevention of oxidation.

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.1. Electroplating
blocks.text: The PCB fragment was plated at a current density of 1 9.4 mAcm ^- 2 for 70 min. Two phosphorus-containing copper slices were used as anodes and directly placed in the plating bath with a working volume of 1500 mL. Constant agitation was performed by continuous air bubble flow with a flow rate of 2.5 Lh ^- 1 during electroplating. The composition of the base electrolyte used for all plating tests was 0.88 M CuSO_4 (Riedel-de Haën, ACS) and 0.54 MH_2S0_4 (Merck, 96%, Ultrapure). The additives used herein were PEG with a molecular weight of 8000 (Fluka), NaCl (Fisher, Certified ACS), bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) (Raschig GmbH, Germany), and DB (Aldrich). They were individually added to the plating bath through dilution from stock solutions that were prepared with properly concentrated contents. The temperature ofthe plating solution was maintained at 25^°C The filling performance of a plating formula was examined through an image of the microvia cross-section obtained from an optical microscope (OM) (Olympus BX51).

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.2. Electrochemical analyses
blocks.text: The electrochemical characteristics and interaction of various additives were characterized by galvanostatic measurements (GMs) using a PGSTAT30 (Auto-Lab) potentiostat with a three-electrode cell. The base electrolyte formulated for the GM was the same as that ofplating ( i.e.,0.88MCuSO_4. and 0.5 4 M H _ 2 S 0 _ 4). The volume of the tested electrolyte was 100 mL and the temperature of the electrolyte was maintained at 2 5 ^ ° C during analysis. A 3-mm-diameter platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE) was employed as a base of WE. Before each electrochemical analysis, a thin copper layer with a thickness of 500 nm was predeposited onto the Pt-RDE in a predeposition bath, which only contained 0.88 M CuSO_4 and 0.54 M H _ 2 S O _ 4, to prepare a Cu-RDE. The counter electrode (CE) was a small copper bar, which was placed in a small glass tube containing the base electrolyte. The end of the small glass tube was sealed with a porous material to prevent direct contact of the additives with the CE during analysis, which in turn produced certain byproducts. A saturated mercurous sulfate electrode (SMSE) served as a reference electrode (RE).

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 2.2. Electrochemical analyses
blocks.text: The GM of the additive injection was performed using the Cu-RDE at a current density of 19.4 mA cm− 2. At the beginning of the GM, the glass vessel contained only the base electrolyte. After the GM was performed for a period, one additive with a given content was injected into the glass vessel to achieve the desired concentration. The potential variation ofthe Cu-RDE could clearly indicate the electrochemical effect of these additives on copper deposition. The GM was carried out twice. One was carried out using the Cu-RDE at 100 rpm, and the other was carried out at 1000 rpm. A potential difference, Δ η, defined by Δ η = η (average at 100 rpm)  (average at 1000 rpm), was evaluated from the GM. This value is a good indicator offilling performance [17,22,23]. Ifthe value is positive, it means that strong convection results in less copper deposition; thus, the plating solution may be effective for bottom-up filling (BUF) of microvia, whereas it is ineffective for BUF when the Δ η value is zero or negative. This approach was also adopted for this study to characterize the electrochemical behavior of these additives, providing further information for the BUF mechanism.

The temperature ofthe etching solution was maintained at 2 8 ^ ° C. The copper foil with a thickness of 50 -m was formed by plating on a stainless steel plate using the required copper plating formula. It was then peeled off from the stainless steel plate. The etching solution contacted only one side ofthe copper foil that did not attach the surface of the stainless steel plate. Each etching rate was measured three times to minimize the possibility of error.

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.1. Effect ofDB addition onfilling performance
blocks.text: Fig. 1 shows the molecular structures of DB and JGB. They are very similar, except for that DB has a functional alcohol group. Alcohol may be oxidized by H_2 SO _4 or by anodic current to be a carboxyl group, which forms a chelating complex with metallic ions and has the ability to form hydrogen bonds with each other or with H_2 O. Hence, small amounts of precipitate always appear in the plating solution after electroplating. Table 1 lists the plating results obtained from various plating formulas, showing that only two formulas resulted in BUF of microvia. One formula had 0.3 ppm SPS and no DB, and the other formula had 1 ppm SPS and 1 ppm DB. The rest of these formulas did not led to BUF but to conformal deposition. PEG–Cl is a well-known suppressor, and SPS–Cl has been confirmed to be an accelerator for copper electrodeposition [5,7,8,10,26–52]. Hence, the results listed in Table 1 indicate that the BUF behavior is caused by a synergistic interaction between the suppressor and the accelerator and that when the accelerator concentration is high, a leveler is an indispensable additive for achieving BUF.

A mirror-like copper surface as well as an excellent filling performance was obtained in case 8, as shown in Fig. 2e and f. blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.2. Electrochemical behavior ofthe additives
blocks.text: Fig. 3 shows potential variations in galvanostatic measurements on a Cu-RDE at two rotating speeds. The individual additive was injected into the base electrolyte in sequence. Fig. 3A shows that DB interacts with chloride ions to be a depolarizer for copper deposition. This electrochemical behavior is different from that of JGB, which exhibits a slight inhibition of copper deposition in the presence of chloride ions [16,18]. The deposition rate was Cu(II) diffusion-controlled before PEG was added in the plating solution because the cathodic potential decreased as the rotating speed increased ( i. e., Δ η < 0). After PEG was injected into the plating solution, the cathodic potential suddenly dropped by a wide margin, and the value of- equaled zero. These results mean that the main contribution for inhibiting copper deposition comes from PEG–Cl, and the deposition rate of copper is not Cu(II) diffusion-controlled but charge-transfer-controlled owing to the existence of PEG–Cl. Interestingly, after SPS was subsequently injected in the plating solution, the value of Δ η thereupon became positive, suggesting that forced convection is unfavorable to the copper deposition.

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.2. Electrochemical behavior ofthe additives
blocks.text: This phenomenon stems from a convection-dependent competitive adsorption ofadditives, whose original occasion is attributed to the potential-dependent adsorption of chloride ions [16,17,23,26].

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.2. Electrochemical behavior ofthe additives
blocks.text: Fig. 3B shows that the cathodic potential was not significantly changed after SPS injection, implying that there was no significant interaction among DB, chloride ion, and SPS at the low potential. The CDA behavior (i.e., - > 0) only occurred after PEG was also present in the plating solution. To further clarify the interaction of these additives, the injective sequence was changed again, as shown in Fig. 4. There was no potential difference (i.e., Δ η = 0) until SPS was injected into the plating solution, showing that copper deposition is not diffusion-controlled in the presence of PEG–Cl–DB. This result, combining with that of Fig. 3, also strongly suggests that the CDA behavior, which leads to BUF, is caused by the interaction of these four additives. This synergy ofadditives results in a slow copper deposition on the board surface and a relatively rapid copper deposition at the bottom of the microvia, which is characterized by the positive Δ η shown in Figs. 3 and 4. Fig. 4 also shows that DB does not enhance the inhibiting effect of PEG–Cl on copper deposition, which is different from that ofJGB [16].

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.3. Effect ofDB concentration onfilling performance
blocks.text: Fig. 5 shows the influence of DB concentration on filling performance. The filling performance of a plating solution is defined by a ratio percentage of two heights, i.e., ( h _ 2 / h _ 1) × 1 0 0 %,, where h is the copper thickness plated inside the microvia and h _ 1 is the thickness ofdielectric layer plus the thickness ofcopper plated on the top surface of PCB [37]. A small amount of DB could markedly improve the filling performance of the plating formula composed of 200 ppm PEG, 60 ppm Cl−, and 1 ppm SPS. The optimal DB concentration causing the best filling performance ranged from 0.5 to 1 ppm, depending on the diameter of the microvias. Similar results were also obtained from the system usingJGB as a leveler [17]. When the DB concentration was higher than 1 ppm, the filling performance declined with the DB concentration, particularly in the big microvia. This result is attributed to the CDA behavior [16,17,23,26] caused by the synergy of these additives, which is characterized by the Δ η values recorded by curve (c) shown in Fig. 5. Three representative - values were evaluated from Fig. 6.

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 3.3. Effect ofDB concentration onfilling performance
blocks.text: The trend of the Δ η value with the increased DB concentration varies with the variation in filling performance. The positive value of Δ η implies that that the rate ofthe copper deposition is inversely proportional to the strength of forced convection [16,17,23,26], which leads to a slow copper deposition on the board surface and a relatively rapid copper deposition at the bottom of the microvia. Hence, the larger the Δ η value, the better will be the filling performance. These results also reveal that Δ η defined in this study is a useful indicator to evaluate the filling performance ofa plating solution employed for microvia filling. However, this evaluation tool is conditional, that is, a leveler must be present in the plating solution [26]. If there is no leveler in the plating solution, a poor filling performance may be obtained, even though a positive Δ η value is correspondingly obtained, as confirmed in Fig. 2c and d. It is notable that the positive Δ η value was obtained at lower cathodic potential because of the leveler-free plating solution, as recorded by curves (a) and (b) shown in Fig. 6.

In addition, an  wave that represents a transient surface composition change, which varies from an accelerator-dominated composition to a leveler-dominated one, appears in Fig. 6. The transient time depends on the DB concentration and the strength of convection. A higher DB concentration or a stronger forced convection leads to a shorter transient time. Moffat et al. [53] proposed a model to explain the competitive adsorption between an accelerator and a leveler and simulated similar transient curves during plating.

blocks.text: The influence ofthe additives on the surface morphology ofcopper deposit was observed using SEM. Fig. 7 shows the top views of the copper deposits obtained from different plating formulas. Only two formulas, namely, PEG + Cl ^- + SPS and PEG + Cl− + SPS + DB, led to a flat plane within a micron range, as shown in Fig. 7e and f. After annealing at 120 ◦C for 1 h, the [1 1 1] orientation rather than the [2 2 0] orientation becomes dominant [54]. blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: A leveler, namely DB, employed for microvia filling was tested in this study. An excellent filling performance is obtained from a copper plating formula composed of 200 ppm PEG, 60 ppm Cl−, 1 ppm SPS, and 1 ppm DB. This plating formula not only results in BUF of microvias but also leads to a mirror-like copper surface. According to electrochemical analyses, the root cause for achieving BUF in the plating solution was attributed to the CDA behavior ofthis formula.

blocks.section: Microvia filling by copper electroplating using diazine black as a leveler > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: Although DB is a derivative of JGB, their electrochemical behaviors are somewhat different. DB cannot enhance the suppression of PEG–Cl on copper deposition, whereas JGB can do that. Nevertheless, DB can effectively suppress the acceleration of SPS–Cl on copper deposition in the presence of PEG. The preferential orientation of the plated copper films is changed from [1 1 1] to [2 2 0] because of the addition of DB, which causes a decrease in the etching rate of the plated copper film and results in fine grains and mirror-like copper surfaces.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating
blocks.text: Zhen Li a,b, Baizhao Tan a, Jiye Luo a, ∗, Jinfeng Qin a, Guannan Yang b, ∗, Chengqiang Cui b, ∗, Li Pan c a School of Chemical Engineering and Light Industry, Guangdong University of Technology, Guangzhou, Guangdong 510006, China b School of Electromechanical Engineering, Guangdong University of Technology, Guangzhou, Guangdong 510006, China c The AKM Electronics Industrial (Pan Yu) Ltd, Guangzhou, Guangdong 510006, China

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > abstract
blocks.text: Leveler is one of the most important additives for super-conformal copper electroplating, which has been widely applied in the fabrication of nanoscale (or microscale) interconnect features in integrated circuits (ICs) and printed circuit boards (PCBs). Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. In this study, a series of triphenylmethane-based (TPM-based) molecules with different nitrogen-containing groups have been designed, synthesized, and investigated as novel levelers for superconformal copper electroplating. Their structure-property relationships are investigated by electrochemical analyses, contact angle measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It is found that the steric hindrance and the type of the nitrogen-containing groups (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) in a leveler not only affect its adsorption ratio and strength on the copper interface, but also affect its adsorption preference on different copper crystalline plane.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > abstract
blocks.text: In combination with Cl−, polyethylene glycol (PEG, suppressor), and bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS, accelerator), all TPM-based levelers show excellent microvia filling performances in copper electroplating and their effective concentrations are related to their antagonistic ability against the accelerator SPS.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Copper electrochemical deposition (ECD) for trench and microvia filling as interconnects in integrated circuits (ICs) or printed circuit boards (PCBs) is one of the most important techniques in modern electronic manufacturing industry [1,2]. For better stability and reliability, the ECD copper in these nanoscale and microscale interconnect features are required to be void-free. Therefore, a technology named “super-conformal” or “bottom-up” copper electroplating has been developed and widely applied in industrial practice. The electroplating process was carried out in an acid copper electrolyte, which was composed of copper sulfate, sulfuric acid, chloride, and trace organic additives. Though the organic additives’ amounts in the electrolytes are very small (generally at several parts per million), the additives play a crucial role in the super-conformal electroplating. The competitive adsorption and differential distribution of the additives on the cathode surface are the origination for the realization of “bottom-up” copper filling electroplating.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: According to the additives’ different electrochemical effects in the electroplating, the additives were categorized as accelerators, suppressors, and levelers, respectively. Bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) [3,4] and its reduced monomer sodium 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) [5,6] are most widely used accelerators. In electroplating, the accelerators can reduce the cathodic polarization and facilitate the copper reduction [7,8]. The suppressors are usually polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) [9,10], polypropylene glycol (PPG) [11,12], or their copolymers [13,14]. In contrast to the accelerators, the suppressors synergistically work with chloride ions to increase the cathodic polarization and thus suppress the copper reduction. Leveler is another important additive used in the electrolyte to fulfill the super-conformal electroplating, which usually are nitrogencontaining molecules and positively charged in the acid electroplating solution. As reported, the levelers can adsorb at the highdensity charge region of the cathode to inhibit the copper deposition and level the copper surface [15].

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In addition, the use of a leveler in the microvia filling electroplating solution can greatly expand the application concentration range of accelerators [16].

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Fig. 1. Molecular structures of TPM-1, TPM-2, TPM-3, TPM-4, and TPM-5.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Currently, most of the reported levelers are nitrogen-containing dyes, such as the Janus Green B (JGB) [17], Alcian Blue (ABPV) [18,19], and Diazine Black (DB)[16] etc., or non-dye heterocyclic aromatic molecules, such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole (AMBT)[20] and 2-mercaptopyridine (2-MP)[21,22] etc. Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear yet, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. More and more research groups began to purposefully design and synthesize various nitrogen-containing levelers to study their structureproperty relationship [23–27]. In our previous study, we reported a triphenylmethane-based leveler TPM-1, in which three pyrrolidine rings (nitrogen-containing functional groups) were linked by a triphenylmethane (TPM) backbone [28]. It was found that the small molecule with three saturated tertiary amines already be able to show strong inhibition effect and promising microvia filling performance in the copper electroplating experiments.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: To further investigate the structural influence of nitrogencontaining groups on their electrochemical properties and microvia filling performance, a series of novel TPM-based molecules with different nitrogen-containing functional groups were designed and synthesized. As shown in Fig. 1, TPM-1 and TPM-3 are tertiary amines with pyrrolidine and piperidine as the nitrogen-containing groups, respectively. TPM-2, TPM-4, and TPM-5 are quaternary ammoniums, in which TPM-2 and TPM-5 were methylated base on TPM-1 with I− and Cl− as the counter anions, respectively, and TPM-4 was methylated from TPM-3. In this study, the TPM-based molecules were used as levelers in the super-conformal copper electroplating and their structure-property relationship were carefully investigated by electrochemical analyses, contact angle measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 2.1. Materials synthesis and characterization
blocks.text: Triphenylmethane based levelers were synthesized in the lab. The reagents and starting materials employed were commercially available and used without further purification. 1 H and ^13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were recorded on a Brucker ADVANCE III 400 MHz spectrometer (1H NMR: 400 MHz, ^13C NMR: 100 MHz). Mass spectra were recorded on a Thermo Fisher TSQ Endura 95 spectrometer with the electrospray ionization (ESI) method. (Detailed syntheses and characterization are given in the supporting information).

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 2.2. Electrochemical measurements
blocks.text: All electrochemical measurements were carried out using an electrochemical workstation (CHI 760E) with a three-electrode system. A platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE, PINE) with a diameter of 5 mm was employed as the working electrode. The counter electrode and the reference electrode were Pt bar and saturated mercury-mercurous sulfate electrode (SMSE), respectively. The volume of the electroplating solution was 50 ml and the temperature were controlled at 2 5 ~ ^° C.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 2.2. Electrochemical measurements
blocks.text: Before the galvanostatic measurements (GMs), a thin copper layer was deposited on the Pt-RDE (10 mA/cm2, 900 s) in the base electroplating solution to prepare a Cu-RDE. The composition of the base electroplating solution was 0.88 mol/L CuSO _4·5H_20 (JHD, analytical reagent, recrystallized from ultrapure water before use) and 0.54 mol/L H_2S0_4. The GMs were carried out with the current density of 20 mA/cm2. The rotating speed of the working electrode was controlled at 100 rpm or 1000 rpm to simulate the forced convection at the bottom of microvia and on the copper surface, respectively. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was carried out by a negative sweep from -0.4 to 0.75 V and then back from 0.75 to -0.4 V with a scan rate of 0.01 V/s

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 2.3. Contact angle measurements
blocks.text: Contact angle measurements were examined by the fully automatic contact angle measuring and contour analysis system (Dataphysics OCA100) using sessile drop method. The copper plate was thoroughly cleaned with ethanol, dilute H_2S0_4, pure water, and treated with plasma before the contact angle measurements. A 3 μl droplet was generated on the top surface of the copper plate. The droplet-solid interface image was collected, and the contact angle of the droplet was measured.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 2.4. Electroplating measurements
blocks.text: Printed circuit boards ( 6 × 8 ~ cm ^2) with many microvias formed by CO _2 laser ablation were used as test samples for filling plating experiments. The diameter and depth of the microvias were 75 and 50~μ m, respectively. Two phosphorus-containing copper slices ( 6 0 × 1 5 0 ~ mm ^2) were used as anode and placed in the electroplating solution with a 1000 mL working volume. The electroplating solution was constantly agitated by air bubbles during electroplating to ensure suficiently convection. The composition of the electrolyte for microvia filling plating was 0.88 mol/L CuSO _4 • SH _2 0 0.54 mol/L H_2 SO _4, 200 ppm PEG (MW6000), 40 ppm Cl− (added as NaCl), 2 ppm SPS and various TPMs. The current density was controlled at 1.8 A/dm2 (ASD) for 45 min. The surface morphologies and crystalline structures of the copper deposits were characterized by a field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, Hitach SU8220) and an X - Iay diffractometer (XRD, Bruker D8 AD-VANCE), resepctively. The microvia filling performances were examined by cross-sectional imaging with optical microscopy (OM).

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.2. Galvanostatic measurements with different additive injection orders
blocks.text: The electrochemical properties of TPM-based levelers were investigated with GMs and CVS methods. Fig. 2 shows the GMs with different injection orders of Cl−, PEG, SPS and TPM-based levelers. As shown in Fig. 2a, with the addition of 40 ppm Cl^-, 200 ppm PEG, and 2 ppm SPS in sequence, the cathode potential went through three changes: rising, sharply decreasing, and slowly rising again. The results are consistent with the literature reports [5,7]: Cl− itself is a depolarizer; however, the Cl− and PEG will synergistically form a barrier layer on the cathode and significantly suppress the copper reduction; SPS is a depolarizer in the presence of Cl−, which can gradually replace the suppressor layer on the cathode leading to a slowly potential increase.
