blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.2. Galvanostatic measurements with different additive injection orders
blocks.text: Following the addition of SPS, 1.484 μmol/L TPM-based levelers were injected into the electroplating solution. The cathode potential drops from 0.559 to 0.673 and 0.712 V for TPM-1 and TPM-2, respectively, which imply that at the same concentration, the inhibition effect of the quaternary ammonium TPM-2 was much stronger than the tertiary amine TPM-1. Comparing the molecular structures of TPM-1 and TPM-2, two differences were found: the quaternary ammonium structure and the I− ion. It has been reported that counter anion in a leveler influence its electrochemical behavior and I− can inhibite the Cu ^2 + reduction [29– 33]. To distinguish the stronger inhibition ability of TPM-2 was induced by the ammonium structure or I−, we designed and synthesized a new molecule TPM-5, which have the same cationic structure as TPM-2 but with Cl− instead of I− as the counter ion. When TPM-5 was injected in the copper electroplating solution, the potential drops from 0.559 to 0.654 V (fast adsorption) and then slowly moves back to 0.547 V(gradually deactivated by the SPS through the ion pairing interactions)[34–36].

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.2. Galvanostatic measurements with different additive injection orders
blocks.text: The result indicates that though with the same cationic skeleton, TPM-5 has a much weaker inhibition effect against SPS than TPM-2. As shown in Fig. 2a, the steady potential after addition of TPM-5 is close to the initial value before the leveler injection, which means the adsorption of TPM-5 on the copper surface is weak and the adsorbed leveler was replaced by SPS gradually in the electroplating process. From the GMs of TPM-2 and TPM-5, it can be concluded that the extraordinarily strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 should be related to the anion I− instead of causing by the quaternized pyrrolidine group. In addition, from Fig. 2a, we can see that the inhibition effect of TPM-5 is also weaker than TPM-1. Therefore, by comparing the molecular structures and inhibition abilities of TPM-1, TPM-2 and TPM-5, it was found that the methylated quaternary ammonium structure actually weakens the leveler’s inhibition effect instead of strengthening it, and the exist of I− is the cause of dramatical improvement of the molecule’s inhibition ability.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.2. Galvanostatic measurements with different additive injection orders
blocks.text: TPM-3, in which three six-membered piperidine rings were introduced to replace the five-membered pyrrolidine rings in TPM-1, has also been added in the electroplating solution to investigate how the ring size of the nitrogen-containing groups affect their electrochemical properties. As shown in Fig. 2a, with the addition of TPM-3, the cathode potential drops from 0.559 to 0.646 V and then slowly moves back to 0.590 V. The results show that the antagonistic effect of TPM-3 against SPS is weaker than the TPM-1. Since the electronic structures of nitrogen atoms in pyrrolidine and piperidine are very close (the pKa value of pyrrolidine and piperidine are 11.27 and 11.22, respectievely [37]), the electrochemical property difference of TPM-1 and TPM-3 should mainly be caused by the steric hindrance, that is, a bigger head group of the nitrogen-containing group leads to a weaker antagonistic effect against SPS. While for the TPM-4, which also has I− as the counter ion, no surprise, the addition of the molecule leading to a strong polarization and the potential sharply drops to approximately 0.712 V just as TPM-2.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.2. Galvanostatic measurements with different additive injection orders
blocks.text: To further verify the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the I− alone or the synergistic effect of I− and the TPM-based counterpart, equivalent amount of I− as in TPM-2 and TPM-4 was injected into the electroplating solution. As shown in Fig. 2a, the addition of I− alone in the presence of Cl−, PEG, and SPS leads a further polarization from 0.559 to 0.662 V, which means I− has a certain kind of antagonistic against SPS, however, the inhibiton ability is much weaker than that of TPM-2 and TPM-4 as shown in the GMs. The results clearly indicate that the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergistic effect of I− and its counterpart rather than I− itself alone. To further confirm whether the synergistic effect is related the quaternary ammoiunm structure, TPM-1 I− and TPM-3 I− with a molar ratio of 1:3 have aslo been injected together into the electroplating solution, respectively. As shown in Fig. 2a, with iodide ions in the electrolyte, the potentials of TPM-1 and TPM-3 also dramatically decreased to 0.710 V and 0.713 V, respectively. The polarization of TPM-1 I− and TPM-3 I− behaved very similarly as TPM-2 and TPM-4.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.2. Galvanostatic measurements with different additive injection orders
blocks.text: Since TPM-1 and TPM-3 have no quaternary ammonium structure, the strong inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 should be caused by the synergistic effect of I− and the whole structure of the TPM-based counterpart, rather than specifically interacted with the quaternary ammonium structures.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.2. Galvanostatic measurements with different additive injection orders
blocks.text: GMs with injection orders of Cl−, TPM-based levelers, PEG, and SPS has also been carried out to investigate the synergistic interaction of the TPM-based levelers with Cl− and PEG without the interference of SPS. As shown in Fig. 2b, following the addition of Cl−, the subsequent injection of TPM-based levelers leaded to potential decreases of approximately 93 mV (for TPM-1), 75 mV (for TPM-2, TPM-4, TPM-1 I−, and TPM-3 I−), 100 mV (for TPM-3), 88 mV (for TPM-5), and 49 mV (for I−), respectively. Comparing the inhibition ability of the TPM-1, TPM-2, TPM-5, and I ^-,, it can be found that in the presence of Cl−, I− leads to the weakest inhibition effect, the TPM-2 (quaternary ammonium salt with I as counter ion) exhibit weaker inhibition effect than TPM-5 (quaternary ammonium salt with Cl− as counter ion), which is further weaker than TPM-1 (tertary amine). Then 200 ppm PEG was added into the electroplating solution. For all TPM-based levelers, the potentials sharply decreased to approximately 0.702 V, which were much lower than the potentials obtained by PEG and Cl− in the absence of TPM-based levelers (approximately 0.667 V, as shown in Fig. 2a).

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.2. Galvanostatic measurements with different additive injection orders
blocks.text: The results imply that the TPM-based levelers synergistically interact with halides and PEG to form stronger barrier layers than those formed by PEG and Cl−. While for the I−,the potential gradually moved back to 0.678 V after the sharp decrease, which is higher than that induced by TPM-based leveler. Finally, SPS was added into the electrolyte and it was found that with TPM-1, TPM-3, TPM-5, and I− presented in the electroplating solution, the cathodic potentials increased by 37 mV, 108 mV, 143 mV, and 39 mV, respectively. While for the electroplating solution contain TPM-2, TPM-4, TPM-1 I−, and TPM-3 I−, instead of increase, the cathodic potential even slightly decreased. These results indicated that with the participate of I−, the TPM-based levelers could synergistically interact with PEG and Cl− forming much stronger barrier layers than those formed by TPM-based levelers without I−.

blocks.text: SPS can hardly replace the complex inhibitors composed of PEG, Cl−, and TPM-2 (or TPM-4, TPM-1 I−, TPM-3 I−), which further demonstrated that the combination of iodide ion and TPM-based levelers rather than any of them alone strongly improve the leveler’s inhibition effect and quenched the activity of SPS on the cathodic surface. To make the interactions more comprehensible, a schematic diagram was provided in Fig. 3.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.3. Cyclic voltammetry measurements
blocks.text: To charactrized the effect of the leveler concentrations on its electrochemical properties, cyclic voltammetry measurements with various concentrations of TPM-based levelers (or I−) in an electroplating solution containing 2 ppm SPS, 40 ppm Cl− and 200 ppm PEG have been carried out. As shown in Fig. 4, the increase of the TPM-based levelers (or I−) concentration all leads to a further polarization. For TPM-1, the addition of 0.05 ppm leveler not only decreases the absolute current density, but also changes the relative current density values in the forward (negative-going) and backward (positive-going) sweep. As reported, the current densities in the return sweep larger than the forward values indicate a positive feedback for the copper electroplating [38,39]. In addition, when the concentration of TPM-1 reaches as high as 8 ppm, an evident negative differential resistance (NDR) phenomenon was observed, which has been widely used to explain the mechanism of extremely bottom-up filling of Cu or other metals with one suppressor as the additive in electroplating [38,40–42].

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.3. Cyclic voltammetry measurements
blocks.text: Similarly, NDR has also been observed with other TPM-based levelers at relatively high concentrations (above 2 ppm for TPM-2 and TPM-4; above 8 for TPM-3; above 20 ppm for TPM-5). Though ternary additives (leveler, suppressor, and accelerator) were used in this research instead of one additive system reported in literature, extremely bottom-up microvia filling effect has also been otained with high concentrations of TPM-2 or TPM-4 (as shown in Figs. 7–2f, 7–2g, 7–4f, and 7–4g), which imply a gradual breakdown of the suppression starting from the microvia bottom. NDR is observed for all high concentration TPM-based levelers, however, only TPM-2 and TPM-4 result in the extremely bottom-up filling. One possible explanation is that due to the strong inhibition strength caused by the synergistic effect of I− and the TPM-based counterpart, the suppression layer formed by high concentration of TPM-2 (or TPM-4) plays a predominant effect on the cathod surface and overshadowed the effect of SPS (as shown in Fig. 3e and f).

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.3. Cyclic voltammetry measurements
blocks.text: While for other TPM-based levelers (or I−), the antagonistic effect of SPS and the inhibitors contributes together to achieve the super-conformal electroplaitng, as described by the curvature enhanced adsorbate coverage (CEAC) [36] or convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) [43] mechanisms.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.4. Galvanostatic measurements at different rotating speeds
blocks.text: As suggested by the CDA mechanism [16,44], the electrolyte convection states inside and outside the microvia have a great influence on the microvia filling performance. Different rotating speeds of the working electrode has been widely used to simulate the convection states of the plating solution on the top (1000 rpm) or at the bottom (100 rpm) of a microvia. The potential difference (Δη=η_100-η_100 0) measured from the two rotating speeds in GMs can be used to predict the microvia filling performance. Generally, a larger positive Δ η value implies a better microvia filling performance.

Before the addition of TPM-based levelers, the cathodic potentials continuously positively shift due to the depolarization effect of SPS, and no CDA phenomenon was observed (the Δ η values obtained from two different rotating speeds all are near zero). blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.6. Microvia filling electroplating with TPM-based levelers
blocks.text: To evaluate the actual microvia filling performance of the TPMbased levelers, electroplating experiments with TPM-based levelers, PEG and SPS have been carried out. Fig. 7 shows a summary of the optical microscope images of microvia cross-sections after electroplating. The microvia cross-sections of TPM-1 (Figs. 7–1a– 7–1g) were quoted from our previous work [28] as a reference for other TPM-based levelers For TPM-2, super-conformal electroplating was observed at the concentration as low as 0.01 ppm (as shown in the Fig. 7–2a). When the concentrations of TPM-2 increased from 0.03 to 2 ppm, fully microvia filling (microvia filling power > 85%) were obtained (as shown in the Figs. 7–2b–7–2e). Above 3 ppm, the microvia filling performance gradually deteriorated (big dimples appeared in the microvia, as shown in the Figs. 7–2f and \mathsfit 7 - 2 g) and the copper surface became uneven. The electroplating experiments are in good accordance with the GMs results as shown in Fig. 5 and Table 1(Δη>0 between 0.01–2 ppm).

blocks.text: As shown in Fig. 2, the strength of TPM-based leveler’s antagonistic effect against SPS is in the following order: TPM-2 TPM-4 > TPM-1 > TPM-3 > TPM-5. Correspondingly, the concentrations for the levelers to achieve full microvia filling performance are followed in a reverse order as: TPM-5 > TPM-3 > TPM-1 > TPM-4 TPM-2. The results are reasonable, because the weaker antagonistic effect of the leveler against accelerator SPS requires higher concentration to achieve the same inhibition power.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 3.7. Surface morphology and crystalline orientation of the Cu deposition
blocks.text: As reported, the electromigration resistance of copper film is affected largely by the (111) orientation [45,46]. The crystalline structure of the copper depositions electroplated with various TPMbased levelers were characterized by XRD. As shown in Fig. 9, without leveler in the electroplating solution, the preferred crystalline orientation of the copper layer is Cu (111). When TPM-1 was added in the electroplating solution, the predominant texture peak was changed from Cu (111) to Cu (220), which means the leveler TPM-1 can hinder the growth of Cu (111). Different from TPM-1, the preferred crystalline orientation of the copper layers deposited with TPM-2, TPM-3, TPM-4 and TPM-5 as levelers is Cu (111) again. Considering the molecular structures, electrochemical properties, and the crystalline orientations, the nitrogen-containing groups in a leveler not only affect its adsorption strength on the copper surface, but also affect its adsorption preference on different crystalline plane.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: In this study, a series of novel triphenylmethane-based molecules (TPM-2 to TPM-5) with varied nitrogen-containing functional groups were synthesized and investigated as levelers for copper super-conformal electroplating. The structure-property relationships of the TPM-based levelers have been studied in detail with electrochemical analyses, surface activity measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It was found that all TPM-based levelers show inhibition effect in the copper electroplating and their antagonistic ability against SPS followed in the order of TPM-2 TPM-4 TPM-1 TPM-3 TPM-5. The inhibition ability of the TPM-based levelers positively correlated to their adsorption ratio on the copper interface.

blocks.section: Structural influence of nitrogen-containing groups on triphenylmethane-based levelers in super-conformal copper electroplating > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the strongest inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergist interaction of the TPMbased structures and the counter ion I−; the replacement of a fivemembered pyrrolidine ring (TPM-1) by a six-membered piperidine ring (TPM-2) leads to a decrease of the leveler’s inhibition ability; the quaternization of a tertiary amine (TPM-1) with Cl− Cl^- as the counter ion leads a much weaker antagonistic effect against SPS (TPM-5). Based on the results, it can be concluded that the minor adjustment of the nitrogen-containing group’s structures in a leveler has a significant impact on its electrochemical properties and microvia filling performance. The steric hindrance and the type (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) of the nitrogen-containing groups need to be comprehensively considered when one designs new levelers for the super-conformal copper electroplating.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil
blocks.text: Yaqiang Li a,b,1, Yuanhang Zhang a,c,1, Ruopeng Li a,*, Xingchen Ma b, Fuxue Wang b, Fan Meng a, Jie Jiang a, Xuesong Peng a,*, Lanchen Li d,*, Maozhong An a,* a School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin, 150001, PR China b College of Chemistry, Institute of Molecular Engineering Plus, Fuzhou University, Fuzhou, Fujian, 350116, PR China c School of Environmental and Chemical Engineering, Shenyang Ligong University, Shenyang, 110159, PR China d Dalian Changfeng Industrial Corporation, Dalian, 116038, PR China

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: This work investigated the influence of Sodium 3- (benzothiazole-2 -ylthio)- 1- propanesulfonate (ZPS) as a single additive on performance of copper foil. Electrochemical analysis indicates that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM confirm that Copper growth obeys 3D diffusioncontrolled instantaneous nucleation and growth process, with ZPS significantly increasing the density of active sites. A comprehensive theoretical framework combining density functional theory calculations, molecula dynamics simulations, and in situ infrared spectroscopy elucidates an adsorption-capturing acceleration mechanism: ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and “catch” free Cu 2+ to the active sites to accelerate the electrochemical reduction process coupled with adsorbed Cl −. Furthermore, a Turing oscillation growth model, supported by finite element simulations and AFM analysis, is proposed to describe the morphological evolution, wherein ZPS preferentially accumulates at valley regions, improving surface flatness through cyclic peak-valley transfer, though with inherently limited ultimate smoothing.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Structurally, XRD shows ZPS promotes Cu (220) orientation, while HRTEM confirms the presence of twin boundaries, and lattice fringe measurements reveal a transition from (111)-dominated to (220)-dominated regions upon ZPS addition. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) further indicates grain refinement (mean size from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and increased twin-boundary density, which contribute to strengthening via Hall-Petch and dislocation-blocking effects. In terms of performance, ZPS improves surface morphology and reduces roughness. Mechanical properties are optimized at 30 mg/L ZPS, with tensile strength reaching 331 MPa and elongation 3.78 %. Finite-element simulation of high frequency signal transmission demonstrates that the lowered roughness effectively mitigates the skin effect, reducing signal loss. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive mechanistic understanding of ZPS and dem onstrates its potential as a single additive for producing high-performance electrolytic copper foils.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: With the progress of 5 G communication technology, there are new requirements for electronic devices, such as laptop, communication station, smart watch and phone and so on [1]. In these devices, printed Circuit Board (PCB), as the “mother board” for integrated circuit and all kinds of electronic components, has attracted researchers’ wide attention in recent years [2]. Copper clad laminate (CCL) is one of the key materials in PCB, consisting of copper foil and substrate, among which copper foil directly affects the electrical performance and mechanical performance of PCB [3]. There are two methods to prepare copper foil in industry, namely, electrolytic copper foil and rolled copper foil, among which rolled copper foil is fabricated by rolling and compressing pure copper [4]. However, the production cost of rolled copper foil is expensive and the thickness is limited [5]. In contrast, electrolyte copper foil is cost-friendly and suitable for scale-up production [6]. In widely-used acid sulfate copper electroplating process, free Cu^2+ obtain electrons and is reduced on Ti cathode surface to form copper foil [7,8].

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: However, it is hard to directly prepare satisfied electrolyte copper foil from acid sulfate copper solution without the aid of additives to satisfy the fabrication requirement of advanced electronic products [9].

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Additives usually consist of organic molecules, which plays roles mainly on the interface between substrate and electrolyte. Thus, it is significantly important to apply specific additives to modulate the nucleation and growth process of copper foil and control the surface morphology to improve the performance of copper foil. As for proposed additives, Zhang et al. [10] studied the influence of DPS and hydrolysis animal protein on surface morphology and mechanical property, while Xiao et al. [11] applied SPS, SH110, gelatin to change surface roughness and tensile strength of copper foil. Alexandrov [12] et al. studied the effect of two composite additives (gelatin-polyacrylamide and thiourea-polyacrylamide) on surface roughness, tensile strength of copper foil. Sun [13] et al. applied three composite additives (SPS, HEC, collagen) to fabricate copper foil with low roughness. Despite the development of diverse additives (surfactants, polymers, dyes, proteins, etc.), poor mechanistic insight has rendered additive design largely empirical, necessitating exhaustive experimental screening with little predictive guidance.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: As investigation method progresses, theoretical calculation [14], spectrum technology [15], microscopic technology [16] are widely used to gain deeper understanding of additives during copper electrodeposition, providing guidance for researchers. An et al. [17,18] coupled in situ Raman spectra and infrared spectra, DFT (density functional theory) calculation to study triphenylmethane-based levelers during copper electroplating and proposed difunctional mechanism of coordination and adsorption, providing insights into future leveler molecular design. Wheeler et al. [19] used ab initio MD simulation method and found that the adsorption strength order is Cl^->Na^+>MPS>H_2O.. The addition of Cl⁻ results in the decline of copper substrate work function, indicating that electrons can transfer more readily from the metal to surface-active species. Meanwhile, sulfide bond of MPS adsorbs onto the copper substrate, whereas the sulfonate group tends to attract Cu ^2 + and reduce Cu ^2 + with Cl − adsorption layer. Broekmann [20] investigated the accelerating mechanism of SPS by STM and found that SPS adsorbs on copper sub strate by disulfide.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Laterally, SPS will break into two MPS molecules, among which one side (sulfide bond) adsorbs on copper substrate and the other side (sulfonate group) catches Cu ^2 +, consistent with Ref [19]. The desorbed MPS will be oxidized to SPS or PDS. Overall, emerging advanced research technology provide support for the underlying mechanism of electroplating additives.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In this work, a novel accelerating additive, namely, accelerator (benzothiazole-2 -ylthio)- 1- propanesulfonate (ZPS) is introduced to prepare copper foil. Electrochemical analysis method, including cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectra, was used to study the effect of ZPS in cathode surface. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM was used to investigate the nucleation and growth process. DFT calcu lation, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and in situ infrared spectroscopy is used to study the accelerating mechanism on the cathode surface. Besides, growth model of copper foil under the influence of ZPS was established based on finite element (FE) simulation. The phase structure and surface morphology under the influence of ZPS is also investigated, while tensile strength and elongation of copper foil is evaluated. Based on FE simulation, the skin effect is studied for copper foil with different surface roughness.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 2.1. Chemicals
blocks.text: The chemicals used in this work, including CuSO_45H_2O,\H_2SO_4, NaCl, Sodium 3- (benzothiazole-2 -ylthio)- 1- propanesulfonate (ZPS) of CAS number of 49625-94-7, are purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd and are analytical-grade (AR). Deionized water was used to prepare all the electroplating solutions. The virgin make-up solution (VMS) consists of 190 g/L CuSO 5H O, 100 g/L H_2S0_4 and 98 mg/L NaCl.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 2.2. Electrochemical tests
blocks.text: Electrochemical tests were carried out at room temperature (298 K). Cyclic voltammetry (CV), electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) and chronoamperometry are measured by Gamry Framework station in traditional three-electrode system, in which Pt rotating disk electrode with diameter of 0.5 cm, saturated mercury sulfate electrode (SSE) and Pt plate with area of 1 × 2 ~ cm ^2 were used as the working electrode, reference electrode and counter electrode, respectively. CV was swept from −0.8 V to 0.2 V vs. SSE with scan rate of 50 mV/s and 1000 rpm. EIS was carried out at −0.45 V vs. SSE with the frequency range of 1 0 ^5 to 1 0 ^- 2 HZ and amplitude of 10 mV on pre-plated (1A/dm2 for 60 s in VMS) Pt rotating working electrode. Chronoamperometry was measured with different ZPS concentration at 1000 rpm. Nicolet IS50 FTIR spectrometer with MCT detector was used to measure in situ infrared spectroscopy during electroplating. The testing solution consists of 1.9 g/L CuSO 4 •5 H 2 O+ 1 g/L H_2SO_4+ 0.98 mg/L Cl −.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 2.3. Theoretical calculation
blocks.text: The optimization for ZPS was carried out by Gaussian software according to density functional theory (DFT) at B3LYP/6–311 G level [21]. Gaussview was used to visualize frontiers molecular orbits (FMO). The electrostatic potential (ESP) was drawn by VMD 1.9.3, as well as ESP distribution were calculated [22]. The interaction between ZPS and Cu^2+ was investigated by applying atoms-in-molecules (AIM) theory and interaction region indicator (IRI) through Multiwfn 3.8 [23].

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 2.3. Theoretical calculation
blocks.text: The adsorption simulation of ZPS on different copper crystal planes was calculated by Vienna Ab-initio Simulation Package (VASP) [24,25]. The structural relaxation and exchange-correlation function was calculated by the general gradient approximation (GGA) parameterized by Perdew, Burke and Ernzerhof (PBE) [26]. The ion-electron interactions were solved by projected augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotentials and 500 eV was set as the cutoff energy of plane wave basis set. 10 − 5 was set as the convergence criterion of self-consistent field (SCF).

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 2.4. Electroplating
blocks.text: Electroplating was carried out in circulating cell with volume of 1 L and the circulating rate was 3 L/min. Phosphor copper plate was used as anode, while polished titanium plate was used as cathode. Before carrying out electroplating, titanium substrate was immersed in acetone at ultrasonic condition for 10 min to degrease oil and laterally was activated by 10 wt. %H_2S0_4. The current density used for electroplating was 30 A/dm2 at 298 K for 40 s and the thickness of prepared copper foil was about 4.5 μm.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 2.6. COMSOL multiphysics simulations
blocks.text: The growth process simulation of copper foil and current distribution simulation was calculated by COMSOL Multiphysics software. Electroplating module, coupled with surface reactions module and diluted species module, were used together to solve the growth process under the influence of ZPS. The parameters used in this work were obtained from experiments and theoretical calculations (details seen Supporting Information). Electrostatics module was used to calculate the current density distribution at high-frequency current.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.1. Electrochemical and nucleation study
blocks.text: In this part, the influence of ZPS on cathode process was investigated. The influencing effect of ZPS on copper electrodeposition was studied by applying cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS), while the nucleation and growth of copper foil was studied by chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.1. Electrochemical and nucleation study
blocks.text: Fig. 1a1 shows the effects of ZPS on electrochemical reduction of Cu^2+ and the onset potential was about −0.525 V. After the introduction of ZPS, the onset potential shifted positively. When ZPS concentration was 40 mg/L, the onset potential was increased to about −0.425 V, indicating that ZPS is of depolarization effect during copper electrodeposition. Besides, it is obvious that the anodic stripping area saw an increase with the rising of ZPS concentration, which demonstrates that the number of deposited copper during cathodic reactions was increased with the addition of ZPS, resulting in the increase of anodic stripping area. As a result, the anodic stripping coulomb was calculated to quantitively evaluate the accelerating effect [29], as shown in fig 1a2. The coulomb was 1.75 C / cm ^2 for VMS, while there is a continuous increasing trend with the rising concentration of ZPS. When ZPS concentration was 5 mg/L, the coulomb was increased to 1.87 C / cm ^2.. With ZPS concentration further increased to higher than 10 mg/L, coulomb rises higher than 2\C/ cm ^2. However, it should be noted that the increasing trend is slowing down with ZPS concentration.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.1. Electrochemical and nucleation study
blocks.text: Especially, when ZPS concentration ranging from 30 mg/L to 40 mg/L, the coulomb slightly increases (about 0.02 C / cm ^2) to 2.17 C/cm^2.. To elucidate the effect of Cl −, the CV tests were carried out in solution without Cl − (Fig. S1). Although anodic stripping coulomb still sees a continuously increase with ZPS, the increase trend is less pronounced than that under Cl − -containing condition, demonstrating that Cl^- play a strengthening role in the acceleration. In summary, ZPS is of accelerating effect for copper electrodeposition.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.1. Electrochemical and nucleation study
blocks.text: The impedance ring in Electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) represents the charge transfer process. As shown in fig. 1b1, it is directly observed that the impedance ring decreases with rising ZPS concentration, demonstrating that the charge transfer process is accelerated. The fitted values for charge transfer impedance ( R _ct) and solution impedance (R s) were shown in fig. 1b2 and fig. S2 according to equivalent circuit (inserted figure). There is no change in terms of R _s regardless of ZPS concentration, illustrating that ZPS has no influence on solution impedance. Fig. 1b shows that the R _c t without ZPS is 5.9 Ω. When ZPS concentration ranges from 5 mg/L to 10 mg/L, R _c t decreases from 5.5 Ω to 5.1 Ω, demonstrating that ZPS can effectively accelerate copper electrodeposition. With ZPS concentration further increased from 20 mg/L to 40 mg/L, there is a slight decline about R _ct (4.9 Ω to 4.6 Ω), which suggests that the accelerating effect is almost maximized, in accordance with CV analysis. Overall, CV study and EIS study indicate that ZPS can accelerate copper growth process.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.1. Electrochemical and nucleation study
blocks.text: The influence of ZPS on nucleation and growth of copper foil was studied by chronoamperometry [30] and ex situ SEM images [31]. blocks.text: Fig. S3 shows that copper foil growth obeys instantaneous nucleation and growth process without ZPS when cathodic potential i s - 0.7 : V and −0.9 V. blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.2. Interface behavior study
blocks.text: Density functional theory (DFT) calculation, molecular dynamics simulation (MD) and in situ infrared spectroscopy were applied to study the interface behavior of ZPS and adsorption-capturing accelerating mechanism was proposed.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.2. Interface behavior study
blocks.text: Fig. S4 shows the optimized structure of ZPS and it is expected that ZPS is of relatively good adsorption behavior since ZPS is of quasi-plane structure. Besides, the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) are used to analyze the possible additive adsorption configuration [33]. Fig. 2a shows the distribution of HOMO and LUMO as well as energy gap, respectively. The HOMO and LUMO are distributed around ring structures and heteroatom (S atom) due to π-π conjugate electron cloud and lone pair electrons, suggesting that adsorption preferentially occurred on these areas. The large energy gap ΔE (E LUMO -E HOMO) illustrates that it is hard for electrons to transfer within ZPS, demonstrating that ZPS is of good stability.

blocks.text: Fig. 2b shows the adsorption difference of ZPS on Cu (111), Cu (200) and Cu (220). Fig. 2c shows that there are three charge transfer area (interaction sites) between ZPS and Cu (220), namely -SO group area, two S atoms area of ZPS and copper substrate. The above analysis confirms the multi-adsorption effect between ZPS and copper substrate, mainly including S atoms and sulfonate group.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.2. Interface behavior study
blocks.text: Based on above analysis, adsorption-capturing accelerating mechanism was proposed. During electroplating, ZPS adsorbs well on copper substrate by multiple sites (heterotoms S and -SO_3^-), different from typical accelerator SPS, which breaks into two MPS molecules on copper surface and adsorbs by sulfide bond [16,20]. Therewith, -SO_3^- captures Cu^2+ moving to the cathode surface, after which Cu^2+ obtains electrons and is rapidly reduced through “bridging effect” of adsorbed Cl − on copper surface, verified by electrochemical tests, similar to the accelerating effect of SPS. Fig. 2i and S17 shows that ZPS- Cu ^2 + complex could adsorb on copper substrate with c l ^- layer to form Δ _ZPS -Cu^2+·_Cl^- surface complex, among which Cl − plays a bridging role to deliver electrons from copper substrate to Cu^2 +. There is obvious charge density difference among ZPS,Cu^2+,Cl^- and copper substrate. PDOS analysis indicates that px, py, pz orbits of O atoms from ZPS interact with dz2 of Cu^2 +, indicating the “capturing effect” of -SO 3 −. Besides, px and py orbits of Cl − have large overlap with dyz and dxz orbits of Cu ^2 +, while pz orbits interact with dz2 orbits of Cu^2 +.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.3. Shape evolution study
blocks.text: The influence of ZPS on copper foil shape evolution was studied by Finite element simulation and AFM [39]. Coupled with Molecular dynamics simulation [40], electrochemical tests [41] and finite element simulation [42], the kinetics and relevant parameters were obtained (detailed in Supporting Information, tab. S1) and discussed in fig. S18- S20. The simulated 2D copper foil growth evolution was shown in Fig. 3a and 3b. Without ZPS, \thinspace Cu^2+ concentration at the valley position was lower than peak position due to limited mass transfer (fig. S21, S22), resulting in a lower growth rate at the valley than in other area and leading to more uneven copper surface.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.3. Shape evolution study
blocks.text: After adding ZPS, the electrode reaction is divided into two distinct kinetic regimes: Accelerator (fast deposition process) occurs on surface regions with high ZPS coverage, characterized by a high exchange current density i _0, ~A~ (twice that without ZPS, i _0, Cu). Inhibitor (slow depo sition process) exists on cathode surface wherever ZPS coverage is low, characterized by the intrinsic slow kinetics of copper reduction without ZPS. Notably, the inhibitor is not a chemical species but the ubiquitous background slow kinetics; the accelerator is a locally emerging state whose spread is limited by the slow geometric evolution of the surface. This contrast between the locally emerging fast process and the ubiquitous slow process satisfies the activator-inhibitor conditions for Turing-type reaction-diffusion patterns [43,44]. Furthermore, a mathematical shape evolution model based on Turing model was established (detailed in supplementary) as follows:

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.3. Shape evolution study
blocks.text: Under the influence of ZPS, the shape evolution exhibits the transfer of valley and peak (Fig. 3a). Further analysis reveals that ZPS surface coverage was improved at the valley position due to geometric change (fig. S23), leading to a higher growth rate at valley position after the introduction of ZPS and the surface flatness is improved as so. However, when valley grows up to the same level as peak, the accumulated ZPS is still higher than original peak position, resulting the continuous accelerated growth (fig. S24) and the original valley changes into peak. In this circumstance, the ZPS will be accumulated in newly-formed valley (original peak) and accelerate the local growth. As a result, ZPS surface coverage exhibits oscillation behavior (Fig. 3c) and shape evolution is characterized by continuous peak-valley transfer, which illustrates that the improved surface flatness is limited. Furthermore, the respective Turing pattern was visualized to better illustrate the application of Turing model. Fig. 3d shows the 3D shape evolution under the influence of ZPS.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.3. Shape evolution study
blocks.text: The fast deposition process area with high ZPS coverage and slow deposition process area with low ZPS coverage evolution were shown in Fig. 3e and fig. S25. The process area evolution and ZPS coverage evolution exhibit typical Turing patterns characterization (spots, stripes), and the transfer between peak and valley arises from the slow geometric evolution of the surface.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.3. Shape evolution study
blocks.text: Based on above analysis, Turing oscillation growth mechanism was proposed. On one hand, the accumulation of ZPS on valley position improve the flatness. On the other hand, the continuous change between valley and peak (oscillation) indicates that the boosting effect of addi tives on surface flatness is limited, overcoming previous diffusionadsorption theory based on suppressor-type additives, in which the surface flatness should be continuously improved to plane ( R _z tending to 0). To verify the mechanism, the cross-sectional profile of copper foil was calculated from AFM images used to measure copper layer deposited with different deposition time (Fig. 3F and 3g). The almost unchanged surface roughness with deposition time confirms the limited improved flatness of copper foil under the influence of ZPS due to the transfer of valley and peak.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.4. Characterization of copper foil
blocks.text: XRD was used to analyze the influence of ZPS on phase structure [45] (Fig. 4a). The diffraction peak of copper foil under ZPS appeared at 43.30◦, 50.43◦ and 74.13◦, respectively. Laterally, the texture coefficient ( R _CT ( hlk)) was calculated to analyze crystal orientation under the influence of ZPS according to Eq. 2 (fig. 4a2). R _CT~(111) stayed basically unchanged regardless of ZPS concentration, ranging from 37.8% to 38.8%. In contrast, R CT (200) sees a continuous decline from 21.2% to 17.4%, while R CT (220) rises from 41.0% to 44.5% with ZPS concentration rising from 0 mg/L to 40 mg/L, suggesting that ZPS is beneficial for the growth of Cu (220) crystal plane and suppress Cu (200) plane.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.4. Characterization of copper foil
blocks.text: To directly observe the internal interface structures at the atomic scale, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) was employed to investigate the microstructural evolution of copper foils influenced by ZPS (bis-(sodium sulfopropyl)-disulfide) [46]. HRTEM observations consistently revealed the presence of twin boundaries on the copper foil surfaces, irrespective of ZPS addition (Fig. 4b and 4c). Quantitative measurements of lattice fringe spacings in the twin-boundary regions demonstrated a distinct crystallographic transition: in the absence of ZPS, the twin-boundary vicinities were predominantly characterized by (111) planes; upon ZPS introduction, the regions transformed to (220) planes (Fig. S26-S29). This finding is in agreement with the XRD analysis, confirming that ZPS facilitates the preferential growth of (220)-oriented grains. Consequently, the enhanced mechanical properties are attributed to the synergistic effects of the favorable slip characteristics associated with the (220) texture and the strengthening contributions from the high-density twin boundaries.

blocks.text: Furthermore, the cross-sectional Inverse Pole Figure (IPF) orientation maps (d1, e1) from EBSD tests indicates that ZPS has a limited effect on grain orientation, with only a slight enhancement of (220) texture. The obtained Cu (220) is of better for improving elongation of copper foil compared with Cu (111) and Cu (200) plane [47] owing to more glide planes [48].

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.4. Characterization of copper foil
blocks.text: The influence of ZPS on grain size was investigated by EBSD. The Image Quality (IQ) maps (d2, e2) show that the addition of ZPS reduces the grain size and induces high density boundaries. Specifically, the mean grain size decreases from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm (d4, e4). According to Hall-Petch strengthening mechanism, grain boundaries act as strong barriers to dislocation motion. Grain refinement dramatically increases the total grain boundary area, leading to sharp increase in strength. As a result, the improved grain boundaries density by ZPS is conducive for enhancing mechanical performance. Furthermore, twin grain boundaries, as a special type of high-angle grain boundary, are characterized by low interfacial energy and high stability, and they exhibit a stronger strengthening effect due to their unique symmetric structure. As revealed by fig. d3, e2, the introduction of ZPS increases the density of twin boundaries (red lines), thereby further enhancing both elongation and tensile strength.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.5. Performance of copper foil
blocks.text: The copper foil without ZPS is uneven and full of large copper grain size, while the surface flatness is improved and the grain size is reduced with ZPS rising from 10 mg/L to 20 mg/L, which is due to ZPS boost the nucleation growth, resulting in more compact and even growth of copper foil. When ZPS was 30 mg/L, copper foil becomes compact and flat and there is no obvious improvement with ZPS increased to 40 mg/L, indicating that accelerating effect of ZPS is achieved the most (Fig. 5b), in accordance with CV analysis and EIS analysis. Apart from surface morphology, the surface roughness was also illustrated (fig. 5c, S30). R _z declines from 2.603 μm to 1.627 μm with ZPS from 0 mg/L to 40 mg/L, further demonstrating that ZPS can improve copper foil morphology.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 3.5. Performance of copper foil
blocks.text: Elongation and tensile strength are key indicators to evaluate the performance of copper foil [50]. Fig. 5d shows the influence of ZPS concentration on mechanical performance of copper foil. The elongation for copper foil obtained in VMS was 2.89%. After adding ZPS, there is an increasing trend (from 3.53% to 3.78%) with the rising ZPS concentration until 40 mg/L. ZPS can accelerate the nucleation and growth process so as to increase the number of copper grain and refining the grain size, which is beneficial to boost the elongation [51]. As for tensile strength, similar results can be found. Tensile strength increases from 295 MPa to 331 MPa with ZPS concentration rising from 0 mg/L to 30 mg/L and then sees a slightly decrease to 327 MPa with 40 mg/L ZPS, which is due to copper foil grain refined by ZPS provides more grain boundary hindering the crack propagation, thereby improving the tensile strength [52]. However, overhigh ZPS leads to grain further reduced, weakening the elongation to some extent [51]. The mechanical performance of copper foil from this work was compared with copper foils from researches in recent years (Fig.

blocks.text: The signal transmission performance is analyzed based on finite element simulation, respectively to evaluate the practical application. The established models were of the same R _z as experimental samples (fig. S32). Fig. 5e shows the schematic diagram of skin effect. The skin depth decreases with the increase of frequency, which means that the current density is mainly distributed on the surface area under high frequency signals, while Fig. 5f shows the relationship among ZPS concentration, signal losses and frequency. At the same frequency, the signal losses rise with the increase of surface roughness. The current distribution on copper surface with different roughness under different frequency was depicted in fig. 5g and 5h. When high-frequency signal transmission is applied, the current density tends to transfer on the copper foil surface. Especially for copper foil with high surface rough ness, current density is gathered on the interface and the phenomena is intensified with rising frequency of signals. As for relatively even copper foil obtained with ZPS, the current density distributes relatively more uniform on copper foil.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: In this study, additive Sodium 3-(benzothiazole-2-ylthio)-1-pro panesulfonate (ZPS) has been systematically investigated for copper foil electrodeposition. Cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectra indicate that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM shows that the 3D diffusion controlled instantaneous nucleation and growth model is not changed but the active sites are increased by ZPS. Theoretical analysis suggests that ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and catch free Cu ^2 + by -SO 3 − to accelerate the electro-reduction coupled with adsorbed Cl − through “bridging effect”. Adsorption-capturing accelerating mechanism was proposed. Molecular dynamics simulation and in situ infrared spectroscopy verify the improved adsorption property of ZPS with increased cathodic polarization. A Turing oscillation growth model, validated by finite-element simulation and AFM, reveals that ZPS accumulates in valleys to locally accelerate growth, improving flatness via cyclic peakvalley transfer, but the smoothing effect is ultimately constrained by this oscillation.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: Structural characterization demonstrates that ZPS selectively promotes the Cu (220) crystal orientation and suppresses the (200) plane, while HRTEM directly visualizes twin boundaries, with lattice fringes showing a shift from (111) to (220) in twin-vicinity regions upon ZPS addition. EBSD confirms grain refinement (mean grain size reduced from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and a marked increase in twinboundary density, which together enhance mechanical performance through Hall-Petch strengthening and dislocation obstruction. Regarding copper foil performance, surface morphology is noticeably improved, while the optimal mechanical properties are achieved at 30 mg/L ZPS, yielding a tensile strength of 331 MPa and elongation of 3.78 %, attributed to grain refinement and twin-boundary strengthening. Finite-element simulation of skin effect demonstrates that the reduced roughness significantly lowers signal loss.

blocks.section: Investigation of single additive ZPS on performance of copper foil > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: Collectively, this work not only establishes ZPS as an effective single additive for industrial copper foil production but also advances the fundamental understanding of additive-induced structure-property relationships, offering a solid foundation for future additive design and process optimization.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating
blocks.text: Bo Yuan, Wenhao Zhou, Xuyang Li, Yiqiu Xie, Xinpeng Yin, Xin Chen, Danyan Shen, Limin Wang Shanghai Key Laboratory for Functional Materials Chemistry and Institute of Fine Chemicals, School of Chemistry and Molecular Engineering, East China University of Science and Technology, 130 Meilong Road, Shanghai 200237, PR China

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Electroplating additives, especially levelers of copper electroplating, are the most critical components of electroplating solutions in the manufacture of printed circuit boards and integrated circuits. A series of carbazole derivatives have been synthesized and used as levelers for through-hole electroplating. Electrochemical tests, theoretical calculations, and simulations were used to compare the various properties of the carbazole de rivatives. Among them, the carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB was preferably subjected to electroplating which was demonstrated by metallographic microscopy, SEM, and XRD. To further investigate the mechanism of leveler Cz-BPDB, the nucleation model theory was used to explain the phenomenon of flat and smooth electroplating surfaces. The electrostatic potential plot and the average local ionization energy plot were employed to analyze the active sites of the Cz-BPDB. Moreover, the galvanostatic measurements were applied to investigate the interaction of the Cz-BPDB with PEG and SPS. Therefore, a more reasonable through-hole electroplating mechanism was proposed in electroplating solution with Cz-BPDB used as leveler.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: This work introduced an excellent performance leveler and contributed to the continuing development of the copper electroplating mechanism.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: With the wide application of 5G communication and related tech nologies, the miniaturization, lightweight, and high stability of various smart devices are increasingly valued and required. In this context, through-hole metallization in the manufacture of printed circuit boards (PCBs) [1,2] and the packaging of integrated circuits (ICs) [3–5] is one of the methods used to address the miniaturization of the devices. Copper, a low-resistance and high-conductivity metal, is also used as a through-hole metallization material for multilayer circuits to achieve faster transmission of electrical signals [6]. Therefore, to realize the metallization filling process of through holes, copper electroplating technology is proposed and developed continuously [7–9].

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: At present, the acidic copper sulfate solution is more commonly used for copper electroplating deposition [1], and the main components of the Virgin Make-up Solution (VMS) are copper sulfate (CuSO 4), sulfuric acid (H SO), and chloride ions (Cl −) [10]. However, in through-hole electroplating, the orifice of through hole has higher current density and higher mass transfer [11]efficiency than the middle of through hole, resulting in very uneven metal deposition of through hole, which affects electrical signal transmission of the circuit and reduces the service life of electronic devices. Researchers have found that this problem can be solved by adding a variety of additives to the VMS, which has sparked increasing interest in the study of copper electroplating additives [12]. The additives of copper electroplating are generally divided into three categories: inhibitors (i.e. polyethylene glycol (PEG) [13–15], polypropylene glycol (PPG) [16] or their copolymers), accelerators (such as bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) [17,18], or 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) [19,20]), and levelers (i.e.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Janus Green B (JGB) [11,21–23], Diazine Black [24], Alcian Blue, Safranin T [25], 2-mercaptopyridine [26,27], or 2,2-Dithiodipyridine [28]). With the synergistic effect of the three additives, a bright and uniform thickness of the electroplating inside and outside through hole is obtained. In previous work, our group reported aliphatic amine organics [29–31] and large conjugated molecules [32–39] as copper electroplating levelers, and all of these levelers performed excellently.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In this work, a family of water-soluble carbazole derivatives were synthesized in high yield. Electrochemical tests were employed to explore the ability to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions. In theoretical calculations, molecular orbital calculations of carbazole derivatives demonstrated the ability of carbazole derivatives to adsorb onto copper surfaces. Furthermore, molecular dynamics simulations visualized the adsorption behavior of carbazole derivatives on copper. After through-hole electroplating experiments, the effect of compound Cz-BPDB as a leveler was demonstrated by various instruments. Metallographic microscopy was applied to test throwing power (TP) values. SEM and XRD were respectively employed to observe the flatness of electroplating surface and the dominant crystal orientation of electroplating layer. In addition, to investigate the mechanism of through-hole electroplating, nucleation model theory, molecular properties, and electrochemical properties were further analyzed.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: This work increased the options for copper electroplating levelers with carbazole materials as a new plating leveler and contributed to the continuing development of the copper electroplating mechanism.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 2.1. Materials synthesis and characterization
blocks.text: Five different compounds (Cz-TMA, Cz-PD, Cz-BPD, Cz-BPDM, and Cz-BPDB) were synthesized via two- or three-step reaction using commercially available carbazole as the starting substrate. The molecular structures and synthesis routes of the five carbazole derivatives are shown in Fig. 1. All the compounds obtained by synthesis were confirmed to be the target products by 1 H NMR, 13 C NMR, and mass spectrometry. (The corresponding spectra and data for carbazole derivatives are shown in the Supporting Information.)

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 2.2. Electrochemical measurements
blocks.text: All electrochemical measurements were performed by an electro chemical workstation PGSTAT302N Auto-Lab with a standard threeelectrode system. The working electrode (WE) was a platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE) with a 5 mm. Moreover, a Pt stick with a diameter of 2 mm was serve as the counter electrode (CE) and the reference electrode (RE) was a silver/silver chloride ( Ag/AgCl) electrode. The VMS included 60 g / LCuSO _4, 100 mL /LH_2SO_4,, and 140μ L/L HCl in all electrochemical tests. In addition, polyethyleneglycol (PEG, MW = 10000) and bis-(sodium-sulfopropyl)-disulfide (SPS) respectively played the role of inhibitor and accelerator.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 2.2. Electrochemical measurements
blocks.text: Before conducting each potentiodynamic polarization test or linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) measurement, Pt-RDE, which was pre-treated for 120 s to form a thin copper layer, was transformed into Cu-RDE. Furthermore, a constant scan rate was 20 mV/s with a scanning po tential range of 0 to −0.8 V in all potentiodynamic polarization tests. The scanning potential ranged from 1.57 to −0.20 V under a constant scan rate of 50 mV/s for all cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements in this essay. In galvanostatic measurements (GMs), a current density was fixed at 1.5 A/dm2.. In addition, a glassy carbon rotating disk electrode (GC-RDE, Ф 5 mm) was used as WE with a copper sheet as CE and an Ag/ AgCl electrode as RE for all the chronoamperometry (CA) tests.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 2.3. Calculational methods and details of simulations
blocks.text: Quantum chemical calculations were conducted on Gaussian 09 program package. The geometry optimizations of all carbazole derivatives were based on density functional theory (DFT) using the B3LYP method with a 6-311G+ basis set. To obtain more precise data on the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy (E HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy ( E _ LUMO), the energy calculations were carried out under B3LYP/6-311G+ (d, p) level. ΔE was defined as Δ E = E _ LUMO · E _ HOMO. The molecular orbital, the electrostatic potential (ESP), and the average local ionization energy (ALIE) were calculated, analyzed, and drawn by using Multiwfn [40–43] and VMD program package.

The MD simulations were shown in simulation boxes ( 4.1 0 × 4.1 0 × 7.1 0 nm ^3) including a carbazole derivative molecule, 1000 water molecules, and Cu (111) surface. blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 2.4. Electroplating experiments
blocks.text: A double-sided copper-clad board with many through holes was used as an electroplating sample. The size of the electroplating board was 15 × ~ 5 ~ cm^2. Moreover, the diameter and depth of through holes on the electroplating board were 300 μm and 3 mm, respectively. Before electroplating experiments, an electroplating board underwent a pretreatment process containing degreased by a degreasing agent, washed with deionized water, and acid washed with 10 % H_2SO_4 solution. The middle of a 1500 mL Harring cell was placed into an electroplating board as the cathode, and two phosphorus-containing Cu plates were placed on both sides of the cell as the anode. During electroplating, a continuous flow of air bubbles was kept for enduring good mass transfer under 1.5 A/dm2 current density and ^7 5 min electroplating time. The electroplating solution formula was based on the VMS with the addition of inhibitor (PEG, MW = 10000), accelerator (SPS), and leveler (Cz-BPDB or JGB).

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.1. Potentiodynamic polarization measurements
blocks.text: Potentiodynamic polarization curves were utilized to assess the ability of electroplating additives to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions in electroplating solutions [32,44]. When the current density began to grow during the scanning potential test from positive to negative scanning, copper ions began to be reduced to copper and deposited on the cathode. The potential at which the current density began to increase was called the deposition potential. After adding organics as additives to the VMS, the higher deposition potential indicated that the organics were more capable of inhibiting the reduction and deposition of copper ions. In addition, a study [45] found that Br − had a positive effect on electroplating. In our studies, a series of comparative tests were done with VMS solutions containing the same concentration of bromine ions (Br −) as a comparison sample.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.1. Potentiodynamic polarization measurements
blocks.text: The five carbazole derivatives and B r ^- were characterized at different concentrations as shown in Fig. 3. The commercial JGB was characterized at different concentrations as shown in Fig. S1 in the Supporting Information. In the VMS without any additives, the current density increased as the scanning potential scanned from positive to negative from 0 V. And as can be seen in Fig. 3(a)-(e), the deposition potential increased as the concentration of carbazole derivatives increased. To exclude the effect of Br − on potentiodynamic polarization tests, a VMS solution containing Br ^- was tested and the results were shown in Fig. 3(f). The deposition potential of the VMS solution con taining Br − was slightly larger than that of the VMS solution and much smaller than that of the carbazole derivatives (Cz-PD, Cz-BPD, Cz-BPDM, and Cz-BPDB), which implied that Br − had a weak effect on the depo sition potential. Fig. 4 shows the potentiodynamic polarization curves of adding 2 μmol/L of various compounds to VMS, which showed the order of the deposition potential (i.e. VMS < Cz-TMA < Cz-PD<Cz-BPD<Cz- BPDM < Cz-BPDB).

blocks.text: As a result, it was obvious that Cz-BPDB was the strongest of the five carbazole derivatives in inhibiting the deposition of copper ions by reduction, and its inhibition ability was greater than that of commercial JGB, which had great potential as a better leveler for copper electroplating.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.2. Cyclic voltammetry measurements
blocks.text: In electrochemical measurements, cyclic voltammetric curves were performed to test the ability of organics to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions in the electroplating solution. The negative current density peak in the cyclic voltammetric curve was the copper deposition peak, which represented the ability of copper ions to be reduced to copper and deposited. While, the positive current density peak was the copper stripping peak, whose area represented the ability of the deposited copper to be oxidized to copper ions. The peak area of the copper stripping peak was positively correlated with the peak area of the copper deposition peak. Therefore, the smaller the peak of the copper deposition peak, the smaller the peak area of the copper stripping peak, which implied the stronger ability of the organics to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions [29,46].

blocks.text: The cyclic voltammetric curves of the five carbazole derivatives and Br − were shown in Fig. 5. The cyclic voltammetric curves of the commercial JGB were shown in Fig. S2. As seen in Fig. 5(a)-(e), the copper stripping peak of the VMS without any organic additives had the largest peak area, and the peak area of the copper stripping peak decreased as the concentration of the additives added to the electroplating solution increased. This indicated the carbazole derivatives had the ability to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.2. Cyclic voltammetry measurements
blocks.text: To exclude the instability of electrochemical workstation instrumentation on electrochemical tests, the ratio of the peak area of the copper stripping peak (Q) of the electroplating solution containing different concentrations of additives to the peak area of the copper stripping peak (Q 0) of the electroplating solution without any additives was proposed and adopted [47]. And smaller value of Q/Q_0 represented greater ability of the organic additive to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions in the electroplating solution. As shown in Fig. 6, five carbazole derivatives all inhibited the ability of copper ions to be reduced and deposited in this order of magnitude (i.e. Cz-TMA < C z - P D < C z - BPD < C z - BPDM < C z - BPDB) and in agreement with the conclusion of the polarization curves. As shown in Figs. 5 (f) and 6, the Q/Q_0 value of VMS containing B r ^- was greater than those of the synthesized carbazole derivatives, which implied a weak effect of Br − on the ability to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions. Meanwhile, all carbazole derivatives were stronger than the commercial JGB in inhibiting the reduction and deposition of copper ions.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.3. Quantum chemical calculations
blocks.text: Quantum chemical calculations were used to evaluate the potential of organics as electroplating levelers, and the results were shown in Fig. 7. According to the front-line orbital theory, E _HOMO and E _LUMO were correlated with the electron-giving and electron-absorbing ability of the molecule, respectively. Higher E _HOMO values represented greater tendency of the molecule to give electrons, while lower E LUMO values meant greater tendency of the molecule to give trapped electrons. Based on previous studies, a smaller value of ΔE represented stronger adsorption of organic molecules on copper [48,49].

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.3. Quantum chemical calculations
blocks.text: As shown in Fig. 7, the HOMO orbitals of carbazole derivatives were distributed on the carbazole conjugated structure and their E HOMO values were close to each other, which indicated the similar electrongiving ability of the carbazole derivatives. However, the E _LUMO values of the five carbazole derivatives differed considerably, which indicated that the electron-capturing ability of the carbazole derivatives was different, with Cz-BPDB having the greatest electron-capturing ability. In addition, the ΔE values exhibited an order (i.e. Cz-TMA < Cz-PD < Cz Δ BPD \ < \ C z · BPDM < \ C z · BPDB) which was consistent with the electrochemical results. Cz-BPDB had the smallest ΔE value, which implied stronger adsorption on copper.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.4. Molecular dynamic simulations
blocks.text: To visualize the adsorption behavior of carbazole derivatives on copper, molecular dynamics simulations were employed to carry out further studies [50,51]. The pre-simulation and post-simulation states of the carbazole derivatives on the Cu (111) surface were shown in Fig. 8. The pre-simulation and post-simulation states of JGB molecules on the Cu (111) surface were shown in Fig. S3. Table 1 showed the adsorption energies of carbazole molecules on the Cu (111) surface. As shown in Fig. 8, carbazole derivatives were not on the copper surface before the simulation; after 500 ps time of simulation, all carbazole derivatives were adsorbed to the copper surface, which was in combination with the results of electrochemical tests, proved that the synthesized carbazole derivatives were adsorbed to the copper surface to prevent the reduction and deposition of copper. While the specific adsorption energy values were given in Table 1, Cz-BPDB had the largest adsorption energy of 133.93 kcal/mol. And the same order of magnitude of adsorption energy was found in electrochemical tests and theoretical calculations (i.e. Cz TMA < Cz - PD < Cz - BPD < Cz - BPDM < Cz - BPDB)

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.5. Copper electroplating experiments and characterization
blocks.text: Based on the above results, Cz-BPDB exhibited optimal performance in the electrochemical tests, calculations, and simulations and was selected as the copper electroplating leveler to be added to the electroplating solution for copper electroplating experiments. Therefore, based on the VMS, various copper electroplating formulas were designed as shown in Table 2, and these formulas were used for copper electroplating experiments in order to characterize the through-hole filling properties (i.e. TP value), the surface morphology and the dominant crystal orientation of the electroplating surface.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.5. Copper electroplating experiments and characterization
blocks.text: After copper electroplating experiments, the cross-sectional images of through holes in Bath 1–5 were taken by metallographic microscope, as shown in Fig. 9 (a)-(e). The through-hole filling performance of JGB as a leveler was shown in Fig. 9 (f). The data from the through-hole copper electroplating experiments were shown in Table 3. According to previous studies, a TP value greater than 100 % implied that the through hole had the same thickness of copper deposited inside and outside the through hole, which was an important indicator of the electroplating filling of the through hole [39,44].

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.5. Copper electroplating experiments and characterization
blocks.text: In Bath 1 electroplating solution without any additives, the TP value of through-hole electroplating filling was 52.87 %, which represented that the thickness of the electroplating in the middle of through hole was only half of which in the through-hole orifice, i.e., the filling effect was poor. In Bath 2 electroplating solution obtained by adding 200 ppm PEG and 2 ppm SPS to Bath 1 electroplating solution, the TP value increased to 66.57 %, but this still did not reach the desired requirement. In Bath 3, Bath 4, and Bath 5 electroplating solutions with 0.1 ppm, 0.3 ppm, and 0.5 ppm Cz-BPDB, respectively, the electroplating layers were dramatically improved. Among them, the TP value of Bath 5 was 104.77 %, which was in accordance with the requirement of through-hole electroplating. It can be concluded that the addition of Cz-BPDB to the copper electroplating solution increased the thickness of the electroplating layer in the middle of the through-hole. blocks.text: Meanwhile, in order to investigate the effect of Cz-BPDB as a levele on the dominant crystal orientation of the electroplating layer, XRD was employed to test the crystallographic orientation of the electroplating layer [39,53], and the test results were shown in Fig. 11. blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.6. Exploration of the mechanism of electroplating additives
blocks.text: The ALIE plot described the reactivity of the electrons in the molecule, where lower values of the average ionization energy indicated weaker binding and higher electron activity [39,50]. As shown in Fig. 13 (a), the low value of the average ionization energy (8.57 eV) was mainly distributed on the carbazole ring of Cz-BPDB, which indicated the high activity of the electrons on the carbazole ring of Cz-BPDB and the easy chemisorption to the electron-rich copper surface for electrophilic reaction. In addition, the ESP plot demonstrated the distribution of electron density, where high electrostatic potential values represent low current density [50,51]. As shown in Fig. 13(b), the high value (179.32 kcal/mol) in the ESP plot was mainly distributed on the positively charged bipyridine conjugate ring of Cz-BPDB, which indicated that the current density here was the lowest in the whole molecule. During electroplating, the positively charged bipyridine conjugate ring of Cz-BPDB tended to physically adsorb to the electron-rich copper surface to prevent the reduction and deposition of the copper ions.

blocks.text: To discuss in further detail the mechanism of additives on the filling of through-hole electroplating, GMs tests were used for solutions with different addition sequences or different rotational speeds [31,57], and the results of these tests were shown in Fig. 14. As shown in Fig. 14(a), at 1000 s, 200 ppm PEG was added to prevent copper ions from reductive deposition. This caused a sharp drop in potential ( - 0.0 4 to - 0.2 5 V) and polarization. SPS promoted the reduction and deposition of copper ions after being added to the 1000 rmp-PSC bath at 2000 s; as a result, the potential significantly rose (from −0.25 to −0.15 V), and depolarization took place. When Cz-BPDB was added to the 1000 rmp-PCS solution, it also prevented copper ions from being reduced and deposited. A polarization and a modest drop in potential ( - 0.2 5 ~to~ - 0.2 6 ~V) were noticed. These showed, respectively, PEG’s antagonistic and synergistic effects with SPS and Cz-BPDB. The 1000 rmp-PSC bath’s potential significantly dropped (−0.15 to −0.23 V) after the addition of Cz-BPDB at 3000 s, and polarization occurred.
