blocks.text: As shown in Fig. 14(b), the PSC electroplating solutions were subjected to GMs tests under different rotational speeds of 1500rmp and 150rmp, respectively. The convection velocity was strong at high rmp. The smaller potential difference (Δη) between high and low rotational speeds indicated that the distribution of additives on through hole was less affected by convection velocity and more uniformly distributed inside and outside through hole. According to a previous study, the convection velocity inside through hole was lower than the convection velocity at the orifice [58]. Simultaneously, the current density at the through-hole orifice was high while the current density inside through hole was low [59].

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.6. Exploration of the mechanism of electroplating additives
blocks.text: As shown in Fig. 14(b), the Δη went from 0 to 5 mV after the addition of PEG at 1000 s, which indicated the small effect of convection intensity on the adsorption and distribution of PEG. After the addition of SPS at 2000 s, the Δη changed dramatically and was about 23 mV, which indicated the large effect of convection intensity on the adsorption and distribution of SPS. Therefore, the stronger the SPS depolarization phenomenon, the larger number of SPS adsorption in the high convec tion environment of 1500 rmp. After adding Cz-BPDB at 3000 s, the Δη was 10 mV and became larger with time, which indicated the large effect of convection intensity on the adsorption and distribution of Cz-BPDB. Under the principle of mutual attraction of anisotropic charges, the stronger the polarization of Cz-BPDB in the high convection environment of 1500 rmp, the more Cz-BPDB is adsorbed to the region of high current density.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 3.6. Exploration of the mechanism of electroplating additives
blocks.text: Based on the above discussion and previous studies [39,60], a reasonable mechanism was introduced. As shown in Fig. 15, the red line represented the current density, and the higher density of the line represented the higher current density. And then, the blue represented the convective intensity, while the dark blue represented the high convective intensity. PEG was more uniformly distributed inside and outside the hole, while the main distribution of the leveler Cz-BPDB was positively correlated with the charge density (i.e., Cz-BPDB was mainly distributed at the orifice). Because PEG and more Cz-BPDB adsorbed to the orifice, the SPS lacked favorable conditions for adsorption at the orifice and adsorbed more to the interior of the holes under the guidance of high convective intensity to promote the reduction and deposition of copper ions inside the holes. It clearly explained the experimental phenomenon of increasing TP values in Fig. 9. Thus, a more reasonable through-hole filling mechanism was proposed for through-hole elec troplating with Cz-BPDB used for the leveler.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: In conclusion, the synthesized carbazole derivatives were used as levelers for copper electroplating. Initially, Cz-BPDB was screened from five carbazole derivatives as the most effective leveler by electrochemical and computational studies. Hereafter, various formulations were designed to investigate the performance of Cz-BPDB. In Bath 5 with 0.5 ppm Cz-BPDB, the TP value of through-hole electroplating reached 104.77 %. Meanwhile, adding Cz-BPDB, the electroplating surface became smooth and flat from roughness as seen by SEM. And after, the dominant crystallographic orientation of the electroplating layer was (111). Further, a series of works were carried out to investigate the mechanism of action of Cz-BPDB. CA tests showed that the nucleation pattern of the VPS + Cz-BPDB solution conformed to the instantaneous nucleation model. The active sites of chemisorption and physisorption of Cz-BPDB were analyzed and localized to the carbazole and pyridine structures of Cz-BPDB in the ALIE plot and the ESP plot. Additionally, the GMs test results illustrated the preferential adsorption sites of the three additives in the electroplating through holes.

blocks.section: Investigation of synthesized carbazole derivative Cz-BPDB as a high-performance leveler for copper electroplating > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: Eventually, a reasonable mechanism for through-hole electroplating is proposed, which helps to promote the copper electroplating leveler to be further investigated and developed.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: In this work, we develop a novel safranine (SA)-based acidic sulfate copper electronic plating process for through-hole copper void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection, and both the molecule actions and synergistic effects of safranine (SA) are carefully explored. Cyclic voltammetry experiments at rotating rates of 200 r/min and 1200 r/min demonstrate that SA itself can accelerate the electro-reduction of copper ion, heighten the inhibiting effect of polyethylene glycol (PEG) and acceleration effect of bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS). The addition of SA to the virgin make-up solution (VMS) containing PEG and SPS makes the relative electric charge (ΔQ) between the low and high rotating rates be increased from 1.27 ± 0.04–22.53% ± 0.05, indicating the higher copper electronic plating amount at the center than that at the mouth of through-hole.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: In situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy together with theoretical calculations further illustrate that the molecule SA is adsorbed on the copper surface through the N atom in the aromatic ring, PEG and SPS can heighten the adsorption of SA on the Cu surface, and both PEG and SPS both synergistically influence with SA to achieve the void-free copper filling of through-hole.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: With the rapid development of electronic products, advanced fabrication technologies for high-density interconnect (HDI) in the printed circuit board (PCB) are widely applied in 5 G communication, energy devices, wearable devices, and other booming fields [1–3]. Metallization of through-hole (TH) is one of the core technologies to realize the conduction of different layers in HDI-PCB [4,5]. Acidic sulfate copper electronic plating is the most universal process for the metallization of TH [6–9]. TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging and TH void-free copper filling are the two common metallization technologies. For the TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging technology, only a homogeneous and conformal copper coating (about 20 µm) on its side wall is needed [10–14], then epoxy resin is used to fill the TH. For the TH void-free copper filling technology, copper coating is fully filled inside the TH without any void. It is worth noting that TH may crack under long-term heating due to the different thermal expansion coeffi cient between the resin and copper, resulting in the blocked signal transmission.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Therefore, compared with TH copper thickening combined with resin plugging technology, TH void-free copper filling technology behaves the advantages of higher reliability and better signal transmission quality. Nowadays, with the acceleration of communication speed, more heat is generated when the signal processing, the copper void-free filling of TH has therefore been widely employed for improving the heat dissipation efficiency.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: The main difficulty in copper filling is the formation of voids in TH with higher aspect ratio due to the uneven local current distribution and tanglesome convection environments caused by the specific geometry of TH [15–17]. The copper deposition amount at the mouth is usually higher than that at the center of TH, resulting in the coating in a void or seam. Therefore, it is particularly crucial introducing the organic additives in the acidic sulfate bath to modulate the copper deposition process at the mouth and center. The key to blind hole filling is the bottom-up growth of copper coating. The key to TH filling is that copper coating rapidly deposits at the center of TH wall until the center is connected to form a butterfly shape structure (two blind holes), and then the two blind holes are filled separately. The accelerator of bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) and suppressor of polyethylene glycol (PEG) are the commonly used additives in the acidic sulfate bath [18–25]. Suppressor, mainly distributed at the mouth of TH, inhibits the copper ion electro-reduction at a definite potential which results in the decrease of reduction current density.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Accelerator, mainly distributed at the center of TH, promotes the copper ion electro-reduction at a definite potential which results in the increase of reduction current density. It is still difficult to realize a void-free copper filling from the bath with only these two additives, and therefore the other additive is further needed. Zheng et al. [12] reported that poly (1-vinyl imidazole co 1, 4-butanediol diglycidyl ether) (VIBDGE) could further heighten the inhibiting ability of PEG in copper electronic plating. Li et al. [13] presented that a copolymer comprising of pyrrole and 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (PBDGE) also could enhance the inhibiting ability of PEG during copper electronic plating. Wang et al. [14] introduced that gentian violet (GVT) behaved with the synergistic inhibiting effect with PEG and the antagonistic effect with SPS. Although considerable studies have been carried out to show the superior performance of additives, up to now, the synergistic action mechanisms of additives are still not clarified.

blocks.text: In this work, we successfully develop a novel and excellent SA-based acidic sulfate copper electronic plating process (additives: PEG, SPS and SA) for the void-free filling of X-shape TH (conducive to the formation of butterfly structure for void-free filling). The intrinsic properties of SA and the interactions among SA, PEG and SPS at the molecule level are expounded through cyclic voltammetry, in situ FTIR experiments and theoretical calculations.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > 3.4. In situ FTIR study of SA interreaction mechanism
blocks.text: In situ FTIR experiments are conducted to further comprehend the interaction mechanisms among SA, PEG and SPS in the acidic sulfate copper electronic plating bath. To improve the detection sensitivity, the base electrolyte (BE) is composed of 2.2 g/L CuSO _4 • SH _2 O,, 0.49 g/L H_2SO_4 and 60 mg/L Cl -, and the concentrations of SPS and SA are adjusted to 60 mg/L and 1 g/L, respectively.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > 3.4. In situ FTIR study of SA interreaction mechanism
blocks.text: The in situ FTIR spectra of BE without and with SA are shown in Fig. 7, and the characteristic peaks and corresponding assignments are listed in Table 5. As shown in Fig. ^7 a, when only Cu ^2 +, sO _4 ^2 - and Cl ions exist in the BE, a characteristic peak (A) arises at about 1202 cm ^- 1 for the absorption of SO_4^2- [29]. By the potential negatively shifting, the peak intensity continually increases due to the accumulation of SO_4^2- for the reduction reactions of Cu^2+ to Cu and H ^+ to H 2 [14]. After SA is added into the BE (Fig. 7b), other two characteristic peaks (B and C) at around 1497 and 1 3 9 7 cm ^- 1 appear at − 0.7 V, which are assigned to the stretching vibration of C––C and C-N in the aromatic ring [30,31]. By the potential negatively shifting, the wavenumbers of the two peaks blue shift in 2 ~ 4 ~ cm^-1 and the peak intensities increase, indicating that SA can be adsorbed on the copper surface through the N atom in the aromatic ring.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > 3.4. In situ FTIR study of SA interreaction mechanism
blocks.text: Theoretical calculations can well analyze the active sites of SA and its adsorption ability on the metal surface. Fig. 8 shows the molecular structure, corresponding frontier molecular orbitals, electrostatic potential (ESP) and adsorption model of SA. As shown in Fig. 8b, the energies of the highest occupied molecular orbital (E HOMO), lowest unoccupied molecular orbital ( E _ LUMO)) and the energy gap ( Δ E = E _ LUMO - E _ HOMO) are − 8.79 eV, − 5.83 eV and 2.97 eV, respectively. Based on the frontier molecular orbital theory, the energies of LUMO and HOMO are related to the electron-accepting and electron-donating abilities of molecules. A lower E _ LUMO means that the molecule possesses a higher tendency to receive electrons, and a higher E HOMO means that the molecule possesses a higher tendency to donate electrons [32]. The ΔE can evaluate the adsorption ability of a molecule. The smaller ΔE corresponds to the stronger adsorption ability [33]. Janus Green B (JGB) is a classic organic additive in the acidic sulfate copper electronic plating bath, which can be regarded as the reference chemical compound to assess the adsorption ability of other additives.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > 3.4. In situ FTIR study of SA interreaction mechanism
blocks.text: Compared with JGB [14], the value of E _ HOMO for SA is lower than that of JGB (−5.75 eV), indicating that it is slightly difficult for SA to donate electrons to the copper surface. The value of E _ LUMO for SA is also lower than that of JGB (−3.68 eV), implying that it is easy for SA to receive electrons from the copper surface to form a back-donation bond. The ΔE value of SA is higher than that of JGB (2.06 eV), signifying that the SA itself possesses weaker adsorption on the copper surface.

blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > 3.4. In situ FTIR study of SA interreaction mechanism
blocks.text: To further understand the specific atoms involved in adsorption, the ESP of SA is calculated and displayed in Fig. 8c. The ESP represents the distribution of electron density, where a low ESP value is equivalent to high electron density [34]. Obviously, the nitrogen atoms at both sides of SA (dark blue region) are susceptible to electrophilic attack, and the nitrogen atoms in the middle of SA (light blue region) are susceptible to nucleophilic attack. Combined with the in situ FTIR spectra results in Fig. 7, it can be determined that SA adsorbs on the copper surface through the N atom in the aromatic ring (light blue region). The adsorption model is proposed in Fig. 8d.

As shown in Fig. 9a, when PEG is added into the electrolyte composed of CuSO _4•5H_2 O, H_2 SO _4, Cl - and SA, though there is no characteristic peak of PEG appearing, the intensities for characteristic peaks B and C of SA slightly increase. blocks.section: Insights into the synergistic effects of safranine in an acidic copper bath on through-hole void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: It is very important to optimize the novel additive for TH copper void-free filling. In this work, we first successfully develop a novel SAbased acidic sulfate copper electronic plating process, and the process behaves the excellent copper void-free filling of TH. The complicated but effective molecule actions and synergistic effects among PEG, SPS and SA are carefully studied for the void-free filling of TH by CV, in situ FTIR experiments and theoretical calculations. This work is undoubtedly beneficial to understanding the interaction mechanisms of additives at a molecular level, and further developing and improving the acidic sulfate copper electronic plating in TH void-free filling.

blocks.section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition
blocks.text: Huizi Shen a, Hoe Chul Kim a, Minjae Sung a, Taeho Lim b,, Jae Jeong Kim a, a School of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Institute of Chemical Process, Seoul National University, 1 Gwanak-ro, Gwanak-gu, Seoul 08826, Republic of Korea b Department of Chemical Engineering, Soongsil University, 369 Sangdo-ro, Dongjak-gu, Seoul 06978, Republic of Korea

blocks.section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Organic additives play an important role in regulating fi lm growth and properties in Cu electrodeposition. 3‑Mercapto‑1‑propane sulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are representative accelerators that promote Cu electrodeposition rate. In this study, the formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS wa determined by measuring the equilibrium constants of thiol–disulfide interchange reactions with the reference thiol/disul fi de pairs by 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy. The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS was 0.153 V (vs. standard hydrogen electrode). Based on this calculation, the cell potentials of Cu(I)(thiolate) formation reaction with either SPS or MPS, which is a key reaction in accelerating mechanism, were also estimated by ultraviolet–visible absorption and 1 H NMR spectroscopies: they were found to be 0.202 V and 0.214 V for SPS and MPS, respectively. The positive cell potential indicates that the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complexes is thermodynamically favorable in the presence of additives.

blocks.section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Cu has been widely used as metallization material in the semi conductor industry owing to its low electrical resistivity and high electromigration resistance. Cu metallization is usually performed by electrodeposition, which e fi ciently yields high quality fi lms by a relatively simple and inexpensive process. Electrolyte for Cu electrodeposition typically contains small quantities of organic additives, which are essential to regulate fi lm growth and properties. Additives are grouped into accelerators, suppressors, and levelers according to their roles in controlling the deposition rate. Among them, 3‑mercap to‑1‑propanesulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are the most representative accelerators in Cu electrodeposition [1].

blocks.section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: The accelerating e f ect of SPS or MPS has been explained by two mechanisms [2]. One describes competitive adsorption between accel erator and suppressor; the displacement of suppressor inhibition layer by SPS or MPS facilitates the approach of Cu ions to electrode surface, enhancing the deposition rate [ 3 - 7 ]. The other mechanism focuses on direct catalytic reduction of Cu ^2 + ion to C u ^+ ion by forming Cu(I) (thiolate) complex [8–11]. The reduction of Cu ^2 + to Cu ^+ is known as the rate-determining step of Cu electrodeposition [12]. Vereecken et al. reported that the amount of C u ^+ near electrode surface is a key factor determining the deposition rate in Cu electrodeposition [13,14].

MPS or SPS in electrolyte can form stable Cu(I)(thiolate) complex, increasing the amount of C u ^+ species near the electrode surface [14]. The corresponding reactions are described as follows.

blocks.text: Herein, the formal reduction potential of SPS ( Eq.. (3)) was obtained, and the cell potentials of Eqs. (1) and (2) were estimated by spectroscopy. The formal reduction potential of SPS was obtained by measuring the chemical equilibrium constants of thiol–disulfide interchange reaction between MPS/SPS pairs and reference thiol/disul fi de pairs, lipoic acid (Lip) and mercaptoethanol (ME). blocks.section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 2.1. Electrochemical analysis
blocks.text: Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed with electrolyte composed of 0.25 M CuSO and 1.0 M H SO. SPS or MPS was also added to the electrolyte. The concentrations of SPS and MPS were 50 μM and 100 μM, respectively, at which the equivalent concentration of thiolate functional group is same: one SPS is reduced to two MPS (Eq. (3)). The electrochemical analysis was conducted in a three-electrode system comprising a Cu rotating disk electrode ( 0.2 \thinspace cm ^2), Cu rod, and Ag / AgCl, /saturated KCl electrode ( Ag/AgCl) as the working electrode, the counter electrode, and the reference electrode, respectively. Temperature was held at 30^°C (303 K) by thermostat during the analysis. The potential applied on the working electrode was swept from 0.15 V to - 0.8 5 : V (vs. Ag/AgCl) at a scan rate of 10 mV/s using a potentiostat (PAR 273A, EG&G Princeton Applied Research Corporation). All the LSV analysis was conducted right after the solution preparation to minimize the extent of reactions, Eqs. (1) and (2).

blocks.text: Chemical equilibrium constants were obtained by measuring the equilibrium concentrations of chemical species by ^1H NMR spectroscopy (Bruker Avance III 400 FT-NM, Bruker). For thiol–disulfide interchange reaction, all the reactants were dissolved in deuterated phosphate bu f er, prepared by dissolving 10 mM phosphoric acid (85% D_3 PO _4 in D_2 O,, Cambridge Isotopes Laboratories) in 50 mL of D_2 O.. The pD of the solution was adjusted to 7 by adding NaOD (30% in D_2 O); the p D was calculated by the following relationship, \pD = \pH + 0.4 [16].

blocks.text: Two test samples were prepared in 5 mm NMR tubes. One comprised 10 mM Lip and 20 mM MPS and the other had 20 mM ME and 10 mM SPS, dissolved in the deuterated phosphate bu f er solution. The NMR tubes containing samples were sealed completely with polytetra fl uoroethylene (PTFE) tape and then kept on shelves at room temperature for 0–45 h before acquiring NMR spectra. The concentrations of the species were determined by measuring the peak areas of the following NMR resonances, Lip: 3.69 ppm, Lip ^red \colon 3.58 ppm, ME ox: 3.86 ppm, ME: 3.69 ppm, MPS: 2.66 ppm and 2.02 ppm, and SPS: 2.86 ppm and 2.15 ppm [17,18].

The solution was kept at room temperature for 0–15 h in a 5–mm NMR tube sealed with PTFE tape before acquiring NMR spectra. blocks.section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: The formal reduction potential of SPS was fi rst determined by using thiol–disulfide interchange reaction with ME and Lip. The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS under the standard condition was 0.153 V (vs. SHE) in aqueous solution. The cell potential of the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complexes, which is the key reaction to explain the accelerating mechanism, was also estimated based on the formal reduction potential of SPS. The cell potential of Cu(I)(thiolate) formation between C u ^+ and SPS was 0.202 V, and the reaction between Cu ^2 + and MPS was 0.214 V. We believe that the thermodynamic values obtained in this study would be helpful in understanding or developing industrial Cu electrodeposition involving SPS.

blocks.section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: A nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compound N-(3-(5-Mercapto-1H-tetrazol-1-yl) phenyl) acetamide (named L) was investigated as a new leveler to develop the microvias Cu fi lling with or without cracked plating in blind via. The synergistic effects of L with other plating additives were investigated by galvanostatic measurements (GMs) and cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements. The GMs show that the Δη values (Potential difference at different speeds of Cu rotating disk electrode) are approximately 24 mV which usually suggests better Cu fi lling performance for the corresponding electrolyte additives. In addition, the optical microscope (OM) measurements indicated that microvias cracked plating was more likely to occur when there is no accelerator in the copper plating solution. The results of OM experiments also show that the microvia super- fi lling would not appear although the copper plating rate at the bottom of the blind hole is higher than that of the outer copper layer of the blind hole if there is no air agitation in the copper plating solution.

blocks.section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Over recent years, the nano or micro-scale blind vias copper fi lling by electroplating has become one of the most practical methods for the fabrication of integrated circuit packaging substrates and circuit boards (PCBs) [1–6]. To achieve high-reliability interconnection by Cu fi lling blind holes between layers of electronic products is a long term and formidable task with high-density interconnection (HDI) technology. The super fi lling of blind holes is commonly regarded as an ef fi cient way and high performance with no void or seam during the microvia metallization process [7–8]. The super fi lling mode means the electrocrystallization rate speed of copper at the bottom of the blind via is much faster than that at the surface of the PCBs so called bottom-up deposition [9–10]. However, cracked plating that grows from the side and bottom of the blind hole penetrates the copper layer at the corners of the blind holes. It is often found as a serious fault in PCB industrial production, as shown in Fig. 1.

blocks.section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Cracked plating is an important reliability failure type of copper electroplating. It is manifested as copper cohesive cracks appearing at the corner locations of the microvias and will result in failures in electric and heat conductivity. The greater harm of the cracked plating phenomenon lies in its concealment. The conductivity of the copper layer for PCBs with cracked plating is usually the same as that of a normal printed circuit board at the early stages, so it is dif fi cult to be detected in electrical testing. However, some problems such as signal interruption and the sudden crash will occur and cause huge economic losses when the electronic devices and products smooth running for a period of time. Hence, there are urgent demands for developing processing guidelines for cracked plating that will lead to stable electroplating structures.

blocks.section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In order to ensure product quali fi ed reliability, many chemical additives have been applied in super fi lling process, including an accelerator (bis(3-sulfopropyl) disul fi de, SPS), a suppressor (polyethylene glycol, PEG or PEP(propylene oxide-ethylene oxide-propylene oxide)), and a leveler (Janus Green B, JGB) [11–15]. Among them, leveler ha important effects with regard to the asymmetric electroplating due to its capability of adsorbing at a high electric fi eld for the cathode sur face, which increase the overpotential of copper deposition and strongly inhibits copper deposition in high current density regions [16–18]. According to the literature [19,20], commonly used levelers for copper electroplating are organic compounds and their derivatives such as quaternary ammonium surfactants, dyestuff substances, nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compounds, and many others. The widely used levelers such as JGB, tricyclazole (TCA), 2-Mercaptopyridine, and 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole (AMBT) play an essential role in greatly hindering the deposition of Cu ion and smooth the surface of the deposited copper fi lm [21–28].

blocks.text: A method to optimize the concentration of Cl − has been established based on cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests at a rotation speed of 1000 rpm, as shown in Fig. 3a. It is usually considered that Cl ^- \ i s the depolarizer of the metal deposition process. When the increase of Cl − in VAS containing SPS, PEP and L, all of these CV plots indicate a clear synergistic inhibitory effect between C l ^- and other additives. The previous research revealed that the C l ^- played a crucial role in the suppressor of PEP and its synergistic inhibitory effect on copper ion deposition. It could be seen from Fig. 3a that the anode copper dissolution peak current gradually decreases with the amount of Cl − increasing from 0 ppm to 120 ppm. The phenomenon indicated that the copper (copper ions) became more and more dif fi cult to dissolve (deposit) due to the anchoring effect of Cl − leading to more PEP molecules adsorbing on the electrode surface [29–30]. The Q was the integral area value of Cu stripping peaks as a function of C l ^- concentrations measured by CV tests as shown in Fig.

It is very important to evaluate the optimal C l ^- concentration for the application and development of the microvias fi lling technology. blocks.section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 2.2. The Q/Q_O values and PEP concentrations dependence
blocks.text: Fig. 5a shows the CV experiment with different concentrations of PEP in the electroplating solution. The strength of suppression of PEP could be evaluated by the integrated area value Q in VAS with a constant concentration of other electroplating additives. Fig. 5b showed the piecewise linear fi tting result of the integrated area value Q/Q_0 of the anode copper dissolution peak. Generally, the smaller Q/ Q_0 value means the higher suppression intensity of copper ion deposition. Fig. 5b shows that the Q/Q_0 value decreases dramatically fi rst and then evolves toward an approximate steady-going value with the PEP increased. Thus, the change rate of Q/Q_0 is divided into two areas, including the linear increase area (PEP concentration less than 10 ppm) and the stable area (PEP concentration greater than 20 ppm). In fact, a critical transition point of Cu stripping peaks occurred when the suppressor concentration was 9.61 ppm, as shown in Fig. 5b. In other words, the 9.61 ppm PEP were adequate to achieve the critical adsorption on the cathode when assumed PEP molecules only constitute a monolayer [32].

blocks.section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 2.3. The Q/Q_O values and SPS concentrations dependence
blocks.text: The CV measured in the electroplating solution with different concentrations of SPS is shown in Fig. 6. It is usually believed that PEP has a small diffusion coef fi cient in VAS, but it can quickly adsorb adsorbed on the Cu surface through the cooperation of Cl − [33]. On the contrary, SPS has a large diffusion coef fi cient and it is strongly adsorbed on active sites in weak convection conditions [34]. The adsorption of SPS on the electrode surface promotes the reduction of copper ions on the cathode surface and accelerates the Cu deposition rate [35]. The peak current and the Q/Q_0 values of anode copper dissolution gradually increase with increasing SPS, as shown in Fig. 6a and b, respectively. The experimental results showed that the copper dissolution became more and more serious with the increase in SPS concen tration. Taking this Δ n value larger means a good fi lling performance, the GMs measured in the electroplating solution with different concentrations of SPS at two different spinning speeds are shown in Fig. 7. So, the optimal SPS was 6 ppm and Δη is equal to 24 mV when the electroplating bath system contains VAS, 200 ppm PEP, 10 ppm L.

blocks.text: The cracked plating of microvia is the main reason for PCBs inter connect faults. This paper further investigates the effect of additives on the cracked plating process based on VAS containing 200 ppm PEP, 60 ppm Cl ^- and 10 ppm L under strong convection intensity. It can be seen from Fig. 13f that the microvia was not fully fi lled and the electroplated coating appeared cracked phenomenon. The results of copper electroplating showed a good agreement compared with the electrochemical experiments (see Fig. 10b). It is usually believed that the accelerator is to increase the cathode current density, control the rate of crystal nucleation and improve the fi lling ability of the microvias [49,50]. From Fig. 13f, we can see fractures and microcracks at the corners of the blind holes. The microcracks or fractures can be caused by the neighboring stress fi eld due to the lack of SPS. So, the severe plastic deformation occurred on the copper plating surface [51]. The cracked plating also revealed that a diagonal line across the bottom of microvia at the corners of the blind holes, as shown in Fig. 13g. Fig.

blocks.text: 13e showed the schematic diagram for the cracked plating without SPS in forced convection. The cracked plating appeared diagonal lines could be attributed to the mechanism: 1)PEP had a large molecular weight led to the relatively dif fi cult diffusion from the bulk solution to the bottom of the hole; 2) The copper ion deposition rate also signi fi cantly retarded and the residual stress increased in electrodeposition process without SPS; 3) The additives concentration distribution on the sides and bottom of the microvia is not uniform. The synergistic effect of the gradient distribution of concentration results in the increased residual stress for the deposited copper fi lm and eventually forms a crack at the junction of the electroplated interfaces.

blocks.section: The synergistic effects of additives on the micro vias copper fi lling > 3. Conclusions
blocks.text: A new nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compound N-(3-(5-Mercapto-1H-tetrazol-1-yl) phenyl) acetamide was found as a leveler for microvias fi lling in HDI board. The Δ G _ads ^0 shown that the L adsorption on the Cu surface was associated with mainly chemical adsorption processes. The optical microscope measurements indicated that the cracked plating was more likely to occur in a diagonal line across the bottom of the microvia at the corners of the blind holes when there is no accelerator in the copper plating solution. The thickness of deposited copper for the bottom of the microvia was larger than the outside without stirring, and this association may be attributed to PEP concentration non-uniform distribution on the sides and bottom of the microvia. Chronoamperometry tests indicate that the Cu electrodeposition nucleation could be considered as an instantaneous mechanism for the initial few seconds. An optimal copper plating solution composed of the virgin acid solution (VAS) only added the PEP, L, and SPS was found and applied to carry out super fi lling of microvias.

blocks.section: Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: A defect free copper interconnect is crucial for ensuring the electrical connection and transmission of high density interconnect printed circuit boards. Leveling agent is a key regulatory factor for achieving dense cop per super filling from bottom to top in blind holes during the electroplating process of high-density interconnect boards. Here, two small molecule five-membered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains, namely 3- amino-5-mercapto-1,2,4-triazole (AMT) and 2–5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT), were selected to be as levelling agents to study their effect on the copper filling behavior on blind holes. Electrochemical tests including cyclic voltammetry solvation (CV) and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) were firstly used to analyze the inhibitory effect of two leveling agents on copper deposition and it was indicated that the MMT has a more significant inhibitory effect on the copper deposition than the AMT.

blocks.section: Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Subsequently, the influence of different concentrations of MMT on the inhibition of copper deposition and the blind hole filling performance were also further analyzed by LSV, CV, and constant current measurement (GM), where an optimal concentration of 7 ppm was obtained for the maximum inhibitory ability on the copper deposition accompanied by the best blind hole filling ability. The characterization analysis from the field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) also illuminates that the MMT leveling agent can effectively reduce the surface roughness of copper filled with micropores and promote the selective growth of copper coatings along the (11 1) crystallographic plane. The adsorption behavior of the levelling agent on the cathode surface during electrodeposition was further also studied by the quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics sim ulations combined with the in situ electrochemical surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy (EC-SERS) experiments.

blocks.text: It has been suggested that the thiol, sulfur, and alkyl groups in the leveling agent MMT molecule are nucleophilic groups, providing preferred active sites for adsorption reactions and thus generating effective inhibition ability on copper deposition formation. Thermal shock experiments based on tin immersion showed the copper layer obtained under the addition of the levelling agent MMT has excellent reliability. The comprehensive results indicated that 2-mercapto-5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT) was an effective levelling agent for the blind hole supperfilling.

blocks.section: Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Blind hole copper electroplating is the primary technology used in the connectivity manufacturing process for printed circuit boards (PCB), semiconductor integrated circuit (IC) chips, and IC packaging substrates [1–3]. The issue of achieving complete filling of high-quality plated copper has become increasingly essential in light of the progress made in integrated and miniaturized electronic devices. This is particularly relevant as high-density interconnect printed circuit boards (PCBs) are transitioning towards through-hole and micro-hole designs with larger depth-to-diameter ratios [4]. In the process of copper plating on such PCB micro vias with a larger depth-to-diameter ratio, there is a very significant difference between a current’s density distribution inside and on the surface of the micro vias. In such an environment, the copper electrodeposition rate in the pore area will be significantly greater than that in the micropores’ bottom region, which will result in the coppe layer covering and sealing the pore area in a preferential manner, leading to internal defects in the pores.

blocks.section: Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In order to achieve bottom-up superfilling of the micropores, a synergistic effect of different addi tives is required, namely accelerators, inhibitors, levelling agents and chloride ions. Accelerators are generally small molecule organic sul phides containing specific functional groups of (-S–S-), sulfhydryl (-SH) and sulphonic acid ( - S O _ 3 ^ -) groups, which typically preferentially adsorb at the micropore’s bottom and can hasten the electrodeposition of copper at the hole’s bottom. SPS and MPS are both common accelerator [ 5, 6 ]. During copper electrodeposition, the inhibitor is usually adsorbed on the cathode surface and interacts with chloride ions to increase the overpotential, thereby achieving the inhibitory effect on the surface deposition of copper, Inhibitors are mainly macromolecular polyether or polyols [7]. The most prevalent inhibitors are polyethylene glycol (PEG), but in addition to PEG there are also polypropylene glycol (PPG) and triblock copolymers of PEG and PPG [8–10]. Levelling agents can be added in very small amounts compared to inhibitors to achieve a strong inhibiting effect and rapid deactivation, leaving the surface flat and smooth.

blocks.section: Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Meantime, levelling agents also show an inhibiting effect o copper deposition but there is no substitute for inhibitors, which can be compared to short-acting inhibitors, while inhibitors show a moderate inhibiting effect and deactivate slowly, and throughout the plating process, the levelling agent gradually covers the copper surface, domi nating the completion of superconformal deposition [4,7]. Traditiona levelling agents such as Janus Green B (JGB), Diazine Black (DB) Methylene Blue (MB), Alsin Blue (ABPV) [11–14]. However, these dye conventional levelling agents are prone to decomposition at high tem peratures, which makes the plating process not easy to control increasing the cost and also leading to copper plating quality problems. In response to the above problems, researchers have continued t develop new environmentally friendly high-performance small molecul copper plating levelling agents, such as benzyl quaternary ammonium containing compounds phenylacetyl chloride (BZC) [15], 2,2-dithiodi pyridine (DTDP) [16], 4,6-dimethyl-2-mercaptopyrimidine (DMP) [17], tricyclazole (TCA) [18], 1-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-2-tetrazole-5-thion (HPTT) [19].

blocks.section: Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating > 3.1. Electrochemical properties of two leveling agents are compared
blocks.text: First, using cyclic voltammetric stripping, which was carried out in a base solution with SPS and PEG, SPS, PEG, and MMT/AMT, respectively, at two rotational speeds of 100 rpm and 1600 rpm, the effect of two types of five-membered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains on the electrodeposition behavior of copper was investigated. The findings are depicted in Fig. 2. The observation of Fig. 2 reveals that the dissolution peaks of copper obtained from electroplating solutions containing two kinds of small molecule five membered heterocyclic compounds additives are significantly smaller than those obtained from the base plating solution whether at the 100 rpm or at the 1600 rpm. The results of the aforementioned inquiry suggest that the introduction of two small molecules consisting of five-membered heterocyclic compounds can effectively enhance cathodic polarization and prevent the deposition of copper. Moreover, it was further observed that the copper dissolution peak was smaller when 5 ppm MMT was added than when 5 ppm AMT was added. This means that the additive MMT is superior to AMT in inhibiting copper deposition through levelling agents.

blocks.section: Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating > 3.1. Electrochemical properties of two leveling agents are compared
blocks.text: The effects of the two levelling agents on copper electrodeposition were explored further using linear scanning voltammetry (LSV), and the findings are displayed in Fig. 3. From this, we can see when 5 ppm AMT and 5 ppm MMT are added whether in weak or strong convection, Copper’s deposition potential significantly shifts towards the negative direction, which is consistent with the results obtained from CV, indicating that the addition of AMT and MMT both can inhibit copper electrodeposition. Moreover, Copper’s deposition potential attained in the plating solution containing MMT shifts to the negative direction to the greatest extent, indicating that the additive MMT has a greater ability to suppress copper deposition compared to the additive AMT.

blocks.section: Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating > 3.2. Electrochemical analysis of the additive MMT
blocks.text: Based on the above results that the MMT levelling agent exhibits a greater inhibitory ability to copper deposition compared with the AMT, Further research has been done to investigate how MMT levelling agent interacts with other additives. Initially, a constant current test was conducted at a rotational speed of 1600 rpm to investigate the effects of different concentrations of MMT additives on the inhibitory properties of copper deposition. As depicted in Fig. 4 displays the curves represent the relationship between potential and time. From Fig. 4, 200 ppm inhibitor PEG was added at 200 s, 1 ppm accelerator SPS was added at 500 s, and 1 ppm levelling agent MMT was first added at 1000 s. When 1 ppm MMT was added, the deposition potential was negatively shifted at 1000 s and the cathodic polarization was increased, which indicated that MMT inhibited the deposition of copper. The deposition potentials at a total of 7 ppm MMT and 9 ppm MMT were essentially the same, so the optimum concentration of levelling agent MMT was tentatively concluded to be 7 ppm.

blocks.text: Furthermore, the objective of this research is to examine the impact of various concentrations of MMT additive on the inhibition of copper deposition behavior by the utilization of cyclic voltammetric solvation analysis. The findings are presented in Fig. 5. As depicted in Fig. ^5, at 1600 rpm, the copper dissolving peak displayed a trend toward decreasing behavior as the levelling agent MMT concentration was raised from zero to 7 ppm. The copper dissolving peak did not further diminish when the MMT additive concentration was raised to 9 ppm; rather, it essentially remained the same as the copper dissolution peak attained at 7 ppm. Therefore, it can be determined that the optimal concentration of the leveling agent MMT with the strongest copper inhibition ability is 7 ppm, which is consistent with the results obtained from the constant flow rate experiment.

As shown in the figure, the peak of copper dissolution under strong convection (i.e., at 1600 rpm) conditions is significantly smaller than that under weak convection conditions (i.e., at 100 rpm). blocks.section: Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: In summary, two small five-membered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains, namely AMT and MMT, were selected as electroplated copper levelling agents in this paper. The electrochemical anal ysis of CV, LSV, and GM showed that MMT has greater inhibitory ability in inhibiting copper deposition behavior compared to AMT. An optima concentration (7 ppm) of MMT added for effectively suppressing copper deposition was obtained by electrochemical analysis from the CV, LSV, and GM experiments based on the addition of different concentrations of MMT additives. The blind hole filling experiment further demonstrates that such an optimal addition concentration for MMT can achieve cop per overfilling in high aspect ratio PCB blind holes. Characterization analyses from FE-SEM, AFM, and XRD also further demonstrate that the coating obtained at this optimal concentration of MMT has the densest and smoothest surface with a typical 111 texture preferential growth. The thermal shock experiment based on tin immersion indicates that the copper layer obtained using MMT as a leveling agent has good reli ability.

blocks.section: Five-membered heterocyclic small molecule compounds as novel levelling agents for blind-hole copper plating > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: It is indicated by in-situ Raman spectroscopy analysis that the adsorption of MMT molecules on the electrode surface is a time dependent process and the C–S, C–N, N––N, and - CH bonds are preferentially adsorbed on the electrode surface. The smaller energy gap value (ΔE = 3.729 (ev)) for the MMT molecule calculated by quantum chemistry further indicates that suggest that the MMT molecules have strong adsorption capacity. Furthermore, Quantum chemical calcula tions based on the electronic potential energy of the MMT molecula structure indicate that the thiol group, sulfur bond, and alkyl groups from the MMT molecular belong to nucleophilic groups and provides the preferred adsorption reaction active sites for interaction with the copper surface, which is consistent with the results from the in situ electrochemical enhanced Raman spectroscopy. The adsorption of these nucleophilic groups on the copper surface effectively inhibits copper deposition and thereby achieving bottom-up copper overfilling in blind holes. These results from the electrochemical analysis and theoretical calculations fully demonstrate that MMT is an effective levelling agent for PCB blind hole filling.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Cobalt electrodeposition is the core technology in chip manufacturing. Butynediol (BD) is the key component in cobalt electrodeposition. In this work, the molecule structure and adsorption ability of BD are successfully revealed by density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The number of transferred electrons (ΔN) value near 0, and the interaction between oxygen atom not alkynyl group in BD and cobalt, demonstrating that BD is physically adsorbed on the cobalt surface. The adsorption energy of BD on hexagonal closepacked (hcp)(101) is −0.67 eV, which is the highest adsorption energy among crystal faces, manifesting that (101) may be a potential preferred orientation. Then the effects of BD on the electroreduction behavior of cobalt is revealed by electro chemical experimental techniques. BD can inhibit the electroreduction of cobalt ions based on kinetics and decreases the diffusion coefficient from 3.43 × 10 − 6 to 1.33 × 10 − 6 cm 2 /s, but the reaction is irreversible with diffusion control whether it contains BD or not. BD can make the charge transfer resistance increase from 241 Ω/cm 2 to 496 Ω/cm 2.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: BD has some effects on the cobalt electroreduction kinetics, it does not change the instantaneous nucleation mechanism. Finally, the morphology, composition and structure of the cobalt coating are characterized by scanning electron microscope (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). BD can refine the grains and improving the uniformity of the cobalt coating. Although the properties of the mixed crystals have not changed, the preferred orientation has changed due to the addition of BD. A new peak of hcp(101) arises resulted from the adsorption of BD to form a retained surface, which are consistent with the calculation results. And the relatively positive values of stress change indicates that BD causes the internal stress of cobalt coating to be tensile stress.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Electrodeposition plays a vital role in advanced chip manufacturing as it is a key technology for electrical interconnects. With the rapid development of technology, the length of metal wiring inside the chip has been significantly extended, at the same time, the number of layers inside the chip has also continued to increase. To improve energy efficiency and performance, the size of transistors and metals must continue to shrink [1–4]. However, this process inevitably exacerbates the size effect (grain boundary and interface diffusion of electrons in metals), significantly increases the current load and resistance, and causes serious RC delay and thermal damage to chip performance. Metal cobalt has a small mean free path and low size effect, making it an ideal metal [5].

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Metal cobalt interconnect layer is mainly prepared by electrodeposition technology. In the process of metal cobalt electrodeposition, additives are key components that can adjust the cobalt deposition rate in via and trench, improve the uniformity of the deposited cobalt film, and thus improve chip performance [6–9]. However, due to the confidentiality of the technology, there are relatively few related studies and reports, but this does not affect its importance and application prospects. Li et al. [10] introduced that dye molecule Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride could refine cobalt grains and achieve microvia superconformal filling. Huang et al. [11,12] showed that dimethylglyoxime had a strong suppression effect and made cobalt a three-dimensional nucleation. Wu et al. [13] discovered that Akyne-PEG4-amine could be used as an inhibitor to achieve nanometer scale superfilling of cobalt electrode position. Kiruba et al. [14] presented that butynediol (BD) would change the interfacial pH to regulate and control the formation of cobalt. It is worth noting that BD as a typical type-II brightener has attracted much attention among the many cobalt additives. Jeyabharathi et al.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: [15] deemed that BD would cause electrochemical oscillation due to the hydrogenation of BD during cobalt electrodeposition. Pan et al. [16] showed that BD and saccharin together could decrease the microhard ness of cobalt deposits as a result of increased grain size. Although it is well known that BD can be used as an additive, the effect of its molecular structure on the interface of cobalt electrodeposition has not been elucidated at a molecular level. Therefore, it is necessary to carry out relevant research. This study demonstrates the adsorption state of BD on cobalt surface and the effects of adsorption on crystal growth and orientation. This enriches the understanding of the role of additives in the cobalt electrodeposition process, revealing that BD achieves uniformity and compact film morphology through interactions with the cobalt surface, which is conducive to promote the development of high-performance chip interconnection technology.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In this work, the molecule structure, adsorption ability and electrochemical property of BD are revealed through density functional theory (DFT) calculation and electrochemical analyses. The effect of BD on the morphology, composition and structure of the cobalt coating were clarified by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray diffraction (XRD).

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 2.1. Reagents
blocks.text: CoSO _4•7\H_2 O, H_3BO_3 and CoCl _2·6\H_20 were purchased from Chron Chemicals Co., Ltd. (China). Butynediol and H_2SO_4 were purchased from Macklin Co., Ltd. (China). All the reagents used were analytical grade.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 2.2. Electrochemical analyses
blocks.text: Electrochemical analyses were performed using CHI electrochemical workstation (CHI760, China). The basic electrolyte composed of 0.3 MCoSO 4^•7H2 O, 0.16 M H_3BO_3 and 0.02 M CoCl ⋅6 H O. The concentration of additive BD was 0.12 mM. The pH of the electrolyte was adjusted by 5 % H_2 SO_4 aqueous solution and stabilized to 3 ~ 4. The temperature of electrolyte was 303 K. A glassy carbon electrode (GCE) with 3 mm diameter, a H [g/Hg_2SO_4 electrode (saturated K_2SO_4 solution, SMSE) and a platinum sheet were acted as the working electrode, reference electrode and counter electrode, respectively. Before experiments, the GCE was firstly polished with 300 nm and 50 nm Al_2O_3 respectively, further ultrasonically cleaned in absolute ethanol and ultrapure water ( 1 8.2 M Ω cm ^- 1). The value of the OCP is about −0.21 V and the stability time is 120 s.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 2.3. Electrodeposition and characterization details
blocks.text: The cobalt electrodeposition experiments were carried out in baths (0.3 M CoSO •7 H O, 0.16 M H_3BO_3 and 0.02 M CoCl _2·6\H_2 O) without and with BD at the temperature of 303 K and the pH of 3–4. The current density was 10 mA/cm2. The electrodeposition time was 10 min. The anode material is cobalt plate (area: 5 × 5 ~ cm ^2, thickness:1 cm), and cathode material is copper sheet (area: 4 × 2 cm ^2,, thickness: 50 μm). The distance between anode and cathode is 6 cm. The morphology of the cobalt coating was characterized by SEM (Zeiss) with an accelerating voltage of 10 kV. Coupled EDS was used to measure the composition. The structure of the cobalt coating was characterized by XRD (Rigaku) with Cu Kα target and wavelength of 0.15406 nm.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 2.4. Calculations
blocks.text: The DFT calculations of BD molecule were conducted by Gaussian 09 program package [17]. Basis sets of 6–311 + + G ^* \ast ^* for H, C and O atoms was employed with B3LYP functional [18]. The solvent effect of water was included by integral equation formalism polarizable continuum model (IEFPCM). The electrostatic potential (ESP) and average local ionisation energy (ALIE) were calculated by using the Multiwfn package [19–22].

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 2.4. Calculations
blocks.text: The adsorption of BD on cobalt surface at different faces was investigated using the slab model DFT calculations with the generalized Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) [23], and the projector augmented-wave (PAW) pseudopotential plane-wave method on the VASP code [24–28]. A2×2×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-point grid was used for all on geometry optimization calculations. The plane-wave energy cutoff was set to 500 eV. The convergence criterion for the total energy tolerance per atom was 1 × 1 0 ^- 6 eV/atom, and the maximum force tolerance was 0.0 2 : eV ·A^-1

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.1. Number of transferred electrons and frontier molecular orbits
blocks.text: The work function of metal and the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of molecule can be used to evaluate the electron transfer and the adsorption ability. The work function of cobalt is about 4.70 eV [29], meaning that the Fermi level of cobalt is about −4.70 V (Assumption: the vacuum energy level is 0). The energy of the highest occupied molecular orbital (E HOMO) of BDis - 7.5 5 eV. If the Fermi level of the metal is close to the HOMO level of the molecule, the driving force for electrons to transfer from the molecule to the metal surface will decrease. This means that electrons are more likely to transfer between metal and molecule, thereby enhancing the interaction between molecule and metal surface. Obviously, the Fermi level value of cobalt is quite different from the HOMO level value of BD, and the interaction between them is relatively weak. The number of transferred electrons (ΔN) can further analyze the ability of the electron transfer between metal and molecule. when the value of ΔN is close to ^ 0, it means that the electron transfer is not obvious, indicating that the interaction is physical adsorption [30].

The relevant formulae are as follows [31,32]. Thereinto, the values of χ _ Co and η _ Co are 4.3 eV and 3.6 eV,, respectively [32].

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.2. Electrostatic potential and average local ionisation energy
blocks.text: Adsorption can be divided into physical adsorption and chemical adsorption, which are related to the electrostatic effects and the reactivity of molecule, respectively. To expound the electrostatic effects of BD, the colored isopleth maps of the ESP and the area distribution of ESP spacings on the equivalent surface for BD are displayed in Fig. 2. The red region and blue region represent the higher and lower ESP, respectively. The maximum and minimum values of ESP are expressed by orange and cyan spheres, respectively. As shown in Fig. 2a, it can be seen that the lower ESP is mainly distributed on the oxygen atoms on both sides, and the higher ESP is mainly located in the hydrogen atoms on both sides, indicating that the electrons are mainly concentrated on the oxygen atoms on both sides, and the holes are primarily distributed in the hydrogen atoms on both sides. The highest and lowest ESP values are 52.67 and −43.90 kcal/mol. This uneven distribution of ESP can easily lead to a strong electrostatic effect [33]. Fig. 2b presents the histogram of the area distribution at different ESP intervals for BD.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.2. Electrostatic potential and average local ionisation energy
blocks.text: Obviously, BD has a relatively high percentage of area in the low ( 10) regions of ESP. The results again manifest that BD can be adsorbed on metal substances in a strong electrostatic interaction [33], and is mainly physically adsorbed by oxygen atoms.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.2. Electrostatic potential and average local ionisation energy
blocks.text: To clarify the reactivity of BD, the ALIE is completed and the results are presented in Fig. 3. The lower the value of ALIE is, the stronger the reactivity is. The cyan spheres represent the lower points of ALIE, which means that these points are easy to attack by electrophilic reaction [33]. The highest and lowest ALIE values are 268.89 and 203.39 kcal/mol. Obviously, the reactive sites are mainly located in the alkynyl group, that is, these regions are prone to chemical adsorption. Moreover, the more spheres there are in the blue regions, the more chemically active the molecule is, and the easier it is to chemically adsorb. Therefore, it can be seen that BD is also prone to chemical adsorption, and the active sites are mainly concentrated at alkynyl group.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.3. Adsorption on cobalt surface
blocks.text: Based on the ESP and ALIE results, it can be found that BD may be chemical and physical adsorption, and the adsorption regions are concentrated at the alkynyl group and the oxygen atoms on both sides, respectively. To further understand the adsorption type of BD, the adsorption structure of BD and its adsorption energy on different crystal faces are completed. Cobalt possesses face centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal closepacked (hcp) structures. Fig. 4 presents the adsorption behavior of BD on different fcc and hcp crystal faces. Table 1 and Table 2 show the energy values of the different structures and the corresponding adsorptions, respectively. As shown in Fig. 4, regardless of crystal faces, BD is adsorbed exothermically. At the co-adsorbed structure, there are interactions between oxygen atom in BD and cobalt, verifying that BD is physically adsorbed on the surface of cobalt metal. Furthermore, the adsorption energy of BD on fcc(111), fcc(200), fcc(220), hcp(002), hcp (100) and hcp(101) are −0.34, −0.37, −0.44, −0.38, −0.08 and −0.67 eV, respectively.

blocks.text: The results indicate that BD is easily adsorbed on the surface of hcp(101), forming a retention surface, which eventually makes (101) a potential preferred orientation.

Fig. 5 presents the cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves at scanning rate of 50 mV/s on GCE in electrolyte without and with BD. It can be observed that the cathodic peak potentials are −0.92 V and −0.91 V without and with BD, which both attributes to the electroreduction of cobalt ions. The results suggest that, based on thermodynamics, BD may have little effect on the electroreduction reaction. It is worth noting that the cathodic peak currents are − 1.9 8 ~ mA/cm2 and − 1.3 0 mA/cm2 without and with BD, indicating that based on kinetics, BD can inhibit the electroreduction of cobalt ions. On account of the above results, BD has the ability to inhibit the occurrence of cathodic reactions. Moreover, in the more positive potential range ( 0.5 ~ 1.0 V),, the current increases sharply, indicating that metal cobalt is oxidized. The anodic current with BD is less than that without BD, which may be due to the adsorption of BD, hindering the dissolution of cobalt.

blocks.section: Molecular structure with adsorption behavior of butynediol and its effects on cobalt electrodeposition > 3.4. Electrochemical behaviors
blocks.text: The chronoamperometric experiments are conducted under different step-potentials to study the cobalt electro-crystallization process. Fig. 9 shows the chronoamperometric curves on GCE in electrolyte without and with BD, respectively. When a certain step potential is applied, a large current is generated in a very short time and then decreases rapidly, which is attributed to the instantaneous charging of the double electric layer. With the extension of time, the current density first increases to a peak value ( j _m, corresponding to the time t _m) _:, and then gradually decreases until it tends to be stable. This is due to the continuous formation and growth of crystal nuclei, and the current density gradually increases, then the number of crystal nuclei continues to increase, the crystal nucleus diffusion area continues to overlap, and the current density reaches a peak value, finally after the diffusion area completely overlaps, there is no nucleation site for new nuclei to generate, only crystal nuclei grow, and the current density gradually decreases until it tends to be stable. If there is no peak current density in the curve, cobalt may grow epitaxially along the substrate.

Furthermore, the more negative the step-potential, the shorter the time corresponding to the nucleation peak current density, which indicates that the more negative the potential (increase in overpotential) is, the more conducive the cobalt nucleation behavior occurs.

The selection of this current density 1 0 mA/cm2 is based on the actual electrodeposition process and the chronoamperometric curve. First, in the process of cobalt electrodeposition, by selecting 1 0 mA/cm2;, a uniform and dense coating can be obtained. Secondly, according to the chronoamperometric curve, it can be seen that the curve at around 1 0 mA/cm2 is stable, which is consistent with instantaneous nucleation. Instantaneous nucleation can generate a large number of crystal nuclei in a short time, reduce secondary nucleation, reduce the growth size of grains, and make the microstructure of the deposited coating relatively finer. blocks.text: The XRD results of the cobalt coating without and with BD are presented in Fig. 13. In Fig. 13a, when there is no BD in the electrolyte, the crystal faces of the obtained cobalt coating is hcp(100), fcc(111) and fcc (220), which indicates that the obtained cobalt is mixed crystal. In Fig. 13b, when the electrolyte contains BD, the crystal faces of the obtained cobalt coating is hcp(100), hcp(101) and fcc(220). blocks.section: ABSTRACT
blocks.text: In this study, SO was used to chemically modify the commonly used leveling agent polydimethyldiallylammonium (PD) in through-hole electroplating, resulting in a more effective leveling agent, PDS, which improved the throwing power (TP), leading to through-hole circuit boards with better metal coverage in difficult-to-reach areas. Furthermore, theoretical and experimental studies were conducted to understand how the −SO structure influences the leveling ability of the leveling agent. The study demonstrates that the −SO - modified additive significantly enhances the copper plating process, resulting in thicker and more uniform deposits in through-holes, which are critical for ensuring high-quality circuit boards.Additionally, this study elu cidates the mechanism of action of the leveling agent on the copper surface, providing theoretical support for the development of copper plating leveling agents. The leveling ability differences between the leveling agents PD and PDS were investigated using Cyclic Voltammetry, constant current method, and Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy. Additionally, the optimal concentrations of the additives were determined.

blocks.section: 1. Introduction
blocks.text: With the rapid development of the electronics industry, an increasing number of consumer products, such as computers, electronic watches, wearable devices, smartphones, and communication equipment, are becoming more intelligent, lightweight, and miniaturized[1–3]. In these advanced electronic products, the Printed Circuit Board (PCB) is a critical component, serving as the main conduit between various electronic elements, enabling them to connect and work together in a coordinated manner. The metallization of PCBs, which enables the interconnection of electronic components, is particularly crucial[4,5]. Through-hole electroplating plays a vital role in this process, with copper electroplating emerging as the mainstream choice for PCB interconnection due to its excellent conductivity and low cost[6]. However, current copper electroplating technology faces challenges in meeting the ever-increasing demands of PCB manufacturing, which has become a bottleneck limiting the improvement of PCB performance [7,8].Therefore, the preparation of high-quality through-hole plating and high-density interconnect circuit boards holds significant industrial and economic importance[9].

blocks.section: 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Currently, the most widely used technology in the through-hole plating process of circuit boards is acid copper plating, which typically involves a conventional acid copper plating solution containing copper sulfate, sulfuric acid, and trace amounts of plating additives[10]. Traditional electroplating additives can be categorized into suppressors, accelerators, and levelers[11–13]. In the context of through-hole electroplating, the key substance capable of enhancing the TP value is the leveler, which, as a crucial component in the acid copper plating solution, requires only a small addition to effectively increase the TP value [14,15]. As a critical metric for assessing the performance of throughhole copper plating, the TP value is calculated as the ratio of the copper thickness on the surface to the copper layer thickness inside the hole [16]. The traditional calculation method is divided into six-point method[17,18], and the specific measurement method is described in detail later.

blocks.section: 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Currently, research on leveling agents for through-hole copper plating mainly focuses on synthesizing new, highly efficient leveling agents, and utilizing methods such as quantum chemical calculations to explain their active sites and reaction mechanisms[18,21,22]. However, the related research is relatively scattered, and the structures of the leveling agents in published papers vary significantly. There is limited research on the relationship between the molecular structure of indi vidual leveling agent molecules and their leveling performance.

blocks.section: 1. Introduction
blocks.text: This study primarily investigates the mechanism of −SO ’s impact on the leveling agent molecule PD, analyzing the reasons behind the differences in leveling capabilities between the PD and PDS molecules. Electrochemical experiments were conducted to compare the leveling capabilities of the two additive molecules, and their optimal working concentrations were determined. Finally, the influence mechanism of the SO_2 structure on leveling capability was analyzed through SEP calculations and HOMO/LUMO orbital calculations.

blocks.text: Electrochemical tests were conducted using a three-electrode system. The working electrode was a Pt disc electrode with an area of 0.785 cm 2, the counter electrode was a Pt sheet electrode with an area of 1 cm ^2, and the reference electrode was a Mercurous sulfate electrode (MSE). Cyclic voltammetry tests were conducted within a potential range o Ω f - 0.8 V to 0.6 V, with a scan rate of 20 \mV/ s, and an electrode rotation speed of 1000 rpm[23]. A total of five cyclic voltammetry cycles were performed, and data from the last stable cycle were collected. Additives were introduced into the test solution every 500 s to observe changes in the system’s potential. In the VMS, 100 mg/L of different leveling agents were added, and AC impedance tests were conducted under open-circuit potential conditions of −0.1 V and −0.2 V. blocks.section: 3.1.1. Cyclic voltammetry stripping tests
blocks.text: Cyclic Voltammetry Stripping (CVS) tests record the current response in the solution by applying changes in voltage[30]. The leveling agent reduces the current response by slowing down the deposition process, resulting in a decrease or reduction of the current in the CVS curve. By observing the changes in the current–voltage curve, the concentration and effectiveness of the additives in the plating solution can be indirectly characterized. CVS were conducted in VMS with varying concentrations of PDS to analyze the effect of its concentration. It was observed that as the concentration of PDS increased, the anodic strip ping coulombs continuously decreased. The results are shown in Fig. 3.

After adding 5 mg/L of PDS, the value decreased to 0.1 43C\ cm ^- 2, representing an inhibition capability of 74.65 %. blocks.text: After adding different leveling agents in the VMS, the degree of polarization in the copper ion deposition process increases rapidly. As the amount of the additive increases, this polarizing effect becomes more pronounced. Research into the effects of the two leveling agents on the trend of anodic stripping coulombs reveals that PD does not polarize the crystallization of copper ions as significantly as PDS. Compared to PDS, the addition of PD results in a lesser reduction in anodic stripping coulombs. Additionally, the saturation concentrations of the two agents differ. Once the concentration of PDS reaches 50 mg/L, further increases in the additive do not significantly enhance the polarizing effect, indicating that the leveling action of PDS has reached its limit at this concentration. Even at a PD concentration of 100 mg/L, the anodic stripping coulombs remain lower than those of PDS, indicating that its inhibitory ability is weaker. blocks.text: The trend of the potential-time curve obtained by adding PDS is very similar to that of PD, with its final saturation concentration being 100 mg/L. However, each time PDS is added, there is an instantaneous rise in potential, which quickly returns to a stable state. blocks.section: 3.1.2. Chronopotentiometry analysis
blocks.text: At 500 s, when 100 mg/L of PDS is added to the solution, the potential in the VMS instantaneously drops to −0.72 V. As the solution system is stirred, the potential slowly rises, which is due to the gradual even distribution of the additive in the solution and the stabilization of the system. As indicated by Curve 1, when 20 mg/L of SPS is added to the system at 1000 s, the potential of the solution rapidly rises to −0.58 V, demonstrating that SPS strongly promotes the deposition of copper ions. At 1500 s, when 100 mg/L of PDS is added to the solution, the potential drops to −0.68 V, indicating that PDS has a strong inhibitory effect on the deposition of copper ions. However, Curve 2 shows that when 100 mg/L of PDS is added to a VMS containing PEG at 1000 s, the potential of the solution actually rises. From the chronoamperometry curves, it can be observed that the addition of both PD and PDS leads to a rise in the potential of the PEG-containing plating solution. This suggests that both additives antagonize PEG and promote the deposition of Cu 2+. However, the potential increase caused by PDS is less pronounced compared to PD.

As the cathodic overpotential increases further, the size of the impedance arcs of the two additives tends to converge, indicating that the inhibitory effects of both leveling agents on the deposition of copper ions are at the same level under these conditions.
