blocks.text: In PCB plating, maintaining smooth and flat layers is crucial to avoid rough or dendritic formations that can compromise stability. SEM and XRD analyses were conducted to evaluate surface micro morphology and crystal orientation. 38,39 Figure 11 displays samples 1–5 plated with formulations 1–5, respectively, at 1000© SEM magnification. Sample 1, plated without additives, exhibits a rough surface with spiral bumps and a (220) crystal orientation, indicating rapid deposition along this plane. After adding inhibitor and accelerator, cathodic potential remained lower, indicating slower copper atom deposition compared to sample 1, resulting in a flatter surface still dominated by (220) orientation. Upon adding 0.1 ppm DCQA -C_8 -MI, the plated layer becomes smooth with enhanced (111) crystal surface and few (100) orientations. This is because after the addition of 0.1 ppm DCQA- C_8-M I, the molecules preferentially adsorb on the raised portion of the copper layer surface due to the tip-discharge efect, thus selectively inhibiting the deposition of copper here. On a macroscopic level, uniform deposition of copper is observed.

blocks.section: 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: In summary, four aryl heterocyclic quaternary ammonium salts containing quinacridone core ( DCQA –C_8–M I, ∂ DCQA –C_8– QLDCQA -C_8- DMAP, DCQA -C_8- DMAP - M e) were synthesized featuring positively charged centers for improved charge loading and cathode surface adsorption as potential electroplating levelers. Evaluation involved cyclic voltammetry and polarization curve tests, identifying DCQA -C_8 -MI as the most efective. It exhibited superior leveling and adsorption properties compared to the commercial agent JGB, indicating potential as a highly eficient leveler. Density functional theory calculations revealed DCQA ^-C_8^\phantom + MI’s enhanced charge dispersion capability, with molecular dynamics simulations confirming preferential adsorption onto copper plate surfaces. Through-hole plating experiments using DCQA -C_8 -MI demonstrated eficient leveling, achieving a uniform layer with a TP value of 113.31 % at 0.3 ppm additive concentration, highlighting its eficacy as a leveler. Meanwhile, the adsorption mechanism of heterocyclic quaternary ammonium salts have been investigated ofering guidance for the exploration of eficient organic additives for copper electrodeposition.

blocks.section: Study of 5‑Alkynylpyrimidines as Cobalt Superfilling Inhibitors
blocks.text: ABSTRACT: Electrodeposition technology is the key core technology for achieving micro/nanoscale interconnection in high-end chip manufacturing. Recently, cobalt interconnect structures have been the ideal choice for constructing electronic pathways in process nodes below 14 nm due to the fact that cobalt has a smaller electron mean free path compared to copper; thus, studying the electroplating filling behavior of cobalt in micronano scale space has become a hot topic in the field of chip manufacturing. In this article, an electroplating solution containing a new 5-alkynylpyrimidine (5-EP) as an inhibitor is designed for electrochemical tests, including cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry. The results indicate that the 5-EP significantly inhibits cobalt electrodeposition. The change in the nucleation mode of cobalt in an electroplating solution with the inhibitor (5-EP) was revealed by chronoamperometry, where cobalt atoms nucleate in a three-dimensional continuous manner instead of three-dimensional instantaneous nucleation.

blocks.text: In situ enhanced Raman spectroscopy is used to further analyze the adsorption of the inhibitor (5-EP) molecules on the cobalt surface during the electroplating process from a spectroscopic perspective. The energy gap value of the additive molecule obtained through quantum chemical calculations is \beginarray r \triangle E = E _ LUMO - E _ HOMO = 3.3 0 2 ~ eV, \endarray indicating that the additive molecule has high reactivity and higher adsorption strength at the metal interface. The calculated electrostatic potential (ESP) values of the molecule range from a minimum of −47.29 kJ/mol to a maximum of 70.89 kJ/mol. Lower ESP values imply higher electron density. Molecular dynamics simulations calculate the adsorption energy of the additive molecule (5-EP) on Co(100) to be −133.96 kcal/mol, indicating that the 5-EP molecule has good adsorption capability. Electroplating experiments reveal that the addition of 6 ppm 5-EP to the plating solution enables defect-free filling of blind holes.

blocks.text: Damascene copper plating technology has remained the best choice for metal interconnects in logic chips and memory chips. 1 As semiconductor processes advance toward 10 nm and below, the use of copper as a conductor material begins to encounter issues with RC delay, which severely impacts the interconnect performance of chips. This has led to bottlenecks in process technology at the 10- and 7-nanometer nodes, 2,3 necessitating the search for new alternative interconnect materials. Researchers have found that metals such as Co, Ni, Mo, and Nb show greater potential than Cu. 4 However, when considering other parameters such as process and material costs, only Co is highlighted as a promising material. It has been reported that Co has already been used in the contact interconnect layers at the 10 nm node and is also considered suitable for use as a conductor in higher metal layers. 5 Compared to copper, cobalt has a shorter mean free path for electrons and a higher melting point. At the nanoscale, cobalt interconnects exhibit minimal size efects and superior resistance to electromigration.

blocks.text: 3.1.2. Cathodic Polarization Curve. Linear scanning voltammetry (LSV) was used to evaluate the inhibitory efect of the inhibitor (5-EP) on the cobalt deposition process. The evaluation was carried out at two diferent rotational speeds: 2000 and 200 rpm. The relevant results are shown in Figure 2. With the addition of 5-EP, it can be noticed that the overpotential increases, and the additive adsorbs on the surface of the electrode, forming a film of material that causes the electrochemical reaction to take place on this film rather than on the electrode surface. In this case, the additives may occupy the active sites on the electrode surface, leading to a negative potential shift. 24,25 Regardless of the rotational speed setting, it is found that the addition of 5-EP leads to a steady shift of the reduction potential in a negative direction. This suggests that the inhibitor (5-EP) increases the cathodic polarization and prevents the reduction of Co ^2 + at the cathode. In addition, the ability of 5-EP to inhibit cobalt deposition was significantly higher at high speeds than at low speeds.

blocks.text: 3.3. Theoretical Calculations and Simulations. 3.3.1. Quantum Chemical Calculations. Quantum chemical calculations were employed to elucidate the adsorption process of the inhibitor (5-EP) and to predict its potential adsorption sites. The molecule was inserted into a Gaussian function for structural optimization and computation. The resulting data were then visualized using Multiwfn and VMD software. 27,28 In accordance with the frontier molecular orbital theory, the energy levels of the HOMO and the LUMO play a crucial role in determining chemical reactions. 29 The HOMO energy ( E _ HOMO) reflects the molecule’s inclination to give away electrons, whereas the LUMO energy ( E _ LUMO) reflects its inclination to receive electrons. A larger E _ HOMO value implies a greater capacity of the molecule to donate electrons, while a lower E _ LUMO value suggests a better ability to accept electron s. 30,31 The computational results are depicted in Figure Sa, b..

The extremely small energy diference ( \triangle E) between the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital ( E _ LUMO) and the highest occupied molecular orbital ( E _ HOMO) suggests that the additive molecules have a strong tendency to absorb and donate electrons at the electrode surface. The value of \triangle E is directly related to the adsorption intensity of the additive molecules on the metal interface. A smaller \bigtriangleup E value indicates a higher adsorption strength of the molecules at the metal interface, leading to stronger inhibitory efects on cobalt electro deposition.

blocks.text: 3.4. Blind Hole Filling Experiment. Based on the electrochemical experimental findings, it is anticipated that the inclusion of additives would enhance the electroplating and filling of cobalt in blind holes. Therefore, an experiment was conducted to examine the impact of the inhibitor molecule (5- EP) on blind hole filling with cobalt. Figure 7 illustrates the cross-sectional images of blind hole filled cobalt deposited at various time intervals. As depicted in Figure 7a, when 6 ppm of 5-EP was added to the electrolyte for electroplating, a Vshaped filling of cobalt deposition in the blind hole was observed after 3 h, due to convection and mass transfer efects. Figure 7b shows that with increased electroplating time, the cobalt layer in the blind hole exhibited a bottom-up filling trend, although superfilling was not yet achieved. As shown in Figure 7c, after 5 h of electroplating, the blind hole was completely filled without voids or gaps. This indicates that 5- EP initially adsorbs at the mouth of the blind hole during the electroplating process, inhibiting cobalt deposition at the entrance.

The surface morphology of the cobalt deposited from the electrolyte with diferent concentrations of the inhibitor (5- EP) was analyzed using SEM. The relevant SEM data are displayed in Figure 9. Figure 9a clearly shows that the cobalt coating obtained from the electroplating solution with additives has a rough and porous surface, characterized by the presence of massive growth clusters. The presence of the inhibitor (5-EP) clearly alters the micro morphology of the cobalt coating. As shown in Figure 8b−d, introducing an inhibitor (5-EP) can efectively improve the quality of the cobalt layer. When 2 ppm of inhibitor (5-EP) was added, the cobalt particle size decreased. When the concentration of inhibitor (5-EP) was increased to 4 ppm, the cobalt particle size was further reduced, and the surface of the plated layer was smooth. When the inhibitor (5-EP) is added up to 6 ppm, the cobalt grain size on the coated surface is minimized, and the coating is smooth and flat in the macroscopic state.

blocks.text: In summary, this study employs 5-ethynylpyrimidine (5-EP) as an inhibitor for cobalt electrodeposition. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) and LSV reveal that 5-EP efectively suppresses the reduction of Co ^2 +. Additionally, electrochemical tests indicate the significant role of the ethynyl functional group ( - C \equiv C -) in the cobalt electrodeposition process. Further studies on the impact of 5-EP on cobalt nucleation showed that in th absence of 5-EP, cobalt nucleation occurred through a three dimensional instantaneous process, whereas the addition of 5- EP shifted the nucleation to a three-dimensional progressive process. 5-EP efectively reduced the surface roughness of the cobalt coating and promoted the growth of cobalt grains in the directions of Co(100) and Co(110). The resistivity of the cobalt coating remained essentially at 10 μΩ·cm. According to quantum chemical calculations and MD simulations, it was discovered that 5-ethynylpyrimidine (5-EP), which contains an ethynyl group ( - C \equiv C -), can efectively adsorb onto cobalt The adsorption energy of 5-EP was calculated to be −133.96 kcal/mol on the Co(100) surface, indicating its strong adsorption capability.

By observing in situ enhanced Raman spectra at different potentials. it was found that as the potential stepped, the peak intensities at 1092cm^-1 (ring vibration, C−H in-plane deformation shear vibration), 1414 cm^-1 (pyrimidine ring skeleton N = C = N plane bending vibration), 1573 cm −1 (overall bending vibration of the pyrimidine ring skeleton), and 2125~cm^-1 (carbon−carbon triple bond ( C \equiv C) stretching vibration) increased. blocks.section: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Literature reports indicate that existing synthesis methods for leveling agents often sufer from complex procedures, high environmental burden, challenging purification processes, and insuficient via filling eficiency. To address these limitations, a novel leveling agent (CDT) was synthesized using environmentally friendly materials through a simplified, cost-efective process that eliminates the need for post-synthesis purification. This study systematically investigates the influence of CDT on blind via filling performance in an acidic copper sulfate plating bath containing polyethylene glycol (PEG), bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS), and chloride ions. The chemical structure of CDT was characterized by Fouriertransform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and gel permeation chromatography (GPC). Quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed that CDT exhibits stronger adsorption on copper surfaces compared to conventional leveling agents. Electrochemical measurements confirmed its ability to suppress copper deposition and helped determine the optimal working concentration of CDT.

blocks.document_id: 5_聚_1_4_丁二醇二缩水甘油醚_2_甲基咪唑与咪唑_作为盲孔镀铜整平剂的研究

blocks.text: Electroplating experiments further demonstrated CDT’s capability to achieve superfilling, indicating its suitability for printed circuit board (PCB) manufacturing. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) results corroborated the validity of the optimal concentration established by electrochemical tests. Finally, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed strong interfacial interactions between CDT and the copper surface. These findings collectively suggest that CDT is a highly promising candidate for advanced leveling agent applications.

blocks.document_id: 5_聚_1_4_丁二醇二缩水甘油醚_2_甲基咪唑与咪唑_作为盲孔镀铜整平剂的研究
blocks.section: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs) are indispensable components in modern daily life. As current electronic devices trend toward lighter, thinner, and smaller designs, PCB technology is correspondingly evolving toward multi-layer and high-density configurations. In the PCB manufacturing industry, blind via technology plays a crucial role as it facilitates conductive connections between the layers of multi-layer circuit boards. Therefore, the metallization technology for blind vias is particularly critical in this rapidly advancing field [1–4].

blocks.document_id: 5_聚_1_4_丁二醇二缩水甘油醚_2_甲基咪唑与咪唑_作为盲孔镀铜整平剂的研究
blocks.section: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: To meet the high-performance demands of current electronic devices, copper electroplating in blind vias must achieve flawless filling without cracks and gaps. This typically involves superfilling or botom-up filling techniques, where superfilling refers to a deposition process during electroplating in which the copper deposition rate at the botom of the blind vias is significantly higher than at the opening and surface, thereby achieving perfect filling of the vias [5]. To accomplish superfilling, an acidic copper sulfate system is com monly used in industrial applications. In this system, the choice of additives is crucial, primarily including accelerators, suppressors, and leveling agents. Accelerators, usually sulfur-containing organic compounds, adsorb on the electrode surface, refine the copper crystal structure, and promote copper nucleation. Their primary function is to combine with chloride ions to achieve depolarization, thus increasing the cathodic current density [6–9]. The most widely studied and used accelerators include SPS and MPS [10, 11].

blocks.document_id: 5_聚_1_4_丁二醇二缩水甘油醚_2_甲基咪唑与咪唑_作为盲孔镀铜整平剂的研究
blocks.section: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: Sup pressors, such as polyether polymers (e.g., PEG and PPG) [12–14], mainly inhibit the deposition of copper during electroplating by adsorbing on the surface of the plated parts and preventing the difusion of Cu ^2 + [15–17]. In systems containing both accelerators and suppressors, the role of leveling agents is indispensable. Leveling agents typically include certain nitrogencontaining organic compounds [18, 19], such as the dye-type leveling agents JGB [20], DB [18], ABPV [21, 22], and heterocyclic non-dye leveling agents such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole [23] (AMBT) and 2-mercaptopyridine [24, 25] (2-MP). Their main func tion is to work synergistically with suppressors to inhibit copper deposition on the surface of the plated parts, optimize current density distribution, enhance filling eficiency, and thereby prevent premature hole sealing that leads to voids [25–30]. Although the most efective leveling agents are often commercial secrets, high costs and poor environmental friendliness in the market make the development of new leveling agents both time-consuming and labor-intensive.

blocks.document_id: 5_聚_1_4_丁二醇二缩水甘油醚_2_甲基咪唑与咪唑_作为盲孔镀铜整平剂的研究
blocks.section: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: The importance of leveling agents in superfilling copper electroplating has been corroborated by numerous researchers. Literatures [34, 35] frequently mention Janus Green B (JGB) as an efective leveling agent that not only enhances the fill rate of blind vias but also reduces the issue of protrusions during filling. Myung Hyun Lee and other researchers [36] synthesized a leveling agent containing two quaternary ammonium groups and hexaglycerol, which successfully achieved seamless and void-free filling of blind vias. Xu and colleagues [29] designed and synthesized quaternary ammonium salts of diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP) with various aryl substituents. Additionally, Kim and others [37] developed a choline-based leveling agent, 1,5-bis(2-N,N,Ntrimethylaminoethyl) pentanedioate diiodide, used as a modulator in copper electroplating solutions. Meanwhile, TCA [23] and DMP [38] have also been reported as potential leveling agents. Their synthesis processes are complex, the purification is challenging, and the raw material costs are high, all factors that are unfavorable for industrial production.

blocks.document_id: 5_聚_1_4_丁二醇二缩水甘油醚_2_甲基咪唑与咪唑_作为盲孔镀铜整平剂的研究
blocks.section: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: This study, based on a comprehensive analysis of existing literature, aims to develop a novel superfilling leveling agent. During the synthesis process, dimethylimidazole, imidazole, and 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether were selected as raw materials, and a detailed characterization of the organic structure of the resulting leveling agent was performed. By integrating quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics simulations, this research thoroughly analyzed active sites and adsorption behaviors to elucidate the interaction mechanisms between the organic molecules and the copper surface. Furthermore, the filling mechanism of the leveling agent was investigated using theoretical calculations, electrochemical measurements, and techniques such as Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS). Additionally, electroplating experiments were conducted to validate the filling eficacy of the leveling agent and confirm its suitability for specific requirements in Printed Circuit Board (PCB) applications.

blocks.text: In this study, the synthesis process for the leveling agent is as follows: Initially, 3.28 g of dimethylimidazole and 0.6 76\g of imidazole were measured and placed into a 100-ml round-botom flask, followed by the addition of an appropriate amount of water to dissolve both dimethylimidazole and imidazole. blocks.text: In this study, the blind hole test boards used were FR-4 copper-clad laminates, with dimensions of 5 × 12 cm, blind hole diameters of 140–160 μm, and hole depths of 7 0 - 8 0 ~ μ m. The thickness of the copper layer inside the holes was achieved to be 4–6 μm through chemical copper deposition and flash plating processes. The composition of the base plating solution used included CuSO _ 4 · 5 H _ 2 O at 220 g/L, H _ 2 SO _ 4 at 60 g/L, and chloride ions at 60 mg/L. Polyethylene glycol (PEG 10000) was used as a suppressor, bis-(3-sulphopropyl) disulfide (SPS) as an accelerator, and the synthesized leveling agent CDT. blocks.text: The theoretical calculations in this paper were conducted using the Gaussian 09 software package. Geometric optimization was performed utilizing Beckestyle three-parameter density functional theory (DFT) and Lee–Yang–Parr correlation functional (B3LYP). The basis set for carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen was chosen as 6-311+g(2 d, p). Water was selected as the solvent. Molecular analysis was conducted by examining the energies of the frontier molecular orbitals, including the highest occupied molecular orbital energy ( E _HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital energy ( E _LUMO). Additionally, the molecular electrostatic potential (ESP) was calculated. The energy gap ( Δ E_gap) was determined using the formula Δ E _gap = E _LUMO - E _HOMO The interaction between CDT and the Cu(111) surface at 298 K was simulated using the Forcite module within Materials Studio (from Accelrys, Inc.).

blocks.text: Quantum chemical calculations are a crucial method for revealing the correlation between molecular structure and inhibition efects [40]. To understand the inhibitory action of CDT, quantum chemical calculations were performed to obtain electronic properties and orbital information of the molecule, predicting active sites and elucidating adsorption mechanisms related to molecular structure. Using Gaussian software, quantum chemical calculations not only optimized the molecular structure of CDT but also calculated a series of properties such as the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO), the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO), the energy gap ( Δ E = E _ LUMO - E _ HOMO)., and the electrostatic potential (ESP). Figure 6a and b displays the molecular distributions of HOMO and LUMO. Calculations yielded an E _ LUMO of − 1.631 eV and an E _ HOMO of - 7.4 1 2 \ eV for CDT, closely matching the E _ HOMO of VIBDGE ( - 7.4 4 0 \ eV) and JGB ( - \ 6.9 8 1 \ eV) [41]. These results suggest that CDT is a potentially viable leveling agent, with an energy gap ΔE of 5.781 eV.

blocks.text: To further understand the role of additives in the electroplating process, molecular dynamics simulations were utilized to provide valuable insights. Using Materials Studio software, molecular dynamics simulations were conducted to explore the adsorption of leveling agent molecules on the Cu(111) crystal surface. The Cu(111) surface was selected for molecular dynamics simulation because it is the most stable, low Miller index copper surface and the most prevalent surface. blocks.text: Based on theoretical calculations, CDT is identified as a potential leveling agent. Thus, electrochemical tests were conducted to further validate its efects, starting with cyclic voltammetry to study the impact of various concentrations of CDT on copper deposition, with results shown in Fig. 9a–b. As observed from Fig. 9, the dissolution peak of copper is highest without any additives. The addition of 200 mg/L PEG and 1 mg/L SPS significantly reduces the copper dissolution peak due to the inhibitory action of PEG-Cl −. The introduction of the leveling agent CDT further decreases the copper dissolution peak, indicating that the addition of CDT enhances cathodic polarization and inhibits copper deposition. To compare the efects of diferent additives on the dissolution peaks of copper, the dissolution peaks at diferent CDT concentrations were quantitatively calculated using cyclic voltammetry, with average values from three parallel experiments presented in Table 2. It is evident that in the base plating solution without additives, the area of the copper dissolution peak is the largest, regardless of the rotation speed.

blocks.text: Linear sweep voltammetry was further employed to analyze the role of CDT within the electrolyte, as depicted in Fig. 9(c-d). The graph illustrates that the addition of additives significantly influences copper deposition. Relative to the base plating solution without additives, the inclusion of SPS and PEG in the electrolyte solution results in a negative shift of the reduction potential. Studies indicate that the inhibitory efect of PEG on copper deposition is due to the adsorption layer of PEG at the cathode interface, which impedes the reduction process of copper ions facilitated by Cl − [50, 51]. With SPS and PEG present in the electrolyte, the introduction of CDT further enhances cathodic polarization behavior. After adding the additives, the cathodic potential at 1000 rpm is more polarized than at 100 rpm, demonstrating that the additives exert a stronger inhibitory efect on copper deposition in areas of strong convection. Upon adding 1 mg/L of CDT, the initial potential of copper begins to shift negatively.

blocks.text: As the concentration of CDT increases, this negative shift in the starting potential becomes more pronounced, indicating that CDT can enhance cathodic polarization by adsorbing onto the copper surface, thus inhibiting copper deposition. This change is consistent with the trends observed in the cathodic peak areas in Fig. 9a and b. Cathodic polarization increases with CDT concentration, as higher concentrations lead to more adsorption on the cathode surface, thereby providing stronger inhibition of cathodic copper ion reduction. When the concentration of CDT reaches 5 \ mg/L, changes in the copper deposition potential become less distinct, like that seen at 6 mg/L, suggesting that saturation inhibition is essentially achieved at 5 mg/L. Thus, the optimal concentration of CDT is confirmed to be 5 mg/L, consistent with results from cyclic voltammetry.

blocks.text: Galvanostatic measurement (GM) was employed to elucidate the interactions among the inhibitor (PEG), accelerator (SPS), and leveling agent [52]. Under a fixed current density of 1.5 A / d m ^ 2,, various additives were sequentially injected, and the time–potential curves at diferent rotation speeds are shown in Fig. 10 for the base electrolyte. The potential diference Δ η (η100–η1000 rpm) at diferent rotation speeds can be used to evaluate the filling efect of the electroplating solution on micro-vias and is also an important parameter for assessing convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) behavior during electroplating [53, 54]. If Δ η > 0,, it indicates that under strong convection conditions, the plating solution efectively inhibits copper reduction, allowing for perfect filling of micro-vias; conversely, when \beginarray r Δ η ≤ 0, \endarray the rate of copper deposition at the mouth of the via exceeds that at the botom, likely leading to voids in the micro-vias and inefective filling. As observed in Fig. 10, after the addition of 200 mg/L PEG, compared to SMSE, the cathode potential drops sharply.

blocks.text: This is because in the presence of Cl −, PEG forms a complex with Cu ^ + ( PEG-Cu-Cl ^ -) [33, 51, 55] that can rapidly adsorb onto the cathode through intermolecular forces, inhibiting the reduction of copper ions [26, 56]. Before the addition of SPS, Δ η values are zero, indicating non-CDA behavior at this stage. At 1000 s, with the injection of 1 mg/L SPS, the potential of Cu deposition gradually increases, enhancing the kinetics of Cu deposition during this phase. At this time, PEG adsorbed on the WE surface is gradually replaced by SPS, and the potential at 100 rpm is slightly higher than at 1000 rpm, indicating CDA behavior during this stage. After injecting 5 mg/L CDT at 2000s, cathodic polarization is enhanced, and the deposition potential rapidly decreases. The cathodic potential difference Δ η between 100 and 1000 rpm for CDT (20 mV) is significantly greater than that reported in the literature for JGB (4.8 mV) [57], suggesting that CDT exhibits beter CDA behavior than JGB. When PEG and Cl − coexist, CDT efectively inhibits the accelerating activity of SPS in copper deposition. High-speed electrodes exhibit stronger cathodic polarization than slow-speed electrodes.

blocks.text: That i s, the higher the rotation speed, the greater the inhibitory efect of CDT on copper deposition, with the copper reduction rate at the botom of the micro-via exceeding that at the mouth. These phenomena are consistent with previous results discussed in cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry, further proving the efectiveness of CDT in filling micro-vias without gaps. CDT can be selected as the leveling agent for micro-via electroplating fill applications.

blocks.document_id: 5_聚_1_4_丁二醇二缩水甘油醚_2_甲基咪唑与咪唑_作为盲孔镀铜整平剂的研究
blocks.section: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating > 3.4 Electroplating experimental analysis
blocks.text: Based on the research and analysis presented, it can be inferred that CDT can serve as a leveling agent for micro-via filling in PCBs. To evaluate the filling efficacy of CDT as a leveling agent, electroplating experiments were conducted at various concentrations of CDT and compared with a commercial JGB formulation. Figure 11 shows the cross-sectional optical microscopy images of the micro-vias after electroplating. As depicted in Fig. 11a, without the addition of a leveling agent, a significant void is observed at the botom of the via, resulting from uneven current density due to varying convection intensities. With the injection of 1 mg/L CDT, the filling performance of the micro-vias notably improves. As illustrated in Figs. 11b–f, the optimal micro-via filling performance occurs at a CDT concentration of 5 mg/L, consistent with the previous electrochemical testing results. When the CDT concentration is increased to 6 mg/L, the filling rate decreases, and the performance deteriorates, indicating that there is a specific operational concentration range for the leveling agent. If the concentration is too low, the inhibitory efect is insuficient, leading to void formation.

blocks.document_id: 5_聚_1_4_丁二醇二缩水甘油醚_2_甲基咪唑与咪唑_作为盲孔镀铜整平剂的研究

blocks.text: Conversely, if the concen tration is too high, it disrupts the balance among the additives, resulting in poor filling performance. The JGB electroplating formula, commonly used in the industry, serves as a benchmark for comparing the filling performance of newly discovered leveling agents. Figure 11h shows the filling efect using the commercial JGB electroplating solution, which is inferior to the efect achieved with 5 mg/L CDT. The JGB formula results in some concavity and does not completely fill the blind vias, whereas CDT achieves superfilling of micro-vias, demonstrating its potential as an efective leveling agent.

blocks.document_id: 5_聚_1_4_丁二醇二缩水甘油醚_2_甲基咪唑与咪唑_作为盲孔镀铜整平剂的研究
blocks.section: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating > 3.5 Efects of CDT on deposit morphology
blocks.text: The influence of different concentrations of CDT on the surface morphology of copper is depicted in Fig. 12. In the absence of CDT in the plating solution, the copper plating surface exhibits a rough, blocky, and distinctly porous appearance. Conversely, compared to the CDT-free condition, the addition of varying concentrations of CDT to the plating solution significantly improves the surface morphology of the copper plating (Figs. 12b–h). The formation of smooth planes is due to the modification of the plating layer after adding CDT, which initiates crystal refinement. However, when the CDT concentration is increased to 5 mg/L, a proliferation of small blocky crystals appears on the copper surface, becoming denser with increasing concentrations of CDT. These results indicate that CDT demonstrates its leveling capability efectively within a certain concentration range, but as the concentration of the leveling agent increases, the synergistic interactions among the additives are disrupted. Similar results have been reported in copper electrodepositing studies [18, 21].

blocks.text: While molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and XPS ofer diferent perspectives—thermodynamic interaction versus chemical bonding—they provide complementary evidence supporting the strong adsorption of CDT on the copper surface. Figure 13a displays the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) full spectrum of a copper sample after soaking for 40 min in an electroplating solution containing CDT. This full spectrum, obtained through detailed scanning, reveals the presence of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, and copper on the copper surface, confirming the adsorption of CDT. Detailed spectra for Cu2p3/2, C1s, and N1s can be found in Figs. 13b–d. In Fig. 13b, the chemi cal states on the copper surface are shown by the peaks of Cu2p3/2 and Cu2p1/2, located at binding energies of 931.8 and 951.6 eV, respectively. The Cu2p3/2 peak in Fig. 13b can be further divided into subpeaks for Cu 2 O (931.8 eV) and CuO (933.7 eV) [58], indicating the formation of a copper oxide layer on the copper surface due to oxidation in air and reaction with water molecules in the solution, predominantly in the form of Cu O [59].

blocks.text: Figure 13c focuses on the N1s spectrum, displaying two peaks at 397.8 eV (C–N or C=N) and 399.2 eV (Cu–N), which deviate slightly from the nitrogen binding energies reported in previous literature, suggesting the possible formation of structures such as Cu–N–C or Cu–N=C on the CDT-modified copper surface [60–62]. The C1s spectrum (seen in Fig. 13d) reveals six diferent peaks corresponding to 283.66 eV (C=C), 284.03 eV (C–C), 284.42 eV (C–H), 284.92 eV (C–N), 285.9 eV (C–O), and 287.63 eV (C=O) [63–65]. The presence of these peaks indicates a rich variety of carbon environments within the CDT molecule, such as double bonds between carbons, single bonds, combinations of carbon with hydrogen, and carbon with nitrogen, providing crucial clues for understanding how CDT achieves adsorption on the copper surface.

blocks.section: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating > 4 Conclusions
blocks.text: In summary, we have selected the nitrogen-heterocyclic compound CDT as an electroplating leveling agent for copper micro-via filling. The synthesis of CDT was successfully confirmed by infrared, hydrogen nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and gel permeation chromatography results. Quantum chemical simulations suggest that CDT possesses the potential to occupy metal vacant orbitals for adsorption. Moreover, molecular dynamics simulations indicate that CDT exhibits strong affinity for copper surfaces. Electrochemical tests revealed that the optimal working concentration of CDT is 5 mg/L. Chronopotentiometric measurements further demonstrated that CDT can synergistically suppress copper deposition when combined with other additives, exhibiting a potential diference as high as 20 mV, which indicates its strong inhibitory efect on copper electrodeposition. Electroplating tests show that the best plating results occur at a concentration of 5 mg/L, consistent with electrochemical findings.

blocks.document_id: 5_聚_1_4_丁二醇二缩水甘油醚_2_甲基咪唑与咪唑_作为盲孔镀铜整平剂的研究
blocks.section: Exploration of poly(1,4‑butanediol diglycidyl ether, 2‑methylimidazole, and imidazole) as leveling agents in blind hole copper plating > 4 Conclusions
blocks.text: Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) results showed that CDT can refine copper grain structures within an appropriate concentration range; however, when the concentration exceeds the optimal level, crystal agglomeration reoccurs. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed the efective adsorption of CDT on the copper surface, and the strong interaction between them provides a foundation for the suppression of copper deposition. Collectively, our research conclusively proves that CDT is a promising leveling agent for copper micro-via filling, providing theoretical guidance for the discovery and improvement of electroplating technologies for micro-via filling.

blocks.section: Synthesis of coumarin derivatives as levelers for Through-Hole electroplating of copper in PCBs and a study on leveling mechanism of optimized leveler
blocks.text: Jingyu Xie 1, Xinpeng Yin 1, Fengyan Lu, Xuyang Li, Limin Wang Shanghai Key Laboratory for Functional Materials Chemistry and Institute of Fine Chemicals, School of Chemistry and Molecular Engineering, East China University of Science and Technology, 130 Meilong Road, Shanghai 200237, PR China

blocks.section: Synthesis of coumarin derivatives as levelers for Through-Hole electroplating of copper in PCBs and a study on leveling mechanism of optimized leveler > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: In this paper, five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts, including a new highly efficient through-hole (TH) electroplating leveler, were synthesized from environmentally harmless coumarin compounds. The inhib itory properties of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts were tested by electrochemical method, leading to the selection of the optimal leveler (C2). The adsorption capacity, adsorption state and adsorption sites of different coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts on copper surface were systematically analyzed, and the reasons for the different inhibition capacity of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts with different molecular structures were explained. The effect of C2 content on throwing power (TP) was studied, when C2 content was only 0.6 ppm, TP value was greater than 100 %. The adsorption behavior of C2 on copper cathode and the interaction between C2 and other additives were studied by the galvanostatic measurements (GMs). SEM and XRD tests were conducted to analyze the effects of different amounts of C2 on the copper plating surface.

blocks.section: Synthesis of coumarin derivatives as levelers for Through-Hole electroplating of copper in PCBs and a study on leveling mechanism of optimized leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: With the continuous improvement of the modern electronic indus try’s requirements for electronic components, the demand for electronic components such as electronic chips that achieve miniaturization and high efficiency has also increased. The realization of high-density interconnection between printed circuit boards (PCBs) through micropore connection is an important means to realize the miniaturization of electronic products, so as to obtain more excellent electrical conductivity and space performance [1–3]. Acid copper electroplating is a key technology for copper interconnects in through-holes (THs), and it is also an indispensable technology in the manufacturing process of PCB. In order to obtain a flat and smooth plating layer and efficient TH filling, electroplating additives need to be added to the electroplating solution [4,5].

blocks.document_id: 6_香豆素衍生物的合成及其作为印刷电路板通孔电镀铜整平剂的应用与优化整平剂整平机理研究
blocks.section: Synthesis of coumarin derivatives as levelers for Through-Hole electroplating of copper in PCBs and a study on leveling mechanism of optimized leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Electroplating additives are generally divided into inhibitors (generally polyethylene glycol and other polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol, polypropylene glycol [6,7]), accelerators (generally containing S–H bonds or S–S sulfonate compounds, such as sodium 3,3′-dithiodipropane sulfonate, bis-(sodium sulfoethyl)-disulfide [8,9]) and levelers (generally N-containing compounds, such as Janus Green B, diketopyrrolopyrrole [10–16]).

blocks.document_id: 6_香豆素衍生物的合成及其作为印刷电路板通孔电镀铜整平剂的应用与优化整平剂整平机理研究
blocks.section: Synthesis of coumarin derivatives as levelers for Through-Hole electroplating of copper in PCBs and a study on leveling mechanism of optimized leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In the process of copper plating, through the interaction of different plating additives, the microhole can be overfilled. In the current research on electroplating additives, electroplating levelers have attracted much attention due to their irreplaceable properties. The leveler is mainly adsorbed on the surface of TH and inhibits the deposition of copper ions on the surface of TH, but has less inhibition on the deposition of copper ions inside TH, so as to achieve the effect of conductive copper interconnection or bottom-up copper electroplating [17–19]. The current research on levelers mainly includes the research of new leveler molecules (small molecule compounds [20–22], quaternary ammonium compounds [23–26] and macromolecular polymers [27,28]), interaction of different electroplating additives [29] and the effect of leveler concentration on filling efficiency and copper electroplating surface morphology [30]. Among them, quaternary ammonium salts have received more attention as leveler due to their superior leveling performance.

blocks.document_id: 6_香豆素衍生物的合成及其作为印刷电路板通孔电镀铜整平剂的应用与优化整平剂整平机理研究
blocks.section: Synthesis of coumarin derivatives as levelers for Through-Hole electroplating of copper in PCBs and a study on leveling mechanism of optimized leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: For example, Myung JunKim [31] synthesized choline-based quaternary ammonium salt levelers and used them in TSV (Through Silicon Via) electrodeposition copper, Jinge Lv [32] designed and synthesized three water-soluble naphthalimide derivatives (NPI) and used them as levelers for microporous electrodeposition. Van Quy Dinh [33] used sulfonated diallyl dimethyl ammonium bromide copol ymer to fill the TSV bottom-up electrodeposition for 5 min to achieve no gaps. These studies have shown that quaternary ammonium compounds have good application prospects in the field of electroplating levelers, but it is still a difficult task to develop electroplating levelers with small additive amount, good leveling effect and environmental friendliness.

blocks.section: Synthesis of coumarin derivatives as levelers for Through-Hole electroplating of copper in PCBs and a study on leveling mechanism of optimized leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In our previous work, we found that the large plane quaternary ammonium salt leveler has more efficient leveling performance than the general quaternary ammonium salts, when the concentration is 0.2 ppm (0.278 μmol/L), a very efficient leveling effect can be achieved [34]. Combining the previous work, and the working principle of the leveler −- the leveler molecules are adsorbed on the copper surface during the electrodeposition process to inhibit the electrodeposition of copper ions [14,34,35], we speculate that ^4, 4-bipyridine can be used to connect rigid planar molecules to synthesize larger coplanar quaternary ammonium salts. If such large flat molecules can be adsorbed on copper surfaces, they have the potential to be effective levelers [15,34]. As a common natural product, coumarins (Fig. 1) are planar compounds with two conjugated six-membered rings, and its ^7 position is relatively electron-rich, indicating that its ^7 position is prone to electrophilic substitution reaction. When a hydroxyl group is present, it is easy to undergo substitution reaction with dibromoalkane, thereby further reacting with ^4, 4-bipyridine to obtain a coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salt.

blocks.document_id: 6_香豆素衍生物的合成及其作为印刷电路板通孔电镀铜整平剂的应用与优化整平剂整平机理研究
blocks.section: Synthesis of coumarin derivatives as levelers for Through-Hole electroplating of copper in PCBs and a study on leveling mechanism of optimized leveler > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Herein, five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts were synthesized by connecting coumarin-based compounds with pyridine-like compounds, including the first synthesis of large plane dicoumarinbased pyridinium quaternary ammonium salt C2 through a four-step reaction. The results of cyclic voltammetry (CV) test and polarization curve test show that C2 can be used as the preferred leveler. The band gap and electron cloud density distribution of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts were obtained by quantum chemistry calculation and molecular dynamics simulation, in order to study the relationship between the molecular structure and inhibitory ability of these levelers. The experimental results of TH copper plating show that in a certain range, the content of C2 has a positive correlation with the TP value of TH electroplating, and can make the surface morphology of copper plating layer more smooth, and optimize the orientation of the crystal surface of copper particles. GMs results show that C2 can exert inhibition alone and has strong convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) behavior.

blocks.text: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were implemented to calculate the adsorption capacity and the adsorption state of compounds A1 − C2 on copper from a theoretical level. In this section, the energy band gap, electron density distribution and adsorption state on copper surface of quaternary ammo nium cations of five coumarin quaternary ammonium salts A1~-~C2 were analyzed by quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics simulations, so as to analyze the reasons for the different inhibitory abilities of five coumarin quaternary ammonium salts.

blocks.text: Fig. 6 shows the optimization results of the geometric structure and electron cloud density of A1-C 2,. The highest occupied molecular orbitals (HOMO) of A1 -C2 are mainly located in the coumarin region, which means that in the molecular structure of A1-C 2,, the coumarin region is more likely than other regions to give electrons to metal ions, thus forming ligand [13]. The lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMO) of A1-C2 are mainly distributed in the pyridine/bipyridine region, which means that compared with other regions, the pyridine/ bipyridine region is more likely to obtain electrons from the copperplated cathode, thus adsorbing on the surface of the copper-plated cathode. Compared with the other four levelers, LUMO of C2 was distributed in more areas, and LUMO was also distributed in the coumarin region connected with alkoxy in C2 molecule, which repre sented more adsorption sites on C2 molecular structure.

blocks.text: As shown in Fig. 13(a), firstly, the VMS was run in constant current conditions for 1000 s, the potential difference was about 0, indicating that the VMS does not have overfill capacity. The potential decreased rapidly with the addition of PEG, representing the rapid adsorption of PEG, while the potential started to rise slowly with the addition of SPS at 2000 s, indicating that the adsorption of SPS is a slow process and its action rate controlled by its rate of adsorption [42]. At 3000 s, the decrease of potential indicates that the depolarization of SPS is inhibited and there is a competitive adsorption relationship between C2 and SPS. At high speed, the potential immediately decreases, indicating that SPS is rapidly replaced by C2 under strong convection. Δη 1 was greater than 0, indicating that the addition of C2 can improve the filling capacity of electroplating solution, which is consistent with the result of throughhole electroplating.

blocks.section: Synthesis of coumarin derivatives as levelers for Through-Hole electroplating of copper in PCBs and a study on leveling mechanism of optimized leveler > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: In summary, this study synthesized five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts and, for the first time, investigated their application as novel electroplating levelers in acid copper plating. Electrochemical measurements were used to analyze the copper plating inhibition ability of five coumarin-based quaternary ammonium salts, leveler C2 with double coumarin structure had the strongest inhibition performance. Quantum chemical calculation and MD simulation show that leveler C2 has the strongest adsorption capacity and the most adsorption sites on copper surface, which is the reason why C2 has the strongest inhibition ability. TH copper plating results show that the leveler C2 has good leveling performance, only need 0.6 ppm addition, can get 103.36 % through-hole TP value. The interaction between C2 and other additives and the mechanism of action were further explored by GMs test. The results of SEM and XRD show that the leveler C2 can make the surface of the copper plating layer smoother and optimize the orientation of the copper crystallographic plane.

blocks.document_id: 7_micromachines_16_00721
blocks.section: Integrated Electrochemical and Computational Elucidation of Nitro Blue Tetrazolium Chloride as an Efficient Leveler for Copper Microvia Superfilling
blocks.text: Abstract: Levelers are indispensable additives for achieving void-free, bottom-up superconformal copper filling of microvias. Establishing the molecular-level correlation between leveler structure and performance is therefore essential to the continued advancement of microelectronic copper-plating technology. Herein, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT) is identified as an efficient leveler for copper microvia superfilling. A multiscale strategy—combining electrochemical measurements, X-ray photoelectron spec troscopy (XPS), density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations—is employed to elucidate the action mechanism of NBT and pinpoint its electroactive sites. Electrochemical tests show that NBT markedly suppresses copper deposition and, together with polyethylene glycol (PEG), effectively resists competitive ad sorption by bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS), thereby enhancing the microvia superfilling performance of the PEG–SPS–NBT additive system.

blocks.document_id: 7_micromachines_16_00721
blocks.section: Integrated Electrochemical and Computational Elucidation of Nitro Blue Tetrazolium Chloride as an Efficient Leveler for Copper Microvia Superfilling
blocks.text: DFT results reveal that the nitro groups and tetrazolium rings constitute the primary adsorption centers on the copper surface; the nitro groups additionally strengthen intermolecular interactions between NBT and PEG. MD simulations further confirm that NBT anchors onto the Cu(111) surface predominantly through these Ν \cal O_2 groups and the tetrazolium ring, while co-adsorbed PEG enhances the overall adsorption strength of NBT. The electroplating experiment demonstrates that NBT can act as an effective leveler for microvia superfilling. Moreover, XPS analyses further confirm the synergistic co-adsorption of NBT and PEG and verify that the Ν \cal O_2 groups and tetrazolium rings are the dominant adsorption sites of NBT. Collectively, the electroplating, XPS, electrochemical, DFT, and MD findings clarify the structure–activity relationship of NBT and provide rational guidelines for designing next-generation copper-plating levelers.

blocks.text: Electrochemical copper deposition offers distinct advantages for constructing microand nano-scale features and is therefore indispensable in manufacturing advanced interconnects such as integrated circuits (ICs) [1,2]. For high-aspect-ratio structures—including Damascene trenches in ICs and microvias in substrates and printed-circuit boards (PCBs)— voids generated during plating remain a persistent threat to electrical performance and reliability [3,4]. Eliminating these defects has therefore become a primary objective in microvia electroplating [5,6].

blocks.document_id: 7_micromachines_16_00721
blocks.section: Integrated Electrochemical and Computational Elucidation of Nitro Blue Tetrazolium Chloride as an Efficient Leveler for Copper Microvia Superfilling > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Industrial practice predominantly relies on organic additive systems to locally regulate the deposition rate for achieving superfilling of microvias. In two-component systems the competitive adsorption of a suppressor and an accelerator is often sufficient for sub-100 nm Damascene features [7–9]; larger microvias, however, require a third component—a leveler— to suppress copper deposition at high-current-density sites (feature mouths and protrusions), thereby ensuring void-free bottom-up growth and surface planarization [10–12]. Among the numerous levelers reported, Janus Green B (JGB) is the most classic, as it can achieve not only superfilling in microvias [13] but also high throwing power (TP) electroplated in through-holes [14]. Additionally, previous studies have demonstrated that the azo group and the positively charged quaternary-ammonium group are the primary active functional groups in JGB [13,15].

blocks.document_id: 7_micromachines_16_00721
blocks.section: Integrated Electrochemical and Computational Elucidation of Nitro Blue Tetrazolium Chloride as an Efficient Leveler for Copper Microvia Superfilling > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Building on this insight, numerous researchers have designed levelers that incorporate either the azo or quaternary-ammonium group. Wang et al. employed gentian violet, which contains a positively charged quaternary-ammonium group, as a leveler for through-hole electrodeposition and demonstrated that this leveler exhibited plating performance as excellent as that of JGB [16]. However, other researchers introduced quaternary-ammonium groups with varying chain lengths onto the quinacridone skeleton to develop a novel leveler [17], and the novel leveler exhibited superior plating performance compared to JGB. Additionally, they also grafted quaternary-ammonium chains onto the Sudan I scaffold, reinforcing electrostatic adsorption while preserving the azo-naphthalene π–π interactions, thereby further enhancing plating performance [18]. Another group employed quaternary-ammonium salts of varying alkyl-chain lengths as plating levelers and further observed that these levelers delivered suppression performance superior to that of polyethylene glycol (PEG) [19].

blocks.text: However, growing evidence indicates that, beyond the classic active groups— positively charged quaternary-ammonium and azo groups—auxiliary modification groups such as electronegative substituents or heteroaromatic rings can markedly reinforce leveler adsorption [20], alter the diffusion ability of molecules [21,22], and enhance synergism with other additives [23]. Dow et al. compared JGB with its derivative Diamond Black (DB), revealing significant electrochemical differences despite the two molecules differing by only a single peripheral functional substituent [24]. Similarly, Wang et al. observed that Safranine T (ST), which lacks several peripheral functional substituents present in JGB, exhibited significantly reduced through-hole throwing power compared to JGB [25], whereas Zhu et al. restored microvia superfilling by introducing hydroxyl (-OH) groups into ST [20]. Therefore, using density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to unravel how individual functional groups dictate adsorption energetics and electron distribution is very necessary.

blocks.text: As is well known, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT), a commercially available tetrazolium dye, has demonstrated excellent performance as a leveler in through-hole copper filling [28–30]. In contrast, blind microvias present a far more challenging environment: with only one opening, electrolyte circulation is severely restricted, the diffusion layer thickens, and a pronounced ohmic and activation overpotential gradient develops. These factors make void-free filling in blind microvias significantly more difficult than in through-holes. To date, however, the suitability of NBT for blind-microvia superfilling has not been reported, nor has its structure–performance relationship been elucidated—an omission that limits the molecular-level insight into tetrazolium-based levelers and the rational design of cost-effective additives. Accordingly, NBT was chosen as the leveler in this study to assess its effectiveness in copper superfilling of microvias, of which the molecular structure is shown in Figure 1.

blocks.text: Electrochemical measurements were carried out to investigate the effect of NBT on cathodic polarization, as shown in Figure 2. From the GM curves at 1000 rpm, it can be seen that injecting just 10 ppm NBT immediately shifts the electrode potential negatively by approximately 160 mV, demonstrating that NBT strongly inhibits Cu ^2 + reduction (Figure 2a). With further increases in NBT concentration, the cathodic potential shift becomes more pronounced, indicating that NBT’s inhibition strength is concentration-dependent. Moreover, pronounced electrode-potential oscillations occur at 100 rpm but are largely attenuated at 1000 rpm, indicating that adsorbed NBT forms labile complexes with Cu ^+ / Cu ^2 + whose stability is governed by Cu ^2 + mass transport rather than by NBT diffusion. As shown in

blocks.document_id: 7_micromachines_16_00721

blocks.text: Figure 2 b, c, this mass-transport sensitivity appears only at lower NBT concentrations; at higher concentrations, adsorption saturates and becomes insensitive to convection. Therefore, the observed instability of the NBT–Cu complex originates from diffusion-limited Cu ^2 + depletion. Specifically, a dense NBT adlayer rapidly complexes Cu ^+ / Cu ^2 + at the cathode surface, depleting the local Cu ^2 + concentration; under weak convection, insufficient replenishment forces the electrode to shift to more negative potentials to maintain the set current density. Once the overpotential reaches the threshold for NBT-Cu^+ complex breakdown, the suppressor film collapses, releasing Cu ^2 + and causing a sudden depolar ization. As the potential drifts positive beyond the collapse window, the NBT–Cu complex re-forms, re-establishing the suppressor layer and driving the potential back negative— thus generating large-amplitude, periodic oscillations. In contrast, vigorous stirring at 1000 rpm continuously supplies Cu ^2 +, prevents local depletion and complex collapse, and thereby damps these oscillations.

The addition of 10 ppm NBT shifts the onset to −0.68 V, with further negative shifts at higher NBT concentrations. On the reverse scan, a pronounced hysteresis loop appears; we define its width Δ E _ hys = E _ break - E _ l recover, where E_break is the forward-scan potential at - 2 5 mA/cm2 onset and E_recover is the reversescan potential at the same current. blocks.text: The CV profiles further validate the strong synergistic suppression by PEG and NBT (Figure 3b). Compared with the PEG-only baseline, the onset of copper deposition shifts progressively negative as NBT concentration increases, confirming enhanced inhibition. blocks.text: Quantum-chemical calculations are a powerful means of elucidating reaction mechanisms and predicting chemical reactivity. Accordingly, DFT computations were performed to analyze the electronic properties and active sites of NBT. For the frontier molecular orbitals (FMOs), the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) identifies the sites most prone to donate electrons, whereas the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) pinpoints the sites most susceptible to accept electrons. As shown in Figure 5, the HOMO of NBT is mainly localized on the two central phenyl rings (Ph1/Ph1 ′) and their adjacent methoxy groups (MeO/ MeO ′), indicating that these π-rich regions are the preferred electrophilic-reaction sites when NBT interacts with other species. Because the HOMO energy (−7.15 eV) is close to the Fermi level of copper (−4.5~−5 eV) [41], these sites can readily donate electron density to surface Cu orbitals, forming σ- or π-type adsorption bonds that anchor the molecule to the surface. In contrast, the LUMO is concen trated on the two tetrazolium rings (Tz/Tz ′) and the nitro-substituted phenyl rings (Ph1- Nitro/Ph1 ′ -Nitro ′).

The dual nitro groups thus endow NBT with a strong affinity for copper. NBT displays a relatively narrow HOMO–LUMO gap ( Δ E _g = E _LUMO - E _HOMO = 3.5 3 : eV)). Such a small gap promotes frontier-orbital overlap, facilitating charge transfer between NBT and the copper surface and, consequently, establishing a robust adsorption strength that underpins its leveling performance [43].

blocks.text: The average local ionization energy (ALIE) quantifies the local propensity for electron removal within a molecule. The lowest ALIE values (≈219 kcal mol ^- 1) occur on themethoxy-substituted phenyl rings (Ph3-Meo, Ph3 ′ -Meo ′) and the adjacent phenyl rings (Ph2, Ph2 ′) (Figure 6c), indicating that these sites are most susceptible to electrophilic attack and can donate electron density to positive species at the cathode, strengthening chemisorp tion [44,45]. In contrast, the local electron-attachment energy (LEAE) quantifies the ability to accept electrons; smaller values mean stronger nucleophilicity [46]. The minimum LEAE (−46.32 kcal mol −1) is found on the tetrazolium rings and the neighboring nitro-substituted phenyl rings (Figure 6d). This confirms that the nitro groups greatly enhance the nu cleophilic reactivity of NBT, enabling efficient electron uptake from Cu 3d orbitals and the formation of robust back-donation π bonds. Such strong adsorption—especially at high-field sites such as microvia mouths—rationalizes the superior leveling performance of NBT. Moreover, this conclusion is fundamentally consistent with the findings derived from FMO.

blocks.text: To fully predict a leveler’s performance, one must assess not only its electronic active sites but also its interactions with other species and their corresponding adsorption sites. Accordingly, DFT calculations were carried out to investigate NBT’s interactions with Cu ^ 2 + ions and with the suppressor PEG. Atom in Molecules (AIM) and interaction region indicator (IRI) calculations were carried out for the NBT - Cu ^ 2 + complex, while the NBT–PEG interaction was analyzed with the independent-gradient model based on Hirshfeld parti tion (IGMH), as shown in Figure 7. As shown in Figure ^ 7 a, the shortest contact between Cu ^ 2 + and NBT is the Cu–N bond to the tetrazolium nitrogen (1.994 Å). The Cu–O distance to the methoxy group is longer (2.177 A), indicating that the Cu–N interaction is stronger than the Cu–O one. To evaluate the bond nature, we calculated the bond-critical-point (BCP) parameters (Table 1). For both Cu–N and Cu–O bonds, the electron density at the BCP (ρ) is below 0.10 a.u. and the Laplacian of electron density ( ∇ ^ 2 ρ _ BCP) value is positive, showing that the two bonds for Cu–N and Cu–O are ionic bonds [47,48].

blocks.text: However, only the Cu–N bond has negative energy density ( H _ BCP) and negative potential energy density (Vr), which confirms that the Cu–N bond is the stronger bond [49]. IRI analysis (Figure 7b) reveals blue isosurfaces between Cu ^ 2 + and the tetrazolium nitrogen, as well as between Cu ^ 2 + and the methoxy oxygen, indicating strong Cu–N and Cu–O interactions. The two-dimensional IRI map (Figure 7c) further supports these observations, confirming robust coordination between NBT and Cu ^ 2 + ions. These findings indicate that NBT coordi nates predominantly with Cu ^ 2 + via the nitrogen atom of the tetrazolium ring, forming a strong ionic bond that retards Cu ^ 2 + reduction. This selective coordination promotes NBT adsorption at Cu-rich sites—such as microvia mouths or cathode protrusions—thereby efficiently inhibiting local deposition.

These assign ments indicate that both PEG and the aromatic/ether fragments of NBT are present on the surface. The N 1s signal (Figure 12c) is resolved into six peaks at 399.6 eV (C–N/C=N of NBT) [28,52,55], 400.2 eV (Cu–N, evidence of NBT binding through nitrogen) [28,57], 401.7 eV (N–N/N=N in tetrazolium) [52,55], 402.4 eV (protonated amine or quaternary nitrogen generated after interaction with Cu) [17,55], 404.1 eV (positively charged tetra zolium N +) [52], and 406.3 eV (nitro-group nitrogen) [52,58]. These results indicate that the tetrazolium ring and nitro groups in NBT can accept electrons from the Cu 3d orbitals and form stable coordination/back-donation π interactions with the surface. These moieties therefore act as the primary adsorption sites of NBT on copper, fully consistent with the DFT predictions.

blocks.section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia
blocks.text: Zewei Lin 1,2 · Zhihua Tao 1 · Yuxuan Huang 1 · Jihua Zhang 2,3 Accepted: 5 May 2025 / Published online: 17 May 2025 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025

blocks.section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Abstract
blocks.text: Tween (TW) compounds, on account of their environmentally benign and non-toxic characteristics, were systematically studied as prospective eco-friendly suppressants in the process of copper plating for blind hole filling. The synergistic efects between TW and other additives were verified by means of chronopotentiometry, cyclic voltammetry, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. The outcomes of the electrochemical tests revealed that the competitive adsorption behavior between bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) and TW is contingent upon the current density and the intensity of convection. Metallographic section analysis demonstrated that TW exhibits outstanding microvia filling capabilities for micro blind vias with a diameter of 150 µm and a depth of 80 µm. Notably, TW-80 was able to attain a filling rate of 96.15% following electrodeposition for 60 min at a current density of 2 A/dm2. Quantum chemical calculations suggested that the relatively smaller band gap and the clustered molecular structure of TW-80 are more conducive to its adsorption onto the electrode surface, leading to the formation of a barrier layer, which in turn restrains the deposition of copper.

blocks.section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Introduction
blocks.text: In the realm of microelectronics manufacturing, acid copper electroplating for microvia filling has emerged as a pivotal process, ensuring reliable electrical interconnections within printed circuit boards (PCBs) and advanced packaging substrates [1–4]. The quality of via filling, characterized by void—free and uniform deposition, directly impacts the performance, reliability, and miniaturization potential of electronic devices [5–7]. To achieve this, a complex mixture of additives, including suppressors, accelerators, and levelers, is incorporated into the electroplating bath [8–11]. Among these, suppressors play a crucial role in controlling the deposition rate at diferent surface sites, preventing over—plating at the via openings and promoting bottom—up filling.

blocks.section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Introduction
blocks.text: The additives utilized in the acidic sulfate copper plating process primarily consist of chloride ions (Cl-) [12], accelerators, suppressors and levelers. These additives interact with one another to enhance the performance of resulting formed copper plating layer [13, 14, 5, 15–17]. Previous research on suppressors for acid copper electroplating has predominantly focused on polymers and surfactants with diverse molecular structures. For instance, polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based polymers have been widely studied and utilized as suppressors due to their ability to adsorb on the copper surface and inhibit the deposition reaction [18, 19]. However, their high molecular weight and complex synthesis processes often lead to issues such as poor bath stability and dificulty in waste treatment, raising environmental concerns. Polyetheramine (PEP) has also been investigated as a potential suppressor, leveraging its unique amine-containing structure that allows for specific interactions with the copper surface [17, 20]. While PEP shows promise in adjusting the deposition rate, its relatively high cost and limited biodegradability pose challenges for large—scale industrial application.

blocks.section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Introduction
blocks.text: Additionally, ethylene—propylene copolymer (EPE) has been explored, as its alternating structure can provide a balance between hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties, influencing the deposition behavior [21, 22]. Nevertheless, EPE may sufer from inconsistent performance under varying electroplating conditions, and its efect on the quality of microvia filling in high—aspect—ratio scenarios remains suboptimal. Moreover, some non—ionic surfactants like Triton X—series have been investigated, but they may exhibit limited eficiency in microvia filling under high— aspect—ratio conditions and can also pose potential toxicity risks.

blocks.section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Introduction
blocks.text: Tween compounds, a class of non—ionic surfactants derived from sorbitan esters and ethylene oxide, have found extensive applications across multiple industries. In the pharmaceutical industry, Tween compounds are commonly used as solubilizers and emulsifiers in drug formulations. They enhance the solubility of poorly water—soluble drugs, improving drug delivery and bioavailability. For example, in the formulation of oral suspensions and injectable emulsions, Tween 80 efectively stabilizes the dispersed phases, ensuring uniform drug distribution [23]. In the food industry, Tween compounds serve as emulsifiers, preventing the separation of oil and water phases in products such as margarine, salad dressings, and ice creams. They also contribute to the texture and shelf—life of food products [24]. In the cosmetics industry, Tween compounds are utilized in creams, lotions, and shampoos for their excellent wetting and emulsifying properties, facilitating the dispersion of ingredients and enhancing product stability [25].

blocks.section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Introduction
blocks.text: Moreover, in the field of biotechnology, Tween compounds are employed in cell culture media to reduce surface tension, promote cell adhesion, and prevent cell aggregation [26].

blocks.section: Tween Compounds as Eco‑Friendly Suppressors for Acid Copper Electroplating Applications of Microvia > Introduction
blocks.text: Against this backdrop, considering their excellent emulsifying, dispersing, and wetting properties, as well as their relatively low toxicity and good biodegradability, Tween compounds present a compelling option for electroplating applications. However, their application as suppressors in acid copper electroplating for microvia filling has remained largely unexplored. This study aims to investigate the inhibitory efects of TW-20 and TW-80 (as shown in Fig. 1) and their synergistic efects with other additives through electrochemical methods, optical microscopy, and quantum chemical calculations. By doing so, it systematically evaluates Tween compounds as eco-friendly suppressors for acid copper electroplating in microvia applications, filling this research gap. The findings of this research are expected to contribute to the development of more environmentally friendly and eficient electroplating processes, meeting the growing demands of the microelectronics industry for sustainable manufacturing.

blocks.text: The electrochemical measurements were performed with a CHI760E (ChenHua) electrochemical workstation, which was furnished with the conventional three electrodes and a 100 mL three-electrode cell capable of accommodating an virgin makeup solution (VMS) of 220 g/L CuSO4·5H2O and 28.33 mL/L H2SO4. A platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE) with a diameter of 5 mm was employed as the working electrode, while a copper strip with a diameter of 4 mm served as the counter electrode. The experiment utilized a mercurous sulfate electrode (SMSE) as the reference electrode. To evaluate the electroplating efects of the additives, the deposition potential at various rotating disk speeds was measured using chronopotentiometry. A pre-plating step was performed to deposit a 500 nm layer of copper on the platinum spinning disk electrode prior to conducting the chronopotentiometry test. The temperature of the electrolyte was maintained at a constant value of 293 ±1K throughout the duration of the experiment. Chronopotentiometry were conducted using diferent current density at 100 rpm and 1000 rpm respectively. The potential diference measured by the chronopotentiometry was defined as Eq. (1).

blocks.text: The PCB test panels had a thickness of 1 mm, with a via diameter ranging from 120 to 150 µm and a via depth of 75 µm. Electroplating processes were conducted in a haring cell with a capacity of 1.5 L and the electroplating solution maintained a flow rate of 2.0 L per minute. The area of the cathode test plate immersed in the electroplating solution measures 50 mm × 60 mm, while the total area of the test plate is approximately 80 mm × 60 mm. In order to enhance the electrical conductivity between the copper plating and the Cu seed layer, the test boards underwent a series of decontamination processes before plating. The specific operational procedure is as follows: acid cleaning agent followed by deionized water rinse, micro-etching, another deionized water rinse, acid dipping, and finally copper electroplating in an acid bath. The electroplating test was conducted at ambient temperature with the current density maintained at 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0 A/dm2 for various plating durations. Continuous agitation was achieved by stirring the solution with flowing air bubbles to ensure thorough mixing of the plating solution and facilitate efective mass transfer in the plating cell.

blocks.text: The molecular structures of TW-20 and TW-80 were optimized using the B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) method with Gaussian09 W software. The optimization of Tween's molecular structure was conducted based on frontier molecular orbital theory, focusing on the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) and the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) [29]. The forcite module and VMD software were respectively adopted to investigate the interaction between copper surface and Tween and visualize the optimized geometry and molecular orbitals [30]. Tween molecular dynamics properties in the aqueous phase such as radius of gyration, radial distribution function and diffusion coeficient were investigated by the Material Studio software at the temperature of 298 K. The COMPASSII force field was utilized to optimize the size and simulate the adsorption process of Tween.

blocks.text: Following the determination of the inhibitory strengths of the two inhibitors, this study utilized the chronopotentiometry to predict the hole-filling capacity of the plating solution consisting of 60 mg/L Cl-, 6 mg/L accelerator, 4 mg/L HPTT and separate batches of 200 mg/L TW-20 or TW-80. The test results are shown in Fig. 4. The analysis of the test results indicated that the plating solutions containing distinct inhibitors all adhered to the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of additives [32], as evidenced by a notable negative shift in the stable potential measured at high rotation speeds. In other words, the inhibitors exhibit a stronger inhibitory efect under conditions of strong convection, thereby complicating the process of copper deposition. Furthermore, it can be inferred from Fig. 4 that the overpotential for copper deposition with TW-80 is higher than that with TW-20, which remains unafected by the intensity of convection. After comparing the potential diference Δη calculated for the two inhibitors at diferent rotation speeds, it becomes apparent that Δη for TW-80 consistently exceeds that for TW-20 at equivalent concentrations.

After the metallographic sample was filled with resin, it was polished and subsequently examined and analyzed using a metallographic microscope. Cross-sectional images were obtained to demonstrate the filled blind holes under diferent inhibitors. Figure 5(a-f) show that an increase in current density led to a gradual decrease in the surface copper thickness for both sets of metallographic samples, while the filling rate gradually improved. This phenomenon can be attributed to the higher likelihood of the accelerator replacing the inhibitor at lower current densities, which prolongs the time required for each additive to reach adsorption equilibrium. blocks.text: To further clarify the interaction of these additives, the synergistic efects of TW with other additives were further investigated through chronopotentiometry, as shown in Fig. 6(a-f). The analysis will be based on TW-80 since the structural similarity between TW-20 and TW-80. As illustrated in Fig. 6(b), the leveling agent HPTT does not influence copper deposition under either strong or weak convection intensities. Following the addition of TW, a slight negative shift in the deposition potential is observed. The subsequent introduction of SPS leads to a positive shift in the deposition potential. Finally, the addition of Cl- results in a rapid negative shift in the copper deposition overpotential and an increase in Δη to 20 mV, indicating the occurrence of convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) behavior.

blocks.text: Comparing the time intervals of 500–1000 s in Fig. 6(b) with the 1000–1500 s interval in Fig. 6(d) reveals that the simultaneous presence of HPTT and Cl- can accelerate the reduction of copper ions, whereas no such efect is observed when HPTT is present alone. Furthermore, a comparison between the intervals of 500–1500 s in Fig. 6(b) and 500–1000 s in Fig. 6(f) indicates that when only HPTT and TW are present in the VMS, HPTT diminishes the inhibitory efect of TW, suggesting an antagonistic interaction between the two. This antagonism reduces the adsorption capacity of both HPTT and TW in regions of strong convection, while exhibiting no significant impact under weak convection conditions. This implies that HPTT accelerates the rate of copper deposition outside blind holes, leading to an increase in the thickness of the deposited copper.
