blocks.section: Electroplated Copper Additives for Advanced Packaging: A Review > 4. ELECTROPLATING ADDITIVES
blocks.text: Initially, SPS adsorbs on the surface of chloride ions, then dissociates on the metal surface, leaving MPS monomers adsorbed on the copper substrate. During the copper deposition process, individual MPS molecules can be released from the electrode surface, enabling SPS in the electrolyte solution to adsorb on the copper substrate. It has been proven that MPS is more efective in replacing chloride ions on the copper substrate compared to SPS. The reaction between Cu (II) and free MPS produces MPS-Cu (I) and SPS. MPS-Cu (I) reacts on the copper substrate, leading to copper deposition on the surface, and subsequently releases SPS, entering the next cyclic reaction. As depicted in Figure 11, Chen et al. 31 confirmed the existence of MPS-Cu + -Cl − through electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.

blocks.section: Electroplated Copper Additives for Advanced Packaging: A Review > 4. ELECTROPLATING ADDITIVES
blocks.text: Figure 11. Mechanism of action of PEG.

blocks.section: Electroplated Copper Additives for Advanced Packaging: A Review > 4. ELECTROPLATING ADDITIVES
blocks.text: The most widely accepted theory regarding the mechanism of the inhibitory agent is that the formation of PEG-Cl − -Cu + hinders the deposition of copper. This theory has also been substantiated by various techniques, including electrochemistry, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, atomic force micros copy, and others. 35,36 In the case of the inhibitor, chloride ions coordinate with PEG to form PEG-Cu (I)-Cl complexes. Its adsorption on the copper surface enhances cathodic polarization, thus inhibiting the deposition of copper. Moreover, leveling agents in the plating solution can form complexes by coordinating with the copper surface through their active sites (such as N, S, Pyridine rings, etc.). The adsorption of this complex on the copper surface enhances the inhibitory efect of PEG-Cu (I)-Cl on the copper surface.

blocks.section: Electroplated Copper Additives for Advanced Packaging: A Review > 4. ELECTROPLATING ADDITIVES
blocks.text: Numerous studies indicate the presence of significant interactions between inhibitors and accelerators, and the manifestation of the accelerating efect depends to a certain extent on the presence of the inhibitor. For instance, in a plating solution containing Cl^- but without PEG, the addition of SPS did not show a significant accelerating efect, and the resulting plated coating was not bright. Mofat et al. 37 demonstrated that the competitive adsorption of SPS and PEG on the copper surface involves the competition for adsorption sites. They argue that the appearance of the accelerating efect is attributed to the disruption of the cathodic inhibition layer by the sulfonic acid group. Moreover, the rate of SPS replacing PEG adsorbed on the copper surface is dependent on the overpotential. The higher the overpotential, the faster SPS replaces PEG.

blocks.section: Electroplated Copper Additives for Advanced Packaging: A Review > 4. ELECTROPLATING ADDITIVES
blocks.text: Dow et al. 38 proposed that when JGB serves as a leveling agent, there is a synergistic efect between JGB, PEG, and chloride ions, enhancing their inhibitory efects. This enhanced efect is realized through the formation of PEG-JGB-Cl − complexes generated during the electroplating process. The synergistic efect is related to the convection intensity, causing the inhibition of PEG-JGB-Cl − complexes in high convection areas and the accumulation of SPS at the bottom of blind holes, thereby achieving overfilling of the blind holes. Bandas et al. 39 studied the catalytic efect of amine leveling agents on SPS at the interface between copper and the electroplating solution, revealing that the influence of leveling agents on accelerators is related to the molecular weight of the leveling agent.

blocks.section: Electroplated Copper Additives for Advanced Packaging: A Review > 5. CHALLENGES AND ISSUES IN ACIDIC COPPERELECTROPLATING
blocks.text: The primary challenge in acidic copper electroplating lies in the incomplete understanding of the mechanisms of additives in the copper plating system, especially those of accelerators and leveling agents. Among them, the mechanism of leveling agents is of paramount importance. As leveling agents are vital for achieving uniform copper coatings, the challenge lies in correctly selecting and using appropriate additives when altering electroplating conditions, particularly in high current density electroplating. 38 Currently, in industrial electroplating practices, the current density for through-hole electroplating is generally strictly controlled below 3 A/dm, 2 and for plating blind holes, it is even lower, typically strictly controlled below 2 A/dm. 2 There are two main impacts of increasing current density.

blocks.section: Electroplated Copper Additives for Advanced Packaging: A Review > 5. CHALLENGES AND ISSUES IN ACIDIC COPPERELECTROPLATING
blocks.text: First, it seriously diminishes the uniformity of the coating, resulting in greater diferences in thickness between the copper surface and the copper coating inside the hole. Excessively thin hole copper can lead to severe damage to the electrical performance and reliability of PCBs, which is strictly prohibited in electroplating production. Second, increasing current density will impact existing additive systems, necessitating the develop ment of new additive systems. However, developing an entirely new electroplating solution system has become increasingly challenging, requiring higher costs and more funding. Furthermore, higher current density will accelerate the consumption of accelerators, increase the dificulty of additive control, and significantly impact coating quality.

blocks.section: Electroplated Copper Additives for Advanced Packaging: A Review > 6. CONCLUSIONS
blocks.text: As chip integration continues to soar, the standards for copper filling capabilities and quality in silicon vias with exceptional aspect ratios, including through-silicon vias (TSVs) and blind vias, have escalated significantly. Presently, domestic inquiries into electroplating additives remain insuficiently exhaustive, with a scarcity of inquiries into the intricate interaction mechanisms among these additives. Consequently, electro plating solutions utilized in domestic chip manufacturing still heavily rely on imports, necessitating the urgent development of high-performance domestic electroplating copper additives. Therefore, the quest for additives that possess low toxicity, environmental friendliness, stability, and electroplating eficacy is paramount for attaining independent chip localization.

blocks.section: Electroplated Copper Additives for Advanced Packaging: A Review > 6. CONCLUSIONS
blocks.text: Accelerators can be tailored toward organic additives devoid of sodium ions, with the objective of minimizing the impact of sodium ion infiltration on chip electrical performance. Future inquiries into leveling agents should concentrate on polyquater nary ammonium salts, small-molecule nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compounds, and inorganic molecules. Additionally, polymers enriched with multiple active functional groups, including ethers, hydroxyl groups, and imidazoles, emerge as a promising research direction for innovative leveling agents.

blocks.section: Electroplated Copper Additives for Advanced Packaging: A Review > 6. CONCLUSIONS
blocks.text: The subsequent electroplating solution development emphasizes the investigation of the electrochemical behavior’s influence on the grain growth and microstructure of electroplated copper during acidic deposition. This encompasses elucidating the copper crystal form transformation, meticulously controlling the microstructure, and comprehension of the copper coating’s mechanical property variations. Furthermore, revealing the regulatory mechanisms of additives on the mechanical properties of the copper coating material is paramount. Establishing a screening and design framework for organic additives with targeted functional groups is imperative, facilitating the creation of electroplating solutions tailored to meet the requirements of diverse semiconductor manufacturing processes.

blocks.section: Filling performance of an Acid Blue 1 leveler on blind microvias†
blocks.text: Cite this: New J. Chem., 2025, 49, 4538 Mingjie Li, a Xuesong Peng, a Jie Jiang, a Yaqiang Li, * ab Fan Meng, a Youzheng Wu, a Maozhong An, a Ruopeng Li,* a Penghui Ren* ac and Peixia Yang * a Received 24th December 2024, Accepted 11th February 2025 DOI: 10.1039/d4nj05470a The void-free blind microvia copper electroplating process is a key technology in HDI PCB manufacturing. This work systematically studied the influence of the Acid Blue 1 (AB1) leveler on blind microvia filling. AB1 exhibits excellent suppression during electroplating, with its efect strengthening as the AB1 concentration increases. Chronopotentiometry was used to study the interaction among AB1, SPS, and PEG. There is a synergistic suppressing interaction between the new leveler AB1 and suppressor PEG, while there is competition between AB1 and accelerator SPS. During electrodeposition, AB1 can adsorb on the copper substrate to reduce active sites and suppress copper electrodeposition, based on theoretical studies and in situ infrared spectroscopy. At the optimized electroplating process, void-free microvia filling is achieved with 20 mg/L AB1 and successive electroplating confirms the stability of AB1.

blocks.text: Based on difusion diferences among additives and the competition between AB1 and SPS, a gradient competitive adsorption superfilling mechanism was proposed to illustrate the filling process of the AB1–SPS–PEG system. AB1 is beneficial to improving flatness and lowering surface roughness of the copper layer, which is conducive to reducing signal losses during high-frequency transmission. Additionally, AB1 can modulate the preferential formation of Cu(111) and Cu(200) and facilitate grain refinement.

blocks.document_id: d4nj05470a
blocks.section: Filling performance of an Acid Blue 1 leveler on blind microvias† > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: High-density interconnect (HDI) printed circuit boards (PCBs) serve as a foundational platform for connecting all kinds of electronic components in electronic products, thus attracting significant research attention. 1 With the trend toward smallersized electronic devices with higher performance, stricter requirements are imposed on PCB design and manufacturing technology. 2,3 Especially in the fields of high-performance computing, high-speed communication, and precision instruments, the reliability and performance of PCBs are directly related to the performance and stability of the final products. Blind microvia filling is a key interconnect technology in the manufacturing process of PCBs, allowing for electrical connections between diferent layers in the circuit board. 4,5 The application of this technology enhances PCB design flexibility, enabling more complex circuit layouts and greater space utilization.

blocks.document_id: d4nj05470a
blocks.section: Filling performance of an Acid Blue 1 leveler on blind microvias† > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Copper is widely used as an interconnect line in blind microvias for PCB manufacturing due to its good electronic (thermal and electrical conductivity) and mechanical (wear resistance and elongation, etc.) properties. 6,7 The filling of blind microvias with copper is achieved through electroplating technology. 8–10 In PCBs, copper not only provides a stable electrical connection but also enhances the structural strength of HDI PCBs, improving heat and wear resistance. 11 Moreover, copper interconnect lines effectively reduce losses in signal transmission and enhance signal integrity, which is especially important for high-frequency and high-speed circuits. 12 During copper electroplating, it is essential to adjust the metal deposition process in local microvias to avoid the formation of void defects caused by the edge effect, which can undermine the properties of the copper interconnect layer. The most common method is the addition of proper additives. 13–15 The additives used in copper electroplating fall into three categories: accelerators, suppressors, and levelers.

blocks.document_id: d4nj05470a
blocks.section: Filling performance of an Acid Blue 1 leveler on blind microvias† > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: 16 The most commonly used accelerator, suppressor, and leveler is bis-(sodium sulfopropyl)- disulfide (SPS), polyethylene glycol (PEG), and Janus Green B (JGB). 17 During electroplating, density functional theory (DFT) calculations, in situ Raman spectroscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) studies reveal that the disulfide bond of SPS will break up, with the sulfurcontaining side adsorbing on the copper base, while the other side (containing a sulfonic acid group) captures free Cu ^2 + to accelerate reduction with adsorbed Cl - through the ‘‘bridging efect’’. 18–20 As for PEG, in situ Raman and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations confirm the formation of PEG-Cu^2+-Cl^- adsorbate complexes, which increase the energy barrier and suppress copper electrodeposition. 21–23 Mass spectrometry (MS) and DFT calculations demonstrate that the azo group of JGB competes with the reduction of Cu ^2 + to obtain electrons, leading to dissociation 24,25 into phenazine derivatives that can also adsorb on active sites to suppress copper growth. 26,27 Among these additives, levelers are key components for achieving defect-free filling in blind vias.

blocks.document_id: d4nj05470a
blocks.section: Filling performance of an Acid Blue 1 leveler on blind microvias† > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: 28 Nowadays, triphenylmethane derivatives are promising levelers and have been used in throughhole and blind-hole filling due to the unlocalized orbital distribution of the tertiary amine structure. 29,30

blocks.document_id: d4nj05470a
blocks.section: Filling performance of an Acid Blue 1 leveler on blind microvias† > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In this work, a novel triphenylmethane derivative, Acid Blue 1 (AB1), was selected as a potential leveler, and the efects of diferent concentrations of AB1 on copper electroplating were investigated. The interactions among three diferent types of additives were studied using galvanostatic measurements. The influencing mechanism of AB1 on the copper cathode surface during electroplating was also studied theoretically and experimentally. The filling performance of AB1 in blind microvias was examined, and the electroplating process was optimized. Additionally, the surface morphology and roughness of the copper interconnect layer were analyzed, and finite element simulation was employed to study the high-frequency signal transmission losses influenced by AB1, while phase structure was investigated by XRD.

blocks.text: 3.1.1 CV analysis. Cyclic voltammetry was used to examine AB1 during electroplating, 42 as shown in Fig. 1a and Fig. S1 (ESI†). The cathodic onset potential decreases as AB1 concentration increases (Fig. S1, ESI†). The onset potential without AB1 was about -430 mV, while it shifts negatively to -575 mV after adding 10 mg L^-1 AB1, indicating that AB1 efectively increases cathodic polarization. In addition, the onset potential decreases from -583 mV to - 6 5 0 mV with additive concentrations rising from 20 mg L^-1 to 150 mg L ^- 1, demonstrating an intensified suppressing efect on copper electrodeposition with higher AB1 concentrations. The anodic stripping area also declines continuously with increasing AB1 concentration, suggesting a reduction in the amount of electrodeposited Cu during the cathodic process. We calculated the anodic stripping coulomb (ASC) values according to eqn (S1) for quantitative evaluation of AB1 (details in ESI†). 43 Fig. 1b shows that the ASC of VMS is 7 1.0 ~C~ dm ^- 2, which decreases by 28% to 51.4 ~C~dm ^- 2 with 10 mg ~L~ ^- 1 AB1, indicating that trace AB1 (10 mg L ^- 1) can significantly suppress copper electrodeposition.

blocks.text: 3.1.3 Chronopotentiometry analysis. It is important to study the interaction among SPS (accelerator), PEG (suppressor), and AB1 (leveler), as it provides a deeper understanding of the filling mechanism in microvias. 45 Traditionally, galvanostatic measurement is applied to study possible interactions by changing the injection order of the three types of additives. Fig. 1c (up) shows the change in cathodic potential after injecting additives into the testing solution. The cathodic potential declines (230 mV) after adding PEG, indicating its suppressing efect. Upon introducing AB1, the cathodic potential further decreases (31 mV), suggesting synergistic cooperation between AB1 and PEG. However, after the addition of SPS, the cathodic potential shifts positively (42 mV), indicating the accelerating efect of SPS in the presence of AB1 and PEG. By altering the additive injection order, SPS can cause a positive shift of 205 mV in cathodic potential after PEG injection, suggesting that SPS can replace PEG to accelerate copper electrodeposition, consistent with previous work. 46 Following AB1 injection, the cathodic potential changes negatively (-191 mV).

blocks.text: 3.2.1 Adsorption analysis. The influencing mechanism was studied using DFT calculations and in situ infrared spectroscopy. 47–49 The AB1 formula and its optimized structure are shown in Fig. S2 (ESI†). Fig. 2a shows the local electron affinity (LEA) distribution, with the blue color indicating high electrophilicity and red representing nucleophilicity. The -SO_3 area (high electrophilicity) in AB1 is conducive to forming interactions with the copper substrate due to vacant d orbitals. The adsorption equilibrium configuration of AB1 on the copper substrate is shown in Fig. 2b and Fig. S3 (ESI†), with color representations detailed in the ESI.† The quasi-plane structure of AB1 adsorbs nearly parallel to the copper substrate, with the -SO_3 functional group connected to the benzene ring of AB1 preferentially adsorbing on the substrate. Fig. 2c shows the 2D charge density difference of the adsorption configuration after equilibrium. The blue and red colors represent charge depletion and accumulation, demonstrating charge transfer between copper and AB1. It is believed that AB1 adsorbs on the cathode surface to reduce active sites and increase cathodic polarization.

blocks.text: To verify the calculated results, in situ infrared spectroscopy was conducted to observe the AB1 adsorption process during electrodeposition, 30 as shown in Fig. 2d. The peaks and their attributions are summarized in Table S1 (ESI†). The characteristic peaks ( - S O _ 3. functional group) at 1080 cm -1 and 1 2 2 0 cm ^ - 1 confirm the adsorption of the – - S O _ 3 functional group of AB1 on the copper substrate. The stretching vibrations of C-N (1630 cm -1), C–C (1420 cm -1), and C–H (3223 cm ^ - 1) of the aromatic ring indicate that AB1 adsorbs parallel to the copper substrate, consistent with the calculated adsorption equilibrium.

blocks.text: 3.2.2 DOS analysis. Density of states (DOS) analysis provides insight into the interaction at the orbital level. 32 Fig. 2e shows the clear orbital overlap among the d orbitals of Cu, the s orbitals of N, and the p orbitals of O, indicating orbital interactions among the copper substrate, N atoms, and O atoms. In contrast, there is no orbital overlap between S and Cu, demonstrating that S atoms are not directly adsorbed on the copper substrate, consistent with the calculated adsorption configuration. To understand the specific orbital interactions in more detail, the PDOS (projected density of state) was calculated, as shown in Fig. 2f. Firstly, the pz orbitals of N atoms exhibit the largest overlap with the dyz and dz2 orbitals of Cu, while a strong hybridization occurs between py and pz orbitals of O atoms and dyz and dz2 orbitals of Cu. DOS analysis confirms significant d and p orbital hybridization among O, N, and Cu, further verifying the adsorption configuration and providing a deeper understanding of the adsorption mechanism. In summary, AB1 can adsorb on the copper cathode to reduce active sites and act as a barrier to suppress the reduction of free Cu ^2 +

blocks.text: 3.3.1 Electroplating performance. The optimization of the electroplating process is shown in Fig. 3, with the used devices illustrated in Fig. 3c. Without AB1, the growth rate at the opening area is higher than that at the bottom and side walls, leading to void defects in microvias with both diameters (125 mm and 150 mm). At an AB1 concentration of 10 mg L ^- 1, the growth rate at the opening area decreases due to AB1 adsorption, which suppresses copper growth. However, this relatively low concentration is not conducive to establishing an efective concentration gradient, resulting in defects forming in the 125 mm microvias and concave growth in the 150 mm microvias. With 20 mg ~L~ ^- 1 \ AB1, an efective concentration gradient is formed, allowing copper to grow from bottom to top without defects in either microvias. Besides, the compact and flat copper morphology from the top view in Fig. S4 (ESI†) indicates that AB1 improves copper quality compared to layers obtained without it. In contrast, the commonly used leveler Janus Green B (Fig.

The influence of morphology will be discussed in Section 3.4.1. When the AB1 concentration increases further to 3 0 mgL ^- 1, the excessive concentration weakens the concentration gradient, causing the bottom-up growth mode to shift to a conformal growth mode in the 150 mm microvias. blocks.text: 3.3.2 Filling mechanism. The difusion property of AB1 was studied using molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, as shown in Fig. S8 (ESI†). Based on the Einstein equation (eqn (S2), ESI†), the difusion coeficient for AB1 ( D _ AB1) is 2  1 0 ^ - 1 0 m ^ 2 s ^ - 1, which is close to the difusion coeficient for PEG ( D _ PEG, 1 × 1 0 ^ - 1 0 m ^ 2 s ^ - 1) ^ 5 0 and one order smaller than that for SPS ( D _ SPS, 5 × 1 0 ^ - 9 ~m ^ 2 ~s ^ - 1). ^ 5 1 This illustrates that the leveler AB1 and suppressor PEG have slower difusion transport compared to the accelerator SPS. Coupled with the interactions among the three additives discussed in Section 3.1.3, namely the competition between AB1 and SPS, as well as cooperation between AB1 and PEG, gradient competitive adsorption superfilling was proposed to illustrate the AB1–SPS–PEG system, with a schematic diagram shown in Fig. 3d. At the initial stage (3d1), different additives are distributed uniformly within the microvias. As the filling process progresses (3d2), a concentration gradient for the additives forms due to their consumption and local diffusion transport limitations within the microvias.

blocks.text: However, the concentration ratio of SPS to PEG and AB1 at the bottom increases compared to that at the opening area due to the differing diffusion properties among the three additives; specifically, D _ SPS is significantly larger than D _ AB1 and D _ PEG.. As a result, the growth rate at the bottom is improved by the increased accelerating effect from the relatively amount of SPS, while growth at the opening area is effectively suppressed since AB1’s mass transport is not limited due to convection, leading to copper growth from the bottom to the top. At the final stage (3d3), the three additives redistribute uniformly at the opening area, resulting in the same growth rate across different areas. No momentum plating phenomena occur in the AB1–SPS–PEG system. 52

blocks.text: 3.4.1 Efect of AB1 on morphology. Fig. 4 and 5a show the surface morphology of the copper layer observed by SEM and Olympus conformal laser microscope. 53 Small bump particles are present on the uneven copper surface electrodeposited without AB1. After introducing 10 mg L ^ - 1 AB1, the surface flatness improves greatly, and the copper layer becomes compact, although large bump morphology remains. As the AB1 concentration continues to rise, the flatness of the copper layer further improves. Using the Olympus conformal laser microscope, the surface roughness ( R _ z) was calculated, as shown in Fig. 5b. R _ z is 128 nm for the copper layer obtained without AB1 and decreases to 92 nm with 10 mg L ^ - 1 AB1. Furthermore, R _ z values obtained from 20 mg L ^ - 1 and 30 mg L ^ - 1 are 83 nm and 75 nm, respectively. The above analysis indicates that AB1 has a micro-scale leveling efect.

blocks.text: 3.4.2 Efect of AB1 on signal loss. The influence of AB1 on signal loss during high-frequency transmission was studied using finite element simulation. 54 Fig. 5c shows that signal loss is influenced by surface roughness and applied frequency. Total loss increases with rising frequency and R _z. Additionally, the total loss with frequency for the copper layer obtained with JGB is also calculated (Fig. S5d, ESI†). In comparison, the signal loss obtained with AB1 is smaller than with JGB at the same frequency due to a lower R _z for AB1. The skin efect for the optimized copper layer with 20 mg L^-1 AB1 and without AB1 is shown in Fig. 5d and e. At a relatively low frequency (10 GHz), current density is distributed uniformly in the copper layer obtained from 2 0 mgL ^- 1. Even at high frequency (100 GHz), the current density remains relatively well distributed. However, for the copper layer obtained without AB1, the current density mainly concentrates near the surface area at 10 GHz. Simulation results indicate that AB1 helps mitigate the influence of the skin efect during high-frequency signal transmission by improving surface flatness.

blocks.section: Filling performance of an Acid Blue 1 leveler on blind microvias† > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: A novel leveler, Acid Blue 1, was used to achieve void-free copper filling in blind microvias. Electrochemical tests (CV and EIS) confirm the suppressive efect on the reduction of Cu ^2 +. During copper electroplating, there is a synergistic suppression between AB1 and PEG, but competition between AB1 and SPS. DFT calculations and in situ infrared spectroscopy provide a deeper understanding of AB1 adsorption configuration on the copper substrate during electrodeposition, indicating that AB1 can reduce active sites and act as a barrier adsorption layer to increase cathodic polarization. After electroplating optimization, microvias with diameters of 125 mm and 150 mm can be filled with 20 mg L^-1 AB1 at 1.5 Adm ^- 2; the good stability of AB1 indicates its industrial potential. A gradient competitive adsorption superfilling mechanism was proposed to explain the filling process for the AB1–SPS–PEG system. The diffusion differences among the three additives and the competition between AB1 and SPS are key to achieving bottom-up growth in microvias.

blocks.document_id: d4nj05470a
blocks.section: Filling performance of an Acid Blue 1 leveler on blind microvias† > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: AB1 improves the copper layer quality, enhances surface flatness, refines the grains, and reduces signal losses during high-frequency transmission. Additionally, AB1 suppresses the formation of Cu(220) while promoting the formation of Cu(111) and Cu(200).

blocks.section: Electrodeposition of Cobalt for Interconnect Application: Effect of Dimethylglyoxime
blocks.text: The state-of-the-art back-end-of-line (BEOL) interconnects are fabricated with copper, which replaced Aluminum in late 1990’s due to its lower resistivity and superior reliability. 1,2 As the interconnect continues to scale, the critical dimension of the BEOL structures has approached the electron mean free path of copper. The copper resistivity in such nanostructures increases exponentially as the dimension further shrinks, 3,4 posing tremendous challenges to the continuous scaling of copper interconnect for 7 nm technology and beyond. While the bulk resistivity of a metal is an intrinsic property of the material its resistivity in these small structures is largely determined by what happens to the electrons when they come across an interface, i.e., the surface of the metal structure in contact with the matrix materials, the boundaries between grains in the metal structure and the internal interface between metal and the embedded impurity species. 5 Metals with shorter electron mean free path are less susceptible to the effect of scaling and may appear advantageous for the interconnect application.

blocks.document_id: DMG_丁二酮肟_
blocks.section: Electrodeposition of Cobalt for Interconnect Application: Effect of Dimethylglyoxime
blocks.text: For example, transition metals including Ni, Co, Mo and Ru were predicted to be potential candidates to replace Cu. 6 In addition to the advantage of a shorter mean free path, some of the candidate metals can potentially provide performance gain through innovative integration schemes. The overall resistance of an interconnect structure is a result of not only the copper but also other materials used in the interconnect structure for a variety of purposes. Such materials include diffusion barrier, adhesion layer, capping layer and sometimes additional elements as the seed layer for copper plating. Therefore, using metals that can serve dual or multiple purposes may allow more volume for the conducting metal and thus a lower overall resistance and an improved RC delay. Furthermore, new materials that enable better integration and lower defectivities can improve the overall performance as well. For example, chemical vapor deposited (CVD) and atomic layer deposited (ALD) Ru was previously studied to replace the Ta diffusion barrier – Cu seed stack. 7–9 Co has recently gained more and more attention as a material to replace the traditional Ta liner.

blocks.section: Electrodeposition of Cobalt for Interconnect Application: Effect of Dimethylglyoxime
blocks.text: 10,11 Compared with Ta, Co provides a better wettability of PVD Cu seed, enables a more conformal Cu seed coverage and therefore improves the extendibility of Cu electroplating in smaller dimensions. 12 In addition, the enhanced grain growth of Cu electroplated on Co seed 13 and the self-formation of a barrier layer enabled by the Mn diffusion through Co layer 14 potentially provide additional performance gain on the reliability of the interconnect structures.

blocks.section: Electrodeposition of Cobalt for Interconnect Application: Effect of Dimethylglyoxime
blocks.text: Recently, selectively electroless deposited Co has been demonstrated to partially or completely replace the Cu in the small vias to improve the via resistance. 15 The bottom up fill of the via structures relied on the selectivity between the exposed underneath metal layer and the dielectrics for electroless deposition process. Electrolytic super conformal deposition of Co and Ni was reported using 2-mercapto-5-benzimidazolesulfonic acid (MBIS). 16–19 A potential dependent adsorption, passivation and desorption of the additive was found to result in a negative differential resistance in cyclic voltammetry and therefore multiple steady states at certain potentials. Super conformal deposition of through silicon vias (TSV) was enabled by controlling the deposition at such potentials, where the bottom and top of a TSV are plated at two different states. Super conformal NiFe filling into sub-50 nm interconnect trenches was demonstrated with a two component additive system using a polymer suppressor and a monomer accelerator. 20 More recently, three component commercial additive has been reported for the bottom up filling of Co for interconnect.

blocks.text: 21 Electrodeposition of cobalt and its alloys has been studied extensively in the past for their magnetic properties. Among them, CoNiFe 22–25 and CoFe 26–28 alloys were used in commercial hard disk drive writing heads for their low coercivities and high moments. The two additives commonly used in magnetic thin film plating, saccharin and thiourea, were studied with scanning tunneling microscope and were found to adsorb on Au(111) surface through physisorption and chemisorption respectively. 29 The different sulfur incorporation behaviors resulted in different coercivities of the deposited films.

blocks.section: Electrodeposition of Cobalt for Interconnect Application: Effect of Dimethylglyoxime
blocks.text: A group of additives including saccharin and thiourea were previously studied for their impacts on the NiFe alloy deposition toward superconformal filling. 20 While polyethyleneimine (PEI) was found to show suppression effect, thiourea and benzenesulfinic acid showed only acceleration effect. In addition, mercapto-benezenimidazole and its sulfonic acid derivative showed suppression followed by acceleration effect. Comparing the molecular structures of these additives in Figure 1, it is clear that PEI only has paired amine groups, which are two CH groups apart. Thiourea and benzenesulfinic acid both have mercapto groups vie an isomerization and a disproportionation reaction, 30 respectively. When both mercapto group and paired amine (or imine) groups are present in the molecules, such as mercaptobenezenimidazole and its sulfonic acid derivative, both suppression and acceleration effects were observed. In addition, when one of the paired amine nitrogen is replaced by oxygen in mercapto-benzoxazole, the suppression effect was significantly weakened and only acceleration effect was observed.

Based on this previous work, it can be speculated that a pair of amine (imine) group is responsible for a suppression effect and a mercapto group for acceleration.

blocks.text: In an effort to search for a suppressing additive for a onecomponent Co deposition chemistry, this paper presents a study of the effect of dimethylglyoxime (DMG) on the electrodeposition of cobalt. DMG and other dioxime have been previously used as an additive in Co electroless deposition, 31 mainly as a stabilizer due to its strong complexing with Co ^2 +. The structure of DMG, particularly in its complexed form with Co ^2 +, remotely mimics many of the molecules in Figure 1. However, DMG has only a pair of conjugated imine groups without any sulfur containing groups. The study of Co electrodeposition in presence of DMG is expected to shed light on the interactions between the conjugated pair of imine groups and the metal ions during the electrochemical reaction.

blocks.text: A three electrode cell with a glass frit separating the cathode and anode compartments was used for electrochemical studies. Saturated calomel electrode (SCE) was used as reference electrode in a reference compartment with a capillary to the cathode. All potential in this paper is with respect to SCE. A 99.95 wt% Co foil was used as the anode. Platinum rotating disk electrode (RDE) was used as the cathode in electrochemical studies. The rotation rate was fixed at 100 rpm unless stated otherwise.

blocks.text: The Co makeup solution contains 0.3 M CoSO_4, 0.4 H_3BO_3, and 0.1 g/L sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS). The pH of Co solution was adjusted to 4.0 with H 2 SO 4. DMG concentrate solution at 2 wt% (20000 ppm, 1 ppm DMG = 8.6 × 1 0 ^- 6 M) was prepared using its sodium salt and was added into the makeup solution to make Co electrolytes with different amounts of DMG. A 0.2 M HCl solution was used to anodically strip the Co deposit on Pt. Metal free solutions was made with 0.4 M Na 2 SO 4, 0.4 H 3 BO 3, and 0.1 g/L sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) with a fixed pH of 4. All salts were at least ACS grade and deionized (DI) water with 18 MOhm was used for all solutions in this study.

blocks.text: The effect of DMG on Co deposition was studied with cyclic voltammetry (CV). A layer of Co was pre-plated on Pt RDE using the makeup electrolyte (DMG free). Potential was scanned from open circuit potential (OCP, typically about 0.48 V SCE) to 1.5 V with a scan rate of 5 mV/sec. The solution resistance was measured using impedance analysis at 0.65 V with a sinusoidal perturbation of 10 mV. It was found that the solution resistance does not change with the addition of DMG. Partial current densities of Co deposition was determined using the Co films deposited at different constant current densities. These films were then stripped at an anodic current density of 10 mA/cm2 in the HCl stripping solution using a rotation rate of 900 rpm. A sudden potential increase was observed once the Co film was completely stripped. The total charge before the potential increase was used to calculate the amount of Co deposited.

blocks.text: Potential transient studies during galvanostatic plating with injection of DMG were also conducted using Pt RDE rotating at 100 rpm. In these studies, small amount of DMG concentrate was injected at the vicinity of the cathode with the potential transients recorded. Gold quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) preplated with Co from a DMG free solution was used to study the current transients at fixed potentials in absence of agitation. Because of the tiny solution volume used in QCM Co electrolyte with double concentration of the desired DMG concentration was used in the injection of DMG. For example, 2 ml of Co solution with 200 ppm DMG was added into 2 ml DMG free Co solution in QCM cell to obtain the injection of 100 ppm DMG. The same chronoamperometry measurements were also carried out on pre-plated Pt RDE with changes in rotation rates. Electrochemical impedance spectra were acquired using Co pre-plated Pt RDE at 100 rpm. All electrochemical studies were conducted using an AutoLab electrochemical station with QCM and frequency analyzer modules.

blocks.text: The effect of DMG on Co deposition was first examined with cyclic voltammetry (CV). A 100 nm layer of cobalt was deposited on Pt disc electrode in the additive free solution before each CV. A change of open circuit potential (OCP) from about 0.3 V to 0.48 V (both vs. SCE) was observed before and after this pre-plating. Potential was then swept from 0.48 V to 1.5 V with a sweep rate of 5 mV/sec. Figure 2 shows the CV curves with different amounts of DMG without and with ohmic drop correction. When no DMG was present in the solution, the cathodic deposition current started at 0.7 V and reached a current density of 2 mA/cm2 at 0.8 V and 4 mA/cm2 at 0.85 V. The forward and backward scans coincided with each other. The addition of 10 ppm DMG did not change the CV behavior. However, when 100 ppm DMG was added into the solution, the deposition was significantly polarized at low current range. The onset of the cathodic reaction did not occur until 0.9 V, after which a sudden jump of the cathodic reaction rate was observed. Furthermore, the suppressed cathodic current at low potential was not observed in the backward scan, resulting in a hysteresis in CV.

blocks.text: Further increase of DMG concentration to 300 ppm resulted in stronger suppression of the cathodic current. This suppression was present regardless of the potential, causing a much diminished hysteresis. Figure 2b presents the same CV curves with the ohmic resistance of solution accounted for using impedance measurement. The sudden current increase in the case of 100 ppm DMG was so significant that the CV showed a S-shaped negative differential resistance after the ohmic correction.

blocks.text: In addition to CVs, potential transients during galvanostatic deposition was studied with injection of different amount of DMG at 100 rpm rotation and two current densities, 3 and 10 mA/cm2. It is evident from Figure 3 that the addition of DMG resulted in a fast and strong suppression effect. For example, the deposition potential at - 3 mA/cm2 increased by 40 mV and 100 mV within 5 seconds after the injection of 10 ppm and 90 ppm DMG into the electrolyte, respectively. Although this potential rise was an overshoot due to the stagnant flow and the potential fell back upon further homogenization, the response time was in the same order of a typical suppressor in copper damascene chemistry, 32 suggesting a fast action of DMG on Co deposition. While the additional injection of 200 ppm DMG (300 ppm in total) resulted in further suppression, experiments with DMG beyond 300 ppm showed that the suppression effect was saturated at 300 ppm. The transient at 10 mA/cm2 followed the same trend.

blocks.text: The suppression effect in potential transient experiments was consistent with the observation on CVs. The depolarization effect upon further injection of large amount of DMG was also observed in CV study. While the depolarization may relate to additional cathodic reactions that DMG introduces, its details are outside the scope of this paper, which focuses on the application in super conformal filling. Because DMG was added in the form of its sodium salt, electrolyte pH was changed from 4.0 to 4.12, 4.85, 5.25, and 6.08 with the addition of 10, 100, 300, and 1500 ppm DMG, respectively. In addition, DMG may also introduce additional side reaction mechanisms. Therefore, the effect on side reactions will have to be excluded to understand the true impact of DMG on Co deposition.

blocks.text: The partial current density was plotted using the potentials obtained from the forward CV scan. The amount of the Co deposited on Pt RDE was obtained using electrochemical stripping method 33–35 at a constant current density of 10 mA/cm2. A sudden potential increase was observed once the Co films were completely stripped. Co was stripped as Co ^2 + in a solution of 0.2 M HCl. 33,36 Therefore, the current efficiencies as well as the side reaction rates can be computed based on the charges during stripping and the deposition. The stripping of pre-deposited Co layer was repeated 4 times to confirm the reproducibility. A current efficiency of 93.9% with a standard deviation of 0.3% were obtained for Co deposition at 10 mA/cm2 from a DMG free electrolyte. The stripping charge for this pre-deposited Co layer was subtracted from the total stripping charge of the Co films of interest.

blocks.text: As shown in Figure 4a, Co deposition was suppressed in the presence of 100 ppm DMG. The suppression was more pronounced as the DMG concentration increased from 100 to 300 ppm. Furthermore, the sudden current increase as well as the s-shaped negative differential resistance in CVs were proved to result from Co deposition. Side reaction current densities were presented in Figure 4b. The CVs in Co-free solutions with and without DMG were included for comparison. The side reaction current density in a DMG free electrolyte coincided with the total current density of Co-free solution. However, the side reaction rates at potentials more negative than 0.9 V significantly increased when DMG was added. On the other hand, the addition of DMG didn’t change the total current density of a metal free electrolyte. Because the Pt electrode was pre-coated with a layer of Co before all experiments, the increased side reaction is believed to be a result of additional side reaction mechanism that involves not only DMG but also Co(II). For example, a catalytic effect of Co (and Ni) was reported for the reduction of DMG.

The fractions of different forms of ligand and metal ions are presented in Figure 5. At pH of 4 or above, DMG is expected to be completely complexed with Co(II). However, even with 1500 ppm DMG and 0.3 MCoSO _4. more than 97% of Co(II) are presented in a non-complexed form regardless of solution pH. When less amount of DMG is used, the percentage of Co(II) in the non-complexed form is expected to be higher. Furthermore, the deposition of non-complexed Co(II) may also involve an adsorbed Co(I) intermediate species. 39–41 Competitive adsorption between different species can result in suppression of Co deposition. blocks.text: The emerge of additional charge transfer loops were reported previously for copper deposition in presence of surface adsorbed suppressors. 43 The competition for surface sites between the intermediate metal species and the suppressors was found sufficient to explain the additional EIS features in copper deposition. In another detailed study on the impedance of NiFe anomalous co-deposition, the addition of Fe into Ni electrolyte was found to enhance the sensitivity of the inductance loop to deposition current. 42,44 The competitive adsorption between the Fe(I)_ads intermediate and Ni(I)_ads intermediate resulted in a more pronounced inductance loop at certain conditions. A competitive adsorption between adsorbed species, such as C o ( I) _ads and [ Co ( DMG) _2 ] _ads, is believed to relate to the inductance loop of Co deposition in this study.

blocks.text: An electrochemical quartz microbalance was used to study the electrodeposition as well as adsorption in absence of agitation. Figure 7a shows the current density and the QCM frequency at a constant voltage of 0.84 V. Upon the injection of 100 ppm DMG, the cathodic current dropped significantly from 2.3 to 1 mA/cm2. At the same time, the slope of the QCM frequency curve decreased significantly, indicating a slower metal deposition rate. A close look at the QCM frequency showed no sudden jump of the mass, which was observed upon injection of polyethylene glycol (PEG) during copper electrodeposition 45 due to the strong fast adsorption of PEG onto Cu surface. This difference suggests that the suppressing intermediate is either more light-weighted or adsorbs more slowly than PEG in the copper case. Furthermore, the current density as well as the frequency slope kept increasing again after a maximum suppression effect. This relaxation of the suppression effect was interrupted by the replenishment of solution at electrode surface using a pipette, where a strong suppression effect was re-established suggesting a depletion and replenishment of a suppressing species at the surface.

blocks.text: Using the mass-frequency coefficient of the QCM, 12.3 ng/cm^2/H z, the partial current densities of Co deposition and side reactions were calculated and presented in Figure 7b. The total current in absence of additives (before t 60 sec) was mainly due to the deposition Co, which was consistent with the CVs in Figure 4. In addition, the cobalt deposition rate was suppressed and the side reaction rate was slightly increased upon the addition of 100 ppm DMG. While the side reaction rate remained constant as the deposition continued, Co deposition rate was gradually enhanced and doubled after 5 minutes. In addition, the current decrease upon the surface solution replenishment was confirmed to result from a strong suppression in Co deposition. The Co deposition current dropped to 0 mA/cm2 at the maximum suppression point, where the total current densities completely result from side reactions.

blocks.text: For a 700 sec long experiment in a solution with 0.3 ~M~CoSO_4 the maximum decay of a mass transport controlled Co deposition rate would result in a current down to 4 mA/cm2 based on the Cottrell’s equation 46 with a typical diffusion coefficient of 1 0 ^- 5 ~cm ^2 / sec. The current densities observed in this experiment is far below this value and therefore the depletion of Co is not believed to occur. This is also consistent with the constant Co deposition rate observed in additive free solution. When DMG was added into the electrolyte, the formation of a surface adsorbed species, for example [Co(DMG) ], suppressed the Co deposition. However, the coverage of this adsorbed species appeared to decrease after reaching a maximum suppression effect. Therefore, this adsorbed species is believed to be broken down or be incorporated into the Co deposit. At a DMG concentration of 100 ppm the concentration of Co ( DMG) _2 in electrolyte was 0.4 mM with all DMG being complexed. As the surface concentration of Co(DMG) 2 in electrolyte is depleted, the equilibrium between the adsorption and consumption of [ Co ( DMG) _2 ] _ads was broken and its surface coverage decreases.

Co electrolyte with 100 ppm DMG was used and the Pt RDE was coated with a layer of 100 nm Co. Upon the start of deposition without agitation, the deposition rate gradually increased from 0.23 mA/cm2 to a steady state of 2.97 mA/cm2. blocks.text: When a rotation rate of 400, 900, 100, and 50 rpm was applied, the current density dropped to about 0.5 mA/cm2. The higher the rotation rate, the faster the current drop. This observation was also consistent with the replenishment experiments in QCM study. A faster rotation rate results in a thinner diffusion boundary layer and a higher supply rate of Co(DMG) _2 to the electrode surface. The concentration of Co(DMG) 2 at the vicinity of electrode starts to restore when excessive Co(DMG) was supplied to the electrode surface. Switching off these high rotation rates caused an immediate drop in current density followed by the gradual current increase as discussed above. The immediate current drop was probably due to the decrease of side reactions, which is under mass transport control or mixed control. A higher rotation rate before the switching caused a longer delay before the current increase. This trend can also be well explained by a higher surface concentration of Co(DMG) _2 in the electrolyte when a higher rotation rate was used. A longer time would be needed to deplete the excessive Co(DMG) _2 in the electrolyte resulted from the higher rotation rate.

blocks.text: In the particular case of 50 rpm, the current dropped extremely slowly when the rotation was switched on and the current drop immediate after the rotation was switched off almost disappeared. These observations suggested that the supply rate of Co ( DMG) _2 to the electrode at this rotation rate was approximately at equilibrium with its consumption rate on the electrode. Therefore there was no excessive Co(DMG) _2 accumulated at the vicinity of electrode and the surface coverage of [ Co ( DMG) _2 ] _ads started to drop immediately after the rotation was stopped.

blocks.text: Based on the above discussion, any rotation rate below 50 rpm is expected to result in partial replenishment and partial suppression effect. Three rotation rates, 25, 12 and 6 rpm, were used and the observations confirmed the expectation. Among them, the highest rotation rate of 25 rpm resulted in the most replenishment and therefore the strongest suppression. In addition, the steady state current at these low rotation rates showed more noise than higher rotation rates because of the intrinsic small fluctuation in rotation control. As discussed above, the partial replenishment and [ Co ( DMG) _2 ] _ads surface coverage are expected to be highly sensitive to the rotation rates.

blocks.text: For the application of Co deposition into deep and narrow damascene trenches (or vias), agitation at the top of trench is expected to be greater than at the bottom of trench. Super conformal deposition would be expected if the agitation at these two locations were controlled at above and below the critical rotation rate, 50 rpm in this case, respectively. Because the trench depth changes as the filling continues, the rotation rate may be engineered to enable the continuous deposition at the bottom while maintaining strong suppression at the top.

blocks.section: Electrodeposition of Cobalt for Interconnect Application: Effect of Dimethylglyoxime > Conclusions
blocks.text: Addition of dimethylglyoxime in a mild acid Co electrodeposition electrolyte suppressed the Co deposition rate and enhanced the side reaction. The potential dependent suppression effect resulted in an S-shape negative differential resistance in CV. A surface adsorbed species, for example [ Co ( DMG) _2 ] _ads, was proposed to be responsible for the suppression. Additional capacitance and inductance loops were observed in impedance spectra upon the addition of DMG, which was consistent with the competitive adsorption between intermediate species, such as C o ( I) _ads and [ Co(DMG) _2 ] _ads ^- A strong rapid suppression upon injection of DMG was observed in potential transients on a rotating disk electrode. However, this suppression effect was relaxed in absence of agitation. As the surface adsorbed species are consumed or decomposed along with deposition, the depletion of Co(DMG) in electrolyte at the electrode surface resulted in a decrease of [ Co ( DMG) _2 ] _ads surface coverage. Replenishment of surface electrolyte re-establish the strong suppression, potentially enabling a preferential deposition at the bottom of narrow features in damascene electroplating.

A critical rotation rate was observed, below which Co(DMG) _2 in electrolyte was partially replenished and [ Co ( DMG) _2 ] _ads surface coverage was partially rebuilt. blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes
blocks.text: Shuzhou Xing, Xinrui Wang, Jie Jiang, Xuesong Peng, Sihai Bi, Youzheng Wu, Mingjie Li, Ruopeng Li,* Yaqiang Li,* Maozhong An, Jiang Qin, and Peixia Yang*

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes
blocks.text: Cite This: Langmuir 2026, 42, 15236−15247

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes
blocks.text: ABSTRACT: Driven by the rapid development of 5G/6G communications, high-performance computing, and artificial intelligence, the metallization of high-aspect-ratio through-holes (THs) in printed circuit boards (PCBs) imposes stringent requirements on the thickness uniformity and interconnect reliability of electroplated copper layers. This study systematically investigates the application of a novel leveler, thiazolyl blue (MTT), for PCB THs’ electroplating, successfully realizing high-quality conformal deposition in high-aspect-ratio (10:1) THs. Electrochemical analyses demonstrate that MTT significantly enhances the cathodic polarization and efectively inhibits the reduction of Cu 2+. Meanwhile, microscopic morphological characterizations confirm Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes
blocks.text: that MTT exhibits excellent leveling capability, reducing the surface roughness of the copper deposit to as low as 0.147 μm. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the high inhibitory eficiency of MTT originates from the dominant interfacial adsorption of MTT at the cathode. with the bulk cation-π interaction with Cu ^2 + contributing as a minor secondary effect at the microscopic level. Crystallographic and interfacial wettability analyses further indicate that MTT effectively refines the grain size and promotes the preferential growth of the Cu(200) plane while improving the wettability of the plating bath. In practical high-aspect-ratio through-hole plating tests, the introduction of MTT substantially increases the throwing power (TP) from 25.2% to 96.8%. Based on these results, a competitive interfacial polarization remodeling mechanism governed by multiphysics coupling is proposed to elucidate the intrinsic role of MTT in promoting conformal through-hole deposition. This work provides a solid theoretical foundation and practical engineering guidance for the fabrication of highly reliable, high-frequency 3D interconnected PCB structures.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 1. INTRODUCTION
blocks.text: Driven by the rapid advancement of 5G/6G communications, high-performance computing, and artificial intelligence (AI), printed circuit boards (PCBs)�the mother of electronic products�are undergoing profound technological revolutions. 1−3 As the fundamental carrier connecting electronic components, the PCB not only provides mechanical support for chips and passive devices but also functions as the neural network sustaining signal transmission and power delivery throughout the electronic system. 4 With the accelerated evolution of PCBs toward high integration, high interconnect density, and high-frequency/high-speed transmission, this trajectory poses two intertwined materials challenges. On the device side, the suppression of electromagnetic interference, interlayer crosstalk, and thermal accumulation in densely packed high-frequency boards has stimulated intensive research into advanced electromagnetic functional materials, with MXene-based two-dimensional absorbers and heterostructured composites emerging as a particularly promising family that delivers eficient GHz-to-THz electromagnetic wave absorption and integrated thermal management.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 1. INTRODUCTION
blocks.text: 5−8 On the interconnect side, the multilayer copper network that mechanically and electrically links the chips must, in parallel, be reformulated to simultaneously sustain signal integrity, ensure robust interconnect reliability, and guarantee long-term service lifespan under increasingly aggressive high-frequency operation�demands that ultimately translate into unprece dentedly stringent requirements on the copper metallization of microvias with high aspect ratios. Copper electrodeposition in high-aspect-ratio through-holes (THs) is the core technology for achieving interlayer electrical interconnection in multilayer PCBs. The quality of this metallization directly dictates the signal integrity, current-carrying capacity, and long-term service lifespan of the electronic devices. 9,10

blocks.text: However, during the practical electroplating of high-aspect ratio THs, the initial current distribution is highly nonuniform due to geometric constraints. The local current density at the via opening is significantly higher than that at the center, accompanied by severe mass transfer limitations of Cu 2+ within the hole. This multiphysics imbalance frequently triggers the “dog-bone” defect, characterized by excessive copper accumulation at the via opening and excessively thin deposits on the inner walls. 11 Such nonuniform deposition severely compromises the electrical and mechanical performance of the interconnected structures, constituting a universal bottleneck in the high-density interconnect (HDI) industry. 12 To overcome this challenge, it is imperative to introduce suppressors, accelerators, and levelers into the acidic copper sulfate bath. 13 The precise synergistic and competitive adsorption among these three additives dynamically modulates the deposition kinetics at diferent spatial locations within the TH, ultimately achieving high-quality conformal interconnection.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 1. INTRODUCTION
blocks.text: Typically, polyether macromolecules (e.g., polyethylene glycol, PEG) serve as suppressors; bridged by chloride ions, they profoundly enhance cathodic polarization and retard copper growth. 14 Sulfonate compounds bearing thiol or disulfide groups (e.g., bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide, SPS) act as accelerators: they capture Cu 2+ at the cathode interface and lower the activation barrier for its reduction. 15 Among the plating formulations, the leveler plays the most critica interfacial regulatory role. By preferentially adsorbing at strongly convected regions (e.g., the opening), the leveler establishes a localized high-impedance barrier that inhibits overplating, 16−18 thereby compelling the spatial electric field lines to redistribute deeper into TH. 19−21 To date, various commercial dyes have been reported as levelers (e.g., Janus Green B, tetrazolium blue chloride, PAN). 22−24 Meanwhile, some researchers have devoted eforts to the synthesis of nove polymeric levelers (e.g., VIBDGE, PBDGE, Sudan-QNL). 25−27 Nevertheless, each of the aforementioned levelers exhibits specific limitations.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 1. INTRODUCTION
blocks.text: Polymeric levelers such as VIBDGE and PBDGE, despite their promising performance, typically require multistep synthesis and tedious purification procedures, which considerably increase the production cost and hinder their practical scalability. Commercial dye-based levelers (e.g., Janus Green B) are readily accessible and have been widely adopted in industry with proven efectiveness; however, as the aspec ratio of through-holes continues to increase, further enhance ment of throwing power remains highly desirable to ensure the thickness uniformity and long-term reliability of the copper interconnects. In this regard, MTT ofers a compelling combination of advantages: it is a commercially available, of the-shelf reagent that can be directly procured at low cost entirely eliminating the need for custom synthesis or purification, and as will be demonstrated in Section 3.5, it delivers a throwing power (TP = 96.8%) that markedly outperforms the conventional leveler JGB (TP = 84.5%) under identical bath composition and process conditions.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 1. INTRODUCTION
blocks.text: Therefore, a systematic investigation of MTT as a tailored leveler for high aspect-ratio PCB through-hole electroplating is of urgent practical significance.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 1. INTRODUCTION
blocks.text: It is worth noting that MTT has previously been explored in other copper electrodeposition contexts. Ogutu et al. first introduced MTT as a single additive for superconformal filling of through-glass vias (TGVs) with aspect ratios up to 10:1 in methanesulfonate-based electrolytes. 28 More recently, Yang et al. compared MTT with iodonitrotetrazolium chloride (INT) in a sulfate-based acidic electroplating system for blind via copper filling and reported that MTT exhibits a conformal type filling tendency rather than the bottom-up superfilling behavior required for microvia applications. 29 However, the performance of MTT in high-aspect-ratio PCB through-hole electroplating�an application scenario in which conformal, uniform thickness distribution rather than bottom-up super filling is the primary objective�has not yet been systematically investigated. The present work therefore complements these prior studies by examining MTT as a leveler within a sulfate based acidic electroplating system specifically tailored for through-hole plating, thereby establishing the suitability of MTT for this distinct application scenario.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 1. INTRODUCTION
blocks.text: It should also be noted that our group recently reported tetrazolium blue chloride (TB) as a leveler for copper through-hole electro plating. Although TB and MTT both belong to the tetrazolium family, their molecular architectures difer considerably: TB bears two methoxy-phenyl substituents on the tetrazolium ring, whereas MTT carries a 4,5-dimethylthiazole moiety together with two unsubstituted phenyl groups. Such substituent diferences lead to distinguishable electrochemical responses and leveling outcomes. At their respective optimized conditions, TB exhibits a relatively large convection-dependent polarization response with Δη ≈ 31 mV, yielding a TP value of 136.7% along with preferential Cu(111) growth, whereas MTT, as demonstrated in the present study, shows a smaller Δη ≈ 19.3 mV and afords a TP value of 96.8% accompanied by a preferential Cu(200) growth (see Sections 3.4 and 3.5).

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 1. INTRODUCTION
blocks.text: A recent comparative investigation by Yang et al. likewise reported that MTT exhibits filling characteristics distinct from those of its nitro-substituted tetrazolium analog INT, further supporting the notion that subtle substituent variations within the tetrazolium family can give rise to markedly diferent leveling behaviors. 29 These observations together underscore that MTT represents a distinct leveler within the tetrazolium family and warrants dedicated investigation for high-aspect-ratio PCB through-hole electroplating applications.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 1. INTRODUCTION
blocks.text: This work systematically investigates the application performance of thiazolyl blue tetrazolium bromide (MTT) as a highly eficient leveler in PCB TH electroplating. Utilizing scanning electron microscopy and laser confocal microscopy, the exceptional microscopic leveling efect of MTT on the surface morphology of the electrodeposited copper layer is intuitively revealed. Furthermore, X-ray difraction and contact angle measurements are employed to deeply analyze its regulatory efects on crystallographic phase evolution and solid−liquid interfacial wettability. More importantly, this study establishes a multiscale analytical framework integrating macroscopic electrochemical analyses with microscopic quantum chemical calculations to comprehensively elucidate the TH filling mechanism of MTT under multiphysics coupling. Ultimately, through precise optimization of the additive concentration ratio and related processing parameters, high-quality conformal electrodeposition in high-aspect-ratio PCB THs is successfully realized.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 2.2. Electrochemical Tests
blocks.text: All electrochemical measurements were performed in a standard three-electrode electrolysis cell, with test control and data collection accomplished using a Gamry Reference 3000 potentiostat/galvanostat (Gamry Instruments, USA). A 5 mm-diameter platinum disk rotating electrode (RDE) was selected as the working electrode (WE). A platinum sheet electrode ( 1 \ × \ 2 \ ~cm ^2) was used as the counter electrode, and a saturated mercurous sulfate electrode (SSE, Hg/ Hg _2 SO _4) served as the reference electrode (RE). Cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements were conducted over a potential window of −0.8 to 0.2 V (vs SSE). Prior to electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) characterization, a copper layer was electrodeposited onto the RDE surface in the virgin makeup solution (VMS) at a constant current density of 1.5 A dm −2 for 60 s, thus converting the Pt-RDE to a Cu-RDE. EIS measurements were executed at 1000 rpm with an alternating current (AC) amplitude of 10 mV, a direct current (DC) bias potential of −0.5 V (vs SSE), and a frequency sweep range of 10 to 10 −2 Hz. For chronopotentiometry (CP) tests, a constant current density of 2 Adm ^- 2 was applied to the electrode system.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 2.2. Electrochemical Tests
blocks.text: Under normal conditions, the rate of cathodic copper electrodeposition is positively correlated with the forced convection intensity of the plating bath because forced convection reduces the thickness of the Cu ^2 + difusion boundary layer. However, the plating bath contains not only Cu ^2 + but also various additives, which greatly complicate the mass transfer process at the cathode surface. According to the convection-dependent adsorption mechanism (CDA), a qualified plating bath system should exhibit the following behavior: a faster copper deposition rate under weakly forced convection and a relatively slower rate under strongly forced convection. 30

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 2.3. Characterization
blocks.text: The microstructure of the electrodeposited copper layers was systematically characterized via multidimensional analytical approaches. A field-emission scanning electron microscope (Zeiss Supra55, Germany) was utilized to observe the surface morphology under an acceleration voltage of 5 kV. The surface roughness parameter (Sa) was quantitatively analyzed using an ultra-depth-of field 3D microscope (Olympus DSX510), and the average roughness (Sa) of each sample was calculated as the mean value of measurements obtained from three diferent regions. X-ray difraction (XRD, Bruker D8) was employed to investigate the preferential crystal plane orientation of the electrodeposited copper layers, and the measurements were performed at a voltage of 40 kV and a current of 40 mA, with continuous scanning at a rate of 0.0 2^°/s over a 2θ range of 20−90°. An optical contact angle meter (Dataphysics-OCA20) was adopted to evaluate the interfacial properties, where 4 μL droplets were used for each test, and the average value was obtained from measurements conducted at five diferent positions.

All visualization results were rendered and output using the VMD 1.9.3 program. 36 The adsorption behavior of MTT molecules on the Cu(111) surface was investigated through calculations performed with the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP). 37,38 For structural optimization, the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) was adopted as the exchange−correlation functional, which was parametrized using the Perdew−Burke− Ernzerhof (PBE) functional. 39 Ion-electron interactions were described and calculated by employing the projector augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotential.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 3.1. Surface Analysis of Electroplated Copper Layer
blocks.text: The regulatory efect of the MTT additive on the surface morphology of the electrodeposited copper layers was systematically investigated utilizing a scanning electron microscope and a laser confocal microscope. As depicted in Figure ^1b, the copper coating electrodeposited in VMS (without MTT) exhibits a distinctly rough and uneven morphology, characterized by the presence of large and coarse crystalline particles on the surface. In sharp contrast, upon the introduction of MTT into the plating bath (Figure 1c−g), the surface flatness of the coatings shows a dramatic enhancement. With an incremental increase in MTT concentration, the crystalline morphology transitions progressively toward a highly compact and smooth state. This observation unambiguously indicates that MTT possesses excellent leveling capability at the microscopic scale, efectively refining the grain size and upgrading the surface quality. This conclusion was further substantiated by the three-dimensional (3D) surface topography mapping. As illustrated in Figures S1 and S2, the surface roughness of the deposited layers decreases precipitously with elevating MTT concentrations, dropping from 0.545 to 0.147 μm.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 3.1. Surface Analysis of Electroplated Copper Layer
blocks.text: Such a smooth surface characteristic is highly advantageous for high-frequency signal transmission in printed circuit boards (PCBs). During high-frequency signal propagation, dictated by the skin efect, 41 the skin depth of the alternating current becomes increasingly shallow at higher frequencies. When the skin depth diminishes to a scale comparable to the surface roughness of the copper traces, the high-frequency current is forced to travel along the tortuous, rugged surface contour, thereby substantially elongating the actual conductive pathway. Consequently, a copper deposit with inherently low surface roughness can substantially reduce the transmission loss of high-frequency signals. In summary, functioning as a highly eficient leveler, MTT can significantly enhance the surface flatness and compactness of the electro plated copper layers, fulfilling the stringent physical requirements for high-frequency interconnects.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 3.2. Electrochemical Analysis
blocks.text: Cyclic voltammetry (CV) is widely employed to preliminarily evaluate the inhibitive eficacy of additives during electrodeposition. 42 As illustrated in Figure 2a, the cathodic onset potential for copper deposition in the virgin makeup solution (VMS) without MTT is approximately −0.43 V. In contrast, the introduction of merely 20 mg/L MTT significantly intensifies the cathodic polarization, causing the onset potential to shift negatively to −0.61 V. With a further increase in MTT concentration, the cathodic overpotential continues to escalate; when the MTT concentration reaches 60 mg/ L, the onset potential further decreases to −0.67 V. This evolutionary trend is highly consistent with the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) results in Figure 1c, robustly confirming that MTT exerts a severe suppressing efect on the copper electrodeposition process. Notably, once the MTT concen tration is increased to 50 mg/L, the increment in overpotential driven by concentration elevation approaches saturation, indicating that the surface adsorption and the corresponding inhibitive efect of MTT have been maximized.

blocks.text: Furthermore, the charge density derived from the integrated area of the anodic stripping peak in the CV curves can be employed as a reliable indicator for the quantitative assessment of the inhibition performance of MTT. Figure 2b reveals that the anodic stripping coulomb of VMS is 1 2 1.8 6~C/ dm ^2, which drastically decreases to 9 1.3 7~C/dm^2 upon the addition of 20 mg/L MTT. When the concentration is elevated to 60 mg/L, the stripping coulomb plummets to 3 2.6 2C/ dm ^2, representing a 73.2% reduction compared to that of VMS. This remarkable decrease in anodic stripping coulomb further corroborates the profound suppression of copper deposition induced by MTT. 43,44 To deeply investigate the interfacial suppression mechanism of MTT, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) analysis was conducted. The radius of the impedance semicircle in the Nyquist plot intuitively reflects the resistance of charge transfer kinetics; a larger radius signifies a more dificult interfacial charge transfer process. The impedance data were fitted using an R _u : ( CPE - R _ct) equivalent circuit model, and the extracted parameters are summarized in Table S1.

The potential diference ( Δ η) between 100 and 1000 rpm under various MTT concentrations can be calculated to evaluate the microvia filling performance; typically, a larger Δ η is more conducive to achieving excellent superfilling. Figure 2g demonstrates that as the MTT concentration increases from 20 mg/L to 50 mg/L, Δη broadens significantly from 3.4 mV to 19.3 mV. However, with a further increase in MTT concentration, Δη follows a descending trend. The relatively high Δη values maintained within the concentration window of 40−50 mg/L suggest that this range is optimal for the conformal filling of through-holes. blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 3.3. Theoretical Insights into the Inhibition Mechanism
blocks.text: In this section, Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations were conducted to unravel the interfacial adsorption and coordination efects of MTT during copper electrodeposition, thereby systematically elucidating its inhibition mechanism at the microscopic scale. The optimized geometric configuration of the MTT molecule is depicted in Figure S3. Frontier Molecular Orbital theory is extensively employed to analyze and predict the interfacial adsorption behavior of molecules. As illustrated in Figure 3a, the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) are predominantly localized on the tetrazole and thiazole rings, indicating that these functional groups serve as active centers for preferential adsorption. 10,48 Furthermore, the surface electrostatic potential distribution histogram (Figure 3c) reveals that the overall MTT molecule is positively charged, 49,50 possessing a remarkably high average surface electrostatic potential of 65.23 kcal/mol. Driven by robust electrostatic attraction during the electrodeposition process, MTT is highly prone to adsorbing onto the cathodic surface, thereby efectively suppressing copper reduction.

blocks.section: Thiazolyl Blue as a High-Eficiency Leveler for Conformal Copper Electrodeposition in High-Aspect-Ratio PCB Through-Holes > 3.3. Theoretical Insights into the Inhibition Mechanism
blocks.text: To further probe the interfacial adsorption dynamics of MTT on the copper substrate, charge density diference calculations were performed to quantitatively assess its adsorption behavior (Figure 3d and e). The pronounced interfacial charge redistribution between the copper substrate and the MTT molecule decisively confirms their close geometric proximity and intense electronic interaction. Further thermodynamic calculations yield a highly negative adsorption energy of - 2.9 3 eV. This value is consistent with�and slightly more conservative than�the magnitude reported for MTT on Cu(111) under an essentially equivalent level of theory (PBE + Grimme D3 dispersion, slab calculation: E _ads ≈ - 8.1 4 \ eV; −785.93 kJ mol −1) by Yang et al., ^2 9 confirming that the strong MTT−Cu(111) interfacial adsorption is robustly captured by the present calculation. Collectively, these quantum chemica analyses substantiate that MTT can robustly adsorb onto the cathode surface during electroplating.
