blocks.text: Rigsby et al. 39 found that H_3 BO _3 could refine grain and reduce coating roughness, as shown in Fig. 6. Furthermore, when the content of H_3 BO _3 was too low, the trenches were sealed in advance, leaving many holes and gaps, as displayed in Fig. 7. The H_3 BO _3 plays a relatively complex role in cobalt electroplating interconnects. During the cobalt electroplat ing process, due to the continuous occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction, the pH value of the local electrolyte near the cathode surface increases significantly. The H_3 BO _3 must be converted into polyborates and the released H ^+ ions will reduce the local pH value and hinder the formation of Co ( OH) _2 near the cathode surface. 40 In addition, polyborates are easily adsorbed on the cathode surface, occupying active sites for atomic hydrogen electro-reduction and inhibiting the hydrogen evolution reaction. 41 Generally, most chemical substances are adsorbed on the electrode surface, which can inhibit the electrodeposition of metal ions. However, as the concentration of H_3 BO _3 increases, the adsorbed polyborate results in an increase in the current utilization rate of cobalt electrodeposition.

blocks.text: 39 That is to say, the mechanism of converting H_3 BO _3 into polyborates on the cathode surface, the mechanism of inhibiting the reduction of atomic hydrogen, the types of polyborates adsorbed on the cathode surface and their adsorption modes, and the mechanism of polyborates capturing metal ions to form complexes to improve current utilization are currently inconclusive. Research on H_3 BO _3 in cobalt electroplating interconnects is still in its preliminary stage and there is room for discussion on the mechanism, but what is certain is that H_3 BO _3 plays an indispensable role in cobalt electroplating from three aspects: stabilizing the pH, inhibiting surface hydrogen evolution, and promoting cobalt electrodeposition for high current utilization.

blocks.text: Metal cobalt is an iron group element, so the additives suitable for electroplating of iron group metals can be used for cobalt electroplating. Alkynol/enol compounds (including sulfonated compounds) are typical additives for cobalt electrodeposition. The molecular structure is shown in Fig. 8. However, to date, there are almost no reports on the use of alkynol/enol compounds for bottom-up superfilling of cobalt, and only a few studies have explored their reaction process on the surface of cobalt electrodes. Jin et al. 42 showed the molecule structure, adsorption ability, and electrochemical property of butynediol. Pan et al. 43 believed that the electrodeposited cobalt can catalyze the occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction, and the atomic hydrogen produced continuously reduced butynediol adsorbed on the cobalt electrode surface. Kiruba et al. 36 reported that butynediol can be reduced to butenediol on the cobalt electrode surface in the electroplating bath through Raman spectroscopy.

blocks.text: Oxime compounds are condensation compounds of hydroxylamine and aldehydes or ketones, which can inhibit cobalt electrodeposition and have the characteristics of potential and difusion dependence. Huang et al. 33,44 reported the efects of three oxime compounds, dimethylglyoxime (DMG), cyclohexane monoxime (CHO), and cyclohexane dioxime (CHD), on cobalt bottom-up superfilling. The structures of DMG, CHO, and CHD are presented in Fig. 9a. At low overpotentials, all three additives have an inhibiting efect on cobalt electrodeposition. At high overpotentials, the three additives lose their inhibiting ability, and, among them, DMG is more likely to be inactivated at a more positive potential. When a more negative potential (large current) is applied, oxime compounds lose their activity. At the same time, since oxime compounds also have mass transfer and difusion dependence, the oxime compounds at the via mouth are continuously replenished but cannot be replenished in time at the bottom. In other words, the cobalt electrodeposition rate is faster at the bottom, and, therefore, cobalt bottom-up superfilling can be achieved.

blocks.text: Dye additives are usually nitrogen-containing compounds, which are often regarded as levelers and applied to copper electroplating interconnects. 45–54 Dye additives have the characteristics of inhibiting metal electrodeposition and difusion dependence, so they can also be used for cobalt electroplating interconnects. Nitrotetrazolyl blue (NBT) and malachite green (MG) are the typical dye-type additives for cobalt electroplating, and their corresponding structures are shown in Fig. 10a. Li et al. 31 showed that NBT has a concentration gradient in the trench structure. As cobalt electrodeposition proceeds, the NBT content at the bottom of the trench is lower than that at the mouth, and therefore cobalt can be filled from bottom to top. Figure 10b shows the proposed difusion-dependent mechanism for cobalt bottom-up superfilling based on the NBT action mechanism. It is worth noting that, unlike copper electroplating, the bottom-up superfilling mechanism of cobalt electroplating is also related to the atomic hydrogen concentration on the electrode surface in addition to the type of additives.

blocks.section: Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication: A Review > Difusion‑Dependent and Induction–Difusion– Adsorption Mechanism
blocks.text: Some dye additives can promote the occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction, which afects the bottom-up superfilling efect by changing the cobalt electrodeposition current eficiency. Ma et al. 55 believed that MG can promote the generation of atomic hydrogen. There was a concentration gradient of MG in the trench, and the MG concentration was high at the trench mouth. At the same time, MG promoted the occurrence of the hydrogen evolution reaction at the trench mouth, resulting in a decrease in the current eficiency of cobalt electrodeposition there. In contrast, the current eficiency of cobalt electrodeposition at the bottom of the trench was high. Therefore, cobalt was densely superfilled from bottom to top. Based on this characteristic, an induction–dif fusion–adsorption mechanism suitable for cobalt bottom-up superfilling was proposed, as shown in Fig. 10c.

blocks.section: Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication: A Review > Diferential Current Eficiency Fill Mechanism
blocks.text: The above-mentioned cobalt bottom-up superfilling mechanism is closely related to the kinds of additives, but there are also some mechanisms that do not limit the kinds of additives, such as the diferential current eficiency fill (DCEF) mechanism. Rigsby et al. 56–58 considered that the local pH changes directly afected the concentration of hydroxide ions involved in the formation of intermediates, Co(OH)_ads, thereby increasing the reaction paths, changing the thermodynamics of cobalt electrodeposition, and adjusting the rate of cobalt electrodeposition. They confirmed that there was a concentration gradient of hydrogen ions in the via (high concentration at the mouth of via), and the current eficiency of cobalt electrodeposition at the bottom of the via was four times higher than that at the mouth by using cyclic voltammetry with electrochemical quartz microbalance technology. The formation of a pH gradient in the longitudinal direction of the via structure led to diferences in the cobalt electrodeposition rate and eficiency, which enabled bottom-up superfilling. Based on the experimental results, the DCEF mechanism was proposed and is shown in Fig. 11.

blocks.section: Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication: A Review > Hydrogen Reduction‑Induced Deactivation
blocks.text: Another mechanism that is not afected by the types of additives is the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation (HID) mechanism. Wu et al. 59,60 verified that the change of pH value afected the inhibiting ability of additives through cyclic voltammetry. During the cobalt electrodeposition process, a large amount of atomic hydrogen accumulates at the bottom of the via due to the large surface-to-volume ratio, and the inhibitor at the bottom of via is continuously protonated and loses the ability to inhibit the electro-reduction of cobalt ions. A schematic of the HID mechanism is presented in Fig. 12. According to the principles described in this mechanism, any additive that undergoes a transition between an inactive state and active state under the influence of hydrogen ions can control and achieve the cobalt bottomup superfilling.

blocks.text: For the S-NDR mechanism, it is often believed that whether or not the deposition is suppressed in metal superfilling is related to the adsorption and deactivation of the suppressant in the bath. If there is a suitable convection difusion gradient in the depth direction of the trench structure, cobalt filling from bottom to top can be achieved. This mechanism is limited by the type of additives, and oxime compounds often have this characteristic. For the difusion-dependent and induction–difusion–adsorption mechanisms, these are closely related to the hydrogen evolution reaction and diffusion. For the DCEF mechanism, this mechanism does not care about the type of additives. As long as a pH gradient can be formed in the trench structure, it can afect the cobalt electrodeposition rate and current eficiency at the bottom and the mouth, making the current density of cobalt electrodeposition at the bottom much higher than that at the mouth. However, to form a suitable pH gradient, the electroplating current density needs to be controlled below the limiting difusion current density of proton reduction in order to prevent the proton consumption rate from being much greater than the mass transfer rate and failing to achieve superfilling. For the HID mechanism, this mechanism also does not care about the type of additive. The specific surface area at the bottom of the trench is large, and more atomic hydrogen gathers here. As long as the additive can be reduced and inactivated by atomic hydrogen, superfilling can be achieved.

The current density efect will still provide more hydrogen in the feature area, and superfilling continues to occur, resulting in mushroom-shaped bulges. blocks.section: Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication: A Review > Surface and Interface Behavior of Cobalt
blocks.text: The surface and interface formed by the electrode and the bath are important reaction sites in the cobalt electroplating process. Diferent from the traditional conventional electroplating, cobalt electroplating interconnects are carried out in the micro-/nanovia or trench with a certain aspect ratio, in which surface and interface structure, potential distribution, metal nucleation and growth mechanism, mass transfer process, additive molecular action mechanism, etc. are more complex. Therefore, it is significantly important to clarify the structure of the surface and interface of electroplating and the mechanism of cobalt electrodeposition to accelerate the fundamental research and improve development eficiency.

blocks.section: Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication: A Review > Nucleation and Growth
blocks.text: The nucleation and growth process of cobalt interconnect wires has a huge impact on their stability and resistivity. Pagnanelli et al. 70 found that increasing the overpotential of cobalt electrodeposition will increase the number of active sites on the surface, resulting in an increase in the density of cobalt nuclei and a significant decrease in grain size. Mehmood et al. 71 confirmed that the overpotential of cobalt electrodeposition is closely related to its growth structure. High overpotential is conducive to the formation of facecentered cubic cobalt clusters with a small core radius. In addition, pH has an efect on the nucleation of micron-scale cobalt, but has no efect on the nucleation of nanoscale cobalt. 72 Mukhtar et al. 73 showed that the concentration of cobalt ion has a significant efect on its nucleation. When the concentration is low, the cobalt nucleus is larger and the structure is hexagonal close-packed. As the concentration is high, the cobalt nucleus is smaller and the structure is facecentered cubic. A schematic is shown in Fig. 13.

blocks.section: Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication: A Review > Nucleation and Growth
blocks.text: The presence of additives can also afect the nucleation behavior of cobalt. Hu et al. 34 reported the nucleation and growth process of cobalt under the action of diferent additives (DMG, CHD). As shown in Fig. 14, there was a twostep nucleation process on the electrode surface, including electro-reduction of cobalt coordination ions (formed by additives and cobalt ions) and direct electro-reduction of cobalt ions. Furthermore, Hu et al. 74 also discovered that the threshold potential for nucleation decreased upon the increase of furil dioxime concentration, and the deposition was found to follow the progressive nucleation behavior for almost all cases.

blocks.section: Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication: A Review > Electrochemical Oscillation
blocks.text: The phenomenon that an autocatalytic reaction causes a positive feedback loop is regard as electrochemical oscillation. 75–78 The self-adsorption/desorption, decomposition and competitive adsorption of additives on the electrode surface may change the kinetic mechanism of metal ion electro-reduction, resulting in electrochemical oscillation, and periodic changes in current or potential within a certain range. 78–81 Numerous studies on electrochemical oscillation for copper interconnects have been reported, 82–85 but, to the best of our knowledge, only one report on the electrochemical oscillation of cobalt interconnects has been published. Hu et al. 86 reported that 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) can lead to an electrochemical oscillation. The main positive feedback loops resulting in oscillation are autocatalytic accumulation and dissolution of cobalt hydroxide, which are triggered by the potential-dependent adsorption and desorption of the Co-MPS complex. Figure 15 shows the potential oscillation phenomen0n and mechanism of cobalt.

blocks.section: Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication: A Review > Potential Future Direction
blocks.text: At present, the study of cobalt electroplating often obtains average information of various thermodynamics and kinetics of the electrode/solution interface and electrode surface processes at the macrolevel by using classical electrochemical research methods and theoretical calculations. However, classical electrochemical research methods find it dificult to identify the characteristics of electrode reaction intermediates and products, and cannot provide mechanism information at the microscopic and molecular levels. Some advanced in situ characterization methods are used in copper electroplating. 96–99 Therefore, advanced electrochemical in situ research methods should be used in the future. In addition, annealing treatment of cobalt coatings is also a future research direction.

blocks.section: Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication: A Review > Conclusions
blocks.text: Electroplating is a critical technology in high-end electronic manufacturing, including integrated circuits. As interconnect dimensions continue to shrink, copper electroplating is increasingly unable to meet the required performance and safety standards. Cobalt, with its superior electrical properties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, is emerging as a promising next-generation interconnect material to replace copper. Although there have been reports on cobalt electroplating, current research has primarily focused on the electrochemical behavior of cobalt ions and additives, the role of additives, and the filling efects in trenches and vias, along with proposed filling mechanisms. However, several key aspects remain insuficiently explored. These include the specific actions and synergistic/antagonistic interactions of components such as boric acid and additives in the plating bath, the mechanisms by which pH, temperature, and individual bath components influence cobalt nucleation and growth, and the surface, interface, and filling processes during cobalt electrodeposition in micro-/nanostructures.

blocks.document_id: 先进芯片制造中的钴电镀互连技术综述
blocks.section: Cobalt Electroplating Interconnects in Advanced Chip Fabrication: A Review > Conclusions
blocks.text: Future research directions should prioritize the development and application of advanced in situ techniques, including morphological, spectroscopic, and energy spectroscopic, to address these challenges. Clarifying these mechanisms will be essential for advancing cobalt electroplating as a viable interconnect technology in next-generation chip fabrication.

blocks.section: Study on the electrochemical deposition behavior and blind hole filling behavior of Cobalt under the regulation of hexamethylenetetramine as a leveling agent > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: The metal cobalt is expected to be the next generation of interconnect materials due to its shorter average free path of electrons and greater resistance to electromigration. Additives especially the leveling agents are key regulatory factors for achieving a bottom-up dense superfilling of interconnect metals in the electroplating process. Here the hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) with methylene structure was chosen as a leveling agent to study the deposition behavior and the blind hole filling behavior of cobalt. The electrochemical analysis showed that the HMTA exhibits an evident inhibition ability on the deposition of cobalt. Moreover, this inhibitory ability has a significant dependence on the rotational speed of the solution and a greater inhibitory effect on the deposition of cobalt occurs at high rotational speeds.The simulation indicates that such a strong inhibition ability on the deposition of cobalt sourced from the preferred adsorption of the leveling agent on the cobalt surface by the nucleophilic active site provided by the methylene structure of HMTA.

Under the action of this leveling agent, the metal cobalt exhibits the expected bottom-up growth behavior in blind holes of Printed circuit board (PCB) The addition of HMTA is also beneficial for obtaining a flat and dense coating with preferred growth of (100) crystal planes. These results indicate that the HMTA is a potential effective leveling agent for the cobalt interconnects processes.

blocks.section: Study on the electrochemical deposition behavior and blind hole filling behavior of Cobalt under the regulation of hexamethylenetetramine as a leveling agent > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Cu interconnect has become a typical interconnect technology for large-scale and ultra large scale integrated circuits due to its excellent conductivity, high reliability, and resistance to electromigration [1]. However, as the feature size of the chip process decreases to below 10 nm, the resistance of Cu interconnect will significantly increase [2], which will seriously affect the reliability and communication speed improvement of the chip [3]. Therefore, finding more suitable conductive materials for filling nanoscale interconnect has become the key to chip micro integration along Moore’s Law. Metal cobalt is expected to replace copper interconnect as the next generation of interconnect materials in chip processes due to its lower average free path of electrons, smaller size effect, and better resistance to electromigration compared to copper [4]. Therefore, cobalt interconnect have become one of the research hotspots in the field of chip processes in recent years. The current chip copper interconnect mainly adopts the damascus electrodeposition process.

blocks.document_id: 六亚基四甲四胺
blocks.section: Study on the electrochemical deposition behavior and blind hole filling behavior of Cobalt under the regulation of hexamethylenetetramine as a leveling agent > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In the damascus electrodeposition process, the application of two typical additives, namely inhibitors and accelerators, is necessary to obtain high-quality electroplating filling layers [5]. Inhibitors and accelerators are selectively adsorbed in the chip groove hole area to suppress copper deposition and at the bottom of the groove to accelerate copper deposition. With the synergistic effect of these two types of additives, copper can achieve dense filling from bottom to top from the groove hole bottom [6]. Given the filling copper process of electroplating copper in damascene, recent research on cobalt interconnect has mainly focused on seeking suitable accelerators and inhibitors to achieve bottom-up cobalt super filling in trenches and some suitable additives for cobalt super filling have been proposed.

blocks.section: Study on the electrochemical deposition behavior and blind hole filling behavior of Cobalt under the regulation of hexamethylenetetramine as a leveling agent > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In the research on cobalt interconnect electroplating accelerators, recent researchers have mainly attempted to use accelerators used in the damascus copper interconnect electroplating process as accelerators for cobalt interconnect electroplating to explore their effects on cobalt deposition behavior and filling ability.These accelerators typically contain specific functional groups such as (-S-S-), thiols (-SH), and sul fonic acids ( - S 0 _ 3) [7]. For example, Ni Xiuren [8] used a series of electrochemical methods to study the depolarization and polarization behavior of sodium 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) and poly vinylpyrrolidone (PVP) during cobalt electrodeposition. It wa concluded that the amide group of PVP and the thiol group of MPS may be adsorption sites for cobalt electrodeposition. Four different sizes o practical cobalt pillars were successfully electrodeposited through electroplating experiments, thereby promoting the application of metallic cobalt in electronic packaging, resulting in uniform cobalt de posits.

blocks.text: Cao Wei [9] studied the adsorption behavior of three additives glutamic acid (DMG), 3-mercaptoacetic acid (SPS), and histidine (HIS) on the cathode surface during cobalt electrodeposition. The result indicate that the adsorption sites during cobalt electrodeposition ar provided by functional groups such as the imine group of DMG, the sulfonic acid group of SPS, and the imidazole group of HIS. However, th actual effects of these three additives need further research. Compare to accelerators, inhibitors play a more critical role in achieving bottom-up cobalt dense super filling, However, inhibitors applied t damascus copper interconnects are not suitable for electroplated cobal interconnects. Therefore, in recent years, research on cobalt intercon nect electroplating filling has mainly explored more suitable inhibitors and proposed some quaternary ammonium salts and nitrogen-containing derivatives as inhibitors for cobalt interconnect electroplating [10]. For example, Hu et al. blocks.text: Wu Yunwen et al. [15] studied the effects of three additives with un saturated carbon bonds, 1,4-butynediol (BYD), 1,4-butenediol (BED) and ethylene glycol (EG), on cobalt electrodeposition to reveal the po tential mechanism of unsaturated carbon atom bonds in cobalt electro deposition. Research has found that cobalt thin films prepared by BYD electrodeposition have lower resistance and more compact morphology After adding BYD, the crystal surface of the Co film changed from a mixture of elongated ridges and particle shapes to a flat particle struc ture. This conclusion indicates that additives can customize the orien tation and properties of cobalt. Then, he studied another additive phenylmethylsulfone (PMSO) [16], as the main additive for cobal electrodeposition. The results indicate that PMSO has a strong inhibitor effect on cobalt electrodeposition, and the sulfoxide groups in PMSO preferentially adsorb on the cathode surface, exhibiting high chemica reactivity.

blocks.text: As the concentration of PMSO increases, the nucleation pro cess of cobalt shifts from non transient nucleation to gradual nucleation and the surface morphology of cobalt also changes from rough to dense and flat, which can effectively fill high-quality cobalt through-silicon via (TSV) grooves, indicating that PMSO is an effective additive for cobalt electrodeposition. At present, most of the leveling agents used in cobalt electroplating are polymer nitrogen-containing compounds, but these leveling agents are prone to decomposition at high temperatures, mak ing the electroplating process difficult to control, resulting in poor experimental stability, which is not conducive to repeated operations, and also leads to quality problems in the coating. However, the high price of macromolecular compounds increases the experimental cost, which is not conducive to the subsequent production process. blocks.section: Study on the electrochemical deposition behavior and blind hole filling behavior of Cobalt under the regulation of hexamethylenetetramine as a leveling agent > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Recently, some studies indicated that the nitrogen-containing com pounds can form coordination bonds with the cobalt surface or Co ^2 + [17–20] by utilizing the lone pair electrons of nitrogen and thereby produce effectively suppress the reduction of cobalt. The HMTA is a kind of nitrogen-containing small molecule compounds containing methylene structures, which indicates that the HMTA is a potential inhibitor for cobalt deposition. Meanwhile, this HMTA is a stable compound that is not easily decomposed at high temperatures. Therefore, in this work, the HMTA molecules was selected to be as leveling agents for cobalt interconnect electrodeposition. The electrochemical experiments including cyclic voltammetry (CV), linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), and galvanostatic method (GM) were first used to analyze the deposition behavior of cobalt under HMTA leveling. The quantum chemistry calculation and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation were used to predict the adsorption active sites and the adsorption behavior of HMTA molecules at the cobalt surface and the corresponding quantum chemistry parameters including the energy gap, electrostatic potential and adsorption energy were calculated.

The nucleation process of cobalt in blind holes and bottom regions were analyzed through timed current experiments. blocks.text: All electrochemical tests, including CV, LSV, and GMs, were performed in a three-electrode system connected to an electrochemical workstation (CHI660C). The working electrode is a platinum rotating disk electrode (Pt-RDE) with a diameter of 5 mm, and the counter electrode (CE) is a platinum wire electrode (Shanghai Raymagnetic Instruments Co., Ltd.), the reference electrode (RE) is a saturated mercurous sulfate electrode (Hg/Hg₂SO₄) (Shanghai Leimagnetic Instruments Co., Ltd.). In the electrochemical tests, the velocity of the working electrode was adjusted to 1600 rpm and 100 rpm to simulate strong and weak convection in the blind hole, respectively [21]. In the voltage range from 0 to −1.6 V, the cyclic voltammetry is scanned, the scanning speed is 0.01 V / s, scanning 2 segments. At a scan rate of 0.02 V/s, the LSV are scanned from 0 \ to - 1.6 \ V. The constant current measurement requires pre-plating for 300 s at 1000 rpm. at a voltage of −0.15 V to deposit a cobalt layer on the working electrode at a set current density of 1. A/dm2. Then accelerator (MPS) and leveling agent (HMTA) were added to the basic plating bath for determination.

After optimization, the energy density distribution and electrostatic potential (ESP) of the frontier orbits (HOMO and LUMO) were detected visually, and the energy gap was calculated by the formula. blocks.text: In order to further study the inhibition ability of HMTA, quantum chemical calculations were also used to predict the adsorption active sites of HMTA on the metal surface. In this paper, we performed quantum chemical calculations on HMTA using Device Studio software. According to the frontier orbital theory, the Homo value represents the tendency of molecules to lose electrons, while the E _LUMO value represents the tendency of molecules to accept electrons. The higher the E HOMO and E_LUMO, the greater the ability to give and receive electrons. The energy gap value (ΔE) is also an important parameter to characterize the adsorption capacity of organic molecules on the metal surface. If ΔE is small, the molecular reaction activity is high The lower adsorption energy indicates that the additive itself has stronger adsorption ability on the metal surface and has greater inhibition on the electroreduction of cobalt ion. blocks.text: In order to explain the effect of the leveling agent HMTA on the crystalline structure of electrodeposited cobalt with HMTA, the crystalline structure of the cobalt layer under different electrolytes were also analyzed by XRD and the corresponding results are shown in Fig. 14. The crystal planes of the cobalt layer obtained in the electrolyte containing 14 ppm MPS are (110), (101), and (110). On this basis, the crystal planes of the cobalt layer obtained by adding 13 ppm HMTA molecules are (100), (002), and (101). From the Fig. 14, it can be seen that compared with the electrolyte containing 14 ppm MPS, the cobalt coating with 13 ppm HMTA molecules showed a decrease in diffraction peak intensity at the (100) crystal plane at 41.27◦ and the (110) crystal plane at 75.73◦, while the diffraction peak intensity related to the (002) crystal plane at 44.04◦ increased. This indicates that the leveling agent HMTA can inhibit the growth of (100) and (100) crystal planes, and preferentially promote the formation of cobalt crystals along the (002) crystal plane.

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: In advanced electronic manufacturing, additives play a pivotal role in achieving high-quality metal interconnect by enabling precise pattern filling during electrodeposition. Currently, due to complex mechanisms, vast molecular spaces and lack of predictive models, the development of additives still relies on inefficient trial-and-error methods. In this work, a machine learning (ML)-based data-driven framework is developed to accelerate the discovery of cobalt electrodeposition additives. Focusing on molecular adsorption dynamics at the cobalt elec trolyte interface during electrodeposition, this work employs quantum chemical properties to guide the construction of machine learning models for identifying molecules with ideal adsorption potential. Bayesian optimization is employed to optimize model accuracy by tuning hyperparameters, and SHAP analysis provides interpretable chemical insights. Three novel additives are identified, which are 2-aminopyrazine (APZ), 1-methylimidazole-4,5-dicarbonitrile (MIDCN), and 2-amino-4-ethylpyridine (AEP).

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: As advanced chip manufacturing technologies trend toward miniaturization in the post-Moore's Law era, cobalt (Co) has been proposed as a promising alternative to replace copper (Cu) in advanced semiconductor applications [1–4] due to its superior electrical performance [5,6] and interconnect reliability at the nanoscale [7]. Electrodeposition is the predominant technique for Co interconnects [8,9]. Organic additives are decisive for modulating deposition kinetics and achieving high quality Co interconnects, such as surface planarization [10] and defectfree superfilling in submicron patterns.

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In recent years, many studies have focused on the development of additives for cobalt superconformal electrodeposition and the underlying superfilling mechanisms [11–16]. It has been found that molecules influence the electrode process through their adsorption and interactions with the metal surface [17]. These interactions can be eluci dated by Frontier Molecular Orbital (FMO) theory [18], where a higher highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) energy indicates a stronger electron donation capability, while a lower lowest unoccupied molec ular orbital (LUMO) energy suggests a greater tendency to accept electrons. Additionally, within the framework of the Hard-Soft Acid-Base (HSAB) principle [19], metallic cobalt ( Co ^0) is classified as a ‘soft acid and therefore exhibits a preferential affinity for ‘soft bases’ — molecules characterized by a narrow HOMO-LUMO gap (ΔE), as chemical hardness η ≈ \varDelta E / 2.

blocks.text: Consequently, in the electrodeposition field, ΔE has been considered as a practical criterion for identifying promising additives [20], as molecules with smaller ΔE values generally exhibit stronger adsorption affinity toward the metal surface and thus exert more significant regulatory effects on the electrodeposition process [21–24]. An et al. blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Organic additives for cobalt electrodeposition typically feature nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), or sulfur (S) heteroatoms. Studies have shown that S-containing molecules functionalized with disulfide (-S-S-), thiol (-SH), or sulfonate (-SO₃H) groups generally exhibit an accelerating effect in cobalt electroplating (e.g. MPS [21] and thiourea [26]). O-containing additives mainly affect metal-ion solvation and complexation [12], rather than functioning through strong interfacial adsorption where ΔE serves as a key predictor. Notably, inhibitory additives play a particularly critical role in cobalt interconnects, as cobalt superfilling can be accomplished with one-component suppressors [27,28]. Nitrogen-containing molecules, which can interact with the electrode surface through π-bonds and the lone pair electrons of nitrogen, and often exhibit suppressive behavior during the deposition process [29], are preferable to S- and O-containing additives for screening strategies targeting interfacial adsorption–dominated suppression. Furthermore, they present enhanced environmental and economic advantages [30].

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Finding effective additives is a challenge in the field of electrode position. Due to the absence of established screening criteria and the vastness of the chemical space of organic compounds, the process of discovering additives through traditional experimental trial-and-error methods resembles searching for a needle in a haystack and is both time-consuming and resource-intensive [31]. Quantum chemical prop erties enable the prediction of adsorption propensity, thereby accelerating additive screening [13]. However, DFT calculations for numerous molecules often require substantial computational resources and time. Therefore, a much more effective and cost-friendly screening method is essential for achieving high-efficiency screening of additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition. With the accumulation of databases in materials science, machine learning and data-driven strategies have made significant progress in materials discovery [32], property prediction and experiment optimization [33] by uncovering the statistical patterns embedded within extensive datasets and constructing quantitative structure-property relationship (QSPR) models [34–36].

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In this work, we propose a data-driven method to identify novel, high-efficiency, and environmentally friendly nitrogen-containing molecules as inhibitors for cobalt interconnections (Fig. 1). The computational details are described in the Methods section. We employed a DFT computational database to construct machine learning models. The molecular descriptors were calculated based on SMILES [39] (Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System) strings. They were further filtered through a three-step dimensionality reduction workflow. Six machine learning models were systematically compared. XGBoost achieved the best R 2 and MAE after Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) [40] analysis was applied to quantitatively evaluate each descriptor's contribution to ΔE predictions. Crucially, these feature analysis insights were translated into chemical implications. ML models were employed for high-throughput screening of a commercial molecular library, from which three promising addi tives were identified. Electrochemical measurements demonstrated the surface polarization capability of the additives.

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 2.1. Datasets and molecular descriptors
blocks.text: To enable comprehensive molecular screening, we extracted and established a CHN subset (over 14000 molecules containing only C, H, and N) derived from QM9 [41]—a public quantum chemistry database widely acknowledged to deliver high-fidelity quantum chemical properties for the comprehensive chemical space of small organic molecules in which all properties were computed via density functional theory (DFT) using the B3LYP functional and the 6-31G(2df, p) basis set. This dataset has been validated in computational chemistry research, covering diverse molecular topologies and functional groups of small organics, which provides sufficient structural diversity to avoid overfitting in subsequent machine learning modeling. We specifically selected the CHN subset to align with the study's focus on nitrogen containing additives, excluding molecules with other heteroatoms that could confound model training and prediction due to fundamentally different electrochemical mechanisms.

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 2.1. Datasets and molecular descriptors
blocks.text: Molecular descriptors were calculated by RDKit [42], which is a widely used open-source cheminformatics toolkit that provides molecular descriptors and fingerprints for machine learning applications. A total of 208 structural and chemical descriptors were calculated. High dimensional features elevate the risk of model overfitting and compromise generalization performance [43], thereby necessitating feature dimensionality reduction to eliminate redundant features while mini mizing the loss of core information. The process of feature engineering is summarized in Fig. 2a. Firstly, the number of features was filtered to 130 based on variance tests (ANOVA) with a threshold of 0.01 [44]. Next, importance scores for the remaining 130 descriptors were obtained using random forest algorithm, serving to further mitigate data vari ability [45]. Twenty-four descriptors were selected according to ranking of importance and 6 structure-based descriptors (prefixed with “fr”) were added to examine whether there is a relationship between func tional groups and target performance.

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 2.2. Machine learning models establishment and evaluation
blocks.text: The machine learning implementation was carried out using Scikitlearn [53], a widely used open-source Python module. The entire dataset was randomly partitioned into three parts, with a split of 60% for the training set, 20% for the test set, and 20% for the validation set. The substantial sample size ensures that this splitting strategy inherently preserves the consistency of target property distributions across subsets (Fig. S1). Specifically, the training set was employed for model fitting, while the test set was strictly held out and reserved exclusively for the final evaluation. The process of hyperparameter search via Bayesian optimization algorithm using the Optuna package [54] was conducted on the validation set [55], with the final parameters determined after at least 500 optimization iterations. Mean absolute error (MAE) and coefficient of determination (R 2) were used to evaluate the performance of different models [56].

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 2.3. Quantum chemical calculation
blocks.text: To verify the accuracy of the machine learning predictions, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the Gaussian 16W package. These calculations adopted the same B3LYP functional and 6-31G(2df, p) basis set as those used for the training dataset to ensure data consistency. Furthermore, to better emulate the electrochemical environment and capture weak intermolecular interactions, Grimme's D3 dispersion correction with Becke-Johnson damping (GD3BJ) and the Polarizable Continuum Model (PCM) with water as the solvent were employed—the former to compensate for the van der Waals forces neglected by B3LYP, and the latter to mimic the solvation effects in cobalt electrodeposition systems.

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 3.1. Performance evaluation of the ML models
blocks.text: The relationship between the optimized descriptors and ΔE was modeled using six ML algorithms, including XGBoost, RF, LightGBM, KNN, Ridge regression, and GB, as illustrated in Fig. 3. Among these, traditional methods (KNN and Ridge regression) exhibited limited predictive accuracy, with test R^2 values of 0.836 and 0.758, respectively (Fig. 3d, e). In contrast, the ensemble-based methods (XGBoost, RF, LightGBM, and GB) demonstrated better predictive performance, indicating that ΔE likely exhibits complex nonlinear relationships which simple linear or distance-based models struggle to capture [57] (Fig. 3a–c, f). The Random Forest (RF) model demonstrated exceptionally high goodness-of-fit on the training set (R^2= 0.9 9 1), yet its per formance on the test set was comparatively lower (R^2= 0.9 4 1), as shown in Fig. 3b. This discrepancy suggests the presence of a certain degree of overfitting, which occurs because the deep decision trees constituting the model overlearn specific details and noise from the training set, compromising the generalizability gained from prediction averaging [58].

The robustness of this model was further vali dated by 5-fold cross-validation (Table S2), ensuring that the predictive accuracy was not a result of favorable data partitioning. blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 3.2. Feature importance analysis by SHAP
blocks.text: Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) was employed to identify the most influential input descriptors [59]. It provides enhanced interpretability compared to conventional methods by elucidating both the magnitude and direction of feature impact on ΔE. Fig. 4a reveals the importance ranking of the descriptors based on the mean absolute SHAP values. It can be concluded that SMR_VSA7 is the primary descriptor influencing ΔE, whereas the six structure-based descriptors (e.g., fr_piperdine, fr_imidazole) exhibit negligible significance. This may be attributed to the fact that although functional groups alter the electronic structure, polarity, and steric environment of molecules, these effects are already captured by global descriptors that represent the molecule's overall charge and configurational properties.

Each data point represents a molecule, where red indicates greater feature values and blue indicates lower values. The x-axis represents the SHAP values of each feature, where positive and negative values indicate positive and negative contributions to the model's predictions, respectively. The predominance of red dots on the left side indicates that SMR_VSA7, BCUT2D_MRHI, and BertzCT exert a negative effect on ΔE—specifically, the larger their values, the smaller the predicted ΔE. In contrast, HallKierAlpha and FractionCSP3 show a positive association with ΔE. SMR_VSA7 rep resents the sum of the van der Waals surface areas of atoms contributing to the molar refractivity value within the range of 3.05 to 3.63 [60,61]. This reflects a relatively high polarizability interval, reflecting the surface exposure of atoms with moderately high polarizability within the molecule. blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 3.3. Screening small molecule and experimental verification
blocks.text: Based on the ML model, we can perform high-throughput ΔE predictions across a large molecular space for preliminary assessment. To rapidly advance these predictions to experimental validation, we employed a commercially available (CA) dataset with unknown ΔE as the prediction set. Every molecule in the dataset is quality-controlled, eliminating delays and costs associated with synthetic feasibility. Spe cifically, we mapped the chemical space of the training set onto the Sigma–Aldrich catalog and retrieved 4355 nitrogen-containing organic compounds. After prioritizing candidates based on the predicted ΔE values, the top 1% were flagged as promising additives. Considering accessibility, toxicity, and cost, we selected three molecules — 2-amino pyrazine (APZ), 1-methylimidazole-4,5-dicarbonitrile (MIDCN), and 2- amino-4-ethylpyridine (AEP) — for subsequent experimental verification (Table S4). These candidates exhibited favorable frontier orbital energy gaps (ΔE), underscoring their adsorption activity on the metal surface. Fig. 5a, d, and g illustrate their chemical structures and predicted ΔE values.

blocks.text: The effects of additives on cobalt electrodeposition were validated by electrochemical characterization. Fig. 6a-c show the potential transients during Chronopotentiometry (CP). A transient polarization appears immediately upon the addition of APZ and MIDCN, and a polarization for AEP is observed at concentrations above 50 ppm. Subsequently, all three additives cause increasingly cathodic polarization, ultimately resulting in voltage drops of 236, 244 and 119 mV for APZ, MIDCN and AEP, respectively, demonstrating a strong interaction between the ad ditives and the cobalt surface. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was used to further investigate the impact on Co electrodeposition at different concentrations of additives (Fig. 6d-f). The magnified views of the cobalt deposition potential range show a negative shift in deposition potential upon additives addition, as a more negative potential is required to drive the deposition reaction. The anodic stripping area decreases with increasing concentration for all three additives, indicating that they can effectively inhibit the deposition of cobalt [64].

blocks.text: In the initial stage of electrodeposition, additives uniformly adsorb onto the cobalt surface. As the deposition proceeds, the additive molecules within the TSV trenches are gradually depleted. Owing to mass transport constraints, the replenishment of additives inside the deep vias occurs at a slower rate than on the upper surface, resulting in a reduced inhibitor concentration within the trenches compared to the via opening. This concentration gradient leads to weaker suppression at the bottom of the via relative to its top. Consequently, the deposition rate is elevated at the bottom in comparison to the top, facilitating bottom-up filling and thereby enabling the formation of void-free interconnect structures.

blocks.section: Data-driven discovery of novel additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition in 3D interconnects > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: In summary, this study established a data-driven framework that integrates machine learning with experimental validation to efficiently identify novel, high-efficiency, and low-toxicity nitrogen-containing additives for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition. A comprehensive description of the molecules' physical properties was obtained using RDKit descriptors, and the key feature set was subsequently identified by integrating three feature selection strategies. Among the six evaluated ML models, XGBoost achieved the best predictive performance for ΔE prediction (R^2= 0.9 4 5). SHAP analysis revealed that descriptors associated with van der Waals surface area (SMR_VSA7) and molecular topology (HallKierAlpha) significantly influence ΔE. These findings provide interpretable insights that can guide the design of additive molecules. The trained model was applied to a commercial molecular database, successfully identifying APZ, MIDCN, and AEP as three promising candidate molecules. Experimental validation demonstrated that the three additives effectively induce cathodic polarization and exhibit significant inhibitory effects even at low concentrations.

blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants
blocks.text: M. A. Rigsby, L. J. Brogan, N. V. Doubina, Y. Liu, E. C. Opocensky, T. A. Spurlin, J. Zhou, and J. D. Reid Lam Research Corporation, 11155 SW Leveton Dr., Tualatin, Oregon 97062, USA Conventional damascene electroplating utilizes a combination of organic additives, namely, a suppressor, an accelerator, and a leveler, to achieve superconformal fill of interconnects. An alternative mechanism for superconformal cobalt fill is proposed here. This mechanism, the Differential Current Efficiency Fill (DCEF) mechanism, utilizes sacrificial oxidants to achieve voidfree superconformal fill. In the DCEF mechanism, the presence of a sacrificial oxidant, such as H +, O 2, or an organic additive, promotes a difference in metal deposition rate between the field and the feature bottom. Addition of a single suppressor-type additive assists in driving the plating rate differential. By appropriately selecting the sacrificial oxidants, organic additives, the waveform, and the mass transport conditions, void-free superconformal cobalt fill can be achieved in a variety of features.

blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Introduction
blocks.text: As interconnect dimensions continue to decrease, the extendibility of conventional copper damascene processing becomes increasingly problematic, in terms of yield and reliability. Small feature openings require thin seed to avoid having them close before the features can be filled (pinch-off) due to large overhang formation during seed deposition. The thin seed is susceptible to agglomeration, which leads to discontinuities and poor nucleation during the electrodeposition process. Reliability is also impacted by the decreasing line dimensions (1-2). Due to the higher current density in smaller lines, void formation occurs more readily, leading to decreasing electromigration lifetime as critical dimensions scale down. A third issue with decreasing dimensions is increasing RC delay and IR drop due to the exponential increase in resistivity with decreasing line crosssection (1-2). As such, the space occupied by the barrier layer within the feature becomes much more valuable.

blocks.document_id: 利用牺牲氧化剂实现钴的超共形填充
blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Introduction
blocks.text: To address these copper damascene extendibility issues, alternative metals, such as cobalt, are being actively explored for fill in smaller line dimensions (1-2). In terms of bulk resistivity, copper is significantly superior to cobalt. However, cobalt may not require a barrier layer, which frees up space within the feature for more metal. Because of the difference in barrier thickness, there may be a cross-over at narrow line widths such that a cobalt line will be less resistive than an equivalent copper line (3). Another benefit of removing the barrier is that the features are more open, decreasing the risk of discontinuous seed or pinch-off. Increasing the relative amount of metal within a line should also be advantageous for electromigration, as more metal would have to move to create a void. Additionally, the higher melting point of cobalt with respect to that of copper should lead to improved electromigration performance (1-2).

blocks.document_id: 利用牺牲氧化剂实现钴的超共形填充
blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Introduction
blocks.text: Superconformal cobalt fill does not follow the conventional damascene process, with suppressors, accelerators, and levelers. Rather, it can be achieved using a single organic additive. Previous studies have investigated the effect of various additives on cobalt fill in sub-micrometer trenches and through-silicon vias (4-6). Fill is typically attributed to a potential-dependent suppression effect that results in an S-shaped negative differential resistance. However, this mechanism may not hold for very small dimensions, on the order of tens of nanometers, as the ability to bifurcate into active and passive regimes is dependent on electrode dimensions (7-8).

blocks.document_id: 利用牺牲氧化剂实现钴的超共形填充
blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Introduction
blocks.text: New insights are presented for superconformal cobalt fill in nanometer-scale features through a proposed mechanism that the authors have termed the Differential Current Efficiency Fill (DCEF) mechanism. In the DCEF mechanism, the presence of one or more sacrificial oxidants promotes a difference in metal deposition rate between the field and the feature bottom by directly altering the deposition rate through current efficiency. Suppressor-type additives may promote the plating rate differential either by altering the kinetics of deposition or by behaving as a sacrificial oxidant, or both. It will be demonstrated that this strategy can be applied to achieve superconformal cobalt fill in nanometer-scale features.

blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Results and Discussion
blocks.text: To explore the mechanism that leads to superconformal cobalt fill, a series of electrochemical tests were done in combination with electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance (EQCM) experiments. Figure 2 compares the electrochemical and corresponding EQCM responses during a slow-sweep cyclic voltammogram at pH 2.5 and pH 4.0. The electrochemical data gives information about the suppression strength of the additives, but is complicated by the competing hydrogen evolution reaction and possible effects of pH on additive behavior, and so this type of data has only limited value. Because the EQCM is sensitive to mass change during the electrochemical process, it gives direct information on the amount of cobalt deposited under a given set of conditions, which is crucial when the system has competing reactions. In comparing these two plots, it is observed that the total current at a given potential is generally greater at the lower pH, but the cobalt partial current is greater at the higher pH. It can be concluded that hydrogen evolution is in strong competition with cobalt deposition and that it is, therefore, consuming a significantly greater portion of the current at lower pH.

blocks.text: From the data in Figure 2, current efficiency is an important factor in electrodeposition of cobalt. To further investigate this effect, EQCM experiments were done over a range of pH and current density. In Figure 3, the current efficiency derived from the EQCM has been plotted as a function of (A) the current density and (B) the potential. From Figure 3A, the current efficiency decreases with decreasing current density, and this effect is significantly enhanced by decreasing pH. Because both the onset of hydrogen evolution occurs at lower overpotential than that of cobalt deposition and the hydrogen evolution reaction kinetics are faster, current efficiency is low at the lower current densities (9). At high current density, the cobalt reduction dominates and the current efficiency is high.

blocks.text: Deposition rate is another factor that must be considered. Because this information is not as obvious from the voltammetric plots of Figure 2, Tafel plots were generated. Figure 4 presents Tafel plots based on the EQCM-derived cobalt partial current density at pH 2.5 and pH 4.0, both with and without Suppressor A in solution. The first feature that stands out is that the charge transfer coefficient is changed by the presence of the additive. This is as expected, because a suppressor-type additive should affect the reaction kinetics. This effect of the additive on the reaction kinetics is critical because of its impact on current efficiency. On the other hand, the charge transfer coefficient is not affected by changing pH. This means that the effect of pH on the cobalt deposition rate is not kinetic, but it rather must be thermodynamic, which is not expected for the direct deposition of a metal. However, the change in thermodynamics of deposition is clearly demonstrated in the plots. The onset potential for cobalt reduction, both with and without additive, shifts by ~-59 mV/pH, which is consistent with a reaction mechanism where hydroxide is involved.

blocks.text: In Figure 5, Tafel plots are again presented, this time with varying potential scan rate at two different pH. At slow scan rate and with no solution stirring during the potentiodynamic deposition, the system approaches an approximate steady state, meaning that the near-surface region is essentially at equilibrium. By increasing the scan rate, the system can be pushed further away from the steady-state condition, and changes in deposition rate may become observable through comparison of the potential shift between the forward and reverse scans. At slow scan rate, pH 2.5 and pH 4.0 exhibit a similar shift in potential that is due to the pH shift that comes from the mass-transport limited depletion of H ^+ near the electrode surface. Under the non-equilibrium conditions of high scan rate, however, a significant increase in the potential shift is observed at low pH, while the shift is unaffected at higher pH. Because the current efficiency is significantly lower at the lower pH, the proton concentration change is larger and the local pH shift during the potential scan is greater.

blocks.text: active sacrificial species ( H ^ +), organic additive) quickly develop within the feature due to the low current efficiency. The concentration gradients lead to a difference in current efficiency, thermodynamic deposition rate, and deposition kinetics between the base of the feature and the field. Bottom-up fill is then driven by the gradient-induced differentials and proceeds up the feature until the transport-induced concentration gradients are dissipated. At this point, fill shuts down, everything is equally suppressed, and deposition continues slowly and conformally. Because of the critical reliance on current efficiency to produce bottom-up fill, this mechanism has been termed the Differential Current Efficiency Fill mechanism (DCEF).

blocks.document_id: 利用牺牲氧化剂实现钴的超共形填充
blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Results and Discussion
blocks.text: Organic suppressor-type additives have been found to be crucial to achieving efficient bottom-up fill through the DCEF mechanism. The additives can play multiple roles in the fill process. By altering the kinetics of the deposition reaction, the additive can significantly lower the current efficiency, which maintains a very slow deposition rate on the field and assists in generating the pH gradient within the feature. Consumption of the organic additive within the feature would also generate an additive concentration gradient under the lower mass transport conditions, which decreases the overall suppression within the feature relative to on the field. Finally, depending on the pK a of the particular additive, its adsorption properties could be altered, further driving the field/base deposition rate differential.

blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Results and Discussion
blocks.text: Figure 7 uses the electrochemical and EQCM data to demonstrate an example of how the DCEF mechanism can work. In this hypothetical case, the starting pH is 2.7, Suppressor A is present in solution, and the applied current is 0.5 mA/cm. When current is initially applied, the potential depends on the bulk pH and suppressor concentration. At this initial potential, the cobalt partial current density is only ~0.1 mA/cm2. corresponding to about 20% current efficiency. As a pH gradient develops within the feature, the potential must shift to maintain a constant current density as the current efficiency and deposition rate change. Assuming in this hypothetical case that the H + concentration at the base decreases by a factor of a little more than ten to pH~4 and that the effective suppressor concentration approaches zero due to consumption and low mass transport, the potential would shift in the positive direction by ~70 mV. At this new potential, the cobalt partial current density at the feature base has increased to ~0.4 mA/cm2, corresponding to ~80% current efficiency.

blocks.document_id: 利用牺牲氧化剂实现钴的超共形填充
blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Results and Discussion
blocks.text: On the field, however, the pH and suppressor concentration will still be equal to the bulk values, so the cobalt partial current there is almost zero. So, in this hypothetical case, the cobalt deposition current at the base is ~13-14 fold higher than that on the field. This represents a significant differential in the deposition rate between the field and feature base, and would lead to rapid growth from the base of the feature with almost no plating on the field. Further, as the feature is filled from the bottom, the gradient changes due to the changing depth, and the deposition shifts back to higher overpotential until a mass-transport-determined steady-state condition is reached, at which point cobalt deposition will again be slow and conformal. Depending on the process, these shifts in potential may be large enough to observe experimentally, potentially providing a means to predict the endpoint of the fill process in simple cases.

blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Results and Discussion
blocks.text: The reliance on current efficiency-induced pH and additive gradients leads to some important implications for the DCEF mechanism. As an example, for high-aspect ratio features, the evolution of fill will be dependent on the current density that is selected. At very low current density, H + and additive will be depleted near the base of the feature only. This will lead to bottom-up deposition, but the fill will shut down too deep within the feature due to the depth of the H + /additive depletion zone. At higher current density, the H + /additive depletion zone will be at a shallower location within the feature, which

blocks.document_id: 利用牺牲氧化剂实现钴的超共形填充
blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Results and Discussion
blocks.text: could lead to undesirably fast deposition on the sidewalls and, therefore, pinch-off and seam formation. If the current density is high enough, the current efficiency will be too high to support formation of the appropriate concentration gradients, and deposition will be conformal rather than bottom-up. Thus, for deep features, stepping the current up during the fill process can assist in moving the depletion zone to more appropriate depths so that bottom-up fill can continue to completion.

blocks.document_id: 利用牺牲氧化剂实现钴的超共形填充
blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Results and Discussion
blocks.text: A similar effect would be expected when simultaneously filling features of varying dimensions. For the feature for which the process conditions were optimized, fill will be bottom-up and void-free. However, because the H + /additive depletion zone depends strongly on the current, the rotation rate, and feature depth, different feature dimensions will fill differently for the given process conditions. Significantly deeper features will likely pinch off and form a seam because the depletion zone is too high in the feature, while significantly shallower features may not fill at all because the depletion zone is too deep. Careful selection of proper waveform, mass transport, and concentrations is therefore critical to achieving superconformal growth across a die.

blocks.document_id: 利用牺牲氧化剂实现钴的超共形填充
blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Conclusions
blocks.text: Superconformal cobalt fill is achieved in high-aspect ratio nanometer-scale features by effective use of sacrificial oxidants through the DCEF mechanism. The sacrificial oxidant may be, for example, H ^+, O _2,, or an organic additive and functions to lower the cobalt deposition current efficiency. By operating at low current efficiency, concentration gradients for the active sacrificial species are developed within the feature. Here, the role of H ^+ as a sacrificial oxidant has been demonstrated. In addition to shifting the reaction at the base of the feature toward cobalt deposition through higher relative current efficiency, it has been shown that shifts to higher pH via H ^+ consumption and lower mass transport lead to faster cobalt deposition rates through the thermodynamics of a CoOH ^+ reaction intermediate. Relatively small pH shifts, which can be achieved through mass transport effects, can lead to significant differences in deposition rates. Due to their impact on the deposition kinetics, suppressor-type additives play an important role in lowering the current efficiency at a given potential, driving the pH gradient formation and limiting plating on the field.

blocks.document_id: 利用牺牲氧化剂实现钴的超共形填充
blocks.section: Superconformal Cobalt Fill Through the Use of Sacrificial Oxidants > Conclusions
blocks.text: Additive gradients, either through concentration gradient formation or through the effect of pH shifts on adsorption and suppression properties, can also create a differential in kinetics within the feature. Bottom-up cobalt fill proceeds when waveform, mass transport, and organic and inorganic solution constituent concentrations synergistically create the appropriate deposition rate differential through the DCEF mechanism. The DCEF mechanism and insights presented here may be applicable to superconformal fill of other metals, as well.

blocks.text: Xiaochuan Ma, 1 Yaqiang Li, 1 Penghui Ren, 1 Peixia Yang, 1 Jinqiu Zhang, 1 Maozhong An, 1,z and Wenquan Lv 2,z Cyclic voltammetry (CV), chronopotentiometry and quartz crystal microbalance were used to study the effect of Malachite Green (MG) on bottom-up growth of cobalt. The addition of MG not only inhibited the reduction of Co ^2 + but also accelerated the hydrogen evolution process. The metal reduction process was enhanced as well as the current efficiency was higher with the increase of pH. The bottom-up growth of cobalt can be achieved with the potential of −1.20 V. Induction-diffusion-adsorption superconformal electrodeposition mechanism was proposed to illustrate the synergistic effect of MG and pH on the growth of cobalt. On one hand, the MG concentration gradient and pH gradient could be formed to achieve a growth rate difference within blind vias so as to obtain bottom-up growth (diffusion-adsorption effect). On the other hand, the growth rate difference was intensified due to the accelerating effect of MG on HER so as to boost the cobalt superfilling (induction effect). © 2023 The Electrochemical Society (“ECS”). blocks.text: However, within the manufacturing process of back-end-of-line (BEOL), the width of interconnect lines has been downscaled to nano level with the density of LSI devices becoming more and more compressed according to the Moore’s Law. Resulting in the increase of the copper resistivity and RC delay, which has become the key factors for restricting the performance of the integration devices. 2,3 For example, the resistivity of a 10 nm-wide Cu interconnect line is more than ten times higher than that of bulk copper due to the severe electrons scattering and grain boundaries scattering. 4,5 As a result, it is of great importance to screen metals with low electron mean free path in the replacement of Cu in order to improve the property of IC. Among these metals with relatively low mean free path, Co was investigated widely as interconnect line after balancing the production cost and IC property. 6–11 Since cobalt not only is of low fine-line resistivity, but also is of strong electromigration resistance. 12,13 Applying electrodeposition method to prepare Co thin films is a cost-friendly, fast, and easy-operating method, and has been applied in many fields.

blocks.text: In this study, Malachite Green (MG), was selected as a suppressor for cobalt electrodeposition. It has been verified that MG adsorbed on the cathode surface to inhibit the reduction of copper and titanium. 35 And the influence of MG on Co metal deposition process have also been discussed before, 36 so this paper mainly studies the influence of MG adsorption on the hydrogen evolution process. The electrochemical tests, including cyclic voltammetry (CV) and linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV), were applied to research the inhibition ability of MG on the deposition process of cobalt, while the influence of MG on HER was also studied by EQCM tests. Superconformal electrodeposition of cobalt was achieved and induction-diffusion-adsorption mechanism was proposed to illustrate the synergistic effect of MG and pH.

blocks.text: The surface morphology of cobalt deposit.—The surface morphology was analyzed to verify the acceleration of MG on HER, as shown in Figs. 6 and S5. SEM images were obtained with and without the existence of the additive MG. As can be seen from Fig. 6a, the Co grain are densely stacked blocks. When the MG concentration is 10 ppm, the grain size becomes smaller and there are much more nanoscale voids on the grain, as shown in the Fig. 6b. It can be concluded that the addition of MG results in the grain refinement because of the inhibition of MG on cobalt deposition. Meanwhile, the MG act as the accelerator for hydrogen evolution which make hydrogen bubble increase and overflow from the coating surface. However, the voids in the plating layer have a negative effect on the physical and chemical properties of the Co deposition and proper wetting agent should be introduced. Therefore, 20 ppm MPS and 10 mM chloride ion were added in the bath in order to obtain cobalt coating with high quality, as shown in Figs. S6a and S6b. After optimizing plating composition and process parameters, a compact uniform film without nanoscale voids can be obtained with or without stirring.

blocks.text: At the initial state, the cathode surface covered with inhibitor MG which suppress the Co reduction and promote the HER. During the electrodeposition, the deposit suppression gradient was formed because of the diffusion-limited of MG. The passive-active transition zone come into being, and then the zone grows until it covers the entire trench due to the induction HER of MG. Meantime, the effective pH gradient is also established due to the mass transport limitation of hydrogen ion, resulting that the current efficiency at the bottom is higher, as shown in stage b in Fig. 10. Compared with the formation of inhibition gradient, the disruption of MG caused by HER is weaker, which is more conducive to the bottom-up superfilling process. In summary, the induction-diffusion-adsorption mechanism, namely diffusion-adsorption effect caused by MG gradient and pH gradient as well as induction effect of MG on HER, was proposed to illustrate the bottom-up growth of cobalt.

blocks.section: Induction-Diffusion-Adsorption Process of Malachite Green for Cobalt Superconformal Electrodeposition > Conclusions
blocks.text: The additive Malachite Green (MG) was used as an effective suppressor for cobalt deposition. The suppressing effect of MG on cobalt electrodeposition was investigated according to cyclic voltammetry and the mass transport of MG is diffusion-controlled. The induction acceleration of MG on HER was obtained by coupling EQCM and cyclic voltammetry as well as surface morphology was used to confirm the acceleration of MG on HER, while the influence of pH on current efficiency was also studied. The formation of hydroxide ions at the electrode surface caused by the HER which leaded to the formation of CoOH ^+ (ads). The induction-diffusionadsorption mechanism was proposed to illustrate the bottom-up growth of cobalt. The MG gradient formed within blind vias due to the limitation of mass transport resulting the inhibition difference at different parts (the growth rate at the bottom is higher than that of the opening), while the pH gradient and the formation of CoOH^+ (ads) caused by MG induction is beneficial to the Cobalt filling in the feature.

blocks.section: Influence of trace tungsten contents on thin-film properties and electromigration behaviors of electroless-deposited cobalt interconnect lines > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Electroless-plated cobalt alloys with tungsten typically exceeding 5 at.% are the common barrier materials for copper metallization. As cobalt is a new interconnect material for advanced microchips, it is worth studying the advanced cobalt-interconnect metallization process that involves extremely diluted cobalt-tungsten (CoW) alloys with an eliminated impurity resistivity and enhanced electromigration reliability. To this aim, we fabricated three different CoW nanolines with 0.03, 0.06 and 0.11 at.% of W using an electroless process, and examined their electromigration behaviors under accelerated stressing conditions, using Co lines as a control. All three W contents, especially 0.06 at.%, mitigate Co electromigration. The mechanism for the electromigration mitigation is due to an improvement of the film s nanomechanical and surface wetting properties, as well as grain-structure refinements. A full account of the relationship between the film properties, grain structures and electromigration testing results is given, reasonably explaining the cause of the reliability optimization.

blocks.section: Influence of trace tungsten contents on thin-film properties and electromigration behaviors of electroless-deposited cobalt interconnect lines > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: The contact critical dimension of the CMOS transistors currently using copper (Cu) as a core interconnect material is expected to reach 18 nm [1], associated with a diminishment of interconnect width towards less than a few tens of nm. The rather long electron mean free path of 40 nm for Cu would induce multiple electron scatterings in such narrow lines, giving rise to a high residual electrical resistivity [2]. Therefore, Cu is not a good interconnect conductor for future technology nodes. Compared to Cu, cobalt (Co) has a much shorter electron mean free path of about 9 nm, leading to the product of the resistivity and mean free path of Co being less than that of Cu: 6.0 5 × 1 0 ^- 1 6 vs. 6.7 0×10^-16Ωm^2 [2]. Considering the resistivity-size effect, Co is considered to be a more appropriate interconnect material than Cu, especially as the line width (or cross section) is reduced down to below a crossover value of about 15 nm [3–5] (or 450 nm 2) [6,7].

blocks.section: Influence of trace tungsten contents on thin-film properties and electromigration behaviors of electroless-deposited cobalt interconnect lines > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Moreover, electromigration is essentially a forced metal diffusion behavior and the key factor that influences the electromigration reliability of a conductive line is the magnitude of its effective valence (Z*) and diffusivity (D): the lower the product of the Z ^* and D, the higher the electromigration reliability. The absolute value of the Z ^* for Co is about 5 to 10 times lower than that of Cu [8,9]. With a higher melting point of 1495 ◦C than 1085 ◦C of Cu, Co has a much lower (about one order of magnitude) self-diffusivity than Cu [10]. Indeed, the product of the Z* and D for Co is two orders of magnitude smaller than that of Cu [11,12]. Therefore, Co has become the new, alternative interconnection material for advanced microchips [1].

blocks.section: Influence of trace tungsten contents on thin-film properties and electromigration behaviors of electroless-deposited cobalt interconnect lines > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Electroless process has long been used to prepare thin barrier/cap layers of Co alloys for Cu-interconnect metallization [13]. The basic components in an electroless cobalt-alloy plating solution are typically cobalt sulfate (CoSO_4) as a source of Co ions and dimethylamine borane (C_2H_9BN), sodium hydroborate (NaBH) or sodium hypophosphite (NaH_2PO_2) as a chemical reductant. The oxidation of the chemical reductant results in the incorporation of boron or phosphors into the deposited Co, creating a solute-strengthening effect that stabilizes the phase structure, stuffs grain boundaries and/or generates an amorphous matrix, which are all beneficial to barrier/cap properties. Moreover, as a refractory metal, tungsten (W) is highly resistant to heat and abrasion. Its addition to the binary Co alloys thus further elevates thermal-mechanical and barrier properties. Therefore, innovate formulations based on sulfate baths with an added W-containing salt, such as tungstate [ 1 4, 1 5 ] or phosphotungstic acid [16], have been developed to fabricate barrier/cap layers of ternary Co alloys with high W contents usually exceeding 5 at.%.
