blocks.section: Influence of trace tungsten contents on thin-film properties and electromigration behaviors of electroless-deposited cobalt interconnect lines > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: To serve as a core-conducting interconnect material, thin metal films need to have an electrical resistivity close to their bulk values. However, high concentrations of alloy components, particularly heavy elements such as W, in thin films of binary or ternary cobalt-based alloys would induce a high impurity electrical resistivity. After thermal annealing, the tungsten-added cobalt binary/ternary films still give a high resistivity value exceeding several tens or even hundreds of μΩ-cm [17,18]. We have recently developed an all-wet self-assembled-monolayer (SAM) seeding and electroless process for cobalt metallization. By using a CoSO _4 -N _2H_4 (hydrazine; a metal-free reductant) bath, thin films and nanolines of alloy-free Co with (after annealing) a low resistivity of≤15 μΩ-cm are fabricated [19]. In this study, we report an extension of our previous work by adding tungstate to the CoSO _4–N_2H_4 bath for the interconnect metallization of various Co alloys with trace W contents (termed CoW) of 0.03, 0.06 and 0.11 at.%, giving a low impurity-component resistivity potentially suitable for future interconnect-material applications.

blocks.text: By using unalloyed Co as a reference, the enhancement of the electromigration reliability of interconnect lines of the various CoW alloys, in particular with 0.06 at.% added W, will be confirmed. The correlation between nanomechanical/wetting properties of the surface films and the difference in electromigration failure profiles and grain structures of the interconnect lines will be analyzed, elucidating why the optimal W content (0.06 at.%) gives the greatest effectiveness of mitigating electromigration failure.

blocks.section: Influence of trace tungsten contents on thin-film properties and electromigration behaviors of electroless-deposited cobalt interconnect lines > 2.3. Electromigration testing and failure analyses
blocks.text: Prior to electromigration testing, the samples of Co,CoW_l,CoW_m and CoW lines were annealed (400\^°C/30 min) using an Ulvac’s Mila-5000 rapid thermal vacuum annealer. All annealing treatments were performed in flowing Ar -H_2 (5 %) that prevented the samples from oxidation. A heating rate of 15~^°C~s^-1 was used and fast cooling was performed by simply switching off the heating. They were then placed on a thermal chuck situated in a probe-station-enclosed dark box, immediately under constant current stressing by using a Keithley 4200- SCS semiconductor parameter analyzer. The onset of electromigration for metallic interconnects under regular operation conditions occurs on a time scale of several years. Here, the interconnect lines were tested under accelerated electromigration conditions using very high current densities of the order of 10^7A cm ^- 2.. Such current densities were about 2–3 orders of magnitude greater than the practical ones. Thus, the electromigration failure of the tested interconnect lines was speeded up.

blocks.text: Nanomechanical scratch testing of thin films of Co, CoW_l,CoW_m and CoW_h was conducted in a Bruker’s Hysitron TI 980 Tribolndenter. The Tribolndenter was equipped with two sensors for precise force and depth measurements using a state-of-the-art piezoelectric actuator. This advanced design allowed us to control each and every measurement by progressively increasing the normal load of a diamond stylus in a controlled fashion, while synchronously collecting the feedback data of normal displacement, lateral force and lateral displacement. Subsequently, the related plots were automatically generated by using a Hysitron TriboScan software. On-site scanning probe microscopical imaging of the whole scratch profile for the feedback of the scratch data was used to derive the nanomechanical properties of the tested films, such as critical load, delamination force, adhesion strength and friction coefficient.

blocks.text: When adsorbed onto the deposit surface, W (VI) ions tend to become an inhibiting component that blocks the self-catalytic sites of Co [25]. Thus, the W (VI) ions depress Co deposition and their reduction reaction into metallic W being incorporated to the main Co deposit is interde pendent upon the main reduction reaction of the cobaltous ions. Specifically, previous studies have shown that adding high contents of tungstate ( WO_3^4+) to the cobalt sulfate ( Co ^2 +) aqueous solutions with WO _3 ^4 + -to-CO ^2 + molarity ratios exceeding 0.3 or even greater than 2, using a given chemical reductant such as hypophosphite or dimethylamine borane, results in a decrease in the deposition rates of Co [25–28]. Here, the pure Co film was deposited by a sulfate-citrate-hydrazine bath. It should be noted that the concentration of the sulfate in this bath was 0.2 M. The CoW_l,CoW_m and CoW_h films were deposited by otherwise this same bath except including quite low tungstate concentrations of about 2.5 0 × 1 0 ^- 4, 1.0 6 × 1 0 ^- 3 and 5.3 0 × 1 0 ^- 3 M, respectively.

blocks.section: Influence of trace tungsten contents on thin-film properties and electromigration behaviors of electroless-deposited cobalt interconnect lines > 3.1. Basic film properties
blocks.text: Thin films of binary cobalt alloys, such as Co(P) or Co(B), are typically deposited by aqueous electrolytes that contain cobalt sulfate, hypophosphite (or borazane) and a citrate chelating agent. Tungstate, as used in this study, is usually added to the above electroless baths for the incorporation of metallic W into the binary alloys for barrier/cap applications. Traditionally, highly concentrated tungstate, in terms of tungstate-to-cobalt sulfate (or W O _ 3 ^ 4 + - t o - C O ^ 2 +) molarity ratios of 0.3 or greater, is used, which results in the incorporation of substantial amounts of metallic W in the range of 2 10 at.% to the Co matrix. In spite of the fact that pure W cannot be deposited by either chemical or electrochemical methods, electrochemical studies suggest that Co serves as a catalyst for the electroless deposition of W; namely, after the deposition of Co on catalytic particles or layers, the deposited Co subsequently serves as another catalyst to activate the codeposition of Co and W.

blocks.text: The W can be reduced from tungstile ions ( WO _ 2 ^ 2 +), and is then simultaneously incorporated into the Co matrix during the reduction of the cobaltous ions via a so-called induced codeposition mechanism [16, 28,29]. Here, the baths with extremely low tungstate–to–cobalt sulfate molarity ratios of 1.2 0 × 1 0 ^ - 3, 5.3 0 × 1 0 ^ - 3 and 2.6 5 × 1 0 ^ - 2 were used to deposit CoW alloys, and the deposited films indeed contained only 0.03, 0.06 and 0.11 atomic percentage of W,, respectively. This result suggests that, for the cobalt-tungsten alloy films deposited by the tungstate-diluted hydrazine baths, the trace W contents are incorporated to the Co film matrixes also via the induced codeposition mechanism, as for the conventional tungstate-concentrated baths. Indeed, the study of the deposition and film properties of tungsten-containing binary/ternary alloys of Co using CoSO _ 4 -N _ 2 H _ 4 bath formulations with diluted tungsten-ion sources is rather limited. The mechanism for plating diluted cobalt-tungsten alloys using the tungstate-diluted baths is worthy of investigation via electrochemical analysis.

During the course of electroless deposition, the W-added Co or Co deposits surrounding the 2 nm-sized catalytic particles are expanded with plating time to become island-like deposits, eventually coalescing themselves into a thin continuous film. As demonstrated by the top-view and cross-sectional (inset) SEM micrographs in Fig. 3a and 3b, respectively, the thin Co and CoW_m films yield similar uniform surface morphologies and microstructures. The two Co and CoW_m films were further annealed to a certain extent (500~^°C/30 min in flowing Ar/H 2 gas), and the associated top-view SEM micrographs are shown in Fig. 3c and 3d, respectively. blocks.text: The values of the adhesion strength, hardness, specific surface energy and electromigration mean time to failure (MTF) of Co, CoW l, CoW_m and CoW_h, as obtained from the preceding sections, are compiled in Table 2 for comparison. According to this table, the extension of the lifetime and reduction in the scaling factor of Co by W alloying correlate closely with the improvement of surface and nanomechanical properties of the thin films. Notably, surface energy is an important thermodynamic factor that decides the wettability of a condensed matter to a heterogeneous supporting substrate. The deposited film with a lower surface energy would have a higher wetting tendency and thus should be with a greater substrate adherence than the counterpart with a higher surface energy. Indeed, the adhesion strength of the Co films after adding 0.03 at.% and 0.06 at.% of W is increased from 35.8 to 43.4 and 56.1 MPa, respectively, concurring well with the respective decrease in the surface energy from 70 to 66 and 60 mJ m^-2 for CoW and CoW _m.

blocks.text: Grain structure is a crucial factor in defining the strength or weakness of thin solid films. Most noticeably, among the four thin-film materials, CoW_m(W\=0.06 at.%) and Co have the best and worst electromigration reliability, respectively. Here, TEM/STEM was used to analyze two narrow lines of CoW_m and Co (the reference sample) after electromigration stressing for a given time at 5.0 × 1 0 ^7 ~A~cm ^- 2 and ambient temperature. The MTFs of Co and CoW_m lines were about 5000 s and 11000 s, respectively. Here, the stressing times of the two Co and CoW_m lines were preset at half of the failure times as 2500 and 5500 s, respectively. Bright-field TEM images were first recorded over broad regions of the two lines along their longitudinal sections, as shown in Fig. 7a and b. It can be seen from Fig. 7a that electrical stressing of the Co line for 2500 s has induced the formation of many dome-shaped voids about 250 nm long and 50−80 nm deep which are located predominantly along the interfaces of the metal line with the surrounding substrate. This situation suggests that electromigration flux divergences of the Co atoms indeed occur at the grain boundaries and interfaces.

blocks.text: As shown in the inset of Fig. 7a, prolonged electromigration stressing for 4200 s causes the voids to grow, spreading themselves transversely into open slits with 300−500 nm in length. Subsequently, the line is ruptured at 5000 s. Fig. 7b shows, however, that stressing the CoW_m line for a much longer time of 5500 s only causes the formation of much smaller voids without the formation of any open slits. The imaging analysis suggests again that CoW_m has a better electromigration resistance than Co. It should be noted that the voids in the Co interconnect line are located predominantly along its interfaces with the underlying substrate. It can be inferred from the void location and wear-out profile evolution that, upon electromigration stressing, the depletion of the Co atoms by grain-boundary diffusion starts from the meta / SiO _2 interfaces where there probably existing the strongest electron crowding effect and atomic flux divergence [36]. Moreover, the dome-shaped voids display a larger length than depth, suggesting preferential electromigration paths for the Co and W-added Co lines.

blocks.text: Fig. 7a and b suggest that adding 0.06 at.% of W to interconnect lines of Co results in a greatly reduced void growth rate, associated with a reduction of the 0.50 scaling factor of pure Co to 0.33. Closely comparing the bright-field TEM micrographs in Fig. 7a, b seems to reveal the existence of a significant grain-structure difference between the Co and CoW_m lines. This difference was further analyzed by STEM HAADF (high-angle annular dark-field) imaging and high-resolution TEM, as shown in Fig. 7c, d (Co) and Fig.~7e,~f~(CoW_m).. The STEM HAADF image in Fig. 7c shows that the Co line is made of large, columnar crystalline grains. It appears that some grains span the height of the entire interconnect line. The incoming mass flux reaching such ‘blocking’ grains tends to induce a flux divergence that is readily to move upwards along their ‘straight’ grain boundaries to the top free surface, later leading to the formation of large voids in the vicinity of these grains. As seen from the micrograph inserted in Fig. 7a, stressing for 4200 s causes Co atoms to migrate along the interfaces, free surface and grain boundaries, which then accumulate on the top free surface.

blocks.section: Influence of trace tungsten contents on thin-film properties and electromigration behaviors of electroless-deposited cobalt interconnect lines > 3.5. Failure-profile and grain-structure analyses
blocks.text: The STEM-HAADF image of the unalloyed Co line (Fig. 7c) exhibits a ‘clean, smooth’ contour, suggesting a relatively low defect density; the line also gives a ‘perfect’ lattice fringe image (Fig. 7d) and [0001] zoneaxis Fourier transform pattern of HCP-Co (inset, Fig. 7d). By contrast, the CoW_m line comprises a stacking of equiaxed grains (Fig. 7b), seemingly offering a more complicated grain structure that could inhibit grain-boundary electromigration. Moreover, the CoW_m line exhibits an HAADF image with an intricate, rough contour (Fig. 7e), suggesting a relatively high defect density. Its high-resolution TEM image (Fig. 7f), taken along the [0001] zone axis, clearly shows the existence of stacking faults on (0001) basal planes, associated with a streaky diffraction pattern of HCP-Co (inset of Fig. 7f). Comparing the unalloyed Co, the equiaxed CoW_m has a more complex grain structure and a higher density of immobile planar defects, which would offer a maze of diffusion routes to retard the void-growth rate.

blocks.text: It should be noted that an STEM-HAADF image is produced by col lecting the high-angle scattered electrons due to Rutherford scattering of atomic nuclei using an annulus detector around the principal axis of a primary incident electron beam. The collected signals are thus highly sensitive to the variation in the atomic number of the atoms in the imaged specimen, as opposed to the conventional TEM dark-field imaging method which utilizes extremely small-angle Bragg diffracted electrons. The high dependence of imaging contrast on atomic number makes STEM-HAADF a facile way to resolve a higher atomic-number alloy from its matrix material, as for the case of the W in Co matrix. However, using STEM-HAADF imaging, high-resolution TEM and STEM-EDX line scanning/mapping turned out to be inconclusive regarding the location of the added W, indicating that 0.06 at.% of W could be beyond the detection limit of the Talos™ F200X microscope.

blocks.text: In sum, the mitigation of Co electromigration by the alloying of extremely diluted W is directly related to an improvement of the film’s mechanical properties and a reduction in the film’s surface energy. Grain-structure refinement also plays a role in the reliability reinforcement.

blocks.document_id: 微量钨含量对化学沉积钴互连薄膜性能及电迁移行为的影响
blocks.section: Influence of trace tungsten contents on thin-film properties and electromigration behaviors of electroless-deposited cobalt interconnect lines > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: An all-wet SAM-seeding and electroless-plating process has been developed to form thin films of Co and extremely diluted CoW alloys with controlled thin-film properties, including deposition rates, alloy compositions, deposit surface morphologies and microstructure stability against thermal stressing. We then extend this all-wet process to fill these metal films into SiO 2 trenches, eventually fabricating nanolines of three different CoW alloys for electromigration-behavior evaluations, using nanolines of Co as a reference. The electromigration mitigation for all three nanolines of Co alloys with 0.03 at.%, 0.06 at.% and 0.11 at.% of added W, termed CoW_l,CoW_m and CoW_h, respectively, under accelerated current stressing conditions of the order of 10^7A cm ^- 2 has been confirmed. Most noticeably, the CoW_m line containing a moderate amount of W, while only 0.06 at.%, yields a significantly reduced current density scaling factor of 0.33, which is much smaller than that of the Co line (0.50). So, it also yields a much slower void growth rate, associated with an electromigration lifetime at least twice as long as that of the Co line.

blocks.document_id: 微量钨含量对化学沉积钴互连薄膜性能及电迁移行为的影响
blocks.section: Influence of trace tungsten contents on thin-film properties and electromigration behaviors of electroless-deposited cobalt interconnect lines > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: While a variety of advanced TEM analyses fail to locate the trace amount of W which is less than one atom in about 1000 cobaltmatrix atoms, the 0.06 at% added W markedly elevates the adhesion strength and hardness of Co from 35.8 to 56.1 MPa and 14.8 to 17.5 μN nm ^- 1, respectively. Moreover, it also reduces Co surface energy from 70 to 60 mJ m ^- 2, favoring the wetting of the electroless deposits onto the underlying substrate. A fourth benefit given by the optimum W content, as found from advanced STEM/TEM analysis, is that the big electromigration-accelerating blocking grains, as exist in the Co line, are absent from the CoW_m line. The full account of the thin-film properties being investigated correlates well with the reliability performance of the four different metallic thin films/interconnects under thermal/electricfield stressing. It also reasonably explains why the ranking of their electromigration reliability being increased from Co, CoW (0.03 at.%), CoW_h (0.11 at.%) to CoW_m (0.06 at.%).

blocks.section: Investigation of novel suppressor Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride on cobalt superconformal growth > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: It is significantly important to develop novel suppressor to achieve cobalt superconformal filling. Linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV) and impedance spectra (EIS) were coupled together to study the effect of novel dye suppressor nitrotetrazolium blue chloride (NBT) on cobalt electrodeposition. The adsorption behavior of NBT on cobalt substrate was investigated by applying density functional theory (DFT) calculation, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and in situ Raman spectra, while the interaction between NBT and cobalt ions ( Co ^2 +) is analyzed based on topology analysis and interaction region indicator (IRI) analysis. Synergistic suppressing mechanism, namely adsorption effect and coordination effect, was proposed to explain the suppressing effect of NBT during cobalt electrodeposition. The cobalt surface morphology analysis under the influence of NBT demonstrates that NBT is of grain refinement, while XRD analysis indicates that the formation of Co hcp (100) is formed preferentially. The superconformal filling of cobalt is achieved in microvias with different diameters. The cobalt layer is of excellent quality due to low surface deposit thickness (SDT).

blocks.section: Investigation of novel suppressor Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride on cobalt superconformal growth > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: With semiconductor technology evolving continuously along the way based on Moore’s Law, the traditional copper damascene process is facing enormous challenges in terms of yield and reliability [1,2]. On one hand, when trench size is decreased to lower than Mean electron free path of copper, the intensified electron scattering at external surfaces and grain boundaries leads to the exponential growth of resistivity of copper interconnect, resulting in severely increased RC delay and IR drop [3,4]. On the other hand, the seed layer and barrier layer increase the proportion of non-conductive material within copper interconnect, further increasing the resistivity [5]. Meanwhile, it is hard to achieve void-defect filling of copper in downscaling interconnect line width since the current density at the opening is increased due to edge effect, which has a negative effect on reliability [6,7]. Among alternative metals, cobalt [8] is regarded as candidate interconnect metal as a result of low line resistivity at advanced node and compatibility to electroplating process compared with Ni [9,10], Ru [11], Au [12], graphene [13,14] etc.

blocks.section: Investigation of novel suppressor Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride on cobalt superconformal growth > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Electroplating technology is key fabrication process to obtain cobalt interconnect [14]. It is essentially important to introduce proper additives to achieve superconformal growth of cobalt [15,16] since the growth rate at the plane and opening of vias is higher than that in the bottom and sidewalls as a result of mass transfer limitation within vias and edge effect at the opening [17,18]. Several additives used for cobalt superconformal filling has been reported in the literature. Josell et al. investigated branched polyethyleneimine (PEI) as suppressor and proposed S-shaped negative differential resistance (S-NDR) model to predict bottowm-up filling of cobalt [19], while Huang et al. studied the effect of oxime additive and believed that amine groups could coordinate with Co ^2 + to suppress the cobalt electrodeposition [20–22]. He et al. studied the influence of inhibitor polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) on cobalt electrodeposition as well as cobalt superconformal electrodeposition was achieved at trench with high aspect ratio [23].

blocks.section: Investigation of novel suppressor Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride on cobalt superconformal growth > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Although several additives have been investigated, researchers pay little attention to the suppressing mechanism and effective special groups of additives based on experimental analysis and theoretical analysis. Advanced analyzing methods, including in situ Fourier Trans form Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) [25], in situ Surface Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (SERS) [26,27] and Scanning Tunneling Microscopy [28], are widely used to study the adsorption behavior of additives. Besides, another emerging method, theoretical calculation is regarded as an effective method for exploiting the suppressing mechanism of additive [29]. For example, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation is widely accepted to analyze the adsorption ability of additive [30,31], while density functional theory (DFT) is often used to predict the effect of additive based on calculated parameters [32] and analyze interaction between metal ions and additive [33,34]. As a result, operando method and theoretical calculation can help researchers better understand the influencing mechanism, which can provide support for future molecule design.

blocks.document_id: 新型抑制剂氯化硝基四氮唑蓝对Co超共形生长的研究
blocks.section: Investigation of novel suppressor Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride on cobalt superconformal growth > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In this work, a kind of dye molecule Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride (NBT), was used as novel suppressor on cobalt electrodeposition. Electrochemical methods including linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV) and electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) were used together to study the influence of NBT on kinetics of Co ^2 + reduction. Density functional theory (DFT) calculation was accepted to obtain the quantum chemical parameters of NBT. Besides, theoretical calculation, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation and in situ Raman spectra were used to study the adsorption of NBT on cobalt substrate. Topology analysis and interaction region indicator (IRI) analysis were accepted to study the coordination between NBT and cobalt ions ( Co ^2 +). The suppressing mechanism of NBT is explained by proposing synergistic suppressing mechanism. The influence of NBT on morphology and crystal orientation is investi gated by SEM and XRD, respectively. Cobalt superconformal growth is achieved at microvias with different diameters.

blocks.text: The suppressing effect of dye molecule Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride (NBT) on cobalt electrodeposition is investigated by LSV and EIS. DFT calculation and MD simulation is used to study the suppressing mechanism. Quantum chemical calculation, MD simulation and in situ Raman spectra confirms the strong adsorption effect of NBT on cobalt substrate. Besides, topology analysis and IRI analysis were applied to study the coordination effect between NBT and Co ^2 +. Synergistic sup pressing mechanism (adsorption effect and coordination effect) is proposed to demonstrate the influence of NBT. The effect of NBT on morphology of cobalt layer is studied and NBT is of grain refinement. What’s more, the introduction of NBT is conducive for the formation of Co (1 0 0) and can suppress the Co (1 1 0) crystal plane. Superconformal electrodeposition is achieved at micovias with different diameters. The relatively low SDT values (15.9 μm for 150 μm, 8.8 μm for 100 μm and 4.9 μm for 50 μm) indicates that NBT is of excellent selectivity.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > Abstract
blocks.text: This comprehensive review explores electroless cobalt deposition, an appealing surface modification technique that offers advantages such as uniform coverage on complex geometries and compatibility with diverse substrate materials without external power. The article systematically examines the critical impact of various bath constituents and operational variables on the characteristics of deposited films. It details the roles of the cobalt source, different reducing agents, complexing agents, pH regulators, and stabilizers. Additionally, the article scrutinizes the influence of deposition parameters like temperature, solution pH, agitation methods, and bath aging. The formation of numerous cobalt-based alloys and composite materials are also discussed. This review aims to guide the development of optimized electroless cobalt plating solutions, highlighting their wide-ranging utility in fields such as microelectronics, data storage, protective coatings, electrolytic green H₂ generation metal matrix composites, and electromagnetic shielding, thereby fostering advancements in intricate material fabrication Keywords Electroless Cobalt Protective coating Thin film

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: Electroless cobalt plating stands out as a versatile and efficient method for depositing a thin layer of cobalt metal on any surface. Unlike traditional electroplating, which relies on external electrical current, electroless cobalt utilizes a chemical reduction process. This eliminates the need for exclusively conducting substrates, complex electrical setup and allows for more uniform deposition on intricate surfaces. The process is steadily gaining traction since its inception by Brenner and Riddell [1] in 1947 due to simplicity of the technique and lower cost of instrumentation. Electroless coating or autocatalytic coating is a category of chemical process that deposits one or more metal layers by autocatalytic reduction of metal cations in a liquid chemical bath. One of the significant advantages of electroless plating is its ability to achieve a more even and conformal coating compared to electroplating. Unlike electroplating, homogeneity of deposit thickness is maintained even in the sharp corners or intricate recesses of the substrate surface [2, 3].

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: This characteristic makes it ideal for applications where uniform coverage is crucial, such as in microelectronics and the fabrication of magnetic thin films. The composition of the electroless plating solution can be tailored to control the properties of the deposited cobalt layer. Electroless cobalt alloy finds applications in various fields. In the microelectronics industry, it is used to create diffusion barriers [4, 5] and seed layers [6, 7] for subsequent electroplating processes. The magnetic properties ofcobalt make it a valuable material for data storage devices and magnetic sensors [8, 9]. Since US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) categorized Cr 6+ containing baths (essential for hard chrome plating) as unsuitable for environment and stressed on alternative approaches [10], cobalt-based plating has also been explored and employed for wear [11–13] and corrosion [14, 15] protection of metallic components. While electroless plating excels at creating thin films, its potential extends far beyond simple flat surfaces.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: Deposition of 3D structures like cobalt microspheres [16, 17] and 1D structures like nanowires [18] or nanotubes [19] has been successfully demonstrated, paving the way for a new generation of micro and nanostructured materials with enhanced functionalities in various fields.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: As research in this area continues, advancements are being made to optimize electroless cobalt plating solutions for specific applications. Although a large volume of research work is available, comprehensive review article on this area is scarce. Shen et al. [20] in 2022 provided a summary on the progress of electroless cobalt deposition narrowly focusing on semiconductor-based electronics application. The main aim of the current article is to discuss and summarize past works on the influence of bath composition and coating parameters on autocatalytic cobalt deposition. The article also includes brief discussion on the development of Co-based alloys and composites structures obtained via electroless path and their intended applications.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 2 Electroless Cobalt Deposition Process
blocks.text: The deposition process involves reduction ofcobalt cations in an aqueous solution ofmetal salt in the presence ofa reducing agent (R) at the surface of a catalytic substrate. Deposition then continues due to the catalytic action of the deposited metal ions. Hence, the process is also named as autocatalytic. In the course of time, four different detailed reaction mechanisms were proposed to account for electroless deposition process [21]. Among them, the electrochemical mechanism has been experimentally validated by Hwang et al. [22] specifically in case of cobalt deposition. According to this proposition catalyst particles jump start the oxidation (loss of electrons) of reducing agent by acting as anode whereas reduction (gain of electrons) of metal cations happens at a different cathodic site with less catalytic activity. blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 2.1 Substrate Pre-treatment
blocks.text: Figure 1 shows all the steps needed to be followed for successful deposition. Ensuring the substrate to be clean and free of contaminants like grease, oil, or oxides is of paramount importance in order to obtain good quality deposit. Electroless cobalt deposition thrives on the inherent catalytic nature of the substrate. However, advancements have opened doors to depositing cobalt on non-catalytic substrates as well. Iron, nickel, cobalt, gold, palladium, and aluminum substrates can act as catalysts [23], while non-catalytic substrates such as copper, magnesium, polymers, carbon, glass etc. are activated using PdCl _ 2 solution [23–25] because Pd nanoparticles act as seeds, providing numerous active sites for the cobalt ions to be reduced and initiate the electroless deposition process [26]. Non-catalytic substrates must be sensitized by dipping into stannous chloride ( SnCl _ 2) solution before palladium activation. It effectively prepares the surface by depositing Sn ^ 2 + ions [25, 27]. The adsorbed Sn ^ 2 + ions act as a reducing agent. They donate electrons to the Pd ^ 2 + ions in the solution. As a result, the Pd ^ 2 + ions are reduced to metallic palladium ( Pd ^ 0) [28].

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 2.1 Substrate Pre-treatment
blocks.text: However, sensitization can be considered unnecessary when the substrate surface chemistry inherently provides sufficient sites for direct palladium ion adsorption and subsequent reduction to its catalytic metallic form [29, 30]. In an effort to find an activation process without using Pd ^ 2 +, Zhang et al. [31] reported successful use of aluminum foil in conjunction with non-catalytic copper substrate. Mukherjee et al. [32] successfully replicated aluminum induced electroless cobalt alloy deposition on copper foil. Hu et al. [33] demonstrated a method of directly depositing a catalytic cobalt seed layer on a copper substrate using a process called galvanic replacement where a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from an ionic solution.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 2.2 Bath Preparation and Deposition
blocks.text: The aqueous bath primarily consists of a cobalt salt as the source of cobalt ions, a reducing agent to convert cobalt cations to cobalt atoms, complexing agent, pH regulator, and stabilizer. The prepared solution is heated and maintained at certain temperature, and activated substrate is immersed in the heated solution for deposition. Deposition process can take time ranging from few minutes to few hours depending on the required yield. Schematic diagram of instrumentation is shown in Fig. 2a. Figure 2b shows the electrochemical reaction scheme at the vicinity of the substrate. The effectiveness of the electroless deposition process, which involves heating the solution and immersing an activated substrate, is intrinsically linked to the chemical makeup of the aqueous bath. The specific constituents, including the cobalt salt, reducing agent, complexing agent, stabilizer, are paramount in dictating the deposition characteristics. Understanding these individual components is therefore essential for optimizing the electroless cobalt deposition.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.1 Cobalt Source
blocks.text: Cobalt (II) salts like cobalt chloride (CoCl) and cobalt sulfate (CoSO_4) are most preferred sources of cobalt ions for depositing Co-based coatings. Deposition rate is slightly higher from sulfate bath than chloride bath [34]. Brenner and Riddell reported that more than 0.17 M Co salt in the bath results in darkening of coating with significantly lower deposition rate [23]. According to the findings of Magagnin et al. [5], 0.1 M cobalt sulfate results maximum deposition; then, the yield decreases. Consequently, usual practice is to keep the concentration of Co salt within 0.1 M. Although no other report is available for successful reduction of Co (III) salts, Djokic [35] in 1998 claimed to have successfully reduced hexamine cobalt sulfate ( [Co(NH_3)_6]_2(SO_4)_3) into elemental cobalt using hydrazine as reducing agent.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.2 Reducing Agent
blocks.text: Reducing agent is the primary driving force for the electroless deposition reaction. They donate electrons to the metal ions in the plating solution. As the metal ions receive electrons, they are reduced to their metallic state. An effective reducing agent must contain two or more reactive hydrogen atoms as it is observed that metal ions are reduced to neutral atoms by autocatalytic dehydrogenation of the reducing agent [21]. Reducing agent can be classified into three different groups depending upon the resulting deposit—P containing reagents, B containing reagents and reagent which yields pure Co. The catalytic activity of the seed layer depends on the reducing agent. For optimal electroless plating, the potential ofcatalyst metal to reach a reference current density ( 1 × 1 0 ^- 4 A. cm ^- 2 [36]) should be slightly more positive than the standard reduction potential of the reductant. Ohno et al. [36, 37] evaluated and summarized the catalytic activity of different metals in the presence of different reducing agents. Different reducing agents with different compositional yields and corresponding catalytic activity of different metals are furnished in Table 1.

[38] observed that increase of hypophosphite concentration up to 0.5 M increases the deposition rate of Co on substrate, with further increase in concentration, deposition rate increases very slightly. Magagnin et al. [5] reported maximum deposition rate at 1.5 M hypophosphite concentration, and further increase drastically reduces the deposition yield. Stoychev et al. [39] also found similar pattern of increasing, reaching a peak and then drastic fall of deposition rate with increasing hypophosphite concentration. blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.2 Reducing Agent
blocks.text: Use of sodium hypophosphite causes incorporation of P in the cobalt matrix. Miksic et al. [40] provided the earliest report on the amount of P present in Co matrix deposited with different hypophosphite concentration. They found that increasing hypophosphite concentration from 0.047 M to 0.24 M resulted in an increase of the P content from 0.5% to 2.5%. Frieze et al. [41] varied the hypophosphite concentration within slightly wider range (0.05 M to 0.5 M). They were able to increase the amount of P from 1% to 5%. Schlesinger et al. [42] obtained Co-P deposits with the amount of P ranging from 3% to 12% and found almost linear relationship between P content and hypophosphite concentration. They also conclusively observed the tendency of decreasing grain size with increasing amount ofP which was previously hinted by the observations of Cortijo et al. [43]. During nucleation and subsequent growth of Co film on the substrate surface, P atoms act as growth inhibitor resulting in smaller grain size [41, 44].

They were able to incorporate maximum of 1.7% B in the Co matrix resulting in a bright and smooth deposit. Addition of further DMAB caused rapid bath decomposition. Saito et al. [48] and Rohan et al. [49] also independently observed linear relationship between deposition rate and concentration of DMAB in the bath. Additionally, Saito et al. [48] reported that amount of B reaches at its peak at 0.075 M DMAB concentration. It is noteworthy that DMAB loses electrons more readily than Co at the vicinity of Cu substrate. Because of this Co can directly be reduced on the otherwise non-catalytic Cu surface without any pre-activation [50]. Morpholine borane (MB) acts in a similar manner as DMAB [51]. blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.3 Complexing Agents
blocks.text: The complexing agent binds with cobalt ions ( Co 2 ^+) in the solution, forming meta-stable complexes [56]. This reduces the concentration of free cobalt ions available for immediate deposition. This controlled release of free cobalt ions help regulate the deposition rate and prevents uncontrolled precipitation of cobalt. By controlling the availability of free cobalt ions, the complexing agent promotes a more even deposition process across the substrate surface. This leads to smoother and more uniform cobalt films with better adherence to the substrate. The complexing agent used in electroless cobalt bath is usually either an organic acid (Citric acid, tartaric acid, succinic acid, malonic acid, glycine, EDTA etc.) or its salt. Cobalt complex formation is depicted in Fig. 4.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.3 Complexing Agents
blocks.text: Brenner and Riddell [23] compared citrate and tartarate salts and concluded that the former produces superior and less porous film than the latter. Pearlstein et al. [47] showed successful use of succinate salt but more than 0.037 M was needed to ensure bath stability. Homma et al. [57] used sodium malonate, a salt of malonic acid, as complexing agent to obtain Co-P film with preferential crystal orientation in perpendicular direction. Saito et al. [48] compared four different complexing agents namely succinic acid and sodium salts of tarataric, citric, and malonic acid in a Co-B bath. In all cases, deposition rates are almost constant up to a certain concentration of complexing agent, beyond which the deposition rate gradually decreases. Higher deposition rates were obtained from succinic acid bath and sodium malonate bath compared to other two. Apart from sodium tartarate, other three complexing agents do not influence B content in the deposit in any significant way. Addition of sodium tartarate favors the amount of B in the deposit. Tarozait et al.

blocks.text: [38] explored the role of glycine in electroless Co-P formation and found that deposition rate initially increases with glycine concentration, reaches a peak and then diminishes. They also observed the negative effect of glycine in incorporating P in the Co matrix. Later, it is reported that glycine concentration in between 0.6 M and 0.8 M can be used to achieve directional crystal growth of Co-B, more than that retards the process [51]. EDTA (Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) [58] and ethylenediamine [59] are also reported to be useful as complexing agents. Ethylenediamine reportedly can be used as complexing agent in conjunction with trace amount of diethylenetriamine or triethylenetetramine to deposit Co-B from DMAB bath without any prior need of Pd activation [60]. Diethylenetriamene also enable the bath to accommodate higher DMAB concentration without premature decomposition [58, 60].

blocks.text: Primary function of a buffer is to maintain a stable pH within the desired range. One of the major differences between the composition of electroless Ni and Co bath arises from the fact that addition of ammonium salts in electroless Ni baths does not bring forth any kind of significant change while in Co bath it behaves differently. It was well observed from the beginning that presence of ammonia in the bath noticeably increases the quality of the deposit as well as the deposition rate especially in citrate baths [47, 61]. Variation of deposition rate with ammonium sulfate concentration is depicted in Fig. 5a. The plot clearly shows steady increase of deposition rates with ammonium salt concentration despite

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.5 Stabilizer
blocks.text: A Co plating bath can spontaneously decompose at any time which is indicated by increased volume of hydrogen gas evolution. To prevent it from happening trace amount of stabilizer such as thiourea can be used, Addition ofup to 0.3 mg/l increases deposition rate, more than that ensues rapid fall of deposition rate [66]. Trace amount of tyrosene [67] or 0.01 M maleic acid [68] can also reportedly stabilize the bath even for prolonged duration of deposition.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.6 pH Regulator
blocks.text: NH OH [9, 23, 40], NaOH [24, 53], or KOH [50] are used as pH regulators for alkaline baths and H_2 SO _4 [47] or acetic acid [60] for acid baths. pH regulator is added continuously to maintain certain predetermined pH level throughout the process. At a pH below 9, the presence of ammonia does not affect the deposition rate of Co-B. However, when the pH is raised above 9 adding NaOH, the deposition rate decreases but addition of NH_4OH to raise the pH above 9 maintains a high deposition rate [69]. In order to avoid alkaline metal or foul-smelling ammonium hydroxide, Tarozaite et al. [51] successfully employed tetramethylammonium hydroxide for alkaline baths.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.7 Other Additives
blocks.text: Wetting agents, also known as surfactants, are generally used to improve the wettability of a substrate by reducing its surface tension. This allows the electroless bath solution to make better contact with the entire surface, leading to more uniform deposition. Although use of surfactants is not very common in electroless cobalt bath, sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) has been reportedly used in some cases where deposition was done on polyethylene terephthalate [24] or boron nitride substrate [70].

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 3.7 Other Additives
blocks.text: Accelerators enhance the deposition rate on a substrate. They can be categorized into two types. The first type is an accelerator solution into which an activated substrate is dipped before being placed in an electroless bath. The second type is an accelerator that can be added directly to the electroless bath in small quantities. NH_4OH, NaOH, H_2 SO _4 etc. fall in the first category. Osaka et al. [71] compared the accelerating effects of 1 M NH_4OH, 1 M NaOH, and 1.1 2MH_2SO_4 during deposition of C o - P. NaOH reportedly demonstrated maximum accelerating effect although the differences between them were found to be small. Shen et al. [72] found that addition of triethanolamine (TEA) directly into a hydrazine bath as an accelerator enhanced the deposi tion rate of pure cobalt up to five times. TEA forms a complex with cobalt ions in the bath which is believed to be more easily reduced. Trace amount (up to ~ 0.01 mMol) of thiourea in the bath can also be considered as accelerator as it can increase the deposition rate [66, 73].

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.1 Temperature
blocks.text: Electroless deposition is possible at room temperature ( 2 5 - 4 0 ~ ^° C) [55, 74]. With increasing temperature, the deposition rate of metal ions increases almost linearly [75–77]. Figure 5b shows the plot of film thickness versus plating time in different bath temperature. From the plot, it is clearly evident that higher the temperature, lesser the needed time to attain a certain film thickness. Although it can be assumed that still higher deposition rate is possible at temperature more than 9 0 ^° C, maintaining pH at this high temperature is very difficult. Hence, 70–90\^°C is found to be the ideal range of bath temperature for electroless cobalt plating. Generally, increasing the bath temperature accelerates the deposition rate because higher temperatures promote faster chemical reactions and increase the diffusion rates of ions to the substrate surface. However, excessively high temperatures can lead to bath instability and spontaneous decomposition. Optimal temperature control is thus crucial for achieving desired plating kinetics and obtaining uniform, dense, and welladhered coatings. Rahman et al.

Equations 3–5 also indicate that higher pH values (i.e., higher OH− concentration) favor cobalt deposition, an observation consistent with findings in electroless nickel plating [79]. Later, it was found that the variation of deposition rate with pH was heavily influenced by the concentration and the type of the complexing agent. As can be seen in Fig. 6a, in alkaline ammoniacal tartarate bath, higher pH favors deposition rate whereas in alkaline non-ammoniacal citrate bath, deposition rate peaks at around pH 7.5–8 and then gradually diminishes. In alkaline citrate bath with low complexing agent concentration (~ 30 g/l), deposition rate peaks at pH 7.8 but with high concentration (~ 100 g/l) of complexing agent, highest deposition rate can be observed at pH 8.5 [80]. Yu et al. [81] observed when Rochelle salt (potassium sodium tartrate) is employed as a complexing agent, the deposition rate initially rises with increasing pH, peaking around pH 10. For optimum deposition rate of Co-P, pH should be kept in between 8 and 10.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.2 pH
blocks.text: Exceeding this value can lead to the formation of cobalt hydroxide depositions, which in turn decrease the deposition rate. Deposition of Co-B is possible from acidic bath. Increasing pH of an acidic DMAB bath from 3.5 to 5 significantly improves deposition rate although at pH 5.5 the bath quickly degrades [47]. Reports on the effect of pH on the amount of P inclusion in the deposit matrix are conflicting. While Chow et al. [44] reportedly observed decreasing P in the matrix with increasing pH, Tarozait et al. [38] observed slight increase in the amount of P inclusion for the same. As discussed earlier in case of deposition rate, here also the differences may arise from the variation in addition of complexing agent. Amount ofB in the Co-B deposit sharply drops and then flattens with increasing pH of morpholine borane bath [51]. Influence of bath pH on the P and B content is shown in Fig. 6b.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.3 Ultrasonication and Stirring
blocks.text: In electroless plating, both ultrasonication and stirring serve the same overall purpose, which is to ensure a uniform and high-quality metal deposition on the surface of the object being plated. Ultrasonication uses high-frequency sound waves to create microscopic vibrations in the solution to dislodge gas bubbles and enhance mass transfer [82]. In electroless Co-P plating, particularly in solutions with low cobalt sulfate concentration as fewer cobalt ions available, the diffusion process becomes more critical for maintaining a steady supply of ions to the substrate surface. The ability of ultrasonication to improve diffusion has a greater impact on accelerating the deposition rate in such scenarios [64]. Ultrasound irradiation reduces the activation energy of the electroless deposition reaction. This essentially means the reaction requires less energy to occur, allowing for a comparable deposition rate at a lower temperature [83]. The mechanism behind this improvement is attributed to ultrasonic cavitation.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.3 Ultrasonication and Stirring
blocks.text: The collapse of cavitation bubbles on the solid surface generates micro-jets which effectively clean the catalytic surface by removing contaminants leading to a larger active surface area for catalysis [84]. Yu et al. [85] found that at high ultrasonication power (100 W), the film exhibits cracks on the surface. This is likely because excessive agitation disrupts the film growth process, leading to weak bonding between the deposited particles and creating cracks. They recommend 90 W for deposition of relatively smaller and more regular shaped crystallites.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 4.4 Bath Aging
blocks.text: Ammonia free alkaline cobalt baths do not show any decrease in deposition rate with aging. Alkaline ammoniacal cobalt bath has short span of deposition life due to dissolution of atmospheric oxygen. The bath ceases to provide significant deposition after 240 min of aging time. Continuous charging of nitrogen gas can prevent this kind of deterioration [63]. Thermally treating the bath by increasing its temperature to 20~^°C higher than operating temperature, keeping there for 45 min and then cooling it back to operating temperature can also reportedly rejuvenate the solution [87]. Various types of electroless cobalt-based deposition baths, including Co-P, Co-B, and pure Co, have been developed. A comprehensive overview ofthe different bath formulations and their resulting deposit compositions is presented in Table 2, providing a valuable resource for researchers and engineers in this field.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 5 Electroless Co Alloys with Other Metals
blocks.text: Apart from hydrazine baths, all electroless Co baths yield binary alloys with either P or B depending on the reducing agent present in the solution. During earlier decades of electroless cobalt research Pearlstein et al. [88] observed that it is possible to produce cobalt alloys by adding other metal salts in the ammoniacal Co-P bath. Although addition of stannate ( SnO _ 3 ^ 2 -) ions fail to produce zinc or tin alloy of cobalt, adding nickel, tungstate, rhenium, or ferrous ions readily produces Ni, W, Re, or Fe alloys of Cobalt. In the following years several binary (Co–Ni [89], Co–Re [90], Co–Sn [32], Co–Fe [91] etc.), ternary (Co–Ni–P [92, 93], Co–W–P [65], Co–Ni–B [94, 95], Co–W–B [50], Co–Fe–P [96], Co–Fe–B [73], Co–Zn–P [97], Co–Mo–P [98], Co–Mo–B [53], Co–Re–P [99], Co–Re–B [100] etc.), and quaternary (Co–Ni–Re–P [99, 101], Co–W–Zn–P [102] etc.) alloys with other metals have been developed. In contrast with the findings of Pearlstein et al. [88], C o - Z n - P was developed by Zheng et al. [97] by adding ZnSO_4 as Zn precursor in the Co–P bath.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 5 Electroless Co Alloys with Other Metals
blocks.text: Electroless Co–Sn was developed using SnCl as Sn ^ 2 + source [32] but no report is available for successful use of \SnO _ 3 ^ 2 - as Sn precursor. Addition of Ni ^ 2 + [ 9 2 ] or Z n ^ 2 + [97] to the bath suppresses the reduction of Co ^ 2 +, and promotes the amount of Ni or Zn in the deposit at the expense of cobalt. Co–Ni or Co–W-based alloys are the most explored ones. In case of Co–Ni-P alloys, within pH range 8.0–9.0 rising pH seems to favor Ni content in the alloy [92] but pH 10 or more favors the amount of Co in the deposit [103]. It is noted that addition of even small amount of Ni salt significantly increases the deposition rate and in general favors Ni content in the deposit [104]. Presence of sodium tungstate ( Na _2 WO _4) in Co bath produces Co-W alloy. While use of hypophosphite as reducing agent produces Co-W–P alloys [105], use of DMAB or borohydride yields Co-W-B alloys [106] and using both hypophosphite and DMAB can result in Co-W–P-B alloy [107]. Various electroless Co ternary alloy baths are furnished in Table 3.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 7 Electroless Co composites
blocks.text: Co composites formed from electroless bath can be of two types – Co matrix composite and core shell composite. Evenly dispersing inorganic foreign particles like WS [115], SiC [116], or BN [70] in the electroless Co bath with the help of a surfactant (CTAB or SLS) and then depositing Co from this bath on an activated surface yield Co-WS, Co-SiC, or Co-BN composite films, respectively. In this type of composites, these nano or micron-sized inorganic particles are evenly distributed in the Co film to form metal matrix composites.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 7 Electroless Co composites
blocks.text: In case of core shell composites, ceramic particle cores or any fiber can be coated with Co to form the composites. The process scheme is shown in Fig. 8c, and SEM image of a core shell composite is shown in Fig. 8c’. Micron-sized WC particles [117, 118], MgO nanoparticles [119], zirconia alumina (ZTA) composite macroparticles [120], or micronsized hydroxyapatite (HA) particles [121] were activated and immersed in the Co bath to coat each particle with cobalt to, respectively, form Co-WC, Co-MgO, Co-ZTA, or Co-HA core shell composite microspheres. A fibrous material like glass fibers [75, 122], SiC whiskers [123], or multiwall carbon nanotubes (MWCNT) [124] can also be activated and placed in the electroless bath to coat each fiber with cobalt in a similar manner to form core shell composite fibers.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8 Applications
blocks.text: Electroless cobalt, a versatile thin film deposited through a chemical process, boasts a distinct set of properties that have driven its adoption in various established industries. However, recent research is also exploring its potential in exciting new frontiers. Major areas of applications are schematically represented in Fig. 9.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.1.1 Magnetic Recording
blocks.text: Magnetic properties ofelectroless Co films, particularly coercivity, have been extensively studied from the beginning. Coercivity is the ability of a ferromagnetic material to resist external magnetic field without being magnetized. Tuneable coercivity of electroless Co-P combined with ultra-thin nature of the deposited film makes it a candidate of interest for high density magnetic recording medium [8, 9, 78]. Ouchi et al. [125] fabricated CoNiP nanodot arrays shorter than 50 nm with high perpendicular magnetic coercivities, using electroless deposition process (Fig. 10a). This is a crucial property for perpendicular magnetic recording technology to increase storage density. Co-P films are promising for magnetic rotary encoders, enabling magnetization into 2048 magnetic pole pairs with uniform output [126]. This improves resolution and accuracy for angle and displacement measurements.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.1.2 Tribological Applications
blocks.text: Electroless Co-P deposits typically have a fine-grained structure, which contributes to their low friction coefficients and good wear resistance. However, the wear and friction behavior of the deposit can be further improved by annealing the deposit at an elevated temperature. Annealing causes the metal grains to grow, which results in a more uniform and stronger deposit. Klingenberg et al. [127]reported the microhardness (VHN) of Co-B to be 716 kg-f/mm 2 and of Co-P to be 883 kg-f/mm 2 after heat treatment at 350 °C. Composite coating like Co-SiC can exhibit high hardness even without heat treatment [116]. Self-lubricating Co-WS film (Fig. 10b) with very low coefficient of friction can be produced via electroless route [115]. It is also reported that presence of cobalt in electroless film enhances corrosion resistance in acidic [128] and saline environment [14].

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.1 Catalytic Activity
blocks.text: Electrolytic hydrogen generation or "green hydrogen" production is a crucial component of a sustainable energy future.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.1 Catalytic Activity
blocks.text: Electrolysis involves the decomposition of water into hydrogen and oxygen gases. The material of the electrodes can affect the rate of hydrogen and oxygen production. Noble metals (Ru and Pt) are often used due to their catalytic properties but they are expensive. Transition metal-based catalysts (Co–B[52], Co-Mo-B [53], Co-P [31, 129], Co-P-B [130] etc.) offer more economical options. Electroless deposition is explored as a promising method for achieving uniform and adherent catalyst layers on electrode surface. Catalytic activity of Co-P significantly depends on phosphorus content, with the coating containing 11 wt% P achieving optimal hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) performance, notably a low overpotential of 98.9 mV at 10 mA cm ^- 2 [131]. Efficiency of Co-P-B catalysts stems from synergistic electronic interactions, where electron transfer from B to Co, often modulated by P, creates active sites and optimizes adsorption capabilities [132, 133].

Electron micrograph of Co-coated Ni foam developed for catalytic water splitting is shown in Fig. 10c.

blocks.text: The ability to form composite coatings with diamond particles on substrates such as plastic balls [138] or polyethylene terephthalate cloth [39] showcases versatility of electroless cobalt in creating magnetic abrasive particles and flexible polishing disks. This is crucial for achieving high-quality surface finishes, which is increasingly important in diverse industries from microelectronics to material processing.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.3 Coating of Composite Reinforcements and Ceramic Particles
blocks.text: Adding small percentage of micro or nano-sized ceramic particles ( Al _2O_3, SiC, MgO, WC, etc.) to metals can make them stronger and tougher as the hard ceramic particles act like tiny obstacles, making it harder for the metal to deform or break. Poor wettability can be a problem in metal matrix composites. If the metal does not adhere well to the ceramic particles, the composite material will be weaker and more likely to fail. One way to improve wettability is to coat the ceramic particles with a different material. This coating can act as a bridge between the metal and the ceramic, making it easier for the metal matrix to spread out and cover the ceramic particles. In recent decades, cobalt is being proven to be a good choice for coating ceramic particles in metal matrix composites [70, 119, 120]. Nambiar et al. [139] successfully developed aluminum matrix composites reinforced with cobalt-coated carbon nanotubes and Al2024 powder, designed for aircraft and automotive applications.

blocks.text: Electroless plating significantly enhances the performance of ceramic particle-based composite coatings obtained through cladding or thermal spraying, particularly for wearresistant applications. By coating SiC [140], WC [136, 141–143], or WC–Co [144–147] powder particles with Ni–P, Co-P, or Ni-Co, desirable features like a more uniform distribution of the binder, higher sintered densities, and improved interfacial bonding can be ensured.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.4 Electromagnetic Shielding Applications
blocks.text: The ability to deposit uniform and compact cobalt layers on substrates like fibers and microspheres, combined with inherent magnetic properties, makes them ideal for creating conductive fillers for polymer composites. This is crucial for developing flexible and lightweight electromagnetic shield ing materials, which are increasingly vital for protecting sensitive electronics from interference and ensuring data integrity in an increasingly pervasive electronic environment. With reported volume resistivities as low as 4.2 × 1 0 ^- 3 - cm on glass fibers [148], electroless cobalt demonstrates excellent electrical conductivity comparable to or exceeding that of electroless copper ( 6.6 3 × 1 0 ^- 3 - cm [149] to 0.0010 - cm [150]) and nickel ( 5.5 0 × 1 0 ^- 3 -·cm [151] to 6.2 5 × 1 0 ^- 3 - cm [152]) in similar applications. Notably, this conductivity is not as low as that achieved with electroless silver ( 6.5 4×10^-4Ω· cm) [153]. In sophisticated electromagnetic (EM) absorption systems, the outer matching layer is engineered to progressively align the impedance of the ambient air with that of the internal absorbing material.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.4 Electromagnetic Shielding Applications
blocks.text: This design ensures minimal surface reflection, facilitating efficient entry of electromagnetic waves for subsequent absorption by the inner layer. Hollow Ni structures coated with magnetic Co-P [154] and Co-MWCNT composite films [124] are developed to address the need for effective matching layer of EM absorbers. They have the potential to be used in stealth technology.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.5 Diffusion Barrier
blocks.text: Diffusion barriers (Fig. 10f) are crucial in microelectronic devices to prevent unwanted interdiffusion of atoms between different materials, which can lead to device failure. Electroless Co-P [4, 5, 108], Co-W–P [86, 105, 155], and Co-W-B [50] can be employed as interfacial layer in microelectronic contacts to prevent the inter diffusion of materials such as copper [156] and lead-free solders [5], ensuring the long-term reliability of electronic devices. A minimal 0.1% addition of manganese oxide (MnO) particles to electroless Co also reportedly improves its resistance to electromigration by physically blocking atomic movement [157]. Electroless deposited Co-P-W films, particularly those with over 12% P and 2% W, serve as excellent barrier layers in structures like through-silicon vias [158]. Compared to chloride free Pd activation, a PdCl /HCl-based activation process is noted to yield superior, residue-free deposition for such Co-P-W capping layers [159].

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.6 Bio-Medical Applications
blocks.text: Electroless cobalt, particularly in the form of iron-cobalt (FeCo) plated carbon nanotubes (CNTs), presents significant biomedical potential, notably in cancer thermotherapy where these magnetic CNTs serve as heat providers to selectively eliminate cancer cells [160]. Beyond direct therapeutic uses, cobalt-based catalysts, such as Co-Fe/Al_2O_3 system (Fig. 10h), are also highly effective in environmental health applications like the advanced oxidation-based removal of harmful emerging contaminants, including antibiotics, from polluted water, showcasing a broader contribution to human well-being through cleaner environments [91].

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 8.2.7 Other Microelectronics/Electrical Applications
blocks.text: Selective electroless cobalt deposition shows promise as a potential replacement for copper in future CMOS devices [59]. Its ability to achieve high selectivity, good film properties, and self-alignment makes it a promising candidate for overcoming the challenges associated with continued device scaling. By enabling bottom-up fill of high aspect ratio features and providing potential benefits in terms of performance and reliability, electroless cobalt could play a significant role in future generations of advanced logic and DRAM technologies [161]. Goel et al.[162] showed that hysteresis loss of grain-oriented high silicon steels, extensively used to manufacture transformer core, can be minimized by applying a coating of Co–Ni-P thin film via electroless route. Yu et al. [163] successfully fabricated thin electroless Co film as flexible electrode for Li–S batteries. This current collector offers advantages over conventional metallic foils, such as aluminum or copper, because it is less dense and exhibits excellent electrical conduction, stemming from its unbroken formation and intimate interface with the electrode material.

blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook
blocks.text: Electroless cobalt deposition is a versatile technique with significant potential in microelectronics, data storage, corrosion/wear protection, HER catalysis, and nanostructure fabrication. Despite advancements, several areas need further investigation for broader industrial adoption:

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook
blocks.text: Enhanced Deposition Rate and Bath Efficiency: A persistent challenge is the low deposition rate and bath efficiency. Future research should focus on novel reducing agents, catalysts, or additives to accelerate kinetics without compromising quality or stability.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook
blocks.text: Tailoring Deposit Properties: More in-depth studies are needed to precisely tailor magnetic, mechanical, anticorrosion, and catalytic properties of electroless cobalt and its alloys for specialized applications. Understanding relationships between bath chemistry, parameters, microstructure, and performance is crucial.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook
blocks.text: Environmentally Friendly Practices: Efforts are vital to develop sustainable plating processes, including nontoxic components, reduced waste, and efficient recycling. Pd-free activation can be a promising step in this direction.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook
blocks.text: Advanced Characterization and Modeling: A deeper understanding of nucleation and growth mechanisms is vital. In situ and ex situ characterization, coupled with computational modeling, can provide insights into reaction pathways and film development, leading to more rational bath design.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 9 Outlook
blocks.text: Addressing these research directions will advance electroless cobalt deposition, leading to more efficient, versatile, and sustainable coating solutions with enhanced properties for future technological applications.

blocks.document_id: 无电镀钴综述
blocks.section: Unveiling the Potential of Electroless Cobalt Deposition: A Review > 10 Conclusions
blocks.text: Electroless cobalt plating is a versatile technique capable of depositing a wide range of cobalt-based coatings, including pure cobalt and various binary and ternary alloys such as Co-P, Co-B, Co–Ni-P, Co-W–P, and Co-W-B. By carefully adjusting the composition of the plating bath and operating conditions, it is possible to tailor the properties of the deposited coatings to meet specific application requirements. These coatings offer numerous advantages, including improved corrosion and wear resistance, enhanced magnetic information storage capabilities, ability to serve as effective barrier layers against copper diffusion or acting as a catalyst in H generation via electrolysis. While many potential applications have been explored, there is still significant room for further research and development in this area. This review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the electroless cobalt plating process by serving as a valuable resource for information on the various chemical baths and operating conditions employed by previous researchers.

blocks.section: Suppressing-accelerating effect of Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride in boosting superconformal cobalt filling > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Achieving cobalt superconformal (bottom-up) growth is significantly important. Electrochemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectra and EQCM-derived Coulomb-voltage curves, were used to confirm the suppressing influence of new suppressor Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride (NBT). In situ Raman spectroscopy was used confirm that NBT can effectively adsorb on cobalt surface. Besides, EQCM-derived Coulomb-voltage illustrates that it is more beneficial for cobalt electrodeposition at high pH. The NBT effect on hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) was studied by LSV and chronoamperometry. Finite element simulation is used to investigate the accelerating effect of NBT on HER and convection. Suppressing-accelerating effect is proposed to illustrate effect of NBT. NBT can not only suppress the cobalt deposition but also can accelerate local convection by intensifying HER, which can in turn strengthen NBT adsorption. SEM analysis demonstrates that convection and NBT can refine grain. High-quality cobalt is achieved with low SDT values ranging from 24 μm to 45 μm and high FP values (75.4 % for 150 μm, 88.9 % for 100 μm and 87.2 % for 50 μm)

blocks.section: Suppressing-accelerating effect of Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride in boosting superconformal cobalt filling > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: With the development of electronic fabrication technology, the interconnect line width has been downscaled to nano size [1,2]. After entering post-Moore era, convectional copper damascene technology is facing enormous challenges in terms of reliability and electronic property of integrated circuit (IC) [3,4]. It is easy to form defects during production due to edge effect at the opening of vias with narrow line width, thus lowering the yield and reliability [5,6]. When the line width is lower than mean free electron path (MFEP) of interconnect materials, the resistivity sees an exponential growth due to severe electron scattering at the boundary [7,8], which increases the IC delay and has a bad influence on electronic property [9,10]. As a result, developing newgeneration interconnect metal is industrially important [11]. Cobalt, due to its low MFEP and compatibility with copper damascene technology, has been used as the interconnect metal at advanced node [12,13].

blocks.section: Suppressing-accelerating effect of Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride in boosting superconformal cobalt filling > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Due to uneven distribution of electric field caused by edge effect and limited mass transfer during electroplating, it is necessary to add effective additives to achieve void-free bottom-up (superconformal) filling [14,15]. Nowadays, researchers have developed some effective suppressors. He et al applied suppressor polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) to achieve superconformal growth based electrochemical methods [16], while Josell et al studied the effect of branched polyethylenimine (PEI) on cobalt deposition and applied S-shaped negative differential resistance (S-NDR) model to predict bottom-up filling [17]. In contrast, Huang et al applied quartz microbalance to study the suppressing effect of dimethylglyoxime and study the influence of HER [18]. Ma et al studied the suppressing mechanism of malachite green on cobalt electrodeposition by coupling AIM method, molecular electrostatic potential and electrochemical method as well as proposed adsorption-transport mechanism to illustrate the influence of malachite green on bottom-up growth [19].

blocks.text: Nowadays, in situ Raman spectra [20,21] and STM [22,23] are widely used to study the adsorption of additives. Besides, HER occurs inevitably during cobalt electrodeposition and has a significant influence on local mass transfer. Nevertheless, there is lack of research on the effect of HER during electrodeposition and the influence of additive on HER [24,25]. Nowadays, finite element method (FEM) is widely used to simulate the practical process to provide more detailed information for researchers [26], like diffusion [27], electric field distribution [28,29], gas releasing process [30], TSV filling simulation [31,32] and so on. Li et al combined experimental and simulated results to propose Gas Microfluidic Pumping (GMP) model to illustrate the effect of gas releasing during HER on the mass transfer [33]. As a result, applying FEM is a good way to help researcher to understand the influence of HER on mass transfer.

blocks.section: Suppressing-accelerating effect of Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride in boosting superconformal cobalt filling > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In this work, we use cyclic voltammetry (CV), electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) and EQCM-derived Coulomb-voltage to investigate Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride (NBT) suppressing effect of during electrodeposition. The adsorption phenomena of NBT on were confirmed by in situ Raman spectra was used to verify the possible adsorption of NBT on cathode during electrodeposition. The influence of pH on current density was studied by measuring EQCM-derived Coulomb-voltage curves, while the acceleration of NBT on HER was analyzed and the influence of gas flow produced by HER with different NBT concentration on flow rate (convection) of electrolytes was acquired by Finite element simulation. Scanning electron micrograph (SEM) was used to observe the convection and NBT on cobalt layer morphology. Finally, superconformal filling in microvias is achieved.

blocks.section: Suppressing-accelerating effect of Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride in boosting superconformal cobalt filling > 2.2. Electrochemical measurement
blocks.text: Electrochemical measurement was controlled by Gamry Framework and was measured in a traditional three-electrode system. The rotating disk electrode (radius of 0.25 cm), saturated mercury sulfate electrode (SSE) and a platinum with the area of 2 cm × 1 cm were used as working, reference and counter electrode, respectively. Inert N_2 was pumped into bath solution to remove oxygen dissolved to exclude the possible oxidization influence before electrochemical tests. The scan rate for cyclic voltammetry (CV) is 5 mV/s and the rotating speed was 1000 rpm, while electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) was carried out at 1.25 V v.s. SSE, 500 rpm. The scan rate for linear sweeping voltammetry (LSV) was 5 mV/s. Besides, electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance (EQCM) was used to study NBT effect on cobalt deposition with 5 MHz gold quartz crystal. Before carrying EQCM tests, the gold quartz crystal was pre plated with cobalt layer at \lfloor A/dm2 for 60 s. Current transients was carried out by chronoamperometry at different cathodic potentials.

blocks.text: Finite element (FE) simulation was carried out by COMSOL Multiphysics. Two-dimensional symmetric model was established to simulate the rotating disk electrode (RDE). The radius of simulated RDE is set as 0.25 cm according to experiments. Electrochemistry module and CFD module were coupled together to simulate the influence of HER with different NBT concentration on the mass transfer of NBT. Tertiary current distribution and bubble flow and laminar flow were used, respec tively. The parameters (exchange current density, charge transfer efficient) were calculated from LSV curves obtained with different NBT concentration and the detailed parameters were shown in Table S1.

During the cobalt electrodeposition, the local pH near the cathode surface sees an increase due to hydrogen evolution reaction. The free Co ^2 + near the surface can complex with OH – to form CoOH^+ adsorbates to boost the reaction rate. When plate is electrodeposited, the pH value in the feature is higher than other parts due to geometry limitation and mass transport limitation. As a result, the current density in the feature is higher since high pH is conducive for the formation of adsorbed cobalt hydroxide intermediate to increase the deposition rate. Besides, the high pH is also good for the improvement for current efficiency according to our previous work [2]. In summary, the difference in terms of pH in the feature and field will benefit the bottom-up growth.
