On one hand, it is NBT who plays a major effect in superfilling process because growth rate difference at the plane and in the bottom can be caused due to effective NBT concentration gradient is formed as a result of geometry limitation and mass transfer limitation (suppressing effect). On the other hand, the accelerating ef fect of NBT on HER will play a supporting role during electroplating. Because the mass transfer at the plane is influenced little compared with that in the microvias due to geometry limitation. The NBT concentration at the plane is relatively higher, which strengthen the HER and gas releasing process in turn further intensify the NBT diffusion and adsorption to suppress the cobalt deposition at the plane. In contrast, the mass transfer is limited in microvias, leading to the NBT concentration is relatively low, which weaken the hydrogen bubble releasing and in turn lower the supplying of NBT from bulk to feature. blocks.section: Suppressing-accelerating effect of Nitrotetrazolium Blue chloride in boosting superconformal cobalt filling > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: In this work, electrochemical analysis methods, including cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectra and EQCM were used to study the suppressing effect of NBT on cobalt electrodeposition. Besides, in situ Raman spectra was used to analyze the suppressing mechanism and NBT can absorb on cobalt surface to suppress the cobalt electrodeposition. EQCM-derived coulomb-voltage curves indicates that high pH is beneficial for the cobalt electrodeposition. Finite element method was accepted to simulate the influence of NBT concentration on convection. Besides, NBT can benefit the HER, which can effectively intensify the local mass transfer during electrodeposition. The intensified local mass transfer can further supply suppressor NBT to cathode surface so as keep the deposition in plane suppressed. Suppressingaccelerating effect is proposed to illustrate the effect of NBT. On one hand, NBT can adsorb on cathode surface to suppress cobalt deposition. On the other hand, NBT can boost the HER and the intensified gas releasing process in turn accelerate the mass transfer of NBT to strengthen the suppressing effect of NBT on cobalt electrodeposition.

blocks.section: Inhibitor Alkyne-PEG4-amine Contributes to Cobalt Superfilling > 1. INTRODUCTION
blocks.text: As the manufacture of integrated circuits advances toward smaller sizes and higher integration densities, the requirements for interconnect materials are becoming more stringent, while the limitations of traditional copper interconnection have become increasingly apparent. 1−6 The resistivity of copper interconnects increases exponentially when the width falls below the copper mean free path, primarily due to frequent electron scattering at interfaces and grain boundaries, which becomes the main factor determining the resistivity. 7,8 In contrast, cobalt interconnects possess better properties, such as very short electronic mean free path, relatively low price, and good compatibility in silicon-based electronic chips. 9−11 Besides, cobalt has a higher melting point, which is more beneficial to reduce the electromigration caused by atomic difusion. 12 These properties are particularly beneficial for applications in advanced integrated circuit assemblies in the post-Moore’s law era. Therefore, cobalt is expected to be a new generation of interconnection material instead of traditional copper.

blocks.text: 13−15 The manufacture process of cobalt interconnects is similar to that of copper interconnects and is compatible with existing electrodeposition processes for copper damascene interconnects. The electrodeposition process for cobalt interconnection is an advanced interconnect technology for integrated circuits that utilizes a wet electrochemical deposition method to bottom-up fill the interconnect structures of semiconductor chips with cobalt metal. Electrodeposition has the advantages of simple operation, easy control of process parameters, and low cost and is considered to be the main technology for cobalt filling at present. 16−18 In recent years, the process of copper electrodeposition has been thoroughly studied, leading to a comprehensive understanding of the bottom-up electro deposition (superfilling) mechanism, which is also applied to cobalt electrodeposition to achieve defect-free interconnect structures. 19,20 The search for suitable additives is the core to fulfill the bottom-up electrodeposition mechanism. Generally, the electrodeposition rate of cobalt changes in diferent positions of the hole due to changing thermodynamics across the additive concentration gradient.

blocks.text: In this work, we propose a cobalt electrodeposition additive which can be used for superfilling. The inhibition efect of alkyne-PEG4-amine (AP4A) was investigated by electrochemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry and chronopotentiometry. Quantum chemical calculations were applied to confirm the inhibition efect of the AP4A molecule on electrodeposition. The results of the cobalt electrodeposition experiment showed that AP4A has significant influence on electrical properties, surface morphology, and crystal structure. In superfilling of nanometer scale structures with high aspect ratios, the additive AP4A was used to achieve bottom-up cobalt electrodeposition successfully. This study provides a targeted solution for superfilled cobalt plating, which has a good role in promoting the development of electroplating in the future.

blocks.text: 2.2. Electrochemical Tests. The electrochemical characteristics of the additive AP4A were assessed through cyclic voltammetry (CV) and chronopotentiometry tests. The experimental setup was established by utilizing a threeelectrode system linked to an electrochemical workstation (CHI660E, Chenhua). The configuration includes a platinum rotating disk electrode with a diameter of 5 mm (Pt-RDE, WE), a platinum plate electrodes (CE), and a saturated Hg/ Hg _2 SO _4 reference electrode (RE). The chronopotentiometry tests were conducted at a steady current of 0.4 ASD (0.4 A/dm2). CV was performed with potential sweeps ranging from −1.5 to 0.2 V, with the scanning rate set at 50 mV/s. The electrode rotates at a speed of 500 rpm in most studies unless otherwise stated in the paper.

blocks.text: 2.4. Electrodeposition. A cobalt plate of 99.99% purity served as the anode. Silicon wafers, measuring 1.5 cm by 1.5 cm, were prepared as cathodes, which were cleaved from a 12 in. diameter silicon wafer with a copper seed layer of 500 nm thickness deposited onto the adhesion layer. Unless otherwise noted, the cobalt films were electrodeposited at a current density of 0.4 ASD with a rotation speed of 500 rpm for a duration of 10 min. Electrodeposition experiments were performed at a constant environmental temperature of 25 ^° C. The morphology of cobalt films was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, TESCAN MIRA3). The surface roughness of the cobalt films was examined by atomic force microscopy (AFM, Oxford Instruments MFP-3D). The crystal structure of the cobalt film was obtained by an X-ray difractometer (XRD, Rigaku Mini Flex 600), operated at 40 kV and 15 mA, in the range from 3 0 ^° to 8 0 ^° with a step of 0.0 2 ^°. The depth profiles of various elements in the electrodeposited cobalt films were obtained using time-of flight secondary ion mass spectroscopy (TOF-SIMS, TESCAN GAIA3). The cobalt film sheet resistance was measured via a four-point probe setup.

A molecule’s HOMO reflects its capacity for donating electrons to metal ions, and its LUMO reflects its capacity for accepting electrons from the metal substrate. Organics with higher E _HOMO values exhibit an enhanced ability to donate electrons, which facilitates their bonding with the d-orbital of metal.

In the electrodeposition process, the constraints of the hole geometry lead to higher electric field and mass-transport conditions at the top of the hole. 36,37 The current and ion concentration at the top of the hole is often higher than at the bottom; as a result, cobalt tends to deposit more rapidly at the top than at the bottom, resulting in the formation of structures containing voids. Besides, as the current density increases, the possibility of void formation also rises, which is attributed to a more pronounced concentration of current at the top of the hole and an increased restriction on mass-transport at the bottom. The cross-sectional view (Figure 5) confirms AP4A’s capability as an inhibitor in cobalt superfilling. In this work, the concentration of AP4A is 5 ppm, which achieved bottom-up cobalt electrodeposition. The bottom-up filling mechanism is depicted in Figure 6. During the process of cobalt electrodeposition, AP4A molecules are adsorbed on the surface of the electrode, modulating the partial electric field strength and current density distribution. In addition, under the influence of mass transport, the molecules have a higher concentration at the top of the hole, leading to a more significant inhibitory efect and slowing down the rate of reduction of the cobalt ions. As a result, the electric field and concentration gradient developed in the presence of the AP4A molecules lead to a higher rate of deposition of cobalt ions at the bottom of the hole than at the top, resulting in the expected bottom-up superfilling.

blocks.text: Abstract: Copper interconnect technology faces limitations due to the electron’s mean free path and electromigration, driving the adoption of cobalt alternatives. This study proposes a novel mechanism to achieve superfilling by tuning the adsorption energy of additive molecules on cobalt surfaces. The adsorption energies of additives are tailored by changing molecular structures with different functional groups. Computational results reveal that carbon–carbon triple bonds critically strengthen adsorption, while ether bonds further enhance binding on distinct cobalt crystallographic planes. Specifically, 1,4-bis(2- hydroxyethoxy)-2-butyne (BEO) containing both triple bonds and ether groups exhibits the highest adsorption energy (−22.62 eV). Replacing ether with hydroxyl groups in 2- butyne-1,4-diol (BOZ) reduces the adsorption energy to −10.39 eV, while eliminating triple bonds in 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (BDE) further decreases it to −8.43 eV. Experimental studies demonstrate that BOZ and BEO preferentially adsorb on the (101) and (110) planes of hexagonal close-packed cobalt (HCP-Co) due to their differential adsorption energies.

blocks.section: Superconformal Electrodeposition of Cobalt into Micron-Scale Trench with Alkynol Derivatives > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Copper is the conventional material for metal interconnect in very large scale integration (VLSI). However, as the process node develops from 180 nm to a remarkable 7 nm [1,2], interconnect sizes continue to shrink, resulting in high resistance and high resistance–capacitance (RC) delay [3–5]. The reason is that copper has a relatively large electron mean free path (39 nm) and needs a relatively thick barrier layer to inhibit electron migration [6,7]. Cobalt is a promising alternative material with an average electron free path of approximately 10 nm and low electron migration [8,9]. Therefore, at the same nanometer scale, cobalt has lower resistance and smaller RC delay [10,11]. The key to replacing copper with cobalt is to be able to produce high-quality cobalt interconnects.

blocks.section: Superconformal Electrodeposition of Cobalt into Micron-Scale Trench with Alkynol Derivatives > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Thin film deposition technology is critical to realize high-quality cobalt interconnects. Physical vapor deposition [12,13] (PVD), chemical vapor deposition [14,15] (CVD), atomic layer deposition [16–18] (ALD), and electrodeposition [19–21] are the primary synthesis methods reported to date. PVD is a widely used film deposition technique, yet its filling efficiency and step coverage remain inadequate, primarily due to one-direction linear de position characteristics. This results in particles with large incidence angles failing to enter the trenches and instead depositing at the trench openings [22]. Consequently, the opening closes before the trench is fully filled [23]. To solve this problem, the industrial sector has de veloped specific PVD technologies, such as ionized PVD and collimated sputtering [24,25]. Nevertheless, the hole problem in small-sized channels still exists. In addition, CVD tech nologies have better filling capabilities, especially when trench widths are around several hundred nanometers, such as plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition [26].

blocks.section: Superconformal Electrodeposition of Cobalt into Micron-Scale Trench with Alkynol Derivatives > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: ALD possesses the unique characteristic of layer-by-layer self-limiting growth, providing exceptional step coverage and film uniformity. However, its deposition rate is exceedingly low, making it particularly suitable for applications such as barrier layers and seed layers [27]. In contrast, electroplating technology is extensively utilized in damascene copper interconnect processes, where it enables bottom-up film growth and demonstrates remarkable filling capabilities [28,29]. During the electroplating process, precise control over parameters such as applied current, anode material, accelerants, inhibitors, planarization agents, and mass transport allows for the fine-tuning of deposition rate, grain size, morphology, impurity content, and stress [30]. This level of control highlights the considerable potential for further advancement of metal-interconnect trench-filling techniques.

blocks.section: Superconformal Electrodeposition of Cobalt into Micron-Scale Trench with Alkynol Derivatives > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Cobalt electroplating is an efficient and cost-effective method for achieving highquality cobalt interconnects [31,32]. By introducing certain organic additives into the plating solution, bottom-up cobalt superfilling can be realized. Superfilling refers to the phenomenon where the metal deposition rate at the bottom of a trench exceeds that in the side wall. This technique is particularly crucial for the fabrication of interconnects with high aspect ratios, as it effectively prevents the formation of voids, ensuring the integrity and reliability of the interconnects. To date, multiple super-conformal filling mechanisms have been proposed by different research groups. The S-shaped negative differential resistance [33,34] has been extensively applied to the overfilling processes of various metals, including copper [35], gold [36], nickel [37], cobalt [38], and zinc [39]. This model suggests that the adsorption and desorption behavior of inhibitors on the electrode surface leads to a nonlinear variation in current density within a specific potential range, resulting in an “S”-shaped curve.

[40,41] introduced the differential current efficiency fill mechanism, emphasizing the critical role of the H + concentration gradient in overfilling processes. They observed that during the electrodeposition of cobalt, the pH gradient rapidly formed within the trenches due to proton transfer, resulting in a disparity between the current efficiency and deposition rate at the trench interior and the opening. This differential effect facilitated the bottom-up filling of cobalt. In parallel, Wu et al. [42] introduced the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation mechanism, which elaborates on how changes in pH and H + concentration affect the inhibitory efficacy of additives, thereby triggering a bottom-up filling mechanism.

blocks.text: In this paper, we propose a mechanism to achieve superfilling by regulating the adsorption energy of molecules on the cobalt surface. By rationally designing the chemical structure of the additive molecules (such as introducing specific functional groups or adjusting the molecular size), the adsorption energy of molecules on the cobalt surface can be regulated. It is worth noting that alkynol additives [43–46] (such as 2-butyne-1,4-diol) exhibit a strong adsorption effect on the (100) and (101) crystal planes of hexagonal close packed (HCP) cobalt, which provides a potential way to regulate the adsorption energy of molecules on the cobalt surface. However, at present, there is still a lack of in-depth research on the filling effect of alkynols in cobalt interconnect trenches and the regulation mechanism of specific groups on the adsorption energy of molecules. We investigate the effects of three organic additives—2-butyne-1,4-diol (BOZ), 1,4-bis(2-hydroxyethoxy)-2- butyne ( BEO), and ^1, 4 -butanediol diglycidyl ether (BDE)—on the morphology, structure, and electrical properties of cobalt electroplating.

Through electrochemical experiments, we compare the polarization capabilities of these additives and analyze their behavior during the electroplating process. blocks.text: The electrochemical experimental setup used was a multi-channel electrochemical workstation (Model M204) manufactured by Metrohm (Herisau, Switzerland). A standard three-electrode system was employed, with a Pt electrode (Tianjin Aida Hengsheng Technology Development Co.,Ltd., Tianjin, China) as the counter electrode, a saturated Ag/AgCl electrode (Tianjin Aida Hengsheng Technology Development C o.., Ltd., Tianjin, China) as the reference electrode, and a Co / TiN / Si patterned wafer (Prepared by magnetron sputtering) as the working electrode. The patterned wafer had a line width of 3 µm and a trench depth of 1 µm. Cobalt electrodeposition was performed using the constant current chronopotentiometry method. During deposition, only one square surface was exposed, while the remaining area was tightly clamped with the Pt electrode, deposited at a current density of 3 mA/cm2 for 56.5 min. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) was performed from 0 to −1.0 V vs. Ag/AgCl using a negative potential scan at a rate of 2 mV · s ^- 1. The stability of the additives during electrodeposition was evaluated in an acidic solution (pH 4.00) of 30g/LH_3 BO _3 (See Figure S1 for details).

blocks.text: To investigate the adsorption interactions between additives and the Co surface, all density functional theory (DFT) calculations, including total energy computations and geometry optimizations, were conducted using the projector augmented-wave method and generalized gradient approximation potentials with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof exchange-correlation functional, as implemented in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package. To account for long-range interactions, the DFT-D3 dispersion correction method of Grimme was employed. The plane-wave energy cut-off was set to 4 5 0 eV, ensuring convergence of bulk energies within 0.001 eV/atom. Cobalt is known to exist in two crystalline phases: the face-centered cubic (FCC) phase and the hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase. In our experiment, cobalt predominantly adopts the HCP phase. Accordingly, the slab models were based on the most stable HCP (002) surfaces, represented by periodic slabs comprising four-layer 6 × 6 supercells with a vacuum layer of 20 Å to ensure accurate surface energy calculations. Monkhorst–Pack k-point sampling of 2 × 2 × 1 was applied.

blocks.text: To clarify the molecular activity and reaction sites of the three additives, BOZ, BEO, and BDE, the DFT was utilized to investigate the molecular electronic structures and orbital energies. Table 1 presents the E _HOMO, E _LUMO,, and the energy gap ( Δ E = E _LUMO - E _HOMO) of BOZ, BEO, and BDE molecules. Generally, for molecules with similar structures, a higher E _HOMO and lower E _LUMO indicate a greater ability to donate electrons to the unoccupied d-orbitals of the transition cobalt metal and a greater ability to accept electrons, respectively. A smaller ∆E suggests a more stable adsorption of the molecule on the cobalt surface [49]. Comparing the E _HOMO values of the studied molecules, it was evident that BEO had a significantly higher E _HOMO,, indicating a stronger electron-donating ability. Furthermore, the ∆E values of BOZ and BEO were significantly lower than that of BDE, suggesting that BOZ and BEO, with carbon–carbon triple bonds, had a greater potential for adsorption on the Co surface.

blocks.text: Figure 1 shows the ESP maps and the average local ionization energy (ALIE) surface distributions of the BOZ, BEO, and BDE molecules, aiming to identify their preferred adsorption sites. The ESP reflects the ability of molecules to approach each other through electrostatic attraction in the early stages of a chemical reaction. The ALIE distribution illustrates the electronic activity of two molecules as their van der Waals surfaces come into close proximity. Figure 1a,c,e show the ESP maps of the studied molecules. The blue regions represent electron-rich areas, while the red regions indicate electron-deficient areas. Clearly, for the BOZ and BEO molecules, the space around the triple-bonded carbon and oxygen atoms exhibited higher electron density. In the BDE molecule, the four oxygen atoms displayed higher electron density. Figure 1b,d,f show the surface distribution of the average local ionization energy for the studied molecules. The blue regions indicate areas with lower ALIE values, signifying stronger electronic activity.

blocks.text: The electrochemical behavior during cobalt electrodeposition was analyzed using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) and the electrochemical deposition method with constant current. The LSV test involved a negative sweep starting from 0 V to −1 V vs. Ag/AgCl with a scan rate of 2 mV · s ^- 1, as shown in Figure 2a. The results indicated that after adding BOZ and BEO, the onset potential for the increase in current density shifted negatively (the potentials of the control group at −0.795 V shifted negatively to −0.838 V and −0.862 V, as shown in Figure 2c). This implies that cobalt deposition was suppressed at the same applied potential, with BEO exhibiting a stronger inhibitory effect than BOZ. The inhibition of cobalt deposition is attributed to the formation of an adsorption layer on the electrode surface by the additives, which alters the electrode properties and increases the energy barrier for cobalt deposition on the substrate [50]. In contrast, no negative shift was observed in the presence of BDE, indicating that the adsorption capability of BDE on the substrate was weaker than that of BOZ and BEO.

blocks.text: It is well known that during the early stages of electrochemical deposition, especially on the cathode surface, a high cathodic overpotential, a large total number of adsorbed atoms, and the low surface mobility of adsorbed atoms are essential conditions for nucleation. The presence of a cobalt seed layer significantly reduces the nucleation requirements, initiating cobalt deposition almost immediately upon applying the current in the absence of additives. However, the adsorption of additives necessitates a certain overpotential to break through the adsorbed layer [54], where the potential gradually decreases and stabilizes. The stabilization deposition potential generally reflects the cathodic polarization ability of the additives. The polarization induced by BOZ and BDE shifted the potential positively (the potentials of the control group at −1.071 V shifted negatively to −1.036 V and −1.038 V, respectively, as shown in Figure 2d). Furthermore, a positive potential shift implies reduced energy consumption in the system. According to reactions (2) and (3), the energy required to reduce Co^2+ is greater than that for H^+.

blocks.text: To investigate the effect of additives on crystal morphology, SEM characterization was performed on the surface and cross-sectional morphology of cobalt films after electrodeposition. As shown in Figure 3, the surface and cross-sectional morphologies of the cobalt films are presented. The super-conformal filling was achieved in the electrolyte with BDE in micro-scale trend. The cross-sectional of Co deposited with the addition of BOZ and BEO showed a gap, although the gap already shrunk compared to the one without additives. It is evident that prolonged electrodeposition allowed sufficient time for the cobalt grains to grow, and the addition of additives significantly altered the morphology of the deposited Co. When Co was deposited in the solution without additives (as shown in Figure 3a), the presence of cobalt dendrites [55] was observed. Under the influence of the tip effect, these cobalt dendrites may lead to the premature narrowing of openings. The addition of organic additives effectively suppressed the formation of dendrites. The cobalt grains became larger and more uniform with the presence of BOZ, BEO, and BDE.

blocks.text: The effect of organic additives on the crystal structure was further investigated by XRD. Figure 4a reveals that cobalt growth in the trench covered with PVD Co as a seed layer was well crystallized. Due to the intense peak of the silicon substrate (100) plane at 69.1 ◦, the right panel of Figure 4a only shows the peak profiles in the ranges of 35–50 ◦ and 75–90 ◦. During cobalt electrodeposition, cobalt preferentially grew along the (100) direction with strong crystallinity in the electrolyte without additives and with BDE. However, in the electrolyte with BOZ or BEO, the preferred orientation shifted to the (002) direction. Additionally, the (002) crystal orientation of Co deposited with BEO was also observed in the TEM image (Figure 4d). The change in the Co preferential orientation may be related to the specific adsorption of additives on certain crystal planes. This adsorption inhibits the growth of the adsorbed planes, causing the crystal to preferentially grow along the non-adsorbed surfaces.

blocks.text: Experimental data indicated that in the additive-free control group, the crystal orientation of the cobalt thin film was (100), with an RTC _( 1 0 0) value as high as 95%. However, upon the addition of BOZ and BEO additives, the preferred growth orientation of the cobalt thin film shifted from the (100) to the (002) orientation. For the samples with BOZ and BEO additives, the RTC _( 0 0 2) values reached 79% and 5 9 %, respectively, representing increases of 30.5 times and 22.8 times compared to the RTC _( 0 0 2) value of the control group (2.6%). This notable orientation transition is likely closely related to the presence of carbon–carbon triple bonds ( C \equiv C) in the BOZ and BEO molecules. A theoretical analysis suggests that the carbon–carbon triple bonds may strongly adsorb onto the (001) and (101) planes of the cobalt thin film, thereby inhibiting the growth of these planes and promoting the (002) plane as the dominant growth orientation.

blocks.text: To further validate this hypothesis, the effect of the BDE molecule, which lacks a carbon–carbon triple bond, on the crystal orientation of the cobalt thin film was also investigated. Experimental results showed that under the influence of BDE, the RTC _( 0 0 2) value of the cobalt thin film was only 0.34%, significantly lower than that observed with BOZ and BEO additives. Although the BDE molecule retains an ether group ( C-O-C),, its lack of a carbon–carbon triple bond structure did not significantly promote the preferred growth of the (002) plane. This phenomenon indicated the critical role of the carbon–carbon triple bond in inducing the transition in crystal orientation. In summary, the carbon–carbon triple bond altered the crystal growth direction of the cobalt thin film by adsorption onto specific crystallographic planes, leading to the preferred orientation of (002).

blocks.text: The sheet resistance of the cobalt films was measured using the four-point probe method to investigate the effect of organic additives on the electrical performance of deposited cobalt. Typically, the sheet resistance of a thin film is influenced by its thickness and resistivity, and the resistivity is affected by factors such as crystal structure, dislocations, defects, and impurities. Since the sheet resistance was measured at nine different locations on the cobalt film, the fluctuations in the measured values reflected the uniformity of the film properties. The non-uniformity of the film properties was quantified by the ratio of the difference between the maximum and minimum sheet resistance values to the average value ( ( Max ~-~ Min) / Avg). Figure 5a shows that compared to cobalt films deposited without additives, the addition of BOZ increased the non-uniformity of the cobalt film, while the addition of BEO and BDE effectively controlled the non-uniformity.

The adsorption conformations and adsorption energies are shown in Figure 6. All molecules tended to adsorb on the Co surface in a parallel manner through their reactive atoms. Consequently, the BEO molecule, which had the most reactive atoms, exhibited a lower adsorption energy on the Co surface compared to BOZ and BDE, indicating the strongest adsorption capability. The adsorption conformations of BOZ and BEO on the Co surface exhibited a zigzag pattern. In contrast, BDE formed bonds with Co only at its two terminal oxygen atoms, leaving the four central carbon atoms unbound to Co. As a result, the inhibition film formed by BDE on the Co surface was looser compared to those formed by BOZ and BEO. To analyze the selective adsorption of molecules on different crystal planes, we first examined the BOZ and BEO molecules.

blocks.section: Superconformal Electrodeposition of Cobalt into Micron-Scale Trench with Alkynol Derivatives > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: In this study, a superfilling mechanism was proposed, in which superfilling was achieved by regulating the adsorption energy of molecules on the cobalt surface. Organic additives containing carbon–carbon triple bonds and oxygen-containing functional groups (BOZ, BEO, and BDE) were examined. The molecular activity and electrochemical behavior analysis revealed that BOZ and BEO exhibited stronger adsorption capabilities on the cobalt surface compared to BDE, owing to their carbon–carbon triple bonds. XRD results indicated that after the addition of BOZ, BEO, and BDE, the cobalt grain size significantly increased. XRD results and adsorption energy calculations demonstrated that the strong adsorption of BOZ and BEO on the (100) and (101) planes of hexagonal close-packed cobalt (HCP_Co) promoted a preferred orientation along the (002) plane of HCP_Co. The adsorption energy of BOZ, BEO, and BDE were −10.39 eV, −22.62 eV, and −8.43 eV, respectively. Cobalt superfilling into micro-size trench was achieved by using BDE molecules as additives with an absorption energy of 8 eV.

blocks.text: Boao Ma a,b, Shihao Zhang a,b, Baimei Tan a,b,*, Wei Li a,b, Yazhen Wang a,b, Xiaoqin Sun a,b a School of Electronics and Information Engineering, Hebei University of Technology, Tianjin 300130, China Tianjin Key Laboratory of Electronic Materials and Devices, Tianjin 300130, China

blocks.document_id: 烟酸作为碱性钴化学机械抛光_CMP_新型缓蚀剂的实验与分子模拟研究
blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > GRAPHICALABSTRACT
blocks.text: The major mechanism of corrosion inhibition effect by nicotinic acid (NA) is to form a passivation film which adsorbs on cobalt (Co) surface so as to strengthen the surface impedance and isolate the corrosion medium. In an alkaline environment (pH 10), NA exists in the form of Nic 2− ions, which are negatively charged. Driven by electrostatic forces and Van der Waals forces between NA molecule (N atom and the carboxyl) and cobalt atom, Nic 2− ions are appealed to the Co(OH) 2, leading to the appearance of Co(II)-NA molecule groups. NA molecules produce a single or multilayer self-assembled Co(II)-NA film on the cobalt surface and further preven the corrosion on Co film.

blocks.document_id: 烟酸作为碱性钴化学机械抛光_CMP_新型缓蚀剂的实验与分子模拟研究
blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Cobalt (Co) is the interconnect metal of integrated circuits with the feature size of 10 nm and below, and Co corrosion is the main problem in cobalt interconnect chemical mechanical polishing (CMP). The introduction of inhibitors is one of the most ideal approaches to reduce corrosion. In this work, useful insights into the corrosion inhibition performance of nicotinic acid (NA), a green inhibitor, on cobalt film in alkaline medium were investigated via electrochemical characterization, surface analysis, quantum chemical calculation, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, as well as the adsorption mechanism at atomic level was explored. NA belongs to anodic erosion inhibitor and its inhibition efficiency reached a maximum of 86.65 % at the concentration of 80 mM pH 10, which was identified by the contact angle and potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) test. The elec trochemical impedance spectra (EIS) suggested that the surface resistance was enhanced to prevent corrosion. Free energy obtained from the Langmuir model indicates that NA molecules are physically and spontaneously adsorbed on cobalt surface.

blocks.document_id: 烟酸作为碱性钴化学机械抛光_CMP_新型缓蚀剂的实验与分子模拟研究
blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: XPS results further confirmed this point, which reveals that NA exists in the form of Nic 2− in alkaline solution and forms a Co(OH)_2(Nic^2-) molecule group (Co(II)-NA) on Co surface. Additionally, quantum chemical calculations based on density function theory (DFT) have approved that C–N bond and carboxyl group are the active sites of NA molecule and form the most significant electrostatic adsorption force with cobalt atoms. Moreover, it can be inferred from MD simulations that NA molecules are spontaneously and physically adsorbed on the cobalt surface at a certain angle. In a word, NA manifests its effectiveness in corrosion inhibition of cobalt and will become a potential cobalt CMP inhibitor. The research methods and results of this paper are beneficial to the study of the adsorption characteristics and inhibition mechanism of inhibitors on the metal surface, and provide a theoretical basis for optimizing the composition of Co CMP slurry.

blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: As the feature size of integrated circuits (ICs) shrinks below 10 nm, cobalt is the most promising material to replace tungsten (W) and copper (Cu) as the front and intermediate lines owing to its great resistance to electromigration and good performance in step coverage [1]. In addition, the barrier layer of cobalt interconnect ICs is thinner than that of copper [2,3]. After cobalt film deposition, the wafer surface is uneven, so chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) is used in IC manufacturing process to realize local and global planarization through the coordina tion of chemical action and mechanical action [4].

blocks.text: However, Co is prone to being corroded by CMP slurry, which con tains many aggressive chemicals, e.g., oxidizers and complexing agents, in which H_2O_2 is widely used to increase removal rate of cobalt as a green oxidizer [5,6]. Yang et al. [7] studied the corrosion of Co in alkaline medium containing H_2O_2 and found that lots of pits were appeared in the presence of 0.1 wt% H_2O_2,, and at some locations, the coating layer was fragmented and peeling occurred. In order to reduce the corrosion of Co surface, many methods and new chemicals have been introduced into the study of cobalt. Badawy et al. [8] investigated the corrosion of Co in alkaline solution and suggested that the potential of Co can be increased by increasing the pH value of the solution to slow down the corrosion rate. Accordingly, all experiments in this study were carried out under alkaline conditions.

blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In recent years, the addition of corrosion inhibitors has been proved to be an effective measure to inhibit corrosion of metal materials [9 11]. Many studies show that organic inhibitor molecules containing elements such as C, N, and O are often more effective in corrosion prevention, among which benzotriazole (BTA) is a common inhibitor and has been broadly commercialized [12 14]. The corrosion inhibition effect of BTA was firstly reported by Cotton et al. [15], and since then researchers have carried out a lot of researches on BTA [ 9, 1 6, 1 7 ]. However, some current studies reported that BTA has a poor inhibition effect on Co corrosion in corrosive medium. Yang et al. [7] characterized the surface morphology of Co in the solution containing BTA and H_2O_2 by SEM, and concluded that BTA could not effectively reduce the pitting caused by H_2O_2 on Co surface. Similarly, Lei et al. [18] suggested that BTA is no longer applicable to Co CMP by means of surface morphology test. In addition, the toxicity of BTA also limits its application in CMP [19,20].

blocks.text: Notably, nicotinic acid, which belongs to the B3 group of vitamins, is widely used as an intermediate in the synthesis of various pharmaceuticals and shows favorable potential in corrosion inhibition effect. Mohamed et al. [23] investigated the polishing behavior and defects of cobalt samples with an aqueous mixture of H_2O_2, oxalic acid (OA), and nicotinic acid at pH 10. The results show that the alkaline solution including 80 mM NA can broadly reduce the corrosion current of cobalt samples and galvanic erosion between cobalt and copper, proving that NA can operate as an inhibitor for Co film in H_2O_2 solution. He et al. [24] concluded that NA offers a composite layer on the cobalt surface, and prevents further Co corrosion, while a combination of 10 mM NA and 5 mM TAZ minimized Co-Cu corrosion as measured by zero resistance galvanometer. Although it is confirmed that NA possesses an inhibition effect on cobalt, further studies on NA, such as the interaction process between NA and Co, the adsorption mechanism of NA on Co surface and so on, have not been reported.

blocks.text: Studying the adsorption of corrosion inhibitor on the metal surface is of great significance to explore the corrosion inhibition mechanism. This work mainly studies the inhibitory effect of NA on cobalt corrosion in alkaline medium, as well as the formation and mechanism of [NA-Co] complex.

blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Studies on the performance of inhibitor molecules only by conventional chemical experiments and characteristic methods are inadequate. The rapid development of theoretical chemistry provides a more scientific explanation for its research. Molecular simulation is a crucial approach to study the molecular chemical activity of corrosion inhibitors from a microscopic perspective [25,27–29]. The adsorption mechanism between inhibitors and metal substrates can be intuitively characterized by molecular simulation technology. Ma et al. [26] probed the effect of potassium oleate (PO) as a viable corrosion inhibitor for Cu films in EDTA–H_2O_2 based solution through combining chemical experiment analysis with molecular simulation. Density functional theory and molecular dynamics approaches were applied to study the inhibition mechanism at the atom level of PO on Cu(111) substrate. Yin et al. [16] evaluated the corrosion inhibition of BTA and TAZ at the molecular level via comparing quantum chemical descriptors. Therefore, it is necessary to further study the quantum chemical properties of NA and micro adsorption mechanism of NA on Co surface.

blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Considering that NA is an inexpensive, green, and easily available organic inhibitor, it was introduced into the alkaline (pH 10) solution. The molecular structure of NA is shown in Fig. 1. Contact angle and PDP measurements were carried out to determine the optimal concentration of NA. The passive film of NA was investigated by EIS, and the reaction between Co and NA was explored by XPS. Density functional theory was employed to study the properties of NA molecule. Several chemical descriptors were calculated to reveal active sites of NA molecule and the electron transfer characteristics between NA and Co atoms, as well as MD simulation was conducted to study the adsorption configuration, adsorption stability and adsorption sites of NA on Co surface. This work provides a more in-depth insight into the development of alkaline cobalt CMP slurry.

blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 2.3. Electrochemical experiments
blocks.text: All PDP measurements were performed on a CHI660E workstation with a three-electrode system (Chenhua, Shanghai). The treated cobalt coupon was wrapped with waterproof tape with an exposed area of 0.3 8 cm ^2, which was used as the working electrode, and saturated mercury electrode (SCE) and platinum (Pt) electrode (the size was 2 cm * 2 cm) as the reference electrode and the counter electrode, respectively. Different concentrations of NA liquids (pH 10) were taken as electrolyte solutions. The open circuit potential (OCP) was tested incessantly for 600 s to acquire more stable results. The Tafel plots of the Co electrode were gained by PDP curve test at the scanning rate of 5 mV/s within the voltage range of OCP ± 0.3 : V The EIS measurements were conducted on cobalt electrode via potentiostat (ZSRS-UI5022), OCP as initial value and 10 mV peak-topeak sine waves with the frequency in the range of 0.1 Hz to 10 kHz as AC perturbation signals. The EIS data were fitted and rectified by the complex nonlinear least squares (CNLS) method in Zsimpwin software.

blocks.text: The Forcite module was employed to operate MD simulations. The ideal Co(111) surface was selected as the adsorption object owing to its high atomic density and low Miller index. The inhibitor molecule and Co (111) crystal system with the size of 6 × 6 × 8 and containing a 40 Å vacuum layer were optimized before the start of each dynamics simulation. In order to obtain stable adsorption configuration of the inhibitor on the Co(111) surface, MD simulation was carried out at the ‘Universal force field and QEq ^* charge. The total energy was calculated by the summation method of the atom-based electrostatic and van der Waals. All MD simulations were based on NVT thermodynamics with an absolute temperature of 298 K, a time step of 1 fs, and a total simulation time of 1000 ps.

blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 3.1. Contact angle test analysis
blocks.text: The adsorption of organic molecules on the metal surface will change its hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity and alters the contact angle of metal surface, while fresh metal surfaces usually present hydrophilicity, hence the contact angle reflects the adsorption effect of the inhibitor [30]. Fig. 2 illustrates contact angle of cobalt samples treated with different concentrations of NA and compared with that treated with CA. After CA treatment, the natural oxide layer on the cobalt surface was removed, and the contact angle of the cobalt surface reduced from 5 5 ^° to 47◦, obtaining the fresh cobalt surface [31]. The contact angle increased to 6 7 ^° following 40 mM NA treatment and increased steadily with the increase of NA concentration until the maximum contact angle reached 8 3 ^° when the concentration was 80 mM. When the concentrations of NA were 90 and 100 mM, the contact angles were 82◦ and 83◦, respectively, which remained basically unchanged compared with that of 80 mM. These results show that when the concentration of NA is greater than 80 mM, the adsorption of NA molecules on the cobalt surface reaches saturation.

blocks.text: With the introduction of NA, both the anode and cathode branches of Tafel curves have the tendency to extend to the region of low corrosion current density. Compared with the cathode branches, the corrosion current density of the anode branches differs from one another markedly, i.e. the reduction reaction rate of dissolved oxygen at the cathode basically remains unchanged, while the metal ionization process occurring at the anode is inhibited. Accordingly, nicotinic acid belongs to the anodic corrosion inhibitor. The linear region of anodic branch, named as passivation region, proves that NA molecules gradually adhere to the cobalt surface to form a protective film and reduce the corrosion degree. It is noteworthy that the slope at the end of the 40 mM NA anode branch (circled in red) sinks, which is caused by the incompactness of the passivation film as the local corrosion medium may interact with the metal through the protective layer to aggravate the metal ionization. The illustration in Fig. 3 shows the PDP test curves of cobalt electrode in NA solutions with concentrations of 80, 90 and 100 mM, respectively.

blocks.text: EIS measurement was used to analyze the passivation effect of physically adsorbed protective film on cobalt surface in alkaline medium. Fig. 5(a) shows the Nyquist impedance spectra of the Co electrodes in different concentrations of NA, which can better understand the structure of passivation layer. Since the Nyquist curve is a 1/4 arc, the charge transfer controls the erosion on cobalt/alkaline medium interface, and the equivalent circuit is a simple model formed by electron exchange on passivation film. In the event that the general shape of the impedance spectra does not change with the introduction of inhibitors, the reaction principle of the corrosive medium could be considered as unaffected [35]. Meanwhile the radius of the spectrum increases with the increase of NA concentration, suggesting that the adsorption film turns to be more completed [36]. The radius of imped ance spectrum reaches the maximum when the concentration of NA is 80 mM, which is consistent with PDP results.

blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: In this work, we focused on nicotinic acid as a potential corrosion inhibitor for cobalt CMP in alkaline medium, and the adsorption behavior of NA was systematically revealed by several characteristic techniques and molecular simulations. The results of contact angel and electrochemical test show that corrosion efficiency reached the maximum value of 86.65 % at the concentration of 80 mM. The adsorption of NA on cobalt surface follows the Langmuir adsorption isotherm, which is a spontaneous physical process. EIS further suggests that with the increase of NA concentration, the passivation film covered on cobalt surface became more complete, resulting in the increase of surface resistance. According to the results of XPS, NA molecules exist in the form of Nic ^2 - ions in alkaline environment, and physically assemble on Co(OH)_2 to form Co(II)-NA molecular groups to isolate the permeation of corrosive medium. DFT calculation and MD simulation indicate that NA molecule is adsorbed on the Co(111) surface at a certain angle through Coulomb force and van der Waals force, which are derived from the interaction of N = C bond and carboxyl in NA molecule and surface cobalt atoms.

blocks.section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: The results of this work on passive film of NA on Co surface and its microscopic properties provide a theoretical basis for optimizing the composition of Co CMP slurry, and also provide support for subsequent researches of exploring synergistic effect of NA and other slurry components. In conclusion, NA is suggested to be an effective potential inhibitor for Co CMP in IC manufacturing process. Its physical adsorption on cobalt surface will help to improve the inhibitor removal effect in post CMP cleaning.

blocks.section: Effect of Saccharin on Crystallization Behavior of Electroless Cobalt Plating > Abstract
blocks.text: In the process of electroless cobalt plating, the saccharin additive can significantly change the surface morphology, texture orientation, and conductivity of the cobalt coating layer. When the amount of saccharin was 3 mg·L –1, the cobalt coating transformed from disordered large grains to a honeycomb structure, with a preferred orientation of (002) facet on hexagonal close-packed (HCP) cobalt crystals. The resistivity of the cobalt film decreased to 14.4 μΩ·cm, and further decreased to 10.7 μΩ·cm after the annealing treatment. When the concentration of saccharin was increased, the grain size was gradually refined and a “stone forest” structure was observed, with the preferred orientation remaining unchanged. The addition of saccharin also slightly improves the purity of cobalt coating to a certain extent. Through the study of the crystallization behavior of cobalt electroless plating, saccharin molecules can adsorb to specific c-sites on the cobalt dense crystal plane, inhibiting the growth of abc stacking arrangement and inducing the crystal growth in ab stacking mode, thereby achieving optimal growth of HCP (002) texture.

blocks.section: Effect of Saccharin on Crystallization Behavior of Electroless Cobalt Plating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: With the continuous development of chips towards high integration, the chip interconnect size is constantly decreasing and copper interconnect technology faces huge challenges. When the interconnect size is reduced to below 7 nm, copper wire conducts exponential growth in resistivity due to its grain boundary scattering [1, 2], leading to chip overheating and increased power consumption, which in turn affects the computing speed and overall device performance [3]. On the other hand, copper interconnects require a barrier layer of approximately 2 nm tantalum nitride (TaN) to prevent copper metal from diffusing into the silicon dielectric layer, thus further increasing the interconnect resistance [4]. Metal cobalt has the advantages of short electron mean free path, resistance to electromigration and good compatibility with semiconductor manufacturing, which has been considered as a new type of interconnect material to replace copper [5–7]. Currently, the pioneer manufacturers such as Intel and TSMC are also proposing to adopt cobalt as a new interconnect metal for advanced chip manufacturing [8].

blocks.document_id: 糖精对镀钴层结构_导电能力的改变
blocks.section: Effect of Saccharin on Crystallization Behavior of Electroless Cobalt Plating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: At present, the cobalt interconnects in silicon chip are realized through electroplating cobalt super-filling. Although there have been reports on the research of electroplated cobalt super-filling in chip microholes [9–11], compared with electrodeposited copper, electrodeposited cobalt is prone to forming holes and cracks due to such issues as hydrogen evolution, homogenization and poor coating quality [12]. Electroless plating is one of the most practical routs to realize cobalt plating in industrial-scale since it presents a good coverage ability, facile processing and low cost. Particularly, additives play a crucial role in electroless plating [13–16]. The appropriate additives not only can improve the quality of the chemical coating, but also enhance its properties such as density, corrosion resistance, wear resistance, and conductivity.

blocks.section: Effect of Saccharin on Crystallization Behavior of Electroless Cobalt Plating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Saccharin (SAC) is a common organic, non-toxic small molecule that can be used as an additive in the electroplating process to improve the quality of coatings, reduce internal stress, refine grains, enhance the glossiness and reflectivity of coatings [17–19]. Altamirano-Garcia et al. [20] studied the effects of sulfates, chlorides, and saccharin on the electrodeposition of cobalt nickel alloys, and found that the addition of saccharin significantly improved the deposition current efficiency and suppressed hydrogen production, thereby improving the density of the alloy coating. Hoghoghifard et al. successfully improved the microwave absorption performance of nickel coated fabrics by adding saccharin to the plating solution [21]. They found that adding saccharin can reduce surface resistivity, refine grain size, enhance hysteresis loss, and ultimately improve the microwave shielding effect of the fabric. Kolonits et al. found that adding saccharin can significantly refine grain size, increase lattice defect density, and thus improve the hardness of nickel films [22].

blocks.section: Effect of Saccharin on Crystallization Behavior of Electroless Cobalt Plating > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Upon electroless cobalt plating, we observed that the addition of saccharin would change the morphology of cobalt plating. Then we systematically studied the effects of saccharin additive on the microstructure, crystallization behavior, and conductivity of cobalt plating. It was found that adding an appropriate amount of saccharin can effectively adsorb specific crystal planes of cobalt crystals, thereby directionally regulating their growth behavior and obtaining cobalt coatings with (002) texture preferred orientation, which promotes the conductivity of cobalt coatings. At the same time, density functional theory (DFT) simulations provided insights into the crystallization behavior of cobalt coatings, revealing that saccharin molecules can adsorb to specific sites on the cobalt dense crystal plane, blocking abc packing and inducing crystal growth in ab stacking mode to form hexagonal close-packed structure (002) texture.

blocks.text: To investigate the interaction mechanism between the saccharin molecule and the cobalt surface, we constructed a slab model of saccharin adsorbed on the Co (002) surface ( 6 × 6 × 2). Structural optimizations and electronic structure analyses are performed using the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP 5.4.4) [25]. The projector augmented wave (PAW) pseudopotential is employed to describe electron-ion interactions [26, 27], while the exchange-correlation effects are treated with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functional [28]. A plane-wave cutoff energy of 500 eV is utilized, with convergence criteria set to 1 × 1 0 ^- 5 eV for energy and 0.0 2 eV · \stackrel \triangledown A^-1 for forces. Brillouin zone sampling is conducted using a2×2×1 Gamma k-point mesh [29]. For the saccharin molecule, geometry optimization and orbital analyses are further carried out using the Gaussian 16 package [30], employing the PBE1PBE hybrid functional combined with the ^6-311C^** basis set.

blocks.text: Fig. 1(a–d) shows the morphologies of cobalt coating after 1 hour of electroless cobalt plating with different amounts of saccharin. When saccharin was absent (Fig. 1a), the surface grains of the cobalt plating layer grew randomly, exhibiting disordered crystal orientation and larger particle size. When 3 mg·L –1 saccharin was added (Fig. 1b), the grains of the cobalt film exhibited typical hexagonal texture characteristics, and the surface became smoother. As the addition amount was higher than 200 mg·L –1 (Fig. 1c), the morphology of the cobalt film was transformed from a hexagonal texture to a “Stone Forest” morphology. When the addition amount was further increased to 1 g · L ^ - 1 ( Fig. \ 1 d), the cobalt film maintained a “Stone Forest” morphology, but the grain size of the cobalt film was further decreased. Combining XRD patterns (Fig. 1e), it can be seen that the diffraction peak of the deposited Co film was located between (002) the hexagonal close-packed structure (HCP) Co phase and (111) the face centered cubic (FCC) Co phase when saccharin was not added.

blocks.text: To further investigate the interaction between saccharin and the Co surface, we calculated the differential charge density map [33]. It can be observed from Fig. 7a that the charge density near the Co surface is decreased (the cyan region) and the charge density near the aromatic ring structure of saccharin is increased (the yellow region), illustrating that electrons transfer from the Co surface to the saccharin molecule. Bader charge analysis reveals a total charge transfer of 0.88 e. Moreover, the Frontier molecular orbital theory is widely used to analyze and predict the adsorption behavior of molecules [34, 35]. The frontier orbital diagram (Fig. 7b) shows that the LUMO of saccharin, acting as an electron acceptor, is predominantly localized on the unoccupied π orbitals of the phenyl ring and the oxygen atoms. Consequently, the interfacial charge transfer can be attributed to the d → π* back donation interaction between the Co surface and the saccharin molecule.

blocks.section: Effect of Saccharin on Crystallization Behavior of Electroless Cobalt Plating > 3.4. Simulation and analysis of the crystallization behavior
blocks.text: Due to the presences of both sulfonic acid groups (–SO H) and aldehyde groups in saccharin, the electron cloud density at certain positions of the benzene ring is relatively reduced. Therefore, the benzene ring on saccharin molecules often exhibits electrophilicity, which meets the calculation result of the differential charge density mentioned above. In the process of electroless cobalt plating, cobalt ions need to be reduced at sites with electron donating properties. Therefore, the adsorption of saccharin molecules on the cobalt surface hinders the continuous growth of cobalt at the c-site during the stacking process (Fig. 5c and Fig. 6c), leading to the formation of ab stacking and HCP cobalt texture. According to Burton-Cabrera-Frank (BCF) theory, [36] surface adsorbed molecules inhibit atomic diffusion and step flow, thereby inhibiting lateral grain growth. When excessive saccharin is added, too many saccharin molecules adsorb to the sites on the densely packed surface of cobalt film, the continuous growth of the crystallization process is also disturbed so that smaller crystallites are obtained.

blocks.section: Effect of Saccharin on Crystallization Behavior of Electroless Cobalt Plating > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: In the process of electroless cobalt plating, the addition of saccharin changes the microstructure of the obtained cobalt layer. The addition of a small amount of saccharin at a concentration of 3 mg·L –1 caused the cobalt plating film to change from disordered orientation to hexagonal texture, with the preferred orientation of (002) facet of HCP Co phase. Continuous increase in the saccharin concentration (>200 mg·L –1) resulted in the refinement of cobalt film grains with a “Stone Forest” morphology. The honeycomb morphologic cobalt coating with the appropriate addition of saccharin (3 mg·L –1) presented a tight grain boundary connection, thereby reducing the resistance to 10.7 μΩ·cm. After studying the cobalt crystallization process and conducting DFT simulations, it is found that the charge density near the aromatic ring of saccharin is increased from the Co surface donation, so that the saccharin molecules can adsorb to specific c-sites on the surface of densely packed cobalt atoms, hindering the abc stacking arrangement. The crystallization process can be tuned to proceed along the ab stacking, thus forming the (002) preferred texture of HCP cobalt.

blocks.document_id: 糖精对镀钴层结构_导电能力的改变
blocks.section: Effect of Saccharin on Crystallization Behavior of Electroless Cobalt Plating > 4. Conclusions
blocks.text: The findings from this study not only provide a detailed understanding of the role of saccharin in electroless cobalt plating, but also offer a theoretical framework for the design and optimization of additives in electroless plating processes.

blocks.section: 化学镀钴过程中添加剂糖精对结晶取向的调控 > 摘要：
blocks.text: 在化学镀钴过程中， 我们发现添加剂糖精的加入可明显改变化学镀钴层表面的形貌、 织构取向及镀层的导电性。 研究表明， 当糖精添加量为 3 mg ·L^-1 时， 钴镀层由无序大晶粒转变为蜂巢状结构， 具有密排六方 （HCP） 钴晶体的 （002） 择优取向， 其电阻率降低至 1 4.4 μ Ω · cm ， 经过热处理后， 电阻率进一步降低至 1 0.7 ~ μ Ω · cm ， 这对于其在芯片中的应用具有重要价值。 当糖精浓度升高时， 晶粒逐渐细化， 呈现 “石林” 状结构， 择优取向不变， 而糖精的加入在一定程度上提高了镀钴膜的纯度。 通过密度泛函理论对钴镀层结晶行为的研究表明， 糖精分子可吸附于钴密排晶面的特定 c 位点， 抑制 abc 堆积方式生长， 诱导晶体按 ab 堆积方式生长， 从而实现 HCP（002） 晶面的择优生长。

blocks.section: Investigation of polyvinylpyrrolidone as an inhibitor for trench super-filling of cobalt electrodeposition > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) is studied in this paper as an inhibitor of cobalt electrodeposition. The suppres sion effect of PVP was analyzed through electrochemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry (CV) and galvanostatic measurements (GM) tests. It is indicated that PVP effectively suppresses the electrodeposition of cobalt and chloride ion accelerates this suppression. Further experiments verify that PVP inhibits the deposition of cobalt through the adsorption on the electrode surface. Quantum chemical calculations were employed to calculate the molecular orbitals of PVP and the electrostatic potential (ESP) energy of the involved molecules. The simulation results imply that the amide group acts as the main electrophilic attack region and facilitates nucleophilic reactions to bond with cobalt. High aspect ratio trench filling on silicon wafer was achieved with the addition of PVP, which confirms that PVP is an applicable inhibitor for the practical electrodeposition of cobalt filling. The mechanism of cobalt trench filling was proposed to explain the role of PVP in the electroplating filling.

blocks.section: Investigation of polyvinylpyrrolidone as an inhibitor for trench super-filling of cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Metals are the basic building materials to establish the conductive interconnection between the electronic components. The inherent properties of the metal are critical factors for achieving high density interconnection and miniaturization in the electronic devices. Compared with copper, cobalt with shorter electron Mean Free Path (MFP) holds the reduced resistance scaling effect and has been considered as a favorable interconnect metal [1 3]. Also, the thermal expansion coefficient (CTE) of cobalt is close to the one of silicon, which enables cobalt to serve as a compatible metal integrated in silicon-based electronic chips. In comparison with aluminum and copper, cobalt is recommended to be one of the next generation interconnection metals by the leading semiconductor manufacturers, such as Intel and Advanced Semiconductor Engineering (ASE), to meet the requirement of the blooming 5 G communication. Generally, inter-layer connections within the silicon chips are electroplated by bottom-up super filling of through-holes, microvias and trenches.

blocks.section: Investigation of polyvinylpyrrolidone as an inhibitor for trench super-filling of cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Additives are usually involved in electrolyte to promote plating properties. Researchers have performed extensive experimental as well as theoretical analysis to investigate the growth mechanism and additive behaviors of bottom-up copper super filling for micro-vias [8 11]. It was found that, the additives with the function of increasing metal deposition overpotential are able to obtain void-free super-filling [12]. Convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of additive causes larger differential current distribution to realize higher deposition rate at the bottom than the one at the surface of microvia [13]. However, researches focusing on the additives involved in cobalt electrodepositing are still inadequate, especially in cobalt super filling.

blocks.section: Investigation of polyvinylpyrrolidone as an inhibitor for trench super-filling of cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Huang et al. found that dimethylglyoxime (DMG) exhibits obvious suppression behavior in cobalt electro-deposition [14,15]. They stated that paired amine groups of DMG enable the strong complexing between DMG molecule and cobalt ion. On the other hand, these groups also contribute to the preferred absorption of DMG on the deposited cobalt surface. DMG is, however, not an appropriate candidate for industrial application because the molecular chain of DMG easily breaks down under electric current. In addition, the low solubility in acidic aqueous solution also hinders the feasibility of DMG. PVP is a neutral non-ionic polymer containing paired amine groups with good complexing ability [16 18]. Notably, PVP is soluble in water and most organic solvents with low toxicity, making PVP a potential additive for cobalt super-filling.

blocks.section: Investigation of polyvinylpyrrolidone as an inhibitor for trench super-filling of cobalt electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: In this paper, PVP was studied as major additive for cobalt super filling by electro-plating. The suppression effect of PVP was investigated by electrochemical experiments and the effect of chloride ion was also studied. Moreover, the active site in PVP molecule was speculated by theoretical calculations to understand the mechanism of suppression. In addition, PVP also displays significant influence on the morphology and crystal phase of electrodeposited cobalt. As for practical application, trench super-filling was realized by electrodepositing with PVP.

blocks.section: Investigation of polyvinylpyrrolidone as an inhibitor for trench super-filling of cobalt electrodeposition > 3.1. Inhibition and maximum ofPVP inhibition
blocks.text: The inhibitive behavior of PVP in the solution was investigated through electrochemical measurements. Fig. 1 shows the significant decrease of cobalt stripping area and hysteretic voltammetric features in the solution with PVP. The current density decreases sharply in the presence of PVP (Fig. 1a). For example, after adding 5 mg/L PVP into plating solution, the stripping peak current density decreases from 2 1 mA/cm2 to 1 2 mA/cm2.. In the meantime, the oxidation peak potential is also shifted negatively by 80 mV (from 0.36 V to 0.44 V vs Hg/ Hg _2 SO _4). The change in stripping peak current density and oxidation peak potential both reveal that cobalt electrodeposition is inhibited by PVP. The CV plot in Fig. 1b highlights that the cobalt deposition potential is negative correlated with the concentration of PVP which shows an enhancing effect on the polarization of cobalt electroplating. In addition, with the increasing concentration of PVP, cobalt electrodepositing was further inhibited, which is supported by the decreasing area of oxidation peaks.

blocks.text: The maximum state of PVP suppression was further studied. As is shown in Fig. 1c, the oxidation peak area of CV was calculated to illustrate the inhibition effect of PVP with different concentrations. The integral of the cobalt stripping peak area is defined as Q_0 without PVP and as Q with PVP, respectively [28]. The curve which displays the value of Q/Q_0 as a function of the concentration of PVP can be divided into three stages (Fig. 1d). Q/Q_0 values undergo a sharp drop with low concentration of PVP and a steady stage with the high concentration of PVP. Notably, an intermediate slope appears in the curve for the PVP concentration range between 15 mg/L and 81 mg/L. When the PVP concentration continues to increase to more than 81 mg/L, the inhibition of PVP in cobalt electroplating reaches maximum.

blocks.text: As well known, chloride ions could affect the quality of metal coating and influence the mechanisms of additives in metal electroplating bath [29, 30]. The impact of Cl in the PVP-involved electroplating system was analyzed through voltammetry curves (Fig. 2a). In contrast with the curves in Fig. 1a-b, the stripping peak current density decreases more sharply when 5 mg/L PVP was added into the solution. These results in CV curve imply that PVP can inhibit the electrodeposi tion of cobalt in both chloride-containing and non-chloride ion plating solutions. However, in the solution with Cl, less amount of PVP is needed to reach the saturation (Fig. 2b). As for the Q/Q_0 value, this ratio decreases with increasing concentration of PVP and process is divided into two stages (Fig. 2b). The phenomenon of first stage that Q/Q_0 values decrease sharply with adding PVP can be observed when the concentration of PVP is less than 10.65 mg/L. In the second stage, Q/Q values maintain relatively stable with further increased PVP concentration. In the absence of Cl (Fig. 1d), PVP in plating solution reaches the saturation at a much higher concentration.

In this work, when the PVP was added in the solution, it preferentially complexes with cobalt ion. blocks.section: Investigation of polyvinylpyrrolidone as an inhibitor for trench super-filling of cobalt electrodeposition > 3.2. Quantum chemical calculation and CDA
blocks.text: The molecular frontier orbital theory suggests that the key of chemical reactions is the HOMO and LUMO of the molecules [20]. The distribution of HOMO and LUMO of PVP was simulated by molecular orbital method (Fig. 3). The HOMO value ( E _ HOMO) of a molecule determines its ability to lose electrons outward, and the LUMO value ( E _ LUMO) represents its ability to accept electrons. Higher E and lower E _ LUMO partly reflect the reactivity of molecule [32]. The E _ HOMO value of PVP is 6.877 eV (Fig. 3e), compared with 7.338 eV of PEG [21], indicating that PVP has relatively stronger electron donating ability. The simulated values imply that PVP is more likely to interact with cobalt cations and have an impact on electrodeposition of cobalt. Fig. 3e shows that the nitrogen element and oxygen element of the amide group are the main contributors to the HOMO orbital, which acts as the main electrophilic attack region. The organics with higher value of E _ HOMO tent to have stronger electron donating ability to bond with the d-orbital of the metal. PVP with amide group may bond with cobalt, facilitates formation of PVP adsorption and inhibits cobalt electroplating.

Areas with low ESP value are the positions of high electron density, which are considered to be more affinitive to the cobalt surface [34, 35]. PVP has lowest ESP value of 131.3 kJ/mol compared with PEG [21] ( 131.6 kJ/mol) (Fig. 3a). The electron density map shows that the carbonyl of the amide group contributes greatly to the electron donating ability of PVP. The amide group probably acts as reaction sites in the electrodeposition reaction by the quantum chemical calculations.

blocks.text: Convection have significant influence on the process of electrodeposition. For the electroplating with rotating electrodes, the higher rotating speed of electrode leads to the greater convection in the solution. PVP can effectively inhibit the electrodeposition of cobalt in strong convection because the potential was quickly reduced by 160 mV when 5 mg/L PVP was added in strong convection (2000 rpm) (Fig. 3c). However, when 5 mg/L of PVP was added at low rotating speed (200 rpm), the potential was reduced by 100 mV and the inhibitory effect was slowly balanced after 2000s. Ji et al. found that electrolyte flow plays an important role in electroplating process [36]. The convection intensity of the solution inside the hole is lower than the one outside. The local convection affects the transport boundary layer in cobalt electroplating. As a result, more PVP molecules are be transmitted from solution to the electrode surface per unit time in strong convection. In Fig. 3c, PVP demonstrates a faster suppression in the strong convective condition, which is conducive to filling holes in electroplating.

blocks.text: Cobalt bottom up filling mechanism is proposed in Fig. 5. In the initial stage of electrodeposition, PVP molecules were quickly adsorbed on the surface, strongly inhibiting the growth of cobalt on the surface. blocks.text: The effect of PVP involved in the electrodeposition of cobalt was further investigated by the characterization of morphology. PVP demonstrates considerable effect on electrodeposited cobalt crystals. The XRD results in Fig. 6a indicate that PVP inhibits the cobalt electrodeposition by affecting the growth of cobalt specific crystal surfaces. The electrodeposited cobalt mainly forms cubic crystals in Fig. 6a. And, it is worth mentioning that PVP reduced the intensity of diffraction peak of cobalt along the direction of 220, indicating that the introduction of PVP inhibited the growth of 220 surface of cobalt without affecting the growth of other crystal planes.

blocks.text: The contact angle test indicates that PVP can improve the wettability of plating solution effectively. As is shown in Fig. 6c-d, the contact angle of the plating solution without PVP is more than 3 0 ^° on the cobalt surface and is reduced to 15° after adding 100 mg/L PVP. Better wettability of the solution enables more hydrogen to be released in time [39] and enhances coating quality in cobalt electrodeposition. PVP can also be used as surfactant in electrodeposited cobalt because the amide group and carbon chains of PVP can act as polar hydrophilic and hydrophobic group respectively. Meanwhile, according to the theory of electro-capillary, polarization can reduce the surface tension and contributes to the desorption of hydrogen, which is consistent with the discussion above.

Sa represents the arithmetic mean of the height values of all the peaks and troughs on plane A in Fig. 6g and Fig. 6h. The larger the value of Sa, the greater roughness of metal surface. blocks.text: As a conclusion, PVP can increase the polarization of electrodeposition, affect the growth of cobalt particles growth and redistribute the cathodic current. PVP works as inhibitor for electrodeposited cobalt and the suppression mechanisms of PVP were demonstrated. Chloride ion can facilitate the adsorption of PVP and helps to accelerate the suppression effect of PVP. The amide group of PVP is probably the reaction site by quantum chemical calculations. Void free filling of silicon trenches was achieved by cobalt super-filling on a sputtered gold layer in this paper.

blocks.section: Investigation of adenosine as a leveling additive with synergetic acceleration–suppression behavior for superconformal cobalt filling in X-shaped through-hole > ABSTRACT
blocks.text: Adenosine (ADO) was selected as a leveling additive for superconformal cobalt filling in X-shaped through-hole. Changes in deposition potential and the generation of new stripping peaks in cyclic voltammetry curves were observed in electrochemical tests of ADO-containing plating solution. The adsorption behavior of ADO on the cobalt surface was investigated using density functional theory calculations, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, and electrochemical in situ Fourier transform infrared (E-FTIR) spectroscopy tests. Furthermore, the Co 2+ with ADO coordination was simulated via interaction region indicator analysis. Based on the changes of the ADO adsorption sites from the MD and E-FTIR analyses, an intramolecular synergistic acceleration–suppression mechanism was proposed to explain the effects of low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression in cobalt deposition. Surface analysis revealed that ADO exhibited a grain refinement effect, and crystal analysis showed that the Co hcp (002) crystalline plane was preferentially formed.

blocks.text: Electronic interconnect technology is the key for realizing advanced packaging and chip interconnection. With the development of semiconductor technology, the line resistance of copper considerably increases because of the large mean free path of electrons, copper cannot meet the process requirements of damascene filling. However, cobalt exhibits good electrical conductivity and a small mean free path of electrons [1,2], which can prevent electron scattering at the surface interface [3]. In addition, the coefficient of thermal expansion of cobalt (13.3 × 10^-6/K) is similar to that of silicon (10 × 10^-6/K) [4,5], and the internal stresses generated during high-temperature annealing are smaller than those generated during high-temperature annealing of copper [6]. Cobalt is considered the most promising alternative metal for nanoscale interconnect technology.

blocks.text: The bottom-up superfilling phenomenon of cobalt has been increasingly studied, and various micro-nanoscale mechanism models have been proposed. Such models include hydrogen-induced inactivation mechanisms [7,8], voltage-dependent suppression mechanisms [9, 10], S-type negative differential resistance mechanisms [11,12], and differential current efficiency filling mechanisms [13]. Rigsby et al. [12] proposed a differential current efficiency filling mechanism and achieved damascene filling of cobalt. Using the differential current filling mechanism, Ni et al. [14] introduced polyvinylpyrrolidone into electrodeposition of cobalt to achieve a superconformal silicon trench filling. Ma et al. [15,16] used the S-type negative differential resistance mechanism with malachite green and achieved micro blind hole filling of cobalt. Li et al. [17,18] achieved micro blind hole filling with different pore sizes using nitrotetrazolium blue chloride, applicable to S-type negative differential resistance mechanism theory. Huang et al. inves tigated the role of oxime additives and concluded that the amine group can suppress cobalt electrodeposition by coordinating with C o ^ 2 + \ [ 9, 1 0, 19].

blocks.section: Investigation of adenosine as a leveling additive with synergetic acceleration–suppression behavior for superconformal cobalt filling in X-shaped through-hole > 1. Introduction
blocks.text: Herein, using adenosine (ADO) as an additive with the lowconcentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression and the differential current efficiency filling mechanism during cobalt deposition, superconformal filling of cobalt in X-shaped through-hole was achieved. Through electrochemical analysis, ADO was observed to exhibit a depolarizing effect on Co ^2 + deposition at low concentrations. However, at concentrations of > 1 0 mg/L, ADO increased the polarization of cobalt deposition and considerably changed the cobalt deposi tion. Through density functional theory (DFT) calculations and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, this electrochemical effect was elucidated in terms of electrostatic potential (ESP) on the molecular surface and the adsorption energy of ADO on the cobalt surface, respectively. The shift in the type of ADO electrochemical action at different concentrations was elucidated in terms of the change in adsorption sites during electrochemical in situ Fourier transform infrared (E-FTIR) spectroscopy tests.

blocks.text: During the electrochemical testing, ADO was observed to have a low concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect on cobalt deposition. The electrochemical tests, MD simulations, DFT cal culations, and E-FTIR tests explained the reasons for the acceleration at a low concentration and suppression at a high concentration.
