blocks.text: DC electroplating was performed to corroborate the effect of ADO on cobalt filling. The through-hole filling of cobalt was conducted in a 1.5 L Haring cell with a current density of 0.5 ~A/dm2 and plated with a DC power supply for 4 h. Cathodic bubbling was employed during the plating process at a bubbling rate of 2.5 L/min. Here, 50 mg/L of ADO was added during plating, and the X-shaped through-hole filling of cobalt was achieved with the SDT value of 1.2 μm. The pH of plating solution was changed nonlinearly during the cobalt deposition because no acidic or basic substances were added to stabilize the pH value. After plating for 1 h, 2 h and 4 h, the pH values of plating solution were observed as 3.2, 2.6 and 2.3, respectively. The rate of cobalt deposition could become slow due to the decrease of pH value [20,59], thereby leading to thin layer of cobalt growth outside the X-shaped through-hole.

blocks.section: Investigation of adenosine as a leveling additive with synergetic acceleration–suppression behavior for superconformal cobalt filling in X-shaped through-hole > 4. Conclusion
blocks.text: During the electrochemical test, it was observed that ADO exhibited a low-concentration acceleration but high-concentration suppression effect. By analyzing the HOMO-LUMO and ESP values, discovered that the ADO adsorption sites could be categorized into two distinct groups: adenine and nucleoside. Subsequent MD simulations revealed that the specific adsorption sites were the –OH within the nucleoside group and the –NH within the adenine group. Furthermore, the E-FTIR test indicated that the –OH in nucleoside group were preferentially adsorbed, and as the concentration of ADO increased, the adsorption of the –NH in adenine group was enhanced. These findings were consistent with the ESP calculations, which identified the –OH in nucleoside group as the maximum point and the –NH in adenine group as the sub-maximum point. Combined with the results of electrochemical tests and IRI sim ulations, it is concluded that the nucleoside groups which containing multiple –OH played an accelerating role in cobalt deposition, while the adenine group which coordinated with Co ^2 + played a role in suppressing cobalt deposition.

blocks.section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition
blocks.text: Zijie Mao 1, Xianglong Du 2, Xindi Xu 1, Yicai Wu 1, Xiaohui Yang 2* Kun Jiang 1, Jun Cheng 2, Zhi-You Zhou 2, Shi-Gang Sun 2 & Wen-Bin Cai.1* Received January 7, 2025; accepted March 9, 2025; published online May 6, 2025 Cobalt (Co) metallization presents a promising alternative strategy for the bottom interconnect in advanced chip manufacture, yet the interfacial structure and functionality ofan organic additive essential for superconformal Co deposition is far from clear given the concurring hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Herein, interfacial electrochemistry for a model additive molecule MBIS (sodium 2-mercapto-5-benzimidazolesulfonate) at a Co electrode is investigated by applying in situ surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy and electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance combined with density functional theory calculations The vertical plane adsorption of MBIS on the Co surface via thiolate reduces the overall reduction current with a higher/lower Faradaic efficiency (FE) towards HER/Co deposition due to the significant blockage of surface Co sites as well as the formation of Co(II) complex with MBIS.

blocks.section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: The interconnect metallization is crucial to attain signal and electrical transmission and thus a central process in chip manufacturing [1–5]. Cu is the most commonly used interconnect metal by means of Damascene Cu plating, however, when a 14-nm (or below) process is adopted, electron scattering at external surfaces and grain boundaries leads to a sharp rise in the resistance of narrow Cu lines in the bottom layers [6]. At the nanoscale, the resistivity of a metal is directly related to ρ _b × λ, where ρ _b represents the bulk resistivity of the metal and λ represents the electron mean free path [7,8]. Co, Ru, Rh, and Mo have lower ρ _b × λ values and thus are expected to exhibit lower resistances in narrow lines. In addition, their higher melting points compared to that of Cu, are also beneficial in reducing electromigration [9]. In particular, Co interconnect by electrodeposition is highly promising for commercial applications because of its low cost and relative ease for plating among the four alternative metals [10,11].

blocks.section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: Unlike acidic Cu electroplating in which hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is negligible, Co electroplating is accompanied by HER given that φ _Co ^2 + / Co = - 0.2 8 : V vs. SHE and φ_H^+/H_2=0 : V vs. SHE [12,13]. In order to achieve bottom-up filling and avoid voids in the vias, a suitable inhibiting additive, such as sodium 2-mercapto-5-benzimidazolesulfonate (MBIS) [14], or dimethylglyoxime among others [15–25], is needed to regulate the kinetics of Co deposition. Several superfilling (superconformal deposition) models have been proposed to account for the additive-assisted filling process, including the S-shaped negative differential resistance (S-NDR) [15,26,27], the differential current efficiency fill (DCEF) model [28,29], and the hydrogen reduction-induced deactivation (HID) model [30,31].

blocks.section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: Notably, despite their significant achievement from a simulation perspective, these models lack a molecular-level insight into the interaction of a specific organic additive with a Co electrode as well as its impact on the Co electrodeposition, which is otherwise highly demanded for the mechanistic understanding and design ofadvanced additives. Along this line, in situ surface molecular spectroscopies are expected to be valuable for this purpose. The use of surface Raman spectroscopy is limited owing to the very low SERS activity at Co surfaces and the very difficult optical focusing with the strong HER condition. This challenge can be well addressed by the application of the in situ ATR-SEIRAS technique which is least metal-specific and free of gas evolution concern [32–40]. Besides, the convincing analysis of ATR-SEIRAS results towards the assignment of vibrational peaks and the determination of adsorption geometries calls for supplemental support of relevant density functional theory (DFT) calculations.

blocks.section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 1 Introduction
blocks.text: In this work, MBIS, an organic additive already validated for nano-vias Co superfilling [14], is selected as the target model molecule. The interfacial structure and mechanistic aspect of adsorbed MBIS at the Co electrode are probed initially by high sensitivity in situ ATR-SEIRAS and DFT calculations. Electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance (EQCM) is applied to quantify the relative contributions of Co deposition and HER in the Co-plating solutions with and without the additive. Potential and pH dependencies of MBIS on Co deposition rates provide an inference to the interfacial functionality of MBIS in Co superfilling.

blocks.text: Figure 1a illustrates the linear sweep voltammograms (LSVs) for Co electrodes in 0.5 MH_3 BO _3 + 0.0 5 M CoSO_4 solutions with and without 25 ppm MBIS at pHs 2 and 3. In the absence of MBIS, the current density increases with the negative potential scan, owing to hydrogen evolution and Co deposition. Lowering the pH from 3 (black line) to 2 (red line) increases the current density at potentials negative of −1.55 V. In the presence of MBIS, the overall reduction current is strongly inhibited from −1.20 to −1.45 V, followed by a sharp increase regardless of pH, which was attributed to the inactivation of the additive [14]. At more negative potentials, the reduction currents largely overlap regardless of MBIS in the solution for a given pH. The closeness of the inactivation potentials for the two pHs suggests that the inactivation process is not H ^+ dependent.

blocks.text: To further investigate the mechanism, the molecular dynamics simulations were performed using classical force fields (see the details in Supporting Information online). Based on the aforementioned results and molecular dynamics simulations, the interfacial mechanism of MBIS on Co electrodes may be proposed (Figure 7). The hydrophobicity of MBIS aromatic rings disrupts the hydrogen bonding of interfacial H_2 O,, leading to the formation of a more ordered H_2O structure in favor of HER (1 of the left panel of Figure 7). The positively charged Co ^2 + ions are driven towards the electrode surface by the electric field, forming an interfacial Co(II)-MBIS complex that requires higher energy input for its reduction (2, 3 of left panel of Figure 7). On one hand, the adsorption of MBIS reduces the number of surface active sites and decreases the apparent overall current. On the other hand, the formation of a Co(II) complex at the MBIS-modified Co electrode inhibit the Co deposition much more significantly than the HER, leading to a decrease in FE _Co and an increase in FE _H _2..

blocks.section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 2 Results and discussion
blocks.text: As a proven additive in the Co superfilling, MBIS essentially displays the feature of a strong inhibitor against Co deposition. The inhibition effect of MBIS is highly dependent on its surface coverage: the higher the coverage, the stronger the inhibition against Co deposition. Thus, the mechanism of the Co superfilling in the vias could be qualitatively unraveled by assuming the existing difference of local surface MBIS coverage inside and outside the vias, which may arise from but not limited to the obstructed mass transport of MBIS and the pH difference caused by HER. The higher and lower MBIS coverages outside and inside the vias lead to slower and faster Co filling outside and inside the vias, respectively, ensuring the Co superfilling (right panel of Figure 7). Based on the above mechanistic understanding at the molecular level, we are constructing (will report in the near future) a simulation model of the Co filling process to quantitatively analyze the distribution of additives in the vias, as well as to predict the conditions for the Co superfilling.

blocks.text: In this study, we have delved into the inhibition mechanism of the additive MBIS in acidic Co electroplating using a synergistic approach inclusive of electrochemical and ATR-SEIRAS measurement as well as computational simulations.

blocks.section: Decoding the interfacial structure and functionality of an organic additive for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition > 3 Conclusions
blocks.text: The MBIS molecule adapts a nearly vertical adsorption configuration on the Co electrode via the formation of thiolate, reducing both partial currents for Co deposition and H _ 2 evolution with a higher FE _ Co and a lower FE _ H _ 2,, as compared to the MBIS-free case. We have revealed at a molecular level that the adsorbed MBIS molecules disrupt the hydrogen bonding of interfacial water, and form a sort of interfacial MBIS-Co ^ 2 + complex, thereby favoring a higher selectivity toward the hydrogen evolution than the Co deposition. Furthermore, variation in the MBIS coverage has been identified with varying pHs or potentials, offering crucial insights into the refinement of electroplating parameters. The MBIS coverage-dependent inhibition effect can qualitatively account for the Co superfilling process. Our work is valuable in understanding the interfacial structure and functionality of a typical inhibitor for superconformal Co plating and lends important guidance for filling simulations.

blocks.text: The effect of DMG on Co deposition was first examined with cyclic voltammetry (CV). A 100 nm layer of cobalt was deposited on Pt disc electrode in the additive free solution before each CV. A change of open circuit potential (OCP) from about 0.3 V to −0.48 V (both vs. SCE) was observed before and after this pre-plating. Potential was then swept from −0.48 V to −1.5 V with a sweep rate of 5 mV/sec. Figure 2 shows the CV curves with different amounts of DMG without and with ohmic drop correction. When no DMG was present in the solution, the cathodic deposition current started at −0.7 V and reached a current density of −2 mA/cm2 at −0.8 V and −4 mA/cm2 at −0.85 V. The forward and backward scans coincided with each other. The addition of 10 ppm DMG did not change the CV behavior. However, when 100 ppm DMG was added into the solution, the deposition was significantly polarized at low current range. The onset of the cathodic reaction did not occur until −0.9 V, after which a sudden jump of the cathodic reaction rate was observed. Furthermore, the suppressed cathodic current at low potential was not observed in the backward scan, resulting in a hysteresis in CV.

blocks.text: Except for PIEP, the TP values follow the order: IPIEP > IPIMP > IPIET. This sequence implies that, compared with the ethoxy and carbonyl group, the hydroxyl group is more effective in enhancing the leveling performance of the oligomers. As distinguished from the electrochemical behaviors of PIPE (Figure 1), the TP value from PIEP is higher than that from the blank. This difference possibly originates from the inhibition of the activity of accelerators and occlusion of the deposition of copper ions, which are caused by the electrostatic pairing between the cationic amine functionalities of PIEP and the negatively charged sulfonates of MPS [28].

Tween (TW) compounds, on account of their environmentally benign and non-toxic characteristics, were systematically studied as prospective eco-friendly suppressants in the process of copper plating for blind hole filling.

The outcomes of the electrochemical tests revealed that the competitive adsorption behavior between bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) and TW is contingent upon the current density and the intensity of convection.

Quantum chemical calculations suggested that the relatively smaller band gap and the clustered molecular structure of TW-80 are more conducive to its adsorption onto the electrode surface, leading to the formation of a barrier layer, which in turn restrains the deposition of copper.
Among these, suppressors play a crucial role in controlling the deposition rate at diferent surface sites, preventing over—plating at the via openings and promoting bottom—up filling.
polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based polymers have been widely studied and utilized as suppressors due to their ability to adsorb on the copper surface and inhibit the deposition reaction
Polyetheramine (PEP) has also been investigated as a potential suppressor, leveraging its unique amine-containing structure that allows for specific interactions with the copper surface
specific interactions with the copper surface
While PEP shows promise in adjusting the deposition rate, its relatively high cost and limited biodegradability pose challenges for large—scale industrial application.

evidence.quote: Based on the ML model, we can perform high-throughput ΔE predictions across a large molecular space for preliminary assessment. To rapidly advance these predictions to experimental validation, we employed a commercially available (CA) dataset with unknown ΔE as the prediction set. Every molecule in the dataset is quality-controlled, eliminating delays and costs associated with synthetic feasibility. Spe cifically, we mapped the chemical space of the training set onto the Sigma–Aldrich catalog and retrieved 4355 nitrogen-containing organic compounds. After prioritizing candidates based on the predicted ΔE values, the top 1% were flagged as promising additives. Considering accessibility, toxicity, and cost, we selected three molecules — 2-amino pyrazine (APZ), 1-methylimidazole-4,5-dicarbonitrile (MIDCN), and 2- amino-4-ethylpyridine (AEP) — for subsequent experimental verification (Table S4). These candidates exhibited favorable frontier orbital energy gaps (ΔE), underscoring their adsorption activity on the metal surface. Fig. 5a, d, and g illustrate their chemical structures and predicted ΔE values.

experiments.label: Reported BD electrochemical-analysis setup
experiments.shared_note: Source-local reported condition groups only; no cross-document or unstated sample equivalence.

evidence.quote: Electrochemical analyses were performed using CHI electrochemical workstation (CHI760, China). The basic electrolyte composed of 0.3 M CoSO4•7 H2O, 0.16 M H3BO3 and 0.02 M CoCl2⋅6 H2O. The concentration of additive BD was 0.12 mM. The pH of the electrolyte was adjusted by 5 % H2SO4 aqueous solution and stabilized to 3 ~ 4. The temperature of electrolyte was 303 K. A glassy carbon electrode (GCE) with 3 mm diameter, a Hg/Hg2SO4 electrode (saturated K2SO4 solution, SMSE) and a platinum sheet were acted as the working electrode, reference electrode and counter electrode, respectively. Before experiments, the GCE was firstly polished with 300 nm and 50 nm Al2O3 respectively, further ultrasonically cleaned in absolute ethanol and ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ cm−1). The value of the OCP is about −0.21 V and the stability time is 120 s.
